pg008_n0005: This textbook, Agriculture for Secondary Schools, is written specifically for Form One students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg008_n0006: It is prepared according to the 2023 Agriculture Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education Form I - IV issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology.
pg008_n0007: Some of the contents on this book have been adapted from the Agriculture for Secondary Schools Student's Book Form One (2021), Form Two (2021), Form Three (2022), and Form Four (2022) which were published in accordance with the 2019 Agriculture Syllabus for Ordinary Level Secondary Education, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology.
pg008_n0009: The book consists of fourteen (14) chapters namely, Introduction to Agriculture, The agricultural soil, Introduction to horticultural production, General principles and practices of vegetable production, Production of amaranth, Production of Chinese cabbage, Production of onion, and Production of tomato.
pg008_n0010: Others are the Introduction to poultry production, General principles and practices of chicken production, Management of layer chickens, Management of broiler chickens, Management of indigenous and dual-purpose hybrid chickens, and Duck production.
pg008_n0011: Each chapter contains texts, illustrations, activities and exercises.
pg008_n0012: You are encouraged to do all the activities and attempt all the given exercises as well as other assignments provided by your teacher.
pg008_n0013: You are also required to prepare a portifolio for keeping records of activities performed in different lessons.
pg008_n0014: Doing so, will enable you to develop the intended competencies.

pg009_n0009: The competencies developed will enable you to appreciate the importance of agriculture and use agricultural principles and practices in your daily life.
pg009_n0012: “The foundation of life, feeding us and supporting our communities”

pg010_n0014: Agriculture is another term for farming.
pg010_n0015: It involves growing and harvesting crops and looking after animals.
pg010_n0016: This work includes caring for crop plants, collecting the crops, preparing them for use, keeping them safe in storage, and selling them.
pg010_n0017: It also includes taking care of animals such as cattle, chickens, bees and fish.
pg010_n0018: The main aim of agriculture is to produce food.
pg010_n0019: This is important because it helps to feed more and more people around the world and it ensures that everyone has enough to eat.
pg010_n0021: Agriculture is a mixture of science and art.
pg010_n0022: Scientists use science to help farming get better.
pg010_n0023: They come up with new ideas and technologies, for example, using special techniques to improve crops and animals.
pg010_n0024: This means they can develop new varieties of crops and animal breeds that are better.
pg010_n0025: Scientists also use Chemistry knowledge to make fertilisers for plants to grow better by giving them the nutrients they need.
pg010_n0026: Likewise, scientists use Biology and Chemistry to control crop pests and diseases.
pg010_n0027: This means that they use the knowledge about living things and Chemistry to manage and prevent problems associated with diseases and harmful insects that can harm crops and animals.
pg010_n0029: Farming is not just about science.
pg010_n0030: It also involves using our hands and our brains.
pg010_n0031: This is called the art of farming.
pg010_n0032: For example, when we do physical work on the farm such as building structures or using tools, we are practising the art.
pg010_n0033: We also use our brains to make important decisions.
pg010_n0034: We decide what crops to grow or animals to raise, how much to grow, and how to do it.
pg010_n0035: We also think about when and where to
pg011_n0003: buy things we need for farming, for example, seeds and tools, and where to sell our products.
pg011_n0004: Therefore, farming is also an art of using our hands and our brains to make crops and animals grow successfully.
pg011_n0008: How does agriculture contribute to the production of food?
pg011_n0010: In what ways do scientists use science to improve farming?
pg011_n0012: How does the art of farming contribute to the success of crop and animal farming?
pg011_n0016: You have learnt that agriculture is both an art and a science.
pg011_n0017: It involves different activities from the beginning to the end of producing animal and crop products.
pg011_n0018: To do these activities well, we need to study specific fields of agriculture.
pg011_n0019: These fields are also called branches of agriculture.
pg011_n0020: Agriculture is broadly divided into five branches as shown in Figure 1.2.
pg011_im005: Diagram of the major branches of agriculture: a central Agriculture circle connected by arrows to five branches—crop production, animal production, soil science, agricultural engineering, and agricultural economics.
pg011_n0031: Crop production involves different activities from planting seeds to selling the crops.
pg011_n0032: Here are some of these activities:
pg012_n0005: Caring for the crop plants by giving them water and nutrients;
pg012_n0008: Protecting the plants from pests and diseases;
pg012_n0011: Harvesting the produce when they are ready;
pg012_n0014: Handling and processing the harvested produce;
pg012_n0022: These activities together form the crop production value chain.
pg012_n0023: It is important to do each activity properly to ensure quality and high crop yields.
pg012_n0024: Different types of crops can be grown for different uses.
pg012_n0025: Some examples are cereals, pulses, oil crops, horticultural crops and aquatic crops such as seaweed and Azolla.
pg012_n0029: Animal production involves different activities from raising animals to selling them and or their products.
pg012_n0030: Here are some of these activities:
pg012_n0043: Helping the animals to produce their young ones;
pg012_n0049: Handling and processing animals and their products;
pg012_n0057: These activities together form the animal production value chain.
pg012_n0058: It is important to do each activity properly to ensure the highest yield and quality of products.
pg012_n0059: Many different types of animals can be raised, such as cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry and fish.
pg012_n0060: When raising livestock, we get various animal products such as meat, milk, eggs, and honey.
pg012_n0061: It is important to plan well and implement good animal production practices to meet the demand for animal products.
pg012_n0065: Soil Science is a part of Agriculture that studies soil.
pg012_n0066: It involves studying the physical, chemical, and biological properties of soil.
pg012_n0067: By learning soil science, we can manage soil better for growing different crops, including animal feeds.
pg012_n0068: Soil is important because it provides a place for plants to grow and it gives them nutrients.
pg012_n0069: It also helps to filter and store water and is a home to many organisms.
pg012_n0070: Understanding soil helps farmers to make good decisions about how to manage their land and improve their crops.
pg013_n0005: Agricultural engineering uses science and technology to make tools, equipment, machines and other agricultural structures.
pg013_n0006: This helps to solve problems and make farming better.
pg013_n0007: Agricultural engineers design things such as irrigation systems for supplying water to the crops, and machines for land preparation, planting and harvesting.
pg013_n0008: In short, agricultural engineering uses science and technology to improve efficiency, productivity and quality in farming.
pg013_n0012: Agricultural economics focuses on managing resources to make profit.
pg013_n0013: Resources like land, capital, workers, and business skills are used in farming.
pg013_n0014: These resources are also known as factors of production.
pg013_n0015: They need to be used wisely in order to reduce costs of production and increase income.
pg013_n0016: This is done by proper planning, increasing yields, reducing costs, and finding the best prices for products.
pg013_n0017: Research in agricultural economics helps to find ways to improve productivity and make farming more profitable.

pg013_n0037: Agriculture provides food, raw materials for industries, medicinal products, career, entrepreneurial and recreational opportunities, and it contributes to foreign exchange.
pg013_n0038: It is an area that touches many aspects of the lives of Tanzanians.
pg013_n0039: Agriculture is a cornerstone of Tanzania’s economy.
pg013_n0040: It provides livelihoods to about 65.6 % of the population, directly or indirectly.
pg013_n0044: Farming in Tanzania is key to feeding the nation.
pg013_n0045: The country produces a variety of crops, such as cereals, pulses and different types of fruits and vegetables.
pg013_n0046: Farming also provides animal products such as meat, milk and eggs.
pg013_n0047: These agricultural products are what we eat.
pg013_n0048: If there is no enough food, people will starve and become weak.
pg013_n0049: Therefore, agriculture is like a back-up to make sure that we always have enough food to eat to meet our dietary needs and make us strong.
pg014_n0005: Agriculture is important for industries in Tanzania as it supplies raw materials.
pg014_n0006: For example, cotton is used in the textile industries, cattle provides hides, while goats and sheep provide skins for the leather industries.
pg014_n0007: Other crops play an important role in food processing industries.
pg014_n0008: For example, maize in maize flour, fruits for fruit juices, and vegetables for canned products.
pg014_n0009: Moreover, agriculture provides raw materials for the chemical industry.
pg014_n0010: These are used to produce fertilisers and pesticides, which are important for the country’s agriculture sector.
pg014_n0011: Therefore, agriculture is not just about producing food.
pg014_n0012: It is also about supporting other industries by providing the raw materials they need to operate.
pg014_n0014: (c) Provision of entrepreneurial and career opportunities
pg014_n0016: Agriculture opens up many business and job opportunities.
pg014_n0017: These are not just in farming, but also in related areas.
pg014_n0018: For example, people can work in food processing and marketing.
pg014_n0019: Processing involves changing raw agricultural products into something else.
pg014_n0020: For example, maize can be processed into maize flour.
pg014_n0021: Marketing involves selling these products to customers.
pg014_n0022: Entrepreneurial opportunities also exist in the food value chain.
pg014_n0023: This includes steps from growing crops to selling the final product.
pg014_n0024: For example, someone could start a business of growing crops, processing them, or selling them.
pg014_n0025: Therefore, agriculture is not just about farming.
pg014_n0026: It also provides many opportunities for people to start their businesses or find jobs in different sectors related to agriculture.
pg014_n0030: Agriculture helps us to stay healthy.
pg014_n0032: Farms in Tanzania grow many plants that can be used to make these medicines.
pg014_n0033: Some of these plants include vegetables, herbs and spices that have medicinal properties.
pg014_n0034: These medicinal plants can help to manage diseases.
pg014_n0035: Therefore, farming not only provides food but also contributes to our health by providing the raw materials needed to create medicinal products.
pg014_n0040: People can visit farms and learn about farming in a leisure way.
pg014_n0041: They can also be involved in carrying out some activities on the farm.
pg014_n0043: Agritourism enables farmers to earn more money.
pg014_n0044: Therefore, agriculture not only provides food.
pg014_n0045: It also offers chances for people to learn about farming and have fun.
pg014_n0046: This can also help farmers earn more money to keep their farms running and invest more to make even more money.
pg015_n0005: Agriculture helps Tanzania to earn money from other countries.
pg015_n0006: It is done by exporting crops such as cashews, coffee, fruits, spices and flowers.
pg015_n0007: It also involves exporting animal products such as meat and milk.
pg015_n0008: This brings in a lot of money from abroad.
pg015_n0009: Therefore, agriculture not only provides food.
pg015_n0010: It also helps Tanzania to earn money from other countries.
pg015_n0011: This foreign money is used to buy things that Tanzania doesn’t make them.

pg015_n0032: Relationship between Agriculture and other subjects
pg015_n0034: The agriculture subject teaches about crop and animal value chains for better returns.
pg015_n0035: Learning proper practices in these chains requires knowledge and skills from Agriculture and other subjects.
pg015_n0036: Agriculture is closely related to other subjects (Figure 1.3) in various ways.
pg015_n0050: Figure 1.3: Subjects related to Agriculture subject
pg015_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing on the vine.
pg016_n0005: In Biology, we learn about living things such as livestock, crop plants, and pests.
pg016_n0006: We study their characteristics and how their body systems function, such as reproduction and nutrition.
pg016_n0007: This knowledge helps us to understand crop production, livestock management, as well as pest and parasite control in agriculture.
pg016_n0008: Genetics, which is studied in Biology, is applied in Agriculture to develop improved crop varieties and livestock breeds.
pg016_n0012: Using knowledge and skills from Chemistry, farmers can analyse and manage soil.
pg016_n0013: By conducting soil analysis and management, farmers can determine the types and amounts of fertiliser to apply.
pg016_n0014: The knowledge and skills of Chemistry are required for the manufacturing and application of agrochemicals.
pg016_n0015: Chemical reactions studied in Chemistry affect the availability and uptake of plant nutrients in roots.
pg016_n0016: Crop production relies on physical, chemical and biological reactions occurring in the soil.
pg016_n0017: Therefore, Chemistry is important in agricultural production.
pg016_n0021: In Physics, we study topics such as mechanics, heat, and light.
pg016_n0022: The knowledge gained from these topics is applied to various agricultural practices.
pg016_n0023: Mechanics, a branch of physics, deals with force on moving objects.
pg016_n0024: In agricultural mechanization, various actions are applied during farm operations, such as cultivation, planting, weeding, and harvesting.
pg016_n0026: Advanced agricultural operations are performed using machines such as tractors, planters, and harvesters, which are designed by using principles of Physics.
pg016_n0030: Computer Science can help farmers make their work easier and more efficient.
pg016_n0031: This is done using special tools and techniques that are part of a field called ‘Agricultural Technology’ ‘AgTech’.
pg016_n0032: One example of this is a technique called ‘precision farming’.
pg016_n0033: In precision farming, farmers can use computers to monitor and manage their crops and animals more carefully.
pg016_n0034: This can help them to grow their crops and take care of their animals more efficiently and safely.
pg016_n0038: When studying Mathematics, various mathematical operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division are learnt.
pg016_n0039: In Agriculture, these operations play an important role in various aspects.
pg016_n0040: For example, they are used to determine
pg017_n0003: the required number of chickens in a given area, and appropriate ratios of male to female animals.
pg017_n0004: Mathematics is also applied to calculate plant population in crop fields, which is essential for optimizing crop yields.
pg017_n0005: Farmers need to understand and apply these mathematical operations correctly to ensure successful agricultural practices.
pg017_n0008: Understanding climate and weather is important for farming.
pg017_n0009: Farmers can learn about climate and weather through Geography.
pg017_n0010: This knowledge helps them to plan farm activities effectively.
pg017_n0011: By understanding climate and weather, farmers can make informed decisions and take appropriate actions.
pg017_n0012: They can prepare fields, plant crops, and harvest at the right time, hence enhancing production.
pg017_n0013: Furthermore, being aware of climate conditions can help farmers minimise risks and improve their chances of success in farming.
pg017_n0016: Business Studies is a helpful subject for farmers.
pg017_n0017: It teaches them how to calculate profits and losses, do accounting tasks, and make smart decisions.
pg017_n0018: Farmers can also analyse their physical and financial records to see how well their farm is doing and make better decisions for managing it.
pg017_n0021: Food and Human Nutrition is a subject in which we learn how to handle and take care of food.
pg017_n0022: This includes learning about proper storage and making the best use of the foods we grow in agriculture.
pg017_n0023: The subject also covers how to prepare meals that are nutritious and balanced, which is important for promoting healthier and energetic families and communities.
pg017_n0026: ‘Historia ya Tanzania na Maadili’ is a subject where we learn about ethics and cultural values, such as the importance of hard working and valuing one’s culture.
pg017_n0027: We also learn about the significance of following rules and guidelines when carrying out tasks in different fields.
pg017_n0028: These aspects help farmers in smoothly running activities related to crop and animal value chains.
pg017_n0029: In ‘Historia ya Tanzania na Maadili’, we also learn to enjoy working, work hard, and willingly follow rules and guidelines.
pg017_n0030: These skills help farmers to carry out agricultural practices that protect the health of consumers and the environment.
pg018_n0007: Language subjects such as English and Kiswahili (in certain circumstances) are very important since they are used as media for communication during the process of learning and doing agricultural activities.
pg018_n0008: Language subjects facilitate communication which is one of the important 21st Century skills.
pg018_n0009: By integrating the knowledge and skills we learn in different subjects, we can enhance our understanding and application of agricultural practices.
pg018_n0010: For example, language helps farmers to understand the needs of their consumers.
pg018_n0011: This is because language helps farmers to talk to other people about their crops and animals.
pg018_n0012: In addition, language helps farmers to understand the rules and regulations of the market, which can help them to sell their products more easily.
pg018_n0013: Therefore, language plays major role of what farmers do to make their work easier and more successful.

pg019_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn about the concept of agricultural soil as well as the physical, chemical and biological properties of soil in relation to crop plant growth.
pg019_n0011: You will also learn about the soil health.
pg019_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to manage the influence of soil on the growth and development of crop plants including animal feeds.
pg019_n0015: “The lifeblood of agriculture, fuels plant growth and sustains ecosystem”
pg019_n0019: Soil can have different meanings in different fields such as engineering or farming.
pg019_n0020: Soil is very important for life on earth.
pg019_n0021: In agriculture, soil is the topmost part of the earth that naturally or with some modification provides nutrients to plants.
pg019_n0022: It also provides support to the plants.
pg019_n0026: Soil is composed of different components such as mineral matter, organic matter, water, air, and living organisms.
pg019_n0027: The solid part of the soil consists of mineral matter and organic matter, making up about half (50%) of the soil.
pg019_n0028: The other half of the soil is occupied by spaces called pore spaces.
pg019_n0029: These are large pore spaces which are normally filled with air (about 25%) and small pore spaces filled with water (about 25%) (refer to Figure 2.1).
pg019_im003: Pie chart showing soil components by volume: mineral matter 45%, organic matter 5%, water 25%, and air 25%, with water and air labelled as pore spaces and mineral matter plus organic matter labelled as soil solids.
pg019_n0031: Figure 2.1: Distribution of soil components by volume
pg020_n0006: Visit different places in your school (near the pitch, under trees, near waste pits, and in the garden).
pg020_n0007: Then, use a hoe to take a sample of top soil at about 30 cm depth, then:
pg020_n0011: Make a list of all the living and non-living things you find in the soil.
pg020_n0014: Using a magnifying glass, observe the soil closely.
pg020_n0015: Look for tiny creatures, for example, worms, insects, and tiny plants.
pg020_n0018: Put the things you found into these groups: living organisms, mineral matters, and organic matters.
pg020_n0020: Write down what you found in your portfolio.
pg020_n0023: Mineral matter (sand, silt and clay) forms the main soil solid particles.
pg020_n0024: Mineral matter also provides essential mineral nutrients that plants need to grow.
pg020_n0025: These nutrients, including nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and others, help to make the soil fertile, which is good for growing crops.
pg020_n0026: Mineral nutrients in the soil may come from the weathering of rocks over a long time or by adding fertilisers to the soil.
pg020_n0027: The weathering process breaks down the rocks and releases the minerals into the soil.
pg020_n0028: Understanding and managing the mineral content in soil is important for successful farming.
pg020_n0029: This knowledge allows farmers to determine the suitability of the soil for various plants and decide how to enrich the soil with minerals.
pg020_n0032: When plants and animals die, their remains break down and release nutrients and humus into the soil.
pg020_n0033: These nutrients include carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and others.
pg020_n0034: These are like food in the soil that are required by plants to grow successfully.
pg020_n0035: Humus is a dark substance that easily breaks into small pieces or crumbs.
pg020_n0036: It helps to improve the structure of the soil, making it easier for plant roots to grow and obtain water and nutrients.
pg020_n0037: Humus also helps the soil to hold moisture, which is important for plants during dry periods.
pg020_n0039: Farmers can improve the soil’s organic matter by adding things such as animal manure or compost.
pg020_n0040: This makes the soil fertile and healthy, which is good for growing crops.
pg020_n0041: Having organic matter and humus in the soil is important for keeping the soil fertile, supporting plant growth, and allowing crop farming to be successful.
pg020_n0044: The soil has living things including plants and animals.
pg020_n0045: Some are big enough to be seen easily, for example, earthworms and insects.
pg020_n0047: Others, for example, bacteria and certain fungi, are very small and can only be seen using a microscope.
pg020_n0049: Soil organisms eat the remains of plants and animals.
pg020_n0050: When they eat, they break them
pg021_n0003: down to release nutrients and humus.
pg021_n0004: Soil organisms can be divided into beneficial and harmful organisms.
pg021_n0005: Beneficial soil organisms are important for keeping the soil healthy and helping plants grow well.
pg021_n0006: To maintain beneficial organisms in the soil, farmers need to employ Good Agricultural Practices (GAPs), for example, applying compost or animal manure, using mulch or cover crops, and rotating crops.
pg021_n0007: On the other hand, harmful soil organisms affect the growth of plants.
pg021_n0011: Water in the soil is found in small spaces.
pg021_n0012: It can come from rain or when farmers irrigate their crops.
pg021_n0013: This water has mineral nutrients dissolved in it.
pg021_n0014: When water and minerals mix, it is called soil solution.
pg021_n0015: Soil water is important because it helps to dissolve mineral nutrients in the soil and it carries them to plant roots.
pg021_n0016: It also provides water for living things in the soil.
pg021_n0017: Farmers can maintain the required soil water through irrigation and drainage.
pg021_n0018: They can also use methods to prevent or reduce water loss from the soil, for example, by adding organic manures, using dry grass mulch and practising conservation agriculture by planting shed trees on the farm.
pg021_n0021: For most crops, conditions are best when the soil pore spaces are filled about equally with water and air.
pg021_n0024: Experiment: Exploring the role of soil water in plant growth
pg021_n0027: Two identical pots, the same type of soil for both pots, a seedling or a small plant for each pot, two containers for holding water, a notebook for recording observations, and a ruler or measuring tape
pg021_n0033: Preparation: Fill both pots with the same type of soil and plant a seedling or a small plant in each pot.
pg021_n0034: Make sure the depth of planting is the same in both pots.
pg021_n0035: This will ensure that any differences in plant growth are due to the soil condition and not the way the plants were cared for.
pg021_n0038: Set up the experiment: Place one pot in a normal growing environment, allowing it to be watered regularly.
pg021_n0040: For the second pot, water the soil sparingly or not at all for a few days.
pg021_n0044: Observe and record: Over a few weeks, observe and record the growth of the plant in both pots.
pg021_n0045: Measure and record the height of the plant, the number of leaves, and the overall health of the plant.
pg021_n0046: You can use a ruler or measuring tape to accurately measure the height of the plant.
pg021_n0047: Write down your observations in your notebook.
pg022_n0004: Analyse the results: Compare the results of the plant in the control pot (with regular watering) to the plant in the experimental pot (with sparing or no water).
pg022_n0005: Explain why you think the results happened the way they did.
pg022_n0008: Air in the soil is like the air we breathe.
pg022_n0009: It fills the spaces between the soil particles, called pore spaces.
pg022_n0010: This air moves between the soil and the atmosphere.
pg022_n0011: Soil air is important for the growth of plants.
pg022_n0012: Plants need oxygen from the soil air for their roots to breathe or respire and grow.
pg022_n0013: Soil organisms also need air to survive.
pg022_n0014: They breathe in the soil air to stay alive.
pg022_n0015: Farmers need to make sure that soil air stays healthy.
pg022_n0016: Here are some things they can do:
pg022_n0020: Avoid compacting the soil too much.
pg022_n0021: When the soil gets squeezed, the pore spaces get smaller and there is less room for air.
pg022_n0024: Don’t overwater the soil, as water can fill up all the pore spaces and push out the air.
pg022_n0027: Take care when using chemicals or fertilisers, as some can harm the soil organisms and affect the air quality.
pg022_n0028: Consult your agricultural extension worker in your area for advice.
pg022_n0033: Experiment: Investigating the role of soil air in plant growth
pg022_n0035: Materials needed: Two identical pots, the same type of soil for both pots, a seedling or a small plant for each pot, a cover or lid for one of the pots, a notebook for recording observations and a ruler or measuring tape
pg022_n0041: Preparation: Fill both pots with the same type of soil and plant a seedling or a small plant in each pot.
pg022_n0042: Make sure the depth of planting is the same in both pots.
pg022_n0043: This will ensure that any differences in plant growth are due to the soil condition and not the way the plants were cared for.
pg022_n0046: Set up the experiment: Place one pot in a normal growing environment, allowing air to circulate in the soil.
pg022_n0048: For the second pot, seal the lid to prevent air from circulating in the soil.
pg022_n0052: Observe and record: Over a few weeks, observe and record the growth of the plant in both pots.
pg022_n0053: Measure and record the height of the plant, the number of leaves, and the overall health of the plant.
pg022_n0054: You can use a ruler or measuring tape to accurately measure the height of the plant.
pg022_n0055: Write down your observations in your notebook.
pg023_n0004: Analyse the results: Compare the results of the plant in the control pot (with good circulation of soil air) to the plant in the experimental pot (with limited circulation of soil air).

pg023_n0022: When you dig a vertical section through the soil, you can see different layers.
pg023_n0023: This vertical section is called a soil profile.
pg023_n0024: The layers in the soil profile are known as soil horizons.
pg023_n0025: They are called horizons because they spread horizontally from side to side.
pg023_n0026: There are four major horizons in a soil profile found in undisturbed soils.
pg023_n0027: These are horizons O, A, B and C (refer to Figure 2.2).
pg023_im002: Typical soil profile showing horizons O, A, B, C and R, from surface vegetation and topsoil down to subsoil, weathered material and bedrock.
pg024_n0003: O horizon: The topmost layer, also known as the organic horizon.
pg024_n0004: It is rich in decomposed organic matter like leaves and plant debris.
pg024_n0005: It has a dark colour and is rich in nutrients.
pg024_n0007: A horizon: It is also referred to as the topsoil.
pg024_n0008: It is a horizon where most plant roots grow.
pg024_n0009: It is generally darker in colour because it has more organic matter than the horizons below.
pg024_n0010: Horizon A is an important horizon for nutrient availability to plants as it contains organic matter, minerals, and micro-organisms.
pg024_n0011: However, horizon A is characterised by eluviation.
pg024_n0012: Eluviation is the process of leaching or washing out soluble minerals and organic matter from the upper horizons of the soil and depositing them in lower horizons.
pg024_n0014: B horizon: It is also known as subsoil.
pg024_n0015: The B horizon accumulates minerals and nutrients leached from the upper layers hence called the illuvial horizon.
pg024_n0016: Horizon B is denser and less fertile than the A horizon.
pg024_n0018: C horizon: The C horizon is the parent material horizon.
pg024_n0019: It consists of weathered rock fragments and it lacks the organic matter and nutrients found in the upper horizons.
pg024_n0021: R: This is not considered as horizon; it rather denotes a bedrock.
pg024_n0022: It is a layer of hard bedrock found at the bottom of all soil profiles.
pg024_n0023: It is the solid rock from which the soil is formed.
pg024_n0024: It constitutes materials that haven’t changed since were formed
pg024_n0026: In fields, the typical soil profile has horizons A, B, and C.
pg024_n0027: In forests, there is an additional O horizon on top of horizons A and B.
pg024_n0028: Not all horizons are present in every soil profile, especially when the soil is disturbed.
pg024_n0029: The presence and characteristics of each horizon vary based on location and soil formation processes.

pg025_n0011: Agricultural soil has certain properties that affect how plants grow.
pg025_n0012: These properties include texture, structure, porosity, soil pH and fertility, as well as living organisms in the soil.
pg025_n0013: These properties can be grouped into physical, chemical, and biological soil properties.
pg025_n0014: In the coming sections, we will learn about these properties.
pg025_n0018: The physical properties of soil are the features or characteristics of soil that can be seen or observed and measured without changing the soil’s composition.
pg025_n0019: These properties include things such as the feel of the soil (soil texture), how the soil particles are packed or arranged (soil structure), and how much space is between and within the soil particles (soil porosity).
pg025_n0020: The physical properties of soil are important because they affect how water and air move through the soil and how plants grow.
pg025_n0021: Generally, the physical properties of soil determine how well the soil can provide the necessary conditions for plants and other organisms to grow successfully.
pg025_n0025: Soil consists of solid mineral particles which are sand, silt and clay.
pg025_n0026: Sand particles are the largest, ranging from 0.05 mm to 2 mm in diameter.
pg025_n0027: Silt particles are smaller than sand but larger than clay, measuring between 0.002 mm and 0.05 mm in diameter.
pg025_n0028: Clay particles are the smallest, measuring less than 0.002 mm in diameter.
pg025_n0029: Solid particles of soil which are greater than 2 mm in diameter are considered as stones and gravels.
pg025_n0030: The relative proportion of sand, silt and clay particles in the soil is referred to as soil texture.
pg025_n0031: Soil texture also refers to the feeling of coarseness or fineness of soil determined by the relative proportions of sand, silt and clay
pg026_n0004: The three main types of soil texture are sand, silt, and clay.
pg026_n0005: Soils which are a balanced mixture of all these three particle sizes together with organic matter are known as loamy soil.
pg026_n0007: When we want to grow crops, we need to pay attention to the type of soil we have.
pg026_n0008: We can group this into four main types: clayey, silty, sandy and loamy.
pg026_n0009: The size of the particles in the soil is what makes these differences.
pg026_n0010: Clay is very small, silt is medium, and sand is large.
pg026_n0011: While some types of soil are good for growing crops on their own, adding things such as manure or fertilisers can make the soil even better for growing.
pg026_n0012: The soil can change over time, so it is important to regularly check and take care of it.

pg027_n0032: Soil texture can be determined using laboratory analysis or simple methods which can be easily carried out in the field such as texture by feeling method.
pg027_n0033: Normally, laboratory analyses of soil texture are costly and take time, while feeling soil texture by hand is cheap, quick, and accurate.
pg027_n0034: Soils are divided into three broad texture groups: coarse-textured soils, medium-textured soils, and fine-textured soils.
pg027_n0035: The term coarse-textured is often used for soils that are dominated by sand.
pg027_n0036: Fine-textured soils refer to soils that are dominated by clay, and medium-textured soils are a more balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay particles.
pg027_n0037: The medium-textured soils are also termed as loam soils.
pg027_n0039: Determination of soil texture by feel method:
pg027_n0040: This method is used to determine the textural class of soil in the field by simple field tests and feeling the constituents of the soil.
pg027_n0041: The soil sample must be in a state between moist to slightly wet.
pg027_n0042: Gravel and other constituents greater than 2 mm in diameter must be removed.
pg027_n0044: Procedure for determining soil texture by feel method
pg027_n0047: Step 1: Take a handful of soil.
pg027_n0048: If the soil is dry, moisten it just enough to determine if it will form a ball when squeezed in the palm (refer to Figure 2.4) go to step 2.
pg027_n0049: If the moist soil does not form a ball, it is sand.
pg027_im002: A hand holding a moist soil ball formed by squeezing soil in the palm.
pg027_n0054: If the moist soil remains in a ball when the hand is opened, bounce the ball in the hand.
pg027_n0055: If the ball breaks when it hits the hand, it is a loamy sand.
pg027_n0056: If the ball does not break, move on to step 3.
pg028_n0003: Step 3: Determine if the moist soil will form a ribbon when a soil ball is extruded between the thumb and forefinger (refer to Figure 2.5).
pg028_n0004: Also, determine how long a diameter ribbon will form when rolled between palms or on a flat table.
pg028_n0006: When starting with dry clays, make sure you allow time for the clays to become moist, and make sure ‘gritty’ particles are not aggregated.

pg028_n0010: The principle behind forming ribbons is related to the cohesion that exists among clay particles.
pg028_n0011: Clays are sticky when moist, and so the ribbon length is proportional to the clay content.

pg028_n0019: between 2.5 cm and 5 cm, the general category of soil texture is clay loam.

pg029_n0014: Soil is made up of sand, silt or clay particles that come together to form a group of particles known as soil aggregates (refer to Figure 2.7).
pg029_n0015: Soil aggregates can be sandy, silty, clayey or loamy.
pg029_n0016: A soil aggregate is like a basket of different types of soil particles.
pg029_n0017: Soil structure is about how soil particles are arranged in an aggregate.
pg029_n0018: An arrangement of soil particles in an aggregate can influence how the spaces between and within soil aggregates.

pg029_n0023: A well-structured soil has a network of tiny spaces.
pg029_n0024: These spaces are between and within the soil aggregates.
pg029_n0025: This network allows water and air to move around.
pg029_n0026: Soil structure helps water and air to move easily, just like air moving through doors and windows in a house.
pg029_n0027: In farming, soil structure is important because it helps plants to grow strong and healthy.
pg029_n0028: It also stops the soil from being washed away when it rains or wind blows.
pg029_n0030: Poor farming practices can damage the soil structure.
pg029_n0031: For example, if big and too much heavy machines are used, they can squash the soil.
pg029_n0032: If we give the soil too much water or too many chemical fertilisers, it can also damage the soil structure.
pg029_n0033: But we can keep the soil structure safe in many ways.
pg029_n0034: One way is by changing the type of crop we grow each season.
pg029_n0036: Crop rotation involves growing a different type of crop on the same piece of land in each year or growing season, using a set pattern (refer to Figure 2.8).
pg029_n0037: Another way is by using organic fertilisers instead of inorganic fertilisers.
pg029_n0038: These are some recommended cultural practices which help to improve soil structure making it suitable for crop production.

pg030_n0028: Soil pore spaces, also known as soil porosity, are open spaces between and within soil aggregates.
pg030_n0029: These spaces are usually filled with water and air.
pg030_n0030: Everything in the soil that is not a solid is in these pore spaces.
pg030_n0031: Based on size, there are two types of pores namely, macro pores and micro pores (Figure 2.9 (a) and (b)).
pg030_im008: Loosely structured sand particles with large pore spaces, showing macropores between the particles.
pg030_n0035: Figure 2.9 (a): Pore spaces in loosely structured sand particles
pg030_im009: Aggregated clay particles forming peds, with many tiny micropores within the aggregates and larger macropores between them.
pg030_n0040: Figure 2.9 (b): Pore spaces in aggregated clay particles
pg030_n0042: When the soil is porous, it can hold more water and nutrients.
pg030_n0043: This is important for plant growth as it allows plants to absorb water and nutrients from the soil.
pg030_n0044: Without sufficient porosity, water and nutrients cannot penetrate the soil, leading to poor plant growth and health.
pg030_n0045: Moreover, soil porosity also plays a role in the airflow in the soil.
pg030_n0046: This is important because it allows the movement of gases, which are essential for the life of plants and soil organisms.
pg030_n0047: If soil is compacted or has low
pg031_n0003: porosity, it can impede this airflow, leading to poor plant growth and health.
pg031_n0004: The following soil properties can influence the amount of pore spaces in the soil.
pg031_n0005: These include soil texture, soil structure, organic matter and soil compaction.
pg031_n0009: Soil texture: Different types of soil have different amounts of pore spaces.
pg031_n0010: For example, sandy soil, which has big particles, has more pore spaces than clay soil, which has small particles.
pg031_n0013: Soil structure: The way soil particles stick together can change the amount of pore spaces.
pg031_n0014: The soil that is packed loosely has more pore spaces than the soil that is packed tightly.
pg031_n0017: Organic matter: The soil that has a lot of organic matter, for example, leaves, has more pore spaces.
pg031_n0018: This is due to the formation of well-aggregated structures.
pg031_n0021: Soil compaction: When the soil is highly pressed down, for example, when people walk on it or when machines are used on it while is wet, it can have fewer pore spaces.

pg031_n0042: Soil plays an important role in supporting plant growth by providing essential nutrients.
pg031_n0043: The chemical properties of soil, including the presence and availability of various elements, and soil reaction influence its fertility and nutrient content.
pg031_n0044: Understanding the chemical properties of soil is like understanding the nutrition facts on a food label.
pg031_n0045: It helps us know what is good for the plants and what is not.
pg031_n0046: On the one hand, Nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) are the primary macro nutrients required in large quantities by plants and they are commonly provided as inorganic fertilisers.
pg031_n0047: Calcium (Ca), Magnesium (Mg), and sulphur (S) are secondary macro nutrients.
pg031_n0048: On the other hand, micronutrients are required in small quantities.
pg031_n0049: These include iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), zinc (Zn), boron (B), copper (Cu), molybdenum (Mo) and chlorine (Cl).

pg033_n0005: Soil reaction, also known as soil pH, is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of the soil.
pg033_n0006: Soil pH ranges from approximately 0 to 14.
pg033_n0007: Soils with pH values less than 7 are said to be acidic soils, those with pH values about 7 are said to be neutral soils and those with pH values above 7 are said to be alkaline soils.
pg033_n0008: Soil pH is normally presented in a pH scale as shown in Figure 2.10.
pg033_n0009: It affects the availability of nutrients to plants and how these nutrients react with each other.
pg033_n0010: The suitable pH range for most plants is between 5.5 and 7.0.
pg033_im002: pH scale from 0 to 14, with 7 marked neutral; acidity increases from 7 towards 0, and alkalinity increases from 7 towards 14.
pg033_n0015: In acidic soils, availability of nutrients is affected.
pg033_n0016: For example, aluminium and manganese can become more available and more toxic to plants, while calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium are less available.
pg033_n0017: When this happens, some symptoms can be observed in plants.
pg033_n0018: These symptoms include stunted growth, yellowing of leaves, and poor fruit development.
pg033_n0019: To manage acidic soil, materials called lime can be applied to soil to increase soil pH and make it more alkaline.
pg033_n0022: In alkaline soils, the availability of nutrients is also affected.
pg033_n0023: For example, phosphorus and most micronutrients become less available.
pg033_n0024: When this happens, some symptoms can be observed in plants.
pg033_n0025: These symptoms include stunted growth, yellowing leaves, and poor fruit development.
pg033_n0026: To manage alkaline soil, acidifying materials can be added to decrease soil pH.
pg033_n0030: The availability of nutrients in the soil is not only influenced by factors such as acidity or alkalinity.
pg033_n0031: It can also be affected by the amount of organic matter in the soil and soil texture.
pg033_n0032: You need to check plants regularly.
pg033_n0033: Look for signs such as slow growth or yellow leaves.
pg033_n0034: This could mean the plants need more nutrients.
pg033_n0035: If possible, you should consult soil scientists for soil testing.
pg033_n0036: Soil testing results will provide information about the soil’s nutrient content and pH, and suggest necessary management actions if the conditions are not suitable for plant growth.

pg034_n0020: Soil is full of both macro-organisms and micro-organisms.
pg034_n0021: Macro-organisms are those that can be seen with the naked eyes, for example, earthworms, beetles, and other insects.
pg034_n0022: Micro-organisms are very small creatures that we cannot see without a microscope.
pg034_n0023: These include bacteria, fungi, and protozoa.
pg034_n0024: Macro-organisms, for example, earthworms, help to break down dead plants and animals in the soil.
pg034_n0025: As they move through the soil, they also create channels that allow air and water to circulate, which is important for plant roots to grow.
pg034_n0026: Micro-organisms play an even bigger role in soil health and crop production.
pg034_n0027: For example, some bacteria can take nitrogen from the air and convert it into a form that plants can use for growth.
pg034_n0028: This process is called nitrogen fixation.
pg034_n0029: Fungi are another type of micro-organism.
pg034_n0030: Some fungi form a beneficial relationship with plant roots, helping the plant to absorb water and nutrients.
pg034_n0031: In return, the plant provides the fungi with sugars.
pg034_n0032: Therefore, both macro-organisms and micro-organisms are very important for soil health and growing crops.
pg034_n0033: They help to break down organic matter, improve soil structure, and provide plants with the nutrients they need to grow.
pg034_n0034: To improve the biological properties of soil, farmers can apply practices that keep soil a safe habitat for soil organisms, such as reducing tillage and using organic matter.
pg034_n0038: Soil is a home for micro-organisms, also called microbes.
pg034_n0039: Some of these microbes help plants to grow, but others can harm them, for example, nematodes.
pg034_n0040: These harmful microbes can enter plants through their roots and stems, causing damage and stopping the flow of water and nutrients.
pg034_n0041: Some of these harmful microbes can also enter plants through their leaves and cause diseases.
pg035_n0003: Before we plant a crop, it is important to check for these harmful microbes in the soil.
pg035_n0004: If we don’t, they can harm our crops.
pg035_n0005: It is also important to understand that managing these harmful microbes can be tricky.
pg035_n0006: It takes time and effort, and we might not always see the results right away.
pg035_n0007: But, if we manage them well, we can ensure that our crops stay healthy.

pg035_n0016: Soil is used for growing crops.
pg035_n0017: Soil is like a plant’s home.
pg035_n0018: Plants need certain things from soil to grow well.
pg035_n0019: These things include sufficient nutrients, favourable soil pH and the presence of good micro-organisms.
pg035_n0020: However, not all soil is suitable for growing crops.
pg035_n0022: Some soil has harmful bacteria, fungi, and nematodes.
pg035_n0023: Some have excessive acidity or alkalinity.
pg035_n0024: Some soil has bad things in it because of pollution.
pg035_n0025: These things can make the soil unhealthy.
pg035_n0027: Looking after soil health is very important in farming.
pg035_n0028: Healthy soil supports and sustains life.
pg035_n0029: It is like our human body that needs nutrients, water, and a healthy environment to stay well.
pg035_n0030: Soils need these things to grow plants and support other organisms.
pg035_n0031: A healthy soil has organisms like bacteria and worms, and non-living particles such as minerals and organic matter.
pg035_n0032: These things work together to keep the soil healthy.
pg035_n0033: A healthy soil helps plants to grow well.
pg035_n0034: It gives plants the right nutrients, supports their roots, and helps them get water and air when they need them.
pg035_n0036: Just like we need to take care of our health, farmers need to take care of the health of their soil.
pg035_n0037: As said earlier, they can do this in different ways.
pg035_n0038: For example, by adding organic matter, which feeds the micro-organisms in the soil.
pg035_n0039: They can also use techniques such as crop rotation.
pg035_n0040: This practice helps to maintain soil health by ensuring that different crops use different nutrients in the soil.
pg035_n0041: It also helps to control pests and diseases, and also makes the soil better at holding water, which is important for keeping plants healthy.

pg037_im003: Chapter Three: Introduction to horticultural production.
pg037_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn about the meaning of horticultural production, types of horticultural crops and their importance.
pg037_n0011: You will further learn about the structures for growing horticultural crops and types of horticultural farming.
pg037_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to explore and venture into a wide range of entrepreneurial opportunities existing in the horticultural sector.

pg037_n0016: “Nourishes our health beautify our gardens and promotes biodiversity”
pg037_n0018: The meaning and importance of horticultural production
pg037_n0020: Horticulture is part of agriculture, combining art and science in cultivating and managing vegetables (olericulture), fruits (pomology), ornamentals (floriculture), and spices crops.
pg037_n0021: It also involves postharvest practices such as handling, processing, and packaging of the crops to extend their shelf life and increase their availability and profitability.
pg037_n0022: Landscaping, which beautifies areas with different garden designs and materials, is also a part of horticulture.
pg037_n0023: Most horticultural products, such as fruits, vegetables, and some spices, are sold or eaten fresh.
pg037_n0030: Provide nutritious food: Vegetables, fruits and spices are the main source of vitamin and mineral nutrients which enable our bodies to maintain good health.
pg037_n0031: In addition, spices improve the flavour of foods and have some medicinal functions for our health.
pg037_n0035: Provide income: When farmers produce horticultural crops commercially, they can earn money to take care of their day-to-day needs.
pg037_n0036: It also enables farmers to save money for emergencies and for further investments to make more money.
pg037_n0037: They can also be sold to foreign countries and thus serve as a source of foreign income.
pg037_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing on the vine.
pg038_n0003: (c) Provide employment: Production of horticultural crops involves intensive operations carried out from the initial point of production to final consumption (value chains).
pg038_n0004: This creates employment for the people involved in carrying out those operations.
pg038_n0006: (d) Stimulate industrial growth: Most horticultural crops provide raw materials for processing and value addition in industries including beverage industries.
pg038_n0008: (e) Provide business opportunities: There are many chances to start a business in the horticultural-related industry.
pg038_n0009: You can do this by working directly with businesses that are part of the crop production process.
pg038_n0010: This is possible as long as there are people who want to buy the produce and their by-products.
pg038_n0011: Alternatively, you can start a business that helps the main horticultural-related businesses to work better.
pg038_n0012: You can identify a business opportunity in horticultural crops by finding out the problems that people have in the crop value chain and coming up with solutions that can make one earn money.
pg038_n0014: (f) Conserve soil: Apart from beautifying environment, crops such as ornamental shrubs and grasses in the landscape provide adequate soil cover.
pg038_n0015: This protects the soil from wind and water erosions.

pg050_n0024: In addition, ready-made pots can be used in raising horticultural crops (refer to Figures 3.74 (e)).
pg050_n0025: However, the use of ready-made bags and pots is relatively expensive compared to the use of locally available materials.

pg052_n0018: Horticultural farming can be grouped in various ways.
pg052_n0019: It can be grouped according to where it is practised.
pg052_n0020: On this basis, there is home gardening (taking place at home) and field horticulture (taking place in fields which may be near or far away from home).
pg052_n0021: Horticultural farming can also be grouped according to purpose.
pg052_n0022: In this regard, there are subsistence and commercial horticultural farming.
pg052_n0024: Subsistence horticultural farming involves producing horticultural crops at
pg052_im001: Ripe red tomatoes hanging on the plant.
pg053_n0003: a minimum level for own use.
pg053_n0004: For example, horticultural crops (particularly vegetables and some fruits) can be planted in mixtures with staple food crops such as maize, sorghum, yams and upland paddy.
pg053_n0005: Home gardening to produce vegetables, fruits, spices or ornamental plants for own use is another example of subsistence horticultural farming.
pg053_n0006: Where land is sufficient, conventional seedbeds are used for home gardening while improvised seedbeds are commonly used where there is a shortage of land.
pg053_n0008: Commercial horticulture involves the production of vegetables, fruits, spices and/or ornamentals in small, medium or large quantities for business purposes.
pg053_n0009: In commercial horticulture, conventional seedbeds or screen houses are used depending on various factors including the amount of capital a farmer is able and willing to invest.

pg054_n0006: General principles and practices of vegetable production
pg054_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn basic principles and practices of vegetable production including planning for vegetable production, land preparation, sowing or planting, management of water, nutrients and pests as well as harvest and postharvest practices.
pg054_n0011: The competencies developed will enable you to combine scientific knowledge, agricultural techniques and sustainable approaches to produce vegetables.
pg054_n0012: This will help you make money and have food to eat at home.
pg054_n0015: “Lays the foundation for successful horticultural farming”
pg054_n0019: When growing vegetables, it is important to remember some few things.
pg054_n0020: Most vegetables are usually perishable, and bulky, and some only grow in certain seasons.
pg054_n0021: They also need resources to grow and can be affected by pests and diseases.
pg054_n0022: It is sometimes not easy to know how much to produce because the market can change.
pg054_n0023: Therefore, to make a plan for growing vegetables, we need to think about:
pg054_n0027: What is to be achieved in vegetable production?
pg054_n0030: What resources are needed for vegetable production?
pg054_n0033: Which types of vegetables can be produced with the available resources?
pg054_n0036: How does one look after the vegetables to make sure they grow well?
pg054_n0039: If one is growing more than one type of vegetable or if growing vegetables and also keeping animals, it is important to consider about how they can all be kept or grown together.
pg054_n0043: Setting goals for vegetable production is a vital step for successful production.
pg054_n0044: Is it to earn money, for food or for other reasons?
pg054_n0045: Think also about how much time and money you can invest in vegetable production.
pg054_n0046: Ensure that your goals are clear, specific, and achievable.
pg054_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing in a cluster on the vine.
pg055_n0003: Availability of resources for vegetable production
pg055_n0005: Starting a vegetable business depends on several resources.
pg055_n0006: Those resources can vary based on your location and the specific vegetables you want to grow.
pg055_n0007: It is important to carefully consider each resource before starting your vegetable business.
pg055_n0012: Land: You need to know where you will grow your vegetables, how much land you have, and the type of vegetable to grow.
pg055_n0015: Climate: You need to know whether the intended horticultural crop is suitable to the climate of the area.
pg055_n0018: Water: You need to know where you will get water from and how much it will cost.
pg055_n0019: You also need to know if you can use this water for your vegetables.
pg055_n0022: Structures: You need to know the needed structures such as buildings and fences.
pg055_n0023: You also need to know how much they cost to keep them in good condition.
pg055_n0026: Tools/equipment: You need to know the tools and equipment you have to use in your vegetable business.
pg055_n0027: You also need to know if you need to rent or borrow tools/equipment and estimate cost.
pg055_n0030: Money for capital: You need to know how much money you have to start your business.
pg055_n0031: You also need to identify the source of fund for establishing and running the business.
pg055_n0034: Management skills: You need to know how to keep records, manage people, and prepare your budget.
pg055_n0037: Labour: You need to know how many people are required for your vegetable business.
pg055_n0038: You also need to know if you can use family or hired labour.
pg055_n0041: Market and marketing: You need to know where your customers are and how you will take your vegetables to them or whether they will take the vegetables directly from your farm.
pg055_n0042: You also need to decide on a reasonable and profitable selling price.
pg055_n0044: Matching vegetable enterprises with the available resources
pg055_n0046: Plan your vegetable enterprises with available resources.
pg055_n0047: These resources include water, land, money and equipment you have.
pg055_n0048: Compare your resources with the needs of each crop.
pg055_n0049: If a crop needs a lot of sun and you have a lot of it, that is good.
pg055_n0050: If a crop needs rich soil and you have poor soil, you may need to apply fertilisers.
pg055_n0051: If you are not sure, ask a local farmer or an expert.
pg055_n0052: They can give you good advice based on their expertise and experience.
pg055_n0053: Use resources such as books, the internet, and local libraries to learn more.
pg055_n0054: Several websites and books can help you to understand which crops are compatible with each other and with your resources.
pg055_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing on the vine.
pg056_n0005: The following can also be put into consideration when planning for vegetable crop production:
pg056_n0009: Crop rotation: If you plan to grow different crops in rotations, you should know how they affect each other.
pg056_n0010: Some crops can help or harm the growth of others.
pg056_n0013: Pests and diseases: Learn about common pests that can harm your crop, for example, insects, birds, wild or domestic animals, weeds and diseases and how to manage them.
pg056_n0016: Harvesting: You need to know when and how to harvest your crops.
pg056_n0019: Risks: Every crop comes with its own risks.
pg056_n0020: Identify them and think before how to reduce them.
pg056_n0022: By considering all these things, you can grow your vegetable crops successfully.
pg056_n0026: When you want to grow more than one type of crop, you have to think about how they fit together.
pg056_n0027: For instance, you might have enough people to help with one crop.
pg056_n0028: But, if you choose another crop that also needs a lot of labour, you might not have enough to help.
pg056_n0029: It is important to do all activities timely and appropriately.
pg056_n0030: In this case, you will be required to prepare a chart showing labour requirements at an appropriate time for each crop.
pg056_n0031: When you want to farm both animals and vegetables, think about how they can be together.
pg056_n0032: This is because some animals and crops don’t mix well.
pg056_n0033: For example, free-range chickens can destroy some vegetables such as amaranth.
pg056_n0034: However, they won’t cause any trouble with the production of cassava.
pg056_n0035: Fencing can help to separate the two enterprises.
pg056_n0039: There are different ways to get involved in the vegetable industry.
pg056_n0044: Production of traditional vegetables: This involves growing vegetables such as nightshade, pumpkin leaves, amaranth, and sweet potato leaves.
pg056_n0047: Organic vegetable production enterprises: This involves of growing vegetables using non-synthetic/industrial or chemical fertilisers and pesticides.
pg056_n0050: Conventional vegetable production enterprises: Growing vegetables that involves using synthetic inputs such as fertilisers and pesticides.
pg056_n0053: Retail marketing of vegetables: This involves selling vegetables in small portions.
pg056_im001: Ripe red tomatoes hanging on the plant in the field.
pg057_n0005: Wholesale marketing of vegetables: This involves selling vegetables in large quantities.
pg057_n0008: Leafy vegetable production: This involves growing vegetables whose edible parts are leaves, such as amaranth, Chinese cabbage, and cowpea leaves.
pg057_n0011: Fruit vegetable production: This involves growing vegetables that are categorised as fruit, such as tomato, pepper, eggplant, and cucumber.
pg057_n0014: Root vegetable production: This involves growing vegetables that are categorized as roots, such as carrot, beetroot, and bulb onion.
pg057_n0017: Assorted vegetable production: This involves growing a combination of several vegetables.
pg057_n0021: Once you have decided on your crops, look at your goals again.
pg057_n0022: Check that your plan meets your long and short-term goals.
pg057_n0023: It is also important to note that planning can be hard, but it is important.
pg057_n0024: Spending more time in planning, put you in good position to do your vegetable farming better.

pg058_n0003: Site selection and land preparation for vegetable farming
pg058_n0005: Site selection involves choosing a location that is suitable for growing the type of vegetables you want to cultivate.
pg058_n0006: Factors to consider include all factors you have already considered in the planning section.
pg058_n0007: Some of the important factors include soil type, climate and availability of water and market.
pg058_n0008: The next step is to prepare the land for planting.
pg058_n0009: This involves several steps such as clearing the land and preparing the soil by turning it over to break it up and make it easier for the roots of the vegetables to grow.
pg058_n0010: It also involves adding organic manure such as compost or farm yard manure to the soil.
pg058_n0012: Types of seedbeds commonly used for vegetable farming
pg058_n0014: Depending on the production season, type of irrigation and the field condition, three types of seedbeds are commonly used in vegetable production.
pg058_n0015: These are raised seedbed, sunken seedbed, and flat seedbed.
pg058_n0018: Raised beds are great for clayey soils or areas with poor drainage.
pg058_n0019: They are also useful for irrigated crops where water flows down the furrows between them.
pg058_n0020: They are usually 100 cm wide and 10 - 30 cm high, but the best height depends on the soil texture and moisture.
pg058_n0021: They can be made with hand tools in small to medium farms and machines in large farms.
pg058_n0022: The advantages of raised beds are better drainage and easier access for hand operations such as weeding.
pg058_n0023: Figures 4.1 (a) and (b) show examples of raised beds.
pg058_n0024: The beds in Figure 4.1 (a) are best suited to high-rainfall areas.
pg058_n0025: The beds in Figure 4.1 (b) have a lip around all four sides which helps to prevent water from running off, especially in drier conditions.

pg058_im003: Two raised seedbeds with lips around all four sides to help hold water.

pg060_n0031: Germination is when a seed grows into a plant.
pg060_n0032: This is a key step in planting.
pg060_n0033: Before we plant our crops, we need to check if the seeds can germinate.
pg060_n0034: We do this with a germination test.
pg060_n0035: This test helps us see if the seeds are live and ready to grow.
pg060_n0036: To do a germination test, follow this procedure:
pg060_n0046: Get some sand and put it in a container such as a bucket or a plate.
pg060_n0049: Put the seeds in the sand.
pg060_n0050: If the container is small, you might need more than one container.
pg060_n0053: Add water to the sand to moisten the seeds.
pg060_n0056: Keep watering the seeds to keep them moist but not wet until they germinate.
pg060_n0057: How much you water, depends on how moist the sand is.
pg060_n0060: When the seeds grow, count them.
pg060_n0061: The number of seeds that germinate will show how many out of 100 seeds you have sown.
pg060_n0062: For example, if 96 out of 100 seeds grew, that means 96% of the seeds germinated.
pg060_n0064: The germination percentage helps us see how good the seeds are in terms of germination.
pg060_n0065: It helps us to choose the best seeds to buy.
pg060_n0066: Seeds are good if they have a high germination percentage, about 95% or more.
pg060_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing on the vine.
pg061_n0003: germination percentage is usually on the packaging of the certified seeds.
pg061_n0004: Seeds with low germination percentages mean more seeds will have to be sown to attain the required plant population.
pg061_n0008: When planting vegetables, it is important to choose the right planting materials.
pg061_n0009: The following are some aspects to consider:
pg061_n0013: Suitability of the planting material to ecological conditions: Choose materials that can grow well in your area’s climate and soil.
pg061_n0016: Purity of the planting materials: Use high-quality seeds or seedlings that are free from contaminants.
pg061_n0019: Germination capacity: Look for materials that have a high germination rate, meaning they are more likely to sprout and grow.
pg061_n0022: Disease resistance: Choose planting materials that are resistant to common diseases in your area, as this will help your plants stay healthy.
pg061_n0025: Certified planting materials: Choose seeds or seedlings that are certified, as they have been tested and proven to be safe and reliable.
pg061_n0029: Appropriate spacing in vegetable production is important for plants to grow well.
pg061_n0030: Each plant needs space for its roots and leaves distribution and enough air to breathe.
pg061_n0031: Proper spacing helps plants get enough sunlight, nutrients, and air circulation, all of which are necessary for plant growth and development.
pg061_n0032: Farmers should follow the recommended spacing by consulting a nearby agricultural extension worker.
pg061_n0033: Before planting, measure and mark the recommended spacing between plants using tape measures or ruler, strings and pegs.
pg061_n0034: As plants grow, regularly monitor their spacing and perform thinning or gap-filling where necessary.
pg061_n0035: This will help you to obtain the rewards of bigger, healthier plants, with higher yields.
pg061_n0039: There are two main methods of planting vegetables: direct seeding and transplanting.
pg061_n0041: (a) Direct seeding (sowing): This is when you put the vegetable seed straight into the garden for it to begin its growth and stay there until harvesting.
pg061_n0042: Direct seeding is cost-effective and it reduces the risk of transplant shock.
pg061_n0043: There are three common methods of direct seeding: broadcasting, drilling and dibbling.
pg061_im001: Ripe red tomatoes hanging on the vine in the field.
pg062_n0005: (i) Broadcasting: This method involves scattering seeds thinly and evenly over the area.
pg062_n0006: When broadcasting vegetable seeds, you might mix them with a similar amount of sand (1 to 1 ratio) to keep them from sticking together and to make for a more even spread.
pg062_n0007: This method is best for crops such as amaranth and lettuce, which have small and light seeds.
pg062_n0008: These plants are shallow-rooted and can be easily thinned out later if needed.
pg062_n0010: (ii) Drilling: Drilling involves opening a shallow furrow in the soil and dropping seeds thinly in a furrow.
pg062_n0011: This method is best for vegetables like carrots where the seeds are small and the plants need to be closely spaced.
pg062_n0012: With drilling, there is a known space between rows but no clear spacing between plants within a row.
pg062_n0013: It is also commonly practised when sowing onion or tomato seeds at the nursery seed-bed.
pg062_n0015: (iii) Direct row planting: This method is best for crops that need to be spaced out, for example, green beans, common peas and okra.
pg062_n0016: These crops are large and they need to be spaced out for optimal growth.
pg062_n0017: There is a known space between rows and within plants in rows.
pg062_n0019: (b) Transplanting: This method involves starting seeds in a controlled area (nursery), allowing them to grow and get stronger, and then transplanting the seedlings to the garden at the right time.
pg062_n0020: Some vegetables that are best planted by transplanting include tomatoes, peppers, and onions.
pg062_n0024: Planting vegetables on time is key to growing them well and selling them when prices are high.
pg062_n0025: Timely planting helps farmers to get the best yield from their land.
pg062_n0026: If vegetables are planted too early or too late, they might not grow well, and farmers might not get enough yield.
pg062_n0027: To sell vegetables when prices are high, they need to be planted at the right time.
pg062_n0028: This can be tricky because it depends on the weather and soil type.
pg062_n0029: Experienced farmers, teachers or agricultural extension workers can also advise on the best planting times.
pg062_n0030: The goal is to plant vegetables when they will grow better and be ready for harvest when prices are high.
pg062_n0031: This will help farmers make more money from their crops.

pg063_n0029: Management of soil fertility for vegetable production
pg063_n0031: Soil is a natural medium where plants grow and get their nutrients.
pg063_n0032: However, sometimes soil becomes unhealthy or infertile.
pg063_n0033: The following subsections will discuss the causes of loss of soil fertility and the use of organic and inorganic fertilisers in maintaining soil fertility.
pg063_n0035: Causes of loss of soil fertility
pg063_n0037: There are several causes of soil fertility lose or depletion, some of which are discussed here.
pg063_n0040: Soil erosion happens when the moving wind or water removes the topsoil from the land.
pg063_n0041: This can happen when there is a lot of rainfall or when the land is not covered with vegetation.
pg063_n0042: When soil erosion happens, the nutrients in the soil can be washed away, making it infertile.
pg063_n0043: To combat this, we can plant trees and other vegetations to protect the soil from being washed or blown away.
pg063_n0044: We can also use contour farming in sloppy areas to minimise soil erosion (refer to Figure 4.4).
pg063_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing on the vine.
pg064_im002: Vegetables planted in curved contour rows on a hillside to reduce soil erosion and conserve water.
pg064_n0006: Water logging happens when too much water stays in the soil for a long time.
pg064_n0007: When this happens, the air in the soil gets pushed out, making it hard for plant roots to breathe.
pg064_n0008: To solve this, we can improve soil drainage by adding organic matter or creating channels to allow excess water to flow out.
pg064_n0011: Leaching is when water washes away nutrients down the soil profile.
pg064_n0012: This happens when it rains a lot or when we use irrigation.
pg064_n0013: The nutrients are carried downwards in the soil, away from where the plant’s roots are.
pg064_n0014: This means that the plant can’t get the nutrients it needs.
pg064_n0015: This is a problem because plants need these nutrients to grow.
pg064_n0016: To prevent this, we can use mulch or cover crops to slow down water movement and reduce nutrient loss.
pg064_n0017: The lost nutrients should also be replaced by applying organic manure or inorganic fertilisers to the soil.
pg064_n0020: These include burning of vegetation cover, crop removal through continuous cropping and grazing, using acid or alkali-forming fertilisers for a long time, and improper weed control methods.
pg064_n0024: When we burn vegetation on the ground, we destroy the plants and the soil.
pg064_n0025: This leaves the ground exposed to water and wind, which can cause the land to erode.
pg064_n0026: This erosion can make the land less fertile and harder to farm.
pg064_n0027: The plants and the soil contain important nutrients like carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulphur.
pg064_n0028: When these are burned, they are destroyed and can’t help plants to grow well.
pg064_n0029: Only a few minerals such as potassium are left in the ash.
pg064_n0030: The mineral nutrients left in ash can also be
pg065_n0003: washed away by water and wind, causing more erosion and loss of fertility.
pg065_n0004: It is better not to burn the vegetation on the ground.
pg065_n0005: Instead of burning, we can compost plant waste to return nutrients to the soil.
pg065_n0008: Crop removal through continuous cropping and grazing:
pg065_n0009: When crops are continuously grown on the same land, it can deplete the soil of nutrients.
pg065_n0011: Grazing can also deplete the soil’s nutrients, especially if the animals are overgrazed.
pg065_n0012: To address this, we can practice crop rotation or use rotational grazing.
pg065_n0013: This helps to maintain a balance of nutrients in the soil.
pg065_n0014: The lost nutrients should also be replaced by applying organic manure or inorganic fertilisers to the soil.
pg065_n0017: Using acid or alkali-forming fertilisers for a long time:
pg065_n0018: Using acid or alkali-forming fertilisers for a long time can change soil pH.
pg065_n0019: Acidic fertilisers can lower soil pH.
pg065_n0021: Alkaline fertilisers can raise soil pH.
pg065_n0022: This also can affect plant growth.
pg065_n0023: Soil pH changes can affect soil micro-organisms and available nutrients.
pg065_n0024: To avoid a pH decrease, don’t use too much acidic fertilisers.
pg065_n0025: To avoid a pH increase, don’t use too much alkaline fertilisers.
pg065_n0026: Always check the soil’s pH before adding fertilisers.
pg065_n0027: You can test the soil at home with a pH meter.
pg065_n0028: You can also seek advice for the selection of fertilisers from a crop extension worker.
pg065_n0029: This will help to keep the soil’s pH balanced for plant growth.
pg065_n0033: Weeds are plants that grow where they are not needed.
pg065_n0034: When we pull them out, we lose the nutrients they have taken from the soil.
pg065_n0035: It is better to let them decompose into humus on the field.
pg065_n0036: But, where weeds cause problems, we should remove them.
pg065_n0037: To enhance weed control together with the management of soil fertility, we can do the following:
pg065_n0041: Weeds that are removed can be composted, which means they are left to decompose naturally.
pg065_n0042: This process turns them into a nutrient-rich compost that can be used to enrich the soil.
pg065_n0046: This involves growing different types of crops in the same piece of land by alternation (refer to Figure 2.8).
pg065_n0047: This method controls weeds which only grow well when in association with certain crops, for example, parasitic weeds.
pg065_n0048: In addition, crop rotation helps to keep nutrients in the soil at a good level.
pg065_n0049: This is done by growing crops of different nutrients needs; those with higher nutrient needs (heavy feeders); and those with lower nutrient needs (light feeders).
pg065_im001: Ripe red tomatoes hanging on the plant in the field.
pg066_n0003: types of crops, we keep the soil nutrients balanced.
pg066_n0004: Also, by interchanging crops that grow deep in the soil with those that grow shallowly, we make sure nutrients in all parts of the soil get used.
pg066_n0005: Shallow-rooted crops take nutrients from the top soil, while deep-rooted crops take them from the bottom.
pg066_n0006: Legumes and rest periods in the rotation also help to keep the soil fertile.
pg066_n0007: This is because they add more nutrients to the soil.
pg066_n0008: Therefore, crop rotation is a good way to reduce weeds as well as to keep our soil healthy and productive.
pg066_n0010: (iii) Use of herbicides: These are chemical substances that can kill weeds.
pg066_n0011: They can be used in recommended amounts to control weeds without causing much soil degradation.
pg066_n0013: (iv) Use of mulch: Mulch is like a grass blanket that we put on the ground to keep weeds down and add organic matter to the soil (refer to Figure 4.5).

pg066_n0017: Accumulation of excessive salts in soil:
pg066_n0018: Soil has salts that come from rocks and rotting plants.
pg066_n0020: But in dry areas, there is no enough rain to do this.
pg066_n0021: This can cause salts to build up in the topsoil.
pg066_n0022: Too much salt can make the soil lose its fertility.
pg066_n0023: This is because the salts can suck water out of plant roots.
pg066_n0024: They can also change the soil’s pH level.
pg066_n0025: To fix this, we can use good farming practices to stop salt from building up.
pg066_n0026: One way is to avoid excessive watering so
pg067_n0003: as not to raise the groundwater.
pg067_n0004: We can also plant crops that are good at coping with excessive salts in the soil.
pg067_n0007: Some nutrients in the soil can be lost through volatilization.
pg067_n0008: Volatilization is when nutrients in the soil turn into gas and rise into the air instead of staying in the soil to feed the plants.
pg067_n0009: The most common nutrients lost through volatilization, especially in hot weather, are nitrogen, sulphur, and to a lesser extent, phosphorus.
pg067_n0010: To prevent this, apply nitrogenous and sulphur fertilisers by incorporating them into the soil rather than leaving them on the surface.
pg067_n0011: Also, avoid applying fertilisers during hot, dry conditions when volatilization is more likely to occur.

pg067_n0020: The use of organic fertilisers in maintaining soil fertility
pg067_n0022: Organic fertilisers are nutrient-carrying materials derived from plants and animal materials also known as manures or natural manures.
pg067_n0023: These materials play a great role in improving soil fertility.
pg067_n0024: They add nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium to the soil, which are needed by plants to grow.
pg067_n0026: There are different types of organic fertilisers including manures.
pg067_n0027: Examples of manures are farmyard manure, compost, and green manure.
pg067_n0028: Farmyard manure is made from the waste of farm animals, for example, faeces and urine, along with beddings and leftover feed.
pg067_n0029: It is important to store it properly to avoid losing nutrients.
pg067_n0030: It can be used in fields after being well-decomposed.
pg067_n0031: Compost is made from organic materials or waste.
pg067_n0032: It is made by piling up farm residues and covering them with animal waste.
pg067_n0033: Compost is ready to use when it turns dark brown or black, soft and easy to spread, and the pile gets smaller.
pg067_n0034: Green manure is made by growing a crop on a piece of land and then incorporating it by ploughing it into the soil at the flowering stage.
