pg068_n0032: The use of inorganic fertilisers in maintaining soil fertility
pg068_n0034: Inorganic fertilisers are made in factories and may contain Nitrogen, Phosphorus and Potassium (NPK) and other nutrient elements.
pg068_n0035: There are two types of fertilisers: single and mixed or compound fertilisers.
pg068_n0036: Single fertilisers have only one nutrient.
pg068_n0037: Mixed or compound fertilisers have two or more of the primary mineral nutrients.
pg068_n0038: When a fertiliser contains all the three primary mineral nutrients, it is called a complete fertiliser.
pg068_n0040: These properties tell us how and when to use them and what rules we need to follow when using them.

pg069_n0024: Management of soil water for vegetable production
pg069_n0026: Soil water helps plants to grow and stay healthy.
pg069_n0028: This is when water turns into water vapour and disappears from the plants’ leaves.
pg069_n0029: Water also leaves the soil through a process called evaporation.
pg069_n0030: The loss of water from both the soil and plants is called evapotranspiration.
pg069_n0031: If we don’t add water to the soil, plants can die.
pg069_n0033: Different types of plants need different amounts of water.
pg069_n0034: Some plants can tolerate high amount of water, and others cannot.
pg069_n0035: Similarly, the amount of water needed depends on the stage of growth and the weather situation.
pg069_n0036: We can check how much water is in the soil by feeling and looking at it.
pg069_n0037: This can be done by squeezing a soil sample and seeing how it feels and looks.
pg069_n0038: If plants have too little water, they start wilting and leaves turn brown.
pg069_n0039: If they have too much water, their leaves can become soft and limp, also can start wilting due to root suffocation and disease infestation.
pg069_n0041: Certain stages of plant growth are more sensitive to water shortage.
pg069_n0042: If we don’t give plants enough water during these growth stages yield and quality of produce are severely affected.
pg069_n0043: We can conserve moisture in the soil through the application of compost or manure over the soil, placing mulch on the soil and practising crop rotation.
pg069_n0044: This helps to reduce the frequency of watering or irrigating the crop.
pg069_n0045: The watering of the plants is called irrigation.

pg072_n0019: Choosing the right irrigation method for vegetable crops depends on several factors such as:
pg072_n0023: The type of the soil: Some methods work better with certain types of soil.
pg072_n0024: For example, furrow irrigation is not suitable for sand soils because it can result into soil erosion and leaching of plant nutrients.
pg072_n0027: The land’s forms: If the land is flat, a method that spreads water evenly might be best.
pg072_n0028: If the land is hilly, a method that can get water to the top of the hills might be better.
pg072_n0031: The weather: In areas with lots of rain, you might not need to water your plants as much.
pg072_n0032: In areas with little rain, you might need to water your plants more.
pg072_n0035: The type of crops: Some crops need more water than others.
pg072_n0036: For example, tomatoes need more water than lettuce.
pg072_n0039: The availability and quality of water: If you have little clean water, you might go for drip irrigation.
pg072_n0040: If your water is dirty or salty can cause clogging in drip lines and drippers therefore, not good for drip irrigation.
pg072_n0041: Little water cannot support furrow irrigation.
pg072_n0044: The costs and benefits: Some methods of watering plants can be expensive but economical at watering.
pg072_n0045: Others might be cheaper but not economical.
pg072_n0048: The amount of work: Some methods require a lot of work to set up and maintain.
pg072_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing in clusters on the plant.
pg073_n0003: Others are easier to set up and maintain.
pg073_n0004: (h) The level of technology and capital: Some methods require a lot of technology and money to set up.
pg073_n0005: Others are simpler and cheaper to set up.
pg073_n0007: Therefore, each of these factors needs to be considered when choosing the best irrigation method for your vegetable crops.

pg073_n0040: Crop pest means any living thing that harms plants.
pg073_n0041: These can be insects, animals, weeds, or even bacteria, fungi and viruses.
pg073_n0042: They are important to understand because they can badly damage our plants.
pg073_n0043: Pests can harm crops in the field and even after they are stored.
pg073_n0044: This is how pests can cause damage to our crops:
pg074_n0005: They eat plant leaves and stems, slowing down their growth.
pg074_n0006: This can make plants produce less because the damaged plant part cannot carryout effectively important physiological processes or functions.
pg074_n0009: Some pests, such as nematodes and moles, damage plant roots causing the plants to wilt and die.
pg074_n0012: Pests, for example, squirrels and rats can dig up seeds, resulting in few plants per unit area.
pg074_n0015: Insects like thrips can harm flowers and fruits, lowering their quality.
pg074_n0018: Some pests can suck plant sap causing the plant to grow slowly and deformed.
pg074_n0021: Pests such as diseases make crop plants ill-healthy and may cause death to the plant.
pg074_n0024: Crop pests can increase the cost of farming because we need to spend money to control them, for example, by buying pesticides.
pg074_n0027: Pests such as weeds compete with vegetable crops for nutrients, water, and light, reducing the quality and yields of the produce.
pg074_n0029: We can manage crop pests in different ways.
pg074_n0030: We can use cultural farming practices, physical or mechanical methods, biological, chemical, or a combination of methods known as Integrated Pest Management (IPM).
pg074_n0034: Cultural pest management is a way to protect plants from pests using good farming practices.
pg074_n0035: This is done by modifying the environment on which the pest lives.
pg074_n0036: For example, we can modify the amount of sunlight, temperature, or the soil’s pH level.
pg074_n0037: This involves the use of resistant varieties, timely planting and weeding, sanitation within and around the field use of mulching materials, removal of diseased plants and crop rotation.
pg074_n0038: This method helps to prevent pests from becoming too many and damaging our crop plants.
pg074_n0039: It makes our farming system stronger and it is less likely to need chemical pesticides.
pg074_n0043: These involve using physical or mechanical means to kill pests and create barriers to prevent pests from getting into contact with their target crops.
pg074_n0044: The methods involved include hand picking, trapping and killing, flooding and overhead irrigation, physical barrier, proper drying before storage and use of lethal temperature.
pg074_n0048: This method involves the use of living organisms which are natural predators (eat others) to control pests.
pg074_n0049: The natural predators can be birds and insects.
pg074_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing in clusters on the plant.
pg075_n0003: is better than using chemical pesticides because it helps to keep the farm’s ecosystem balanced.
pg075_n0004: Farmers tend to introduce good natural predators into the farm.
pg075_n0005: Examples include parasitic wasps preying on whitefly and mealy bugs, ladybird beetle preying on aphids, praying mantis preying on the giant looper, weaver ants preying on white scales, chicken preying on stainers, chameleons preying on most insects, and cats preying on rats, mice and moles, wasps and poultry preying on bollworms.
pg075_n0006: When a farm has conducive environment, it encourages these good creatures (predators) to live.
pg075_n0007: In this way, the farm’s ecosystem helps to control the pests.
pg075_n0009: By using biological pest management, farmers help to keep the environment healthy and sustainable.
pg075_n0010: However, it is important to note that biological pest management needs careful planning and management.
pg075_n0011: The farmer needs to introduce/maintain the right good creatures and make sure they have the conditions they need to stay alive and thrive.
pg075_n0012: Biological pest management controls pests while keeping the farm environment healthy and balanced.
pg075_n0013: However, the process is a bit slow in some cases.
pg075_n0017: Chemical pest control is a method of controlling pests using chemicals, also known as pesticides.
pg075_n0018: These chemicals come in different forms, such as powders, liquids, and gases.
pg075_n0019: They can be sprayed, dusted, or fumigated onto soil and crop plants.
pg075_n0020: Pesticides are grouped based on their formulation, the type of pest they target, and how they work.
pg075_n0021: Some pesticides are designed to kill specific types of pests for example, insecticides kill insect pests, nematicides kill nematodes, rodenticides kill rodents, fungicides kill fungi, bactericides kill bacteria and herbicides kill weeds.
pg075_n0022: Pesticides can also be either synthetic or bio-pesticides.
pg075_n0023: It is recommended to use bio-pesticides (that is the pesticides coming from animal and plant by-products).
pg075_n0025: Key factors for pest control using pesticides:
pg075_n0026: When using pesticides to control pests, consider these factors:
pg075_n0030: Know the targeted pest: It is important to know what kind of pest you are dealing with.
pg075_n0031: Different pests need different kinds of pesticides.
pg075_n0034: Choose the right pesticide: Not all pesticides work the same.
pg075_n0035: Choose one that is known to work well against the targeted pest.
pg075_n0038: Rotating different pesticides: Sometimes pests get used to a certain pesticide in such a way that the pesticide becomes no longer effective on the targeted pest.
pg075_n0039: In this case, you should try a different one.
pg075_n0042: Choose the right time: The best time to use pesticide is when pests are most likely to be harmed by the pesticide.
pg075_n0043: It is recommended to start using pesticide
pg075_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing on the plant.
pg076_n0003: when the number of pests is high enough to cause economical loss.
pg076_n0004: Avoid using pesticides when it is about to rain as this can wash away the chemical.
pg076_n0008: Use the right amount: Too much pesticide can be harmful, and too little might not work.
pg076_n0009: Make sure to use the right amount.
pg076_n0012: Monitoring: After using the pesticides, keep on observing to see if it worked.
pg076_n0014: Safety precautions in the use of pesticides:
pg076_n0015: Pesticides are toxic chemicals and should be handled with care.
pg076_n0016: Therefore, when using pesticides, you should take the following precautions:
pg076_n0020: Always check the date they expire and read the instructions carefully.
pg076_n0023: Wear protective gear, such as masks, gloves and field boots.
pg076_n0029: Don’t let the pesticide touch your food or water.
pg076_n0032: Wash your hands and clothes after handling pesticides.
pg076_n0035: Don’t smoke or eat while using pesticides.
pg076_n0038: Clean the spraying equipment after using it.
pg076_n0041: Store the chemicals in a safe place, out of reach of children and animals.
pg076_n0044: Don’t throw leftover containers in gardens.
pg076_n0047: Always wait for the recommended time before harvesting a treated crop, that is, adhere to the withdrawal period.
pg076_n0050: Keep a record of dates and all the chemicals you use.
pg076_n0051: This helps you to determine when to harvest your crops.
pg076_n0053: It is important to note that while chemical pest control is faster and more predictable than other methods, it can be expensive and harmful to humans, animals, and the environment.
pg076_n0054: Therefore, it is important to use these chemicals safely and responsibly, considering their effects on the environment and other beneficial organisms.
pg076_n0057: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is a way to control pests using a combination of various pest control methods such as cultural, biological, physical, and chemical controls.
pg076_n0058: These methods are chosen based on information about pests and their interactions with the environment.
pg076_n0059: The following are some steps to follow when using IPM:
pg076_n0063: Choose pest control methods that are safe for crops, soil, air, water and people.
pg076_n0066: Use differences between crops and pests to give crops a competitive advantage over pests.
pg076_im001: Ripe red tomatoes hanging on the plant in a garden.
pg077_n0005: Try to reduce the pests’ survival in the soil.
pg077_n0008: Use weed control practices to stop weeds from growing.
pg077_n0011: Make pest control practices flexible and able to adapt to different seasons.
pg077_n0014: Combine different approaches to suppress, block or repel the pests.
pg077_n0016: When using integrated pest management, start with the least harmful methods.
pg077_n0017: These include prevention or cultural practices, physical control methods, and biological control methods.
pg077_n0018: If these don’t work, consider using non-native predators.
pg077_n0019: Only use chemical control methods if necessary, and always start with naturally occurring materials.
pg077_n0020: The following is an example of some strategies to implement IPM in vegetables:
pg077_n0024: Choose varieties that are resistant to pests.
pg077_n0025: This can help to reduce the need for pesticides.
pg077_n0028: Rotate your crops to prevent pests from building up in the soil.
pg077_n0029: This can be done by planting different types of vegetables in the same area each year.
pg077_n0032: Use biological control agents such as ladybird beetles and parasitic wasps to control pests.
pg077_n0033: These natural enemies can help to keep pests under control.
pg077_n0036: Keep your vegetable plants clean by removing plant debris and weeds.
pg077_n0037: This can help to prevent the growth of pests.
pg077_n0040: Use pheromone traps to monitor and control pests.
pg077_n0041: These traps can help you to identify when pests are present and take action.
pg077_n0044: Use insecticidal soap or neem oil to control pests.
pg077_n0045: These natural substances can be effective in controlling pests without harming other plants or animals.

pg078_n0025: Harvesting and postharvesting practices in vegetable production
pg078_n0027: Harvesting is a process of removing the entire plant or economic parts after maturity for consumption, marketing, storage or processing.
pg078_n0028: Harvested part(s) or the whole plant to be harvested must have attained the right stage of maturity.
pg078_n0029: Therefore, it is important to have knowledge of maturity indices for different types of vegetable crops as over-mature and premature harvest affects negatively the quality of the produce and shelf life.
pg078_n0030: The method of harvesting depends on the type of vegetable crop.
pg078_n0031: Ensure proper harvest without causing any damage to the plant or produce.
pg078_n0033: Postharvesting practices in vegetable crop production
pg078_n0035: Postharvesting practices in vegetable crops refer to the processes that follow after vegetables are harvested.
pg078_n0036: These practices intend to make the vegetables ready for eating, easy to handle and last longer.
pg078_n0037: These practices depend on what kind of vegetables we have, how we want to use them, and when we want to use them.
pg078_n0038: For most vegetables, these practices might include cooling, cleaning, sorting and grading, packaging, storing, or transporting them.
pg078_n0039: We can also use special treatments like refrigeration, heat treatment, and modified atmosphere packaging to keep our vegetables fresh and good to eat for a longer time.
pg078_n0040: Figure 4.7 shows a summarised flow of postharvest practices in vegetables.
pg079_im002: Flow chart of postharvest practices in vegetables: harvesting leads to pre-cooling, then cleaning or disinfecting, then sorting and grading, then packaging. From packaging, vegetables may go directly to marketing, or go to storage or transport to market or a processing plant, then to processing, and finally to marketing.
pg079_n0006: Precooling is a way to quickly get rid of heat after harvesting vegetables.
pg079_n0007: This is important because the heat can make the vegetables spoil faster.
pg079_n0008: Precooling helps to remove field heat from vegetables after they are harvested.
pg079_n0009: It also helps to stop the vegetables from losing water and spoiling.
pg079_n0010: In this way, vegetables can be kept fresh for a long time and retain their taste.
pg079_n0011: Precooling can be achieved by placing vegetables in a cool place, such as a refrigerator or a cool room.
pg079_n0012: If refrigerators or cool rooms are not available, the vegetables can be placed in a cool shaded area, charcoal evaporative cooler or zero energy cooling chamber.
pg079_n0015: Farmers and people who handle vegetables need to clean or disinfect properly.
pg079_n0016: This is important to prevent diseases and incidences of food-related illnesses that can be transmitted to people who eat the vegetables.
pg079_n0019: When we sort vegetables, we get rid of the ones that are spoiled, damaged, or diseased.
pg079_n0020: This is important because it stops the production of a harmful gas called ethylene and also it avoids contamination which can affect other vegetables.
pg079_n0021: Grading involves organising vegetables based on characteristics such as their colour, size, shape, how ripe they are, or how mature they are.
pg079_n0022: Grading helps us to easily identify and handle the vegetables based on certain common parameters.
pg079_n0025: Packaging of vegetables is about protecting them from harm.
pg079_n0026: We put them in boxes or bags to keep them safe from being damaged.
pg079_n0027: This also helps us to easily carry or handle them.
pg079_n0028: However, if we use the wrong materials for packaging, it can cause the vegetables to get damaged, leading to losses.
pg079_n0029: In Tanzania, we often use wooden crates, cardboard boxes, woven palm baskets, plastic crates, nylon sacks, jute sacks, and polythene bags for packaging.
pg079_n0030: However, some of these materials may not protect the vegetables well.
pg080_n0003: The packaging materials should allow the vegetables to breathe, which helps to prevent them from getting too hot.
pg080_n0004: An ideal packaging material should be smooth and not too tall or large, as this could cause too much pressure on the vegetables at the bottom of the pack.
pg080_n0005: This pressure can cause internal injuries, which can reduce the quality of the vegetables after they have been harvested.
pg080_n0008: Storage of vegetables is important because it keeps them fresh for a long time.
pg080_n0009: However, some vegetables are hard to keep fresh for a long time.
pg080_n0010: For short-term storage, we can keep them at room temperature if there is good airflow to stop them from getting too hot.
pg080_n0011: For longer-term storage, we can keep them at cooler temperatures and high humidity.
pg080_n0012: We can also use a charcoal evaporative cooler or zero-energy cooling chamber to preserve vegetable produce (refer to Figure 4.8 (a) and (b)).
pg080_n0013: Therefore, to prevent a lot of our harvested vegetables from spoiling, we need to find and use good storage methods.

pg080_im003: Zero-energy cooling chamber made of brick with a thatched roof, containing trays of vegetables for cool storage.
pg080_n0022: Transporting the vegetables to the market needs special means of transport that keep vegetables cool and safe.
pg080_n0026: Processing of vegetables is a way to make vegetables last longer.
pg080_n0027: This can be done by canning, drying or freezing them.
pg080_n0028: Based on the size of the produce and the level of technology, you can choose whether to carry out the processing in a large factory or a small backyard.
pg080_n0029: To learn more, you can ask your local crop or food processing experts.
pg080_n0032: We need to sell our vegetables in a way that losses are minimised as much as possible and at a reasonable good price.

pg082_n0016: Amaranth is a fast-growing vegetable crop that can be grown all year round in Tanzania.
pg082_n0017: It can be grown for its leaves or seeds.
pg082_n0018: It is an easy crop to grow with very quick returns, and has few simple requirements.
pg082_n0019: Amaranth is rich in vitamins A, B, C, and minerals such as calcium and iron.
pg082_n0020: Some amaranth grains are also high in protein.
pg082_n0021: You can eat amaranth alone or mix it with other vegetables.
pg082_n0022: Amaranth can grow in many different soil and weather conditions.
pg082_n0023: It is also a good way for farmers to earn money by selling its leaves or grains.

pg083_n0009: In planning for amaranth production, consider which variety to grow; for market or home consumption.
pg083_n0010: Other considerations include when to produce the crop, reliable seed sources and arrangement of marketing strategies as the crop takes a short time to be ready for harvesting.

pg083_n0025: First, you need to choose where to plant the amaranth.
pg083_n0026: Next, you need to prepare the place where you will plant the amaranth.

pg083_n0028: After planting, you need to consider water management to the crop plants and keep the amaranth safe from pests and diseases.
pg083_n0032: Amaranth grows well on different types of soil.
pg083_n0033: However, it prefers a well-drained soils such as loamy, sandy loamy, or silty loamy which is rich in organic matter.
pg083_n0034: A pH level between 4.5 and 7.5 is suitable for the crop.
pg083_n0035: Amaranth thrives well in hot and humid weather.
pg083_n0036: The best temperature for amaranth is between 18 and 25 degrees Celsius.
pg083_n0037: Amaranth does not tolerate waterlogging conditions.
pg083_n0038: If there are free-range animals around, you should put a fence around the place.
pg084_n0005: To prepare a seedbed for amaranth, follow these steps:
pg084_n0009: Clear the site, then plough it to a depth of at least 25 centimetres.
pg084_n0010: Afterwards, harrow and level the soil to create the finest tilth.
pg084_n0013: Remove weeds and debris to reduce competition for resources.
pg084_n0016: Apply a well-decomposed farmyard manure of about 25 tons per 1 hectare (about 2 kg per 1 m²) at the time of fine ploughing.
pg084_n0019: Use sunken beds during dry seasons when there is an insufficient amount of water; or use raised beds during excessive wet or rainy seasons.
pg084_n0022: Level the seed beds to ensure no depression patches on the seed bed surface to avoid damping off diseases.
pg084_n0024: Seed selection and planting of amaranth
pg084_n0026: Amaranth seeds come in many types, each with its own characteristic features.
pg084_n0027: Some are good for grain, while others are better for leafy vegetables.
pg084_n0028: It is important to buy high-quality seeds from trusted sellers, for example, research centres or registered seed distributors.
pg084_n0029: If you can’t find registered seed sellers, you can buy seeds from local markets or grow your seeds at home.
pg084_n0030: Before using them, it is important to check their germination rate.
pg084_n0031: Amaranth seeds are very small, so during sowing, they are usually mixed with sand for easier handling.
pg084_n0032: The common ratio is 1 gram of seed to 100 grams of sand.
pg084_n0033: They are usually sown directly into the soil.
pg084_n0034: Sometimes, they are grown in a nursery first, then later transplanted in the main field.
pg084_n0035: However, this method is not practical for large fields.
pg084_n0037: Seeds can be directly sown in the field by broadcasting or sown in rows by drilling method.
pg084_n0038: By broadcasting method, seeds mixed with sand are spread thinly and evenly over the seed bed.
pg084_n0039: Sowing by drilling method requires you to go through the following procedures:
pg084_n0043: Make furrows that are 0.5 to 1.0 cm deep.
pg084_n0044: Drill seeds mixed with sand into these furrows, then, lightly cover the seeds with soil.
pg084_n0047: When growing amaranth to be harvested by uprooting, keep furrows 15 - 20 cm apart.
pg084_n0048: For amaranth picked by piece meal (bit by bit) space furrows 30 cm apart.
pg084_n0049: After planting, thin out the plants to maintain a distance of 15 cm between each plant.
pg084_n0052: Water the bed gently to keep the field moist.
pg084_n0053: The amount of water in the soil will decide how much and how often to irrigate.
pg084_n0055: If you follow the spacing properly, you will need about 2 - 2.5 kg of seeds per
pg085_n0003: hectare. This is the same as 0.5 g of seeds per square meter of a bed.
pg085_n0004: Usually, it takes about 3 days from sowing to germination.
pg085_n0008: Amaranth is a crop that needs a lot of nutrients.
pg085_n0009: You can use organic or synthetic fertilisers based on the plant’s needs.
pg085_n0010: If you want to harvest the whole amaranth plant, it is advisable to improve the soil’s fertility before planting.
pg085_n0011: This can be done by adding about 20 - 25 tons of well-decomposed manure per hectare (2 - 2.5 kg per m²) at the ploughing stage.
pg085_n0012: You can also use other chemical fertilisers such as Nitrogen, Phosphorous, and Potash (NPK) at planting.
pg085_n0014: Also, spraying the crop with 1% urea or diluted cow urine after every harvest can help the plants to grow more and yield more.
pg085_n0018: Amaranth requires a constant amount of water, especially during germination and at the early growth stage.
pg085_n0019: You should water the plants regularly, but not too much because too much water can lead to a disease called damping off.
pg085_n0020: It is better to water the plants when the air temperature is lower, like in the morning or evening.
pg085_n0021: There are several ways to water amaranth plants, including watering through furrows, overhead watering or basin irrigation and using watering can (especially for small scale or home garden).
pg085_n0025: Practices to minimise weeds and weed seeds must be employed before sowing.
pg085_n0026: This may involve deep ploughing to kill both annual and perennial weeds.
pg085_n0027: The use of non-selective systematic herbicides may be applied to kill weeds such as nut grass before ploughing.
pg085_n0028: Irrigation to a ploughed land before sowing will promote the growing of new weeds which will have to be removed before sowing.
pg085_n0029: Other practises, for example, hand pulling and weeding, can be applied after the crop has been established.
pg085_n0033: Amaranth plants can be harvested shortly after planting.
pg085_n0034: This means that the problems with pests must be dealt with early, even before sowing.

pg087_n0054: Harvesting and postharvesting management of amaranth
pg087_n0056: Amaranth plants grow at different growth rates.
pg087_n0057: Usually, they are ready to harvest 3 to 4 weeks after sowing.
pg087_n0058: Harvesting can be done in two ways.
pg087_n0059: First, you can pull out the fully grown plants together with their roots and cut off the roots.
pg087_n0060: Second, you can pick the young, tender leaves/branches throughout the growing season.
pg087_n0061: Put the harvested produce under shade.
pg087_n0062: Next, wash the amaranth to remove dirt and insects.
pg087_n0063: Finally, put the amaranth in a clean container or box to stay fresh until it is sold.
pg087_n0064: For grain amaranth, the crop is ready for harvesting when the seeds start to shatter.
pg088_n0003: The seeds can be threshed and winnowed, then stored in a cool, dry place.
pg088_n0004: Value addition can be through processing amaranth into flour or using it to make various food products.
pg088_n0005: Under good care and the right conditions, one hectare of amaranth can produce around 25 tons of green leaves and 2 to 5 tons of grain (seeds).

pg089_n0008: In this chapter, you will learn how to grow Chinese cabbage, from planting to selling.
pg089_n0009: The competencies developed will enable you to earn money and get food from the Chinese cabbage you grow.
pg089_n0012: “Plant with care and it will soon flourish; a symbol of patient and growth”
pg089_n0014: Getting started with Chinese cabbage production
pg089_n0016: Chinese cabbage is a type of leafy vegetable.
pg089_n0017: The crop grows quickly and it can be ready in 45, 60 or 80 days.
pg089_n0018: It doesn’t need many resources to grow.
pg089_n0019: It can be eaten in many ways.
pg089_n0020: It can be cooked as a vegetable or used in salads while in raw state.
pg089_n0021: It is full of dietary fibres, and minerals such as calcium, potassium, magnesium, sodium, iron, and zinc.
pg089_n0022: It also contains vitamins such as vitamins A, C, K, and niacin.
pg089_n0023: Chinese cabbage comes in two main types.
pg089_n0024: One type (non-headed) is like a long, thin cabbage.
pg089_n0025: It has a thick, stalk and dark green leaves that can grow up to 30 cm (refer to Figure 6.1 (a)).
pg089_n0027: It forms a head, just like a regular cabbage.
pg089_n0028: It is often cylindrical and elongated (refer to Figure 6.1 (b)).

pg089_n0037: Before starting your Chinese cabbage farm, you should think about a few things.
pg089_n0038: First, decide how much Chinese cabbage you want to produce.
pg089_n0039: Next, choose the type of Chinese cabbage you want to grow.
pg089_n0040: Then, decide when you want to start
pg090_n0004: You also need to know how many resources you will need.
pg090_n0005: Lastly, think about when and where you will sell your cabbages.
pg090_n0006: It is also important to estimate the expected profit from selling the cabbages.
pg090_n0013: Use the internet or a library to find out about different types of Chinese cabbage that are commonly grown in Tanzania.
pg090_n0014: Look for information about how Chinese cabbage is grown, cared for, harvested, processed, and marketed.
pg090_n0017: Go to your school garden or a nearby Chinese cabbage farm.
pg090_n0018: Learn from the gardener how Chinese cabbage is grown, taken care of, harvested, processed, and sold.

pg090_n0025: This section will help you to explore the techniques of growing Chinese cabbage right from planning to postharvesting practices.
pg090_n0026: You will learn about choosing the right seeds and how to plant them.
pg090_n0027: You will also cover the management of water and nutrients to the crop plants, protection of the crop against various pests including diseases and postharvest practices.
pg090_n0031: Chinese cabbage needs a fertile and well-drained soil.
pg090_n0032: It likes soil that can hold water well.
pg090_n0033: The best soil pH is between 5.5 and 7.6.
pg090_n0034: The cabbage grows well in temperatures of 15 - 22oC.
pg090_n0035: If it gets colder, the cabbage will start to flower and stop making leaves.
pg090_n0036: It grows best at heights of 500 – 1500 m above sea level.
pg090_n0037: When choosing a site, look for a sunny area with good drainage.
pg090_n0038: Make sure there is a reliable source of water for irrigation.
pg090_n0039: Avoid areas where water can gather and cause waterlogging.
pg090_n0043: To prepare the soil for Chinese cabbage, you start by digging it up.
pg090_n0044: Afterwards, you remove all the weeds and unwanted things.
pg090_n0045: You then smoothen the dug soil using a harrow or rake.
pg090_n0046: The next step is to add well-decomposed manure to the soil.
pg090_n0047: This manure can come from your farm animals or compost.
pg090_n0048: You should use about one bucket of 20 litres of manure for every square metre of soil.
pg090_n0053: The seeds should be clear, strong, and free from mould.
pg090_n0054: Seeds with spots, cracks, or discolouration should be avoided.
pg090_n0055: Larger seeds usually grow into stronger plants.
pg090_n0056: Choose the type that is mostly demanded
pg091_n0004: Chinese cabbage seeds can be sown directly in the seedbed.
pg091_n0005: They can also be sown first in a nursery and then transplanted to the seedbed.
pg091_n0006: An average of 5 – 6 kg of seeds (for direct sowing) and 1.2 – 1.7 kg (to be transplanted) can be sufficient per hectare.
pg091_n0009: Seeds of Chinese cabbage can be directly sown in the field using the dibbling method.
pg091_n0010: Place 2 - 3 seeds in each hole, 25 -35 cm apart between holes and 30 - 40 cm apart between rows.
pg091_n0011: This depends on the type of Chinese cabbage.
pg091_n0012: Keep the seedbed moist by watering.
pg091_n0013: When the seedlings are about 6 - 10 cm tall, thin them out to leave only one plant per hole.
pg091_n0014: Also, fill in gaps where seeds did not grow.
pg091_n0017: First, prepare your nursery bed well.
pg091_n0018: Drill shallow furrows about 25- 30 cm apart.
pg091_n0019: Sow seeds by drilling thinly and covering them with a thin layer of soil.
pg091_n0020: Water the nursery lightly and cover it with dry grass mulch to keep the soil moist.
pg091_n0022: Once the seedlings start to grow, remove the grass cover.
pg091_n0023: Place a partial shade about 60 - 100 cm high to protect the seedlings from strong sunlight and heavy rain.
pg091_n0024: It is recommended to grow seedlings in trays as this helps to reduce shock to the plants during transplanting.
pg091_n0025: Transplanting seedlings from ordinary nurseries with bare roots can cause transplanting shock.

pg092_n0005: Seedlings are moved from the soil nurseries or seedling trays to a permanent seedbed when they are 3 - 4 weeks old, about 6 - 10 cm tall and have 4 true leaves.
pg092_n0006: Before moving, seedlings should be hardened off.
pg092_n0007: This is done by reducing watering and shade at the nursery a few days before taking them to the main field.
pg092_n0008: Seedlings should be planted 25 - 35 cm apart in a row and 30 - 40 cm apart between rows.
pg092_n0009: To help with this, use a long, straight wooden pole or marked rope to mark the spaces.
pg092_n0010: It is advisable to transplant seedlings when the weather is cool.
pg092_n0011: This helps to reduce transplanting shock.
pg092_n0012: Also, water the plants a little bit, but not too much after transplanting.
pg092_n0013: Too much water can cause diseases such as damping off and root rot.
pg092_n0017: Under normal conditions, you need to water the crop plants about 2 to 3 days per week.
pg092_n0018: But you need to think about the soil type, weather situations, and the plant’s age.
pg092_n0019: You can use drip, sprinkler, watering can or furrow methods to water the plants.
pg092_n0023: For the crop to grow well, nitrogenous fertilisers, for example, CAN should be used at least three times.
pg092_n0024: The first application should be two weeks after the plants are in the field.
pg092_n0025: The other two applications should be two weeks apart.
pg092_n0026: For each plant, one tablespoon of fertiliser is enough.
pg092_n0030: You should keep the fields free from weeds throughout the growing season.
pg092_n0031: We use different methods to manage weeds.
pg092_n0032: These include applying mulch, pulling weeds by hand, and hoeing by hand.
pg092_n0033: It is advisable to manage weeds early when they are small and easy to pull out.
pg092_n0034: This is before the plant canopy, or the top part of the plant shades the space between the plants.
pg092_n0035: As the plants grow, they cover the space between them.
pg092_n0036: This covering stops weeds from growing.
pg093_n0004: This helps to keep the field clean and healthy for the crop plants.
pg093_n0006: Management of insect pests and diseases
pg093_n0008: Insects and diseases in Chinese cabbage can cause serious damage.
pg093_n0009: The common insect pests and diseases and their management practices are presented in Figures 6.3 to 6.8 and 6.9 to 6.10 respectively.
pg093_n0014: What they do: Feed on leaves.
pg093_n0015: How to know them: Look for mines on leaves (refer to Figure 6.3).
pg093_n0016: How to manage them: Rotate crops and use bio-based pesticides.
pg093_im002: Leaf miner maggots feeding inside a leaf, leaving winding pale tunnels.
pg093_n0018: Figure 6.3: Maggots of leaf miners feeding on a leaf
pg093_n0023: What they do: Suck sap from leaves.
pg093_n0024: How to know them: Look for flies that leave honeydew on leaves (refer to Figure 6.4).
pg093_n0025: How to manage them: Pick them up, encourage natural enemies, and use recommended insecticides.
pg093_im003: Whitefly resting on a green leaf.
pg093_n0032: What they do: Feed on leaves.
pg093_n0033: How to know them: Look for moth pupae and larvae on leaves (refer to Figure 6.5).
pg093_n0034: How to manage them: Use bio-pesticides and recommended insecticides.
pg093_im004: Diamondback moth caterpillars feeding on leaves with holes from damage.
pg093_n0036: Figure 6.5: DBM caterpillars feeding on leaves
pg094_n0005: What they do: Suck plant sap.
pg094_n0006: How to know them: Look for small soft-bodied insects on leaves and stalks (refer to Figure 6.6).
pg094_n0007: How to manage them: Encourage natural enemies and use recommended insecticides.
pg094_im002: Colonies of aphids clustered on the leaves and stem of a plant.
pg094_n0013: What they do: Feed on plant stem near the base.
pg094_n0014: How to know them: Check for plant stems that have been cut off near the base (refer to Figure 6.7).
pg094_n0015: How to manage them: Use bio-based pesticides
pg094_im003: A cutworm curled on the soil at the base of a young leafy plant.
pg094_n0021: What they do: Feed on plant leaves.
pg094_n0022: How to know them: Look for white hairs on beet armyworm eggs and larvae on plant leaves (refer to Figure 6.8).
pg094_n0023: How to manage them: Use recommended pesticides.
pg094_im004: Leaf damaged by beet armyworm, with chewed holes, scraped patches and black droppings.
pg094_n0025: Figure 6.8: Damage caused by beet armyworm
pg095_n0006: How to know it: Leaves show V-shaped lesions (refer to Figure 6.9).
pg095_n0007: How to manage it: Use disease-free seedlings, and rotate crops.

pg095_im003: Chinese cabbage plant severely affected by black rot, with yellowing, rotting leaves spreading from the base.
pg095_n0014: How to know it: Black or brown infected veins (refer to Figure 6.10).
pg095_n0015: How to manage it: Plant on raised beds, and avoid water logging.

pg095_n0035: Harvesting and postharvesting management of Chinese cabbage
pg095_n0037: Chinese cabbage takes 40-100 days to mature.
pg095_n0038: Non-headed types are ready to eat when the leaves are big enough.
pg095_n0039: How you harvest it depends on demand of the market.
pg095_n0040: Some markets want the very tender leaves inside, which requires to cut off the leaves at the base, above the soil.
pg095_n0041: For markets that want moderately tender
pg096_n0003: leaves, you carefully pick off the mature outer leaves, letting the inner leaves keep on growing.
pg096_n0004: Headed types are harvested when the leaves are tightly packed together.
pg096_n0005: You cut off the whole head at the soil level.
pg096_n0006: This is best when the leaves are strong and before the seed stalks start to grow, usually 50 - 100 days after planting.
pg096_n0008: Postharvest management of Chinese cabbage includes the following:
pg096_n0012: Cleaning: Clean the cabbage with clean and safe water before packaging.
pg096_n0013: Always wash your hands before and after handling Chinese cabbages.
pg096_n0016: Packaging: Place harvested cabbages in clean containers.
pg096_n0020: Storing: Use cooling facilities which may include refrigerator, charcoal evaporative cooler or zero-energy cooling chamber for storage.
pg096_n0023: Sun drying: Dry cabbages by slicing and spreading in the sun.
pg096_n0024: Store dried cabbages in airtight containers or bags.
pg096_n0027: Marketing: Continue to identify more potential buyers in local markets.

pg098_n0009: In this chapter, you will learn how to grow bulb onions, from the start to selling them.
pg098_n0010: The competencies you develop will enable you to earn money and have onions for your meals.
pg098_n0013: “Offers a rewarding path to grow a resilient, high-demanding crop and essential to kitchens worldwide”
pg098_n0016: An onion is a type of bulb vegetable.
pg098_n0017: It has a short, underground stem with fleshy leaves at its base forming a bulb.
pg098_n0018: This bulb stores food for the onion plant.
pg098_n0019: Onion is usually a biennial crop, meaning that it takes two growing seasons to complete its lifecycle.
pg098_n0020: In the first season, a seed grows into a plant with leaves and a bulb.
pg098_n0021: Nutrients then build up in the bulb.
pg098_n0022: In the second season, plant grows from the bulb, and produces flowers, and then seeds.
pg098_n0023: Onion bulbs can be of different colours, such as red, white, and yellow.
pg098_n0024: This is shown in Figures 7.1 (a) to (d).
pg098_im003: Red onions with roots and green leaves attached
pg098_im004: Purple onions growing in the field with bulbs partly above the soil
pg098_im005: White onions growing in neat rows in a field
pg098_im006: Yellow onions growing in the soil with green tops
pg099_n0003: Bulb onions are very popular and they are eaten as most spices do.
pg099_n0004: This means you can add them to your meals to make them taste better.
pg099_n0005: Onions are also full of nutrients that are good for our bodies.
pg099_n0006: They contain minerals such as calcium, iron, and potassium.
pg099_n0007: These minerals help our bodies use other foods well and work properly.
pg099_n0008: Onions also have vitamins B6, B9, and E.
pg099_n0009: These vitamins also help our bodies to use other foods well and work properly.
pg099_n0010: Therefore, not only do onions taste good, but they are also good for our health.
pg099_n0014: Growing onions is one of the ways to earn money.
pg099_n0015: This is how you can do it well.
pg099_n0016: Choose where you will grow your onions.
pg099_n0017: If it is a big area, make sure you have enough water and labour force.
pg099_n0018: Think about how to get your soil ready for planting, look after it, and keep it healthy.
pg099_n0019: Decide if you will hire people to help you in the weeding or if you will use herbicides to kill weeds.
pg099_n0020: Also, plan how to deal with other onion pests and diseases if they occur.
pg099_n0022: Before you start producing onions, it is important to know what types of onions people prefer.
pg099_n0023: This is why you need to do a market survey.
pg099_n0024: Go to the marketplaces and see what and how much people are buying.
pg099_n0025: This will help you decide what type of onions to grow, how much to grow, when to grow and how to get the best prices.
pg099_n0026: Finally, think about where and how you will store your onions if the market is not good during harvesting, and you need to wait for better prices.
pg099_n0027: Growing onions can be very rewarding if you plan well to make your onion business successful.
pg099_n0031: Use the internet or a library to find out about:
pg099_n0034: (a) Different types of onions that are commonly grown in Tanzania;
pg099_n0036: (b) How onion is grown, cared for, harvested, processed, and marketed; and
pg099_n0040: Go to your school garden or a nearby onion farm.
pg099_n0041: Learn from the gardener how onion is grown, taken care of, harvested, processed, and sold.
pg099_n0043: Write down the lessons you have learnt from the tasks 1 and 2 above.
pg099_n0047: This section will guide you through the process of growing onions.
pg099_n0048: We will start by choosing the best site for onion production.
pg099_n0049: Then we will prepare the seedbed, select the right onion variety, raise seedlings at the nursery and transplant the seedlings.
pg099_n0050: We will also learn how to manage water, and nutrients, and deal with weeds, insect pests and diseases.
pg099_n0051: Remember that successful farming is all about careful planning and regular work effort.
pg100_n0003: Choosing a site for onion production
pg100_n0005: We need to think about the type of soil, its pH level, altitude of the place, amount of rainfall and temperature requirement.
pg100_n0006: Good conditions can make big and healthy onions.
pg100_n0007: Onions can grow in many soil types, but they like loamy soil that drains well and has a good amount of organic matter.
pg100_n0008: The soil pH should be between 5.5 and 6.8.
pg100_n0009: The place should be at an altitude of 0 - 1900 m above sea level.
pg100_n0010: A rainfall of 500 - 700 mm per year is good, but most onions are grown under irrigation.
pg100_n0011: The best temperature for onions is between 15 and 25 degrees Celsius.
pg100_n0012: Higher temperatures can make the onions form bulbs faster, but the bulbs get smaller.
pg100_n0013: Lower temperatures can make the onions start to form flowers earlier instead of bulbs in the first growing season.
pg100_n0017: Onions on a small scale can be grown in different seedbeds including improvised beds.
pg100_n0018: These can be made from materials such as used containers, tyres, sacks, polythene bags and pots filled with soil or other growing media.
pg100_n0019: For large-scale production, onions are grown in open fields or greenhouses.
pg100_n0021: To prepare seedbeds in an open field, follow these steps:
pg100_n0025: Dig the soil at least 25 - 30 cm deep.
pg100_n0026: Then smoothen and level it to create a fine soil.
pg100_n0029: Make seedbeds based on the season, type of irrigation and field condition.
pg100_n0032: Add about 25 - 40 tons of manure or compost per hectare (equivalent to 20 kg/m²) during land preparation.
pg100_n0035: Spread about 20 g/m² of inorganic fertiliser such as Di-Ammonia Phosphate (DAP) or Triple Sulphate Phosphate (TSP).
pg100_n0036: For a small seedbed, measure its area.
pg100_n0037: Then work out how much to use on that bed.
pg100_n0039: Remember, these steps are for open fields.
pg100_n0040: If you are using improvised seedbeds, you may need to adjust the steps based on the materials you have.
pg100_n0041: For example, you may need to add more soil if you are using containers or pots, or you may need to use different types of compost or manure.
pg100_n0042: Always try to use what you have and what is available in your area.
pg100_n0044: Selection of seed variety and planting of onion
pg100_n0046: Onions come in many different varieties.
pg100_n0047: Some are hybrids, others are not.
pg100_n0048: Some of these varieties are presented in Table 7.1.
pg100_n0050: New types of onions are always being developed.
pg100_n0051: Keep learning about new varieties of onions that you can grow.
pg101_n0003: Table 7.1: Some common bulb onion varieties
pg101_n0016: Small to medium-sized, round, purple-red, strong taste
pg101_n0018: 150 days, up to 39,500 kg per hectare
pg101_n0023: Big, round, red, very strong taste
pg101_n0025: 150 days, up to 39,500 kg per hectare
pg101_n0030: Big, round, dark red, can resist diseases
pg101_n0032: 110 - 120 days, up to 61,800 kg per hectare
pg101_n0039: 90 - 100 days, up to 62,000 kg per hectare

pg101_n0055: When choosing which onion to grow, think about these factors:
pg101_n0059: Disease resistance: Some onion varieties are more resistant to diseases than others.
pg101_n0060: It is advisable to choose a disease-resistant variety to ensure a healthy crop.
pg101_n0063: Market demand: Consider the preferences of your potential customers.
pg101_n0064: In Tanzania, onions are commonly used in various dishes, so varieties that are flavourful and have a longer shelf life are often more popular.
pg101_n0067: Growth duration: The time taken for an onion variety to mature can influence your choice.
pg101_n0068: If you want a quicker harvest, choose a variety that matures early.
pg101_n0069: Always find out more and ask local crop extension workers or experienced onion farmers for advice.
pg101_n0070: This will help you decide on the best onion variety to grow.
pg101_n0074: Onion seeds are usually not sown directly in the field.
pg101_n0075: We use nursery beds, which can be raised, sunken or flat.
pg101_n0076: These beds should be levelled to prevent water from gathering in one place.
pg101_n0077: If water gathers and stays, it can create a good environment for the development of fungal diseases.
pg101_n0078: The amount of seed used is between 5 - 7 kg per hectare.
pg101_n0079: This depends on the space between plants and the variety of onions
pg102_n0004: It is advisable to ask seed sellers or local crop extension workers about the best time to sow and the amount of seed to use.
pg102_n0005: The following are the steps to grow onion seedlings in the nursery:
pg102_n0009: Drill lines 15 – 20 cm apart and 1- 1.5 cm deep across the nursery bed.
pg102_n0012: Put seeds in the lines thinly.
pg102_n0013: Cover them lightly with a fine soil.
pg102_n0016: Spread light dry grass mulch on top.
pg102_n0019: Water lightly to avoid too much moisture.
pg102_n0020: Too much water can make it easier for the ‘damping off’ disease to develop.
pg102_n0023: The seeds start to grow after 5 - 10 days.
pg102_n0024: After this time, remove the mulch.
pg102_n0025: If you delay this step, the seedlings will become too thin and slender.
pg102_n0028: Water when needed to keep the soil moist for the seedlings.
pg102_n0031: Put up shade that is about 1 m high to protect seedlings from strong sunlight.
pg102_n0034: Check the plants often and deal with any pest or disease problems.
pg102_n0035: Checking and controlling the ‘damping-off’ disease and cutworms are very important at this stage.
pg102_n0039: Transplanting should be in the cool part of the day.
pg102_n0040: Plant the seedlings after 35 to 50 days or when they have 3 - 5 leaves and the stem is like a pencil thickness.
pg102_n0042: For easy field management, divide the field into plots and water them before transplanting.
pg102_n0043: Before transplanting, water the nursery full 2 hours before to make it easier to uproot the seedlings.
pg102_n0044: When planting, put the seedlings 15 - 20 cm from one row to another and 7 - 10 cm from one seedling to another in the rows.
pg102_n0046: After transplanting, water the seedlings moret often until they are well established.
pg102_n0048: The way you plant can change based on the type of onion and what people want in the market.
pg102_n0049: Also, you can use tools such as dibblers to help plant at the right distance.
pg102_n0050: Figure 7.2 shows examples of transplanting dibblers.

pg103_im002: Rectangular transplanting dibbler on a prepared bed, used to make evenly spaced holes for seedlings.
pg103_im003: Farmer pushing a wheeled transplanting dibbler along a seedbed to make evenly spaced planting holes beside vegetable rows.
pg103_n0007: Onions need to be watered regularly.
pg103_n0008: They need more water as they grow and less as they get older.
pg103_n0009: The watering should stop 10 – 15 days before you plan to harvest the onions.
pg103_n0010: There are different ways to water onions, including furrow irrigation and modern methods such as drip irrigation.
pg103_n0014: In addition to organic manure incorporated during land preparation, inorganic fertiliser is also needed.
pg103_n0015: You need to add 180 kg of Nitrogen per hectare at different times; 60 kg before planting, 60 kg at the leaf stage, and 60 kg at the 4th week.
pg103_n0016: Too much nitrogen can be bad.
pg103_n0017: If you add too much nitrogen at late times, the onion leaves will grow too quickly affecting the onion from forming bulbs properly.
pg103_n0018: Likewise, apply 170 kg of potassium per hectare.
pg103_n0019: Before transplanting, add 110 kg of potassium then 60 kg of potassium 7 - 8 weeks before you harvest.
pg103_n0020: Your teacher and a local agricultural extension worker can assist you in determining the recommended type and amount of fertilisers.
pg103_n0022: Managing weed pests in onion fields
pg103_n0024: Onion plants cannot compete with weeds for space, water, and nutrients.
pg103_n0025: Use a special type of herbicide to kill perennial weeds before you start preparing the land or before planting.
pg103_n0026: Use another type of herbicide immediately after transplanting.
pg103_n0027: It is not recommended to use a hand hoe at this stage as it can hurt the onions.
pg103_n0028: If possible, cover the soil with mulch.
pg103_n0029: This can stop weeds from growing.
pg103_n0030: You can use leaves or straw for mulching.
pg103_n0031: Combine different methods to control weeds.
pg103_n0032: Don’t rely on just one method.
pg103_n0033: You can ask local crop extension workers or agricultural input suppliers for advice.
pg103_n0034: They can advise you on the best method to use.
pg103_n0035: Keeping the field free from weeds is important for growing healthy onion plants.
pg104_n0003: Managing other pests and diseases in onions
pg104_n0005: Onions are commonly attacked by thrips, onion maggots and nematodes.
pg104_n0006: They are also affected by diseases such as purple blotch, onion bacterial soft rot, downy mildew and onion black mould.
pg104_n0011: What they do: Suck the juice from plants.
pg104_n0012: How to know them: You can see leaves that are shiny and have spots (refer to Figure 7.3).
pg104_n0013: How to manage them: Rotate the type of crop you grow, and use recommended pesticides.
pg104_im002: Onion leaves damaged by thrips, showing silvery shiny streaks and small spots.
pg104_n0015: Figure 7.3: Bollworm fruit damage & an adult moth
pg104_n0020: What they do: Eat the side roots of onion plants.
pg104_n0021: How to know them: You can see small white worms, affected plants that look like they are shrinking or dying (refer to Figure 7.4)
pg104_n0022: How to manage them: Change the type of crop, use manure or compost, and clean the field.
pg104_im003: Onion plant attacked by maggots, with small white larvae feeding around the base in the soil.
pg104_n0024: Figure 7.4: Plant attacked by onion maggots
pg104_n0029: What they do: Attack the roots or stems of onion plants.
pg104_n0030: How to know them: You can see plants with deformed roots or stems, and some tiny balls in the soil (refer to Figure 7.5).
pg104_n0031: How to manage them: Use special pesticides during farm preparation.

pg104_im004_seg002_v1: Deformed onion plants with twisted, stunted leaves caused by nematode infestation.

pg105_n0006: How you know it: Small white spots on leaves become large purple blotches (refer to Figure 7.6).
pg105_n0008: How to manage it: Use resistant varieties.
pg105_im002_seg001_v1_crop_v1: Onion leaves with elongated purple-brown blotches caused by purple blotch disease.
pg105_im002_seg002_v1_crop_v1: Onion leaves showing sunken purple blotch lesions and drying at the tips.
pg105_n0022: How to know it: Bulb softens and water-soaks (refer to Figure 7.7).
pg105_n0024: How to manage it: Avoid overhead irrigation when onions form bulbs.
pg105_n0025: Don’t let irrigation water touch leaves.
pg105_im003_seg001_v1_crop_v1: Rotting onion bulb with dark soft decay caused by bacterial soft rot.
pg105_im003_seg002_v1_crop_v1: Cut onion bulbs with watery softened inner layers showing bacterial soft rot.
pg105_n0033: How to know it: Leaves turn pale green, then yellow and die.
pg105_n0034: Look for grey to purplish mounds on leaves (refer to Figure 7.8).
pg105_n0036: How to manage it: Use resistant varieties, start with high-quality seeds, space plants properly, avoid overwatering, use recommended fungicides, rotate crops, and do thorough field cleaning at the end of the season.

pg106_n0006: How to know it: Small black spore masses on leaves (refer to Figure 7.9).
pg106_n0007: How to manage it: Handle bulbs carefully to avoid bruising.

pg106_n0031: Harvesting and postharvesting management of onion
pg106_n0033: Onions are ready for harvesting after 90 - 150 days, depending on the variety of onions.
pg106_n0034: Alternatively, we can start harvesting when 50 - 75% of the onions have bent their necks.
pg106_n0035: We can uproot the onions by hand or using equipment like a fork or other advanced equipment such as a harvester.
pg106_n0036: If we do it by hand, we water the area first to soften the soil before pulling out the onions.
pg106_n0037: Then, we lay them flat on the top of the beds with their roots up.
pg106_n0041: After harvesting, we have to perform some practices to keep the onions good for a long period.
pg107_n0004: This is when we dry the parts of the onions that are above the soil.
pg107_n0005: This helps to keep the onions fresh for longer.
pg107_n0006: We can do this in the field or a special place if the weather is bad.
pg107_n0009: The moisture on the onions should be reduced from about 86% to about 12%.
pg107_n0010: In reducing it, use a process called ‘casing’.
pg107_n0011: Cover the onions with straw or leaves to create a pile.
pg107_n0012: Turn the pile regularly to let air circulate.
pg107_n0013: This takes a few days to a few weeks, depending on the weather and the size of the crop.
pg107_n0014: As the moisture decreases, the onions become harder and their smell changes.
pg107_n0015: They also start to brown at the top, a sign that the moisture has been reduced.
pg107_n0018: After the onions have been cured and dried, we sort and grade them.
pg107_n0019: This is done to separate the onions based on their size, shape, and quality.
pg107_n0020: This is to ensure easy packaging ready for marketing.
pg107_n0023: Keep the onions in a cool place with a temperature of 25 - 35ºC.
pg107_n0024: The air should be dry with a humidity of 65 - 70%.
pg107_n0025: Onions are usually put in mesh bags.
pg107_n0026: They can also be put in smaller bags for consumers.
pg107_n0027: The onions need to be kept in a cool, dry place until they reach the consumers.
pg107_n0030: Once the onions are ready, they need to be sold or stored until the price in the market is high.
pg107_n0031: You should use several ways to sell your onions for a good price and make a good income.
pg107_n0032: These are some of the ways you can use to market your onions:
pg107_n0036: You can sell your onions directly at your farm.
pg107_n0037: This could be to local people who want fresh onions or to restaurants and hotels that need onions for their dishes.
pg107_n0040: If the price of onions is low in the market, you can store your onions and sell them when the price is higher.
pg107_n0043: You can use social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter to sell your onions.
pg107_n0044: You can post pictures of your onions and their price.
pg107_n0045: You can also share stories about how you grow your onions.
pg107_n0048: Food influencers are people who have many followers on social media.
pg107_n0049: They can help you by sharing your opinions with their followers.
pg107_n0050: For example, they can post pictures of your onions and recommend them to their followers.
pg108_n0003: (e) Collecting email addresses: You can collect email addresses from people who visit your farm or your social media pages.
pg108_n0004: Once you have these addresses, you can send them newsletters with updates about your farm and your onions.
pg108_n0006: (f) Using data analysis: By looking at the data from your social media pages, you can learn more about what people want and how to sell more onions.
pg108_n0008: (g) Setting a price: Based on the quality of the onions, how big they are, or the price of onions in the market, you have to decide earlier the price for which you will sell your onions.

pg110_n0015: Tomato is a fruit vegetable that can grow all year round.

pg110_n0017: Tomato is full of vitamins A, B, and C.
pg110_n0018: It also has minerals such as iron and phosphorus.
pg110_n0019: Moreover, it has a special ingredient called lycopene.
pg110_n0020: This helps to protect our bodies from certain diseases, for example, heart diseases and cancers.

pg111_n0006: They stop growing taller when they start to produce fruit.

pg113_n0013: Ecological requirements and site selection for tomato production
pg113_n0015: Tomatoes grow in the soil that is well-drained, such as sandy loamy or clay loamy rich in organic matter.
pg113_n0016: The soil should be slightly acidic with a pH between 5.5 and 6.5.
pg113_n0018: They grow well between 20 - 25°C in the day and 15 - 17°C at night.
pg113_n0019: Temperatures above 35°C or below 10°C can harm the plant.
pg113_n0020: Tomatoes need more than 600 mm of rainfall in a growing season.
pg113_n0021: Too much rain can cause leaf diseases.
pg113_n0022: Also, irregular watering can damage the tomato fruits.
pg113_n0023: Tomato needs at least 6 hours of direct sunlight during flowering.
pg113_n0024: Too much sunlight can cause damage to the fruits.
pg113_n0025: To choose a good place to grow tomatoes, you should look for a place that gets at least 6 hours of direct sunlight each day.
pg113_n0029: Tomatoes can be grown both outdoors and indoors.
pg113_n0030: They can be grown in soil or soilless growing media.
pg113_n0031: The following are the steps to prepare land for growing tomatoes:
pg113_n0035: Mark out the land for growing tomatoes.
pg113_n0036: The area can be measured in acres, hectares or square metres;
pg113_n0039: Clear the land and remove any rubbish;
pg113_n0042: Plough the land to a depth of 20 - 25 cm;
pg113_n0045: Harrow the land to break up big lumps of soil; then,
pg113_n0049: Choose the type of seedbed based on the way of watering, management practices and the season.

pg113_n0053: Tomato seeds are of different varieties.
pg113_n0054: Some are hybrids and others are open-pollinated varieties.

pg113_n0056: But remember, these are just a few.
pg113_n0057: Scientists are always developing new varieties of tomatoes.
pg113_n0058: Keep exploring to find new varieties of tomatoes that are doing much better in your area.

pg115_n0003: Nursery preparation for tomato seedling production
pg115_n0005: You can grow tomato seedlings in two ways: on trays or in the soil.
pg115_n0007: Procedures for growing on a tray
pg115_n0011: Choose trays with cells, for example, 105, 128 or 200;
pg115_n0014: Fill the trays with soil such as compost or peat moss;
pg115_n0017: Put one seed in the middle of each cell, half a centimetre deep;
pg115_n0020: Cover the seed with soil, but not too much;
pg115_n0023: Keep the trays safe, away from the sun and rain; then,
pg115_n0026: Water them with a sprayer to keep the soil moist.
pg115_n0028: After 20 to 30 days, your seedlings are ready to move.
pg115_n0034: Make a seed bed 50 to 100 cm wide, 15 to 20 cm length;
pg115_n0037: Add a well-decomposed manure to the soil;
pg115_n0040: Clean the soil with dry grasses and straws, or chemicals;
pg115_n0043: Water the soil, but not too much;
pg115_n0046: Make rows in the soil 15 to 20 cm apart;
pg115_n0049: Put seeds in the rows, and cover them with soil;
pg115_n0052: Cover the seeds with dry grass mulch, and lightly water them;
pg115_n0055: Remove the grass after 5 to 7 days when the seeds have germinated;
pg115_n0058: Protect the seedlings by putting an overhead shade; then,
pg115_n0061: Water them as needed, remove weeds, and control pests.
pg115_n0063: After 20 to 30 days, you can move the seedlings to the main field.
pg115_n0067: Seedlings are ready to be moved to the main field at about 20 to 30 days from sowing (around 12 - 20 cm tall).
pg115_n0068: Before transplanting, seedlings need to be hardened for a week by less watering.
pg115_n0069: This helps them to be strong when they are moved.
pg115_n0071: The following are some important practices to follow when transplanting the seedlings:
pg115_n0075: Make holes about 10 cm deep and diameter.
pg115_n0076: Then, transfer each seedling with its soil from the nursery into these holes and cover them firmly with soil;
pg115_n0079: If you are transplanting seedlings in raised or flatbeds, transplant them 60 - 90 cm apart in the row (between the rows) and 50 - 60 cm apart in the same row (between the plants);
pg115_n0082: If you are growing seedlings using drip irrigation, transplant them at 120 - 150 cm apart in the row (between the rows) and 30 - 50 cm apart in the same row (between the plants);
pg116_n0005: If you are growing seedlings using drip irrigation and they are indeterminate varieties, transplant them 150 cm apart in the row (between the rows) and 50 cm apart in the same row (between the plants);
pg116_n0008: After moving the seedlings, water them immediately.
pg116_n0009: The amount and frequency of watering depend on the moisture of the soil;
pg116_n0012: To keep the appropriate number of plants in the field, replace dead plants (gap filling) 10 days after transplanting them.
pg116_n0014: It is better to transplant seedlings prepared in a ground nursery early in the morning, evening, or on a cloudy day.
pg116_n0015: This helps to reduce the shock when they are transplanted.
pg116_n0016: Seedlings prepared on trays can be transplanted at any time.
pg116_n0018: Management of water for tomato plants
pg116_n0020: Tomatoes need sufficient water to grow properly.
pg116_n0021: The more they grow, the more water they need.
pg116_n0022: This is especially true after they are transplanted from their pot to the garden, and when they are flowering and making fruits.
pg116_n0023: The best times to irrigate tomatoes depend on the season.
pg116_n0024: In the dry season, plants can be irrigated 3 to 4 times a week.
pg116_n0025: In wet season, you can water them less often.
pg116_n0026: You can irrigate tomatoes in different ways including furrow and drip irrigation.
pg116_n0027: You can also water just the base of the plant with a bucket or hose pipe.
pg116_n0028: Remember, it is important to water tomatoes, but too much water can also harm them.
pg116_n0029: Therefore, it is advisable to irrigate tomatoes when the soil is dry.
pg116_n0031: Management of nutrients for tomato plants
pg116_n0033: There are two main sources of nutrients you can use to help tomatoes grow well.
pg116_n0034: The first is organic manures, for example, farmyard and compost manure.
pg116_n0035: The second is chemical or industrial fertilisers.
pg116_n0036: If you only use organic manure, you should apply about 12 - 25 tons per hectare per cropping season.
pg116_n0037: For high-yield tomato varieties, you should apply 100 - 150 kg/ha of nitrogen, 65 - 110 kg/ha of phosphate and 160 - 240 kg/ha of potash.
pg116_n0039: Industrial fertilisers should be applied at a range between 40 - 120 kg/ha of nitrogen, 30 – 90 kg/ha of phosphate, and 30 - 90 kg/ha of potash.
pg116_n0040: When applying industrial fertilisers, be careful not to let them touch the young or wet plants, as this can burn them.
pg116_n0041: The way a tomato plant takes up nutrients depends on the type of fertiliser and how it is applied.
pg116_n0042: You can apply it directly to the soil, about 10 cm away from the stem and 5 cm deep, using either the ring or dibbling method.
pg117_n0003: There are also foliar fertilisers, which are water-soluble and come in liquid or powder form.
pg117_n0004: They contain different macro and micronutrients and they are applied to the leaves, where they are absorbed.
pg117_n0005: It is also very important to ask a local extension worker or a competent registered agro dealer about the right amount and the best way to apply fertilisers.
pg117_n0011: One week after transplanting: Use a complete NPK fertiliser high in phosphorus e.g., 10:40:10 at the manufacturer’s recommended rate.
pg117_n0012: Repeat once in the 3rd week after transplanting;
pg117_n0015: When new leaves appear (2-3 weeks after transplanting): Use an NPK fertiliser high in nitrogen e.g., 20:10:10 at the manufacturer’s recommended rate;
pg117_n0018: When flowers form (4-6 weeks after transplanting): Use a complete NPK fertiliser according to the manufacturer’s recommendation to promote flowering and fruit development.
pg117_n0019: A tomato plant can continue to flower and fruit for 3-4 months.
pg117_n0023: Trellising is a practice of supporting tomato plants using lines held by posts at definite spacing.
pg117_n0024: Posts of approximately 3 m long are placed at an interval of 1.5-2m apart (refer to Figure 8.3 (a)).
pg117_n0025: This is good for indeterminate tomato varieties.
pg117_n0026: Staking is the practice of providing support to tomato plants using poles of wood or metal rods.
pg117_n0027: The stake is placed firmly 15 cm beside the growing plant and the plant is tied to it in stages as it grows (refer to Figure 8.3 (b)).
pg117_n0028: This is suitable for semi-determinate tomato varieties.
pg117_n0029: Trellising and staking aim at keeping plants and fruits firmly off the ground.
pg117_n0030: A combination of poles and ropes to support tomato plants from the sides is also used (refer to Figure 8.3 (c)).
pg117_n0031: Trellising and staking in tomatoes reduce losses from fruit rots when fruits touch the soil and from sunburn when fruits are not shaded by foliage.
pg117_im002: Tomato plants in a field supported on a trellis made of wooden posts and hanging strings.
pg117_im003: A tomato plant tied to a wooden stake, with flowers and ripening fruits supported upright.
pg118_im002: Tomato plants supported by vertical poles and several horizontal ropes used for trellising.
pg118_n0003: Figure 8.3 (c): Combination of poles and ropes to support tomato plants
pg118_n0009: It stops plants from touching the ground.
pg118_n0010: This makes it harder for diseases to spread from the soil to the plants;
pg118_n0013: It lets plants grow upwards, using more vertical space.
pg118_n0014: This helps to make more crops in a small area;
pg118_n0017: It helps to let more air and sunlight reach the plants.
pg118_n0018: This keeps the leaves dry and less likely to get diseases; and
pg118_n0021: It keeps plants away from the pathways.
pg118_n0022: This makes it easier to do farm work such as harvesting.
pg118_n0026: Pruning is a way to help tomato plants grow better.
pg118_n0027: It is important for indeterminate tomato plants.
pg118_n0028: By pruning, we divert nutrients for making tomatoes instead of extra branches.
pg118_n0029: This makes the tomatoes grow faster and bigger.
pg118_n0030: Pruning also helps to keep the plant healthy by letting in more air and reducing humidity.
pg118_n0031: You can do pruning by pinching off the extra branches or using a hand pruner (refer to Figures 8.4 (a) and (b)).
pg118_n0032: Remember, not all tomato plants need pruning.
pg118_n0033: Prunning is only applicable to indeterminate varieties.
pg118_n0034: For determinate and semi-determinate varieties, pruning is not necessary.
pg119_im002: Hand pinching off a side shoot from a tomato plant stem during pruning.
pg119_im003: Hand pruner cutting a side shoot from a tomato plant during pruning.
pg119_n0005: Figure 8.4 (b): Pruning using a hand pruner
pg119_n0009: Mulching is the practice of covering the soil with a layer of dry grass, straw or plant remains (refer to Figure 8.5).
pg119_n0010: Where grass straw is used it is advisable to make sure that the materials are free from seeds to prevent weed invasion.
pg119_n0011: Mulching helps to conserve soil moisture by preventing or reducing evaporation.
pg119_n0012: It also helps to reduce soil erosion and control weeds, particularly the ones with broad leaves.
pg119_n0013: Moreover, when mulch decomposes it adds organic matter to the soil.
pg119_im004: Tomato rows staked in the field with dry grass mulch covering the ground between plants.
pg119_im005: Young tomato plants growing in soil covered with dry grass mulch.
pg119_im006: Staked tomato plant surrounded by dry grass mulch in the garden.
pg119_n0015: Figure 8.5: Grass mulch in the tomato garden
pg119_n0019: Weeds should be controlled right away from the early stages of crop establishment because, at this stage, weeds can badly affect plant growth and it can result into low crop yields.
pg119_n0020: Measures for weed control should begin with correct land preparation together with cultural practices to control weeds such as manual hoeing, mulching
pg120_n0004: The following cultural practices can be integrated for effective weed management in tomatoes:
pg120_n0008: Deep tillage and exposing soil to sunlight before transplanting help to destroy the weed seeds;
pg120_n0011: Removal of any previous crop residues and using of sanitary practices to avoid introducing weed seeds;
pg120_n0014: Keeping the field weed-free for 4 – 5 weeks after transplanting to suppress weed competition and avoid low crop yield;
pg120_n0017: Regularly, practising hand weeding between plant rows;
pg120_n0020: Applying mulches which are free from weed seeds;
pg120_n0023: Planting different crops on a field each season and repeating the same crop after at least three growing seasons (crop rotation).
pg120_n0024: This practice interrupts life cycles of pathogens and pests of the crop.
pg120_n0026: Management of pests and diseases in tomatoes
pg120_n0028: Tomatoes can be harmed by several pests and diseases.
pg120_n0029: It is important to know what they are and how they harm the crop.
pg120_n0030: You also need to know how to deal with them.
pg120_n0031: The following are some of them.
pg120_n0036: What they do: Feed on tomato plants’ sap, causing leaf curling, yellowing and transmission of plant viruses.
pg120_n0038: How to identify them: Look for tiny, soft-bodied insects on the underside of leaves (refer to Figure 8.6).
pg120_n0040: How to manage them: Spray a solution of soap, cow or rabbit urine to affected plants; intercropping with other crops; use recommended pesticides.
pg120_im002: Aphids clustered on the underside of a tomato leaf.
pg120_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing on the vine.
pg121_n0006: What they do: Feed on the underside of tomato leaves, causing yellowing wilting and spread of viral diseases.
pg121_n0008: How to identify them: Look for tiny white insects that you can see on the underside of tomato leaves (refer to Figure 8.7).
pg121_n0010: How to manage them: Use a kerosene and soap spray, plant resistant cultivars with hairy leaves, encourage natural predators, and rotate crops.
pg121_im002: Underside of a tomato leaf covered with whiteflies.
pg121_n0012: Figure 8.7: Whiteflies on the underside of a tomato leaf
pg121_n0017: What they do: Larvae and caterpillars feed on tomato leaves and fruits.
pg121_n0019: How to identify them: Look for the larvae, caterpillars and the damaged leaves and fruits (refer to Figure 8.8).
pg121_n0021: How to manage them: Apply the recommended insecticides
pg121_im003: Green bollworm caterpillar feeding on and damaging a tomato fruit.
pg121_im004: Adult bollworm moth with pale brown triangular wings spread out.
pg121_n0023: Figure 8.8: Bollworm fruit damage & an adult moth
pg121_n0028: What they do: Attack tomatoes, causing white to yellow spots on leaves.
pg121_n0030: How to know them: Look for tiny white or yellow spots on leaves, check for small, red or orange mites under the leaves, notice if leaves turn yellow and fall off, and a thin white or yellow cobweb-like substance on the plant (refer to Figure 8.9).
pg121_n0032: How to manage them: Keep the field free from weeds, and use recommended pesticides.
pg121_im005: Tomato leaves damaged by spider mites and covered with fine web-like strands.
pg121_n0034: Figure 8.9: Tomato affected by spider mites
pg122_n0006: What they do: Feed on plant roots, causing swelling and deformation of the root.
pg122_n0007: How to identify them: Look for deformed roots and swollen roots (refer to Figure 8.10).
pg122_n0008: How to manage them: Plough soil several times to expose the worms to the sun.
pg122_n0009: Rotate the crop with other crops not belonging to the Solanaceae family.
pg122_im002: Tomato roots with swollen lumps and deformities caused by nematodes.
pg122_n0012: Figure 8.10: Tomato roots with lumps caused by nematodes
pg122_n0017: What they do: They cut stems of the newly emerged or transplanted plant at ground level.
pg122_n0018: How to identify them: They cut stems of the newly emerged or transplanted plant at ground level (refer to Figure 8.11).
pg122_n0019: How to manage them: Keep the field free from weeds, and use recommended insecticides.
pg122_im003: Cutworms on soil beside a tomato seedling cut at ground level.
pg122_n0021: Figure 8.11: Cutworms and affected tomato seedlings
pg122_n0026: How to identify it: Look for irregular spots on the top of the leaves (refer to Figure 8.12).
pg122_n0027: How to manage it: Keep your crops free from weeds, use recommended preventive fungicides, and maintain good cultural management of your crops.
pg122_im004: Tomato plant affected by late blight, with dried brown leaves and a rotting fruit.
pg122_n0029: Figure 8.12: Tomato affected by late blight
pg123_n0006: How to identify it: Look for yellowing that starts from the base of the stem and goes upwards (refer to Figure 8.13).
pg123_n0007: How to manage it: Keep your field free from weeds, avoid too much watering, and control insects and nematodes in the soil.
pg123_im002: Tomato plants with fusarium wilt, showing yellowing and wilting leaves from the lower stem upward while green fruits remain on the plant.
pg123_n0009: Figure 8.13: Tomato affected by fusarium wilt
pg123_n0014: It is caused by a deficiency of calcium.
pg123_n0015: How to identify it: Look for sunken, brownish-black spots on fruits (Figure 8.14).
pg123_n0016: How to manage it: Keep your plants well-watered, use mulches to reduce the amount of nitrogen fertiliser you apply, and supply your plants with enough calcium.
pg123_im003: Tomato fruits affected by blossom end rot, with dark sunken brownish-black patches at the blossom end.
pg123_n0018: Figure 8.14: Tomato fruits affected by blossom end rot
pg123_n0023: This is a physiological disorder in tomato fruits caused by over-exposure to hot and bright sunlight.
pg123_n0024: How to know it: Look for pale white or yellow patches on tomato fruits (refer to Figure 8.15).
pg123_n0025: How to manage it: Choose heat-tolerant varieties of tomatoes and supply your plants with balanced nutrients.
