pg124_n0041: Harvesting and postharvesting management of tomato
pg124_n0043: Tomato takes an average of 70 - 90 days to mature and become ready for harvesting depending on variety and climatic conditions.
pg124_n0044: Maturity indices of tomatoes include an increase in fruit size, a change in skin colour and an increase in juice and sugar content.
pg124_n0045: The main criterion is fruit colour change.
pg124_n0046: Depending on the market demand, tomatoes can be harvested at six different stages as shown in Figure 8.16.
pg125_im002: Stage I mature green tomato with the whole surface completely green.
pg125_im003: Mature green tomato, fully green all over.
pg125_im004_crop_v1: Turning tomato with green changing to yellow-orange as ripening begins.
pg125_n0015: It has a definite break in colour from green to tarnish-yellow
pg125_n0019: Some tomatoes show a change in colour from green to tarnish-yellow, pink, red or a combination of the colours
pg125_im005: Pink stage tomato with about one-third to over half of the fruit turning pink-red.
pg125_im006: Light red tomato with most of the surface ripened to pinkish red or red.
pg125_im007: Red ripe tomato with more than 90 percent of the surface fully red.
pg125_n0028: About 30%-60% of the tomatoes have changed to pink or red colour
pg125_n0032: 60%-90% of tomatoes have pinkish-red or red colour
pg125_n0036: More than 90% of the tomatoes have attained red colour
pg125_n0037: Figure 8.16: Different stages of tomato maturity and ripeness
pg125_n0039: Harvesting should be done in the morning or late evening to maintain their quality and extend shelf-life.
pg125_n0040: The fruits are removed from plants by gently twisting or rotating them from the stem without fruit stalk.
pg125_n0041: However, cherry tomatoes are harvested in bunches.
pg125_n0042: When harvesting, do not drop the fruits rather put the fruits gently in a harvesting container.
pg125_n0043: Postharvest management of tomatoes includes the following:
pg125_n0045: (a) Sorting: Do sorting and grading under shade, inorder to avoid the adverse effects of rain, heat and sunlight that can speed up tomato fruit spoilage.
pg125_n0047: (b) Packaging and transporting: Tomatoes are commonly packaged in bamboo, wooden, and plastic crates.
pg125_n0048: However, stackable plastic and wooden crates are best.
pg125_n0050: Lining the crates can prevent fruits from getting bruised, but may stop air from circulating.
pg125_n0051: Packaging helps to protect the tomatoes from pests, loss of moisture, and damage.
pg125_n0053: Transport tomatoes in covered, ventilated trucks.
pg126_n0003: (c) Storage: Store tomatoes at 12 - 15°C for best results.
pg126_n0004: You can store them in a charcoal cooler or zero-energy cooling chamber where temperatures are a bit higher than this.
pg126_n0005: You can store your tomatoes for 2 – 14 days.
pg126_n0007: (d) Marketing: You can sell tomatoes at the farm, local market, or even at distant markets.
pg126_n0008: Common sizes are 20-litre plastic buckets and crates.
pg126_n0009: At lower levels, 10-litre, 5-litre buckets, and bunches are popular.
pg126_n0010: Prices can change quickly, often within a week.
pg126_n0011: Generally, August to October are months with low tomato prices, while December to May are months with high prices in Tanzania.

pg127_n0015: The meaning and importance of poultry production
pg127_n0017: At your home, school or community, you may have seen various birds as shown in Figures 9.1 (a) - (f).
pg127_n0018: In the coming activity, you will explore various things about those birds as well as other birds which are not shown in the figures.

pg128_n0018: Poultry is a general term for domesticated birds.
pg128_n0019: It includes several species such as those shown in Figures 9.1 (a) to (f).
pg128_n0020: These are chicken or domestic fowl, turkey, duck, goose, guinea fowl, and pigeon, respectively.
pg128_n0021: Poultry production or farming is an enterprise that deals with keeping birds either for home consumption or for commercial purposes of either eggs or meat production.
pg128_n0022: Some poultry species such as peafowls, parrots and partridges can be kept for ornamental or game/sports purposes.
pg128_n0023: The poultry species shown in Figures 9.1 (a) to (f) can be kept for home use or business purposes.
pg128_n0027: Poultry are reared in different forms regarding the way they are confined or let free, get fed, and how their produce is collected or harvested.
pg128_n0032: Pay a visit to the school poultry unit and nearby poultry farms.
pg128_n0034: Observe and enquire about the ways used to: (a) confine the birds, (b) give the birds feed and water, (c) harvest the produce from the birds, and (d) record production and sales (both digital and manual).
pg128_n0036: Summarise your findings and the lessons you have learnt in this activity in your portfolio.
pg128_n0038: The selection of a given system for poultry production depends on various factors such as the availability of land, type of poultry, climatic conditions, labour availability and amount of capital the farmer is able and willing to invest.
pg128_n0039: You will understand how these factors influence the selection of poultry production systems as you learn the respective systems.
pg128_n0040: There are three major systems for poultry production.
pg128_n0041: These are free-range systems, semi-intensive systems and intensive housing systems.
pg128_n0045: In this system, birds are left free during the day to search for food.
pg128_n0046: During the night, birds are locked inside a house to protect them from bad weather and predators.
pg129_n0003: system is suitable only where adequate land is available to ensure desired stocking density and to avoid overcrowding.
pg129_n0004: Fields or parts of fields or plots can be kept free from crops to allow birds to move freely from one plot to another in search of food.
pg129_n0005: Nearly 250 adult birds per hectare can be reared using this system.
pg129_n0006: Figure 9.2 shows an example of the free-range system of poultry production.
pg129_im002: Free-range poultry system with chickens scattered across a grassy field and poultry houses in the background.
pg129_n0008: Figure 9.2: Example of the free-range system of poultry production
pg129_n0011: A free-range system of poultry production is preferred for small-scale organic production of poultry meat and eggs.
pg129_n0012: With this system, housing costs and capital investment are low.
pg129_n0013: However, losses due to predatory animals can be high, wild birds may bring diseases unless proper care is taken, and scientific management practices may not be easily adopted.
pg129_n0015: To take care of poultry in a free-range system, it is recommended to do the following:
pg129_n0019: Secure night housing for the chicken.
pg129_n0020: The house is best built off the ground on slats to allow good ventilation and cooling;
pg129_n0023: Supplementary feeding in the evening is to be given to the chicken when they return to the house, for example, grains;
pg129_n0026: Laying birds must be provided with clean, dry dark places (nests) to lay their eggs.
pg129_n0027: There should be a ratio of one nest for five birds in the house and the dry
pg130_n0003: grass or other dry litter should be placed in the nests;
pg130_n0004: (d) Protect mother hens with their young chicks against predators, rain, coldness and wind by providing a box or shelter made of blocks on the ground; and
pg130_n0005: (e) Ensure that unproductive and old laying birds together with extra male birds should be culled.
pg130_n0009: In this system, birds are partly reared in houses and partly in fenced areas.
pg130_n0010: When it is practised in a permanent area, there should be a poultry house(s) followed by a run.
pg130_n0011: At night, birds are confined to houses and during the day, they are given access to runs.
pg130_n0012: The houses should be stationary and runs have to be fenced with wire mesh or any other suitable fencing materials that are locally available.
pg130_n0014: The runs have to be planted or provided with suitable forage to supply birds with green forage.
pg130_n0015: Fencing of the runs may also be designed in a way that allows rotational runs especially when forage is grown inside the run.
pg130_n0016: In this system, one hectare is estimated to accommodate an average rate of 750 birds.
pg130_n0017: With this system, scientific management operations can be applied to a certain extent and there is more economical use of land compared to a free-range system.
pg130_n0018: However, there is a high cost for fencing and the need for routine cleaning and removal of litter materials from the run.
pg130_n0019: Figure 9.3 shows an example of a poultry house and run.
pg130_im002: Wire-mesh poultry run in a semi-intensive system, with chickens feeding on grass inside a fenced enclosure and poultry houses behind.
pg130_n0021: Figure 9.3: Poultry house and run (semi-intensive system)
pg131_n0003: When runs are not permanent, they are not fenced then movable houses are preferably used.
pg131_n0004: Fold houses and coops are the common movable poultry houses.
pg131_n0005: Fold houses are small movable houses with a run attached to them.
pg131_n0007: To take care of poultry in a semi-intensive system, it is recommended to do the following:
pg131_n0011: The runs have to be rotated to give time for the grass to grow and allow for disease-causing organisms to die;
pg131_n0014: Nests should be supplied in the house for the birds to lay eggs;
pg131_n0017: Fresh feed and water must be supplied daily.
pg131_n0018: Feed and water containers must also be washed daily;
pg131_n0021: Programmes for vaccinating and deworming the birds should be followed;
pg131_n0024: Chicks can be kept in a special brooding box or a small area made for them (brooder).
pg131_n0028: In this system, birds are confined to houses either on the ground or on wire-netting floors in cages or slats.
pg131_n0029: This housing system is more efficient, convenient and economical for modern commercial poultry production.
pg131_n0030: It has three categories which are deep litter system, slatted floor system and cage or battery system.
pg131_n0031: These sub-divisions of the intensive poultry system are further elaborated here.
pg131_n0034: In this system, the floor of the house can be made of rough concrete or rammed earth.
pg131_n0035: It is then covered with dry litter materials up to the depth of about 8 cm in the broiler and 15 cm in the layers’ house.
pg131_n0036: However, for egg-laying birds, a 5 cm layer of litter material should be added every two weeks until it reaches the right depth.
pg131_n0037: The birds stay inside a house all the time.
pg131_n0038: Arrangements for feed, water, nests and perches are made inside the house.
pg131_n0039: Several litter materials such as rice husks, sawdust, old newspaper, wood shavings, chopped straw, dried leaves and crushed nutshells can be used depending on their cost and availability.
pg131_n0041: In the deep litter housing system, the welfare of birds is maintained to some extent.
pg131_n0042: The system also offer manure which is useful in crop production.
pg131_n0043: Bacterial and parasitic diseases may be a problem because of the direct contact between birds and litter.
pg131_n0044: Respiratory problems may also emerge due to dust from the litter.
pg131_n0045: Besides, the cost of litter may be an additional expenditure on production cost if it is not readily
pg132_n0002: available. Figure 9.4 shows an example of birds’ confinement in a deep system.
pg132_im002: Deep litter poultry house with many chickens confined on dry floor litter, with feeders, drinkers, nesting boxes and perches inside the shelter.
pg132_n0004: Figure 9.4: Example of deep litter system of confining birds
pg132_n0006: When poultry droppings pile up, they make the litter thick.
pg132_n0007: It is crucial to keep the litter dry.
pg132_n0008: Do this by mixing the litter regularly.
pg132_n0009: If the litter gets too wet, it can clump together.
pg132_n0010: This is not good for the poultry.
pg132_n0011: When the litter is wet, it can become a home for harmful micro-organisms.
pg132_n0012: So, keep stirring the litter often to break the build-up of these harmful micro-organisms.
pg132_n0013: If there are more chicken droppings than litter, add more fresh litter.
pg132_n0014: This helps to keep the litter dry and it reduces the build-up of ammonia, which is harmful to poultry.
pg132_n0015: When the litter gets more than 30 cm deep, remove it and bring in fresh litter.
pg132_n0016: Follow the procedures you have already learnt to bring in fresh litter.
pg132_n0019: In this system, birds are confined in a house with a slatted floor.
pg132_n0020: This floor can be made of iron rods, plastic or treated wooden poles, usually 0.6 - 1 m above the ground level to facilitate the fall of droppings through slats.
pg132_n0021: Wooden poles or iron rods can be used lengthwise of the house with interspaces of 2.5 cm between rods or poles.
pg132_n0022: The house should be roofed with water-proof material.
pg132_n0023: If the poultry pen is roofed with an iron roof, then it needs to put some insulation under the roof.
pg132_n0024: Feeding, watering and egg collection have to preferably be done from outside the house due to the size of this type of building.
pg132_n0025: Figure 9.5 shows a section of a slatted floor poultry system.
pg133_im002: Many chickens in a poultry house standing on a slatted floor system, with feeders and drinkers placed above the slats.
pg133_n0003: Figure 9.5: Example of slatted floor system
pg133_n0006: The slatted floor system for poultry is good.
pg133_n0007: It needs less space for each bird.
pg133_n0008: There is no need for bedding or litter.
pg133_n0009: It is easy to clean up droppings because they fall through the slats.
pg133_n0010: This system also helps to keep the house clean.
pg133_n0011: It stops parasites and diseases from spreading because birds don’t touch their droppings.
pg133_n0012: The system also allows a lot of ventilation into the house.
pg133_n0013: However, it is more expensive to start with, than regular solid floors.
pg133_n0014: It is hard to get feeds back if they fall through the slats.
pg133_n0015: The system also doesn’t let you use the building as much.
pg133_n0016: Flies can get in through the slats, making the fly problem worse.
pg133_n0020: This system is mainly used for commercial egg production.
pg133_n0021: In this system, poultry are confined in compartments surrounded by bars or wire.
pg133_n0023: The cage is large enough to permit limited movement and it allows a bird to stand and sit comfortably.
pg133_n0024: The cages are usually made up of strong galvanized wire and they can be fitted with stands on the floor of a house or hung from the roof.
pg133_n0025: The number of birds per cage varies from 1 to 4 depending on cage size, the size of the bird, and the farmer’s preference.
pg133_n0027: The cages are arranged into rows or layers called tiers.
pg133_n0029: The cage should have a sloping floor for easy rolling and collection of eggs.
pg134_n0003: drinkers are attached to cages from outside except nipple drinkers where a pipeline is installed through or above cages.
pg134_n0004: In medium-scale egg production, feeding and egg collection are done manually.
pg134_n0005: In large-scale poultry farms, auto-operated feeding trolleys and egg collection belts can be used.
pg134_n0006: Depending on the type of cages, the droppings are collected in trays fitted below the cages, on belts, on the floor or in deep pits under the cages.
pg134_n0007: Figure 9.6 shows a section of the cage system of a poultry house.
pg134_im002: Rows of laying hens kept in stacked wire cages inside a poultry house, with eggs rolling onto collection trays at the front.
pg134_n0009: Figure 9.6: Section of cage system of poultry house
pg134_n0012: Advantages of cage poultry housing system
pg134_n0019: There is no wastage of feed and space;
pg134_n0022: It is difficult for the birds to catch pathogens that will cause them infections;
pg134_n0025: Vices such as egg eating and pecking are minimal;
pg134_n0028: Sick birds can be easily identified and isolated for treatment;
pg134_n0031: Unproductive birds can be easily identified and culled;
pg134_n0034: Birds have more protection from internal parasites and soil-borne illnesses;
pg134_n0037: There is less cracking of eggs as the birds cannot perk on the eggs and the eggs are cleaner;
pg135_n0005: It is easy to collect eggs; and
pg135_n0010: Challenges of cage poultry housing system
pg135_n0014: It involves high initial investment costs;
pg135_n0017: Handling of manure may be a problem.
pg135_n0018: Generally, flies become a greater nuisance;
pg135_n0021: The laying birds may be subjected to an illness called cage layer fatigue.
pg135_n0022: The bird lies on its side giving the impression that it is affected by paralysis, hence named cage paralysis or cage layer fatigue.
pg135_n0023: It may be due to calcium and phosphorus deficiency;
pg135_n0026: Broilers reared in this housing system have high incidences of breast blisters especially when the weight is more than 1.5 kg; and
pg135_n0029: The incidence of blood spots in eggs is higher.
pg135_n0031: Note that there is a wide range of poultry species that may slightly differ in management.
pg135_n0032: The details for poultry production systems elaborated in the previous section are general and, in some cases, more applicable to chickens.
pg135_n0033: Depending on the poultry species to be produced, some modifications or additional facilities may be required, for example, a pond facility is required for housing waterfowls such as ducks and geese.
pg135_n0034: Therefore, advice should be sought from teachers, local extension workers or other poultry experts to practise particular poultry production systems properly.

pg135_n0048: Selection of a suitable poultry production system
pg135_n0050: Several people rear poultry in small, medium or large size of production by using one or a combination of the systems learnt.
pg135_n0051: Choosing a system which suits your needs is a task which involves making a thorough analysis of several aspects before choosing a particular system.

pg136_n0009: (a) Poultry species, purpose and level of production;

pg136_n0029: Incubation in poultry production is the process of providing suitable conditions for a fertile egg to hatch into a chick.
pg136_n0030: For the chick to develop, the egg must be kept under suitable conditions of temperature, humidity and ventilation.
pg136_n0031: Brooding refers to the special care given to chicks immediately after being hatched in order to ensure their health and survival.
pg136_n0032: Incubation and brooding in poultry can be done naturally by the female birds or artificially by a farmer through the use of artificial incubators and brooders.
pg136_n0033: In choosing or deciding the type of incubation and brooding suitable for your poultry farming enterprise, you will need to be well informed on the way how each operates.
pg136_n0034: You will also have to be informed of the advantages and disadvantages of each type of incubation and brooding.
pg136_n0035: The following are some of the important features of natural and artificial incubation and brooding.
pg136_n0039: In small-scale production, poultry incubate their eggs naturally by female birds sitting on them in the nests.
pg136_n0040: This keeps the eggs warm enough to hatch.
pg136_n0041: This is also called natural incubation.
pg136_n0042: Different species of poultry have different incubation periods or hatching times (refer to Table 9.1).
pg136_n0043: After hatching, natural brooding is done by female birds.
pg136_n0044: They provide warmth to chicks and protect them against predators.
pg136_n0045: There are some kinds of birds which are better brooders than others.
pg136_n0046: For successful natural incubation, it is important to find and use the birds which are good egg sitters.
pg136_n0047: The farmer should provide clean water and high-quality feeds to both female birds and chicks.
pg136_n0048: Table 9.1 shows incubation periods for different poultry species while Figures 9.7 (a) and (b) show natural incubation and brooding.
pg137_n0003: Table 9.1: Incubation periods for different poultry species
pg137_im002: Hen sitting on eggs in a straw nest during natural incubation.
pg137_im003: Mother bird brooding and caring for newly hatched chicks in a straw nest.
pg137_n0045: Advantages of natural incubation and brooding
pg137_n0049: The system does not require high costs for investment.
pg137_n0052: With suitable conditions, hatchability is higher than artificial incubation.
pg137_n0055: It applies to small-scale poultry breeders/home flocks.
pg137_n0060: Disadvantages of natural incubation and brooding
pg137_n0064: Possibility of disease infection and parasitic infestation is high.
pg137_n0067: Broody bird takes care of a small number of eggs.
pg137_n0070: Broody bird may die before hatching thus losing the whole batch.
pg137_n0073: Hatching may be poor due to an uncontrolled environment.
pg138_n0005: In commercial farms where a large number of birds are kept, incubation is done artificially by the use of egg incubators.
pg138_n0006: Their capacity ranges from 60 to a million eggs in one machine.
pg138_im002: Open egg incubator containing trays of eggs, with a temperature control panel on the left side.
pg138_n0016: A large number of chicks may be hatched at a time.
pg138_n0019: Sanitary measures are carried out easily.
pg138_n0022: Infertile eggs can be removed from the incubator at any stage of incubation.
pg138_n0031: There are high initial and running costs.
pg138_n0034: It requires skilled labour hence high labour cost.
pg138_n0037: There is a high possibility of egg contamination if the collection of eggs is from contaminated sources.
pg138_n0040: Production of chicks may stop completely due to the breakdown of machines especially where spare parts and technicians are not reliably available.
pg138_n0044: Where a large number of chicks are to be reared at once, artificial brooding is done.
pg138_n0045: This is done by keeping chicks in a structure called a brooder where feeds, water, and heat are provided.
pg138_n0046: Artificial brooding starts when chicks are one
pg139_n0003: day old and last at 4 to 6 weeks of age, depending on weather conditions.
pg139_n0004: However, chicks can be reared in the brooder for 6 - 9 days in hotter areas and 12 - 21 days in colder areas.
pg139_n0005: Most brooders should be round because corners encourage overcrowding.
pg139_n0006: A square brooder can also be used provided that the corners are made round by using plywood or boxes.
pg139_n0007: In large commercial poultry farming, the brooding house is expected to be at least 100 metres from other buildings on the farm.
pg139_n0008: Figure 9.9 shows chicks in brooder rings.
pg139_im002: Chicks crowded inside circular brooder rings with feeders, drinkers and hanging bulbs for warmth.
pg139_n0012: The following brooder temperatures have to be maintained: Day 1-2 (34 - 35°C); Day 3 - 4 (32 - 33°C); Day 5 - 6 (30 - 31°C); Day 7 (29 - 30°C); and Day 8 onwards 28 - 30°C.
pg139_n0013: The brooder temperature requirement is similar for all types of chicks.
pg139_n0014: There are various sources of heat for a brooder.
pg139_n0015: These include gas brooder lamps, electric bulbs with 100 Watts, infrared bulbs, charcoal burners, clay-pot burners and lanterns.
pg139_n0016: Figures 9.10 (a) to (d) show some examples of heat sources for brooders.

pg140_n0007: Temperature and humidity in a brooder have to be properly managed for chicks to live comfortably.
pg140_n0008: This can be achieved by using an accurate thermometer and hygrometer (preferably digital) to measure the temperature and humidity during the process regularly.
pg140_n0009: Temperature and comfort in the brooder can be monitored by observing the response or behaviour of chicks to the brooder temperature and other conditions, for example, chicks’ distribution as shown in Figures 9.11 (a) to (d).
pg140_im004: Chicks evenly distributed around the brooder, showing correct temperature.
pg140_im005: Chicks huddled close to the heat source, showing the temperature is too low.
pg140_im006: Chicks crowded around the edge away from the heat source, showing the temperature is too high.
pg140_im007: Chicks crowded on one side of the brooder, showing extreme discomfort.
pg141_n0003: When the temperature is correct, chicks spread evenly, their noise level shows satisfaction and chicks distribute themselves as shown in Figure 9.11 (a).
pg141_n0004: When the temperature is too low, chicks crowd to the heat sources in the brooder and will make noisy and continuous unhappy sounds to seek attention.
pg141_n0005: Their distribution can be as shown in Figure 9.11 (b).
pg141_n0006: When the temperature is too high, chicks stay away from the sources of heat, make no noise, and pant while drooping their heads and wings.
pg141_n0007: Their distribution can be as shown in Figure 9.11 (c).
pg141_n0008: Sometimes chicks show extreme discomfort which might be caused by an uneven light distribution, external noises or unpleasantly cold air blowing through a brooder.
pg141_n0009: This kind of distribution of chicks (refer to Figure 9.11 (d)) requires investigation to find out the actual cause and provide a solution.

pg141_n0015: Planning for a poultry farming enterprise
pg141_n0017: The goal of a poultry farm is to make money by managing it well.
pg141_n0018: But to do that, the farm needs to be planned carefully.
pg141_n0019: Before starting a poultry farm, there are a few things to think about.
pg141_n0024: When choosing a site for a poultry farm, there are important factors to consider.
pg141_n0025: Considering those factors will help in selecting the right site for a poultry farming enterprise.
pg141_n0029: (i) Local government laws: Make sure the farm is in an area where poultry farming is allowed by the local government.
pg141_n0031: (ii) Wind direction: Select a location that takes advantage of wind direction to minimise pollution from the poultry house and avoid transmission of diseases from one poultry house/farm to another.
pg141_n0033: (iii) Natural terrain and landscaping: Look for a site that can use the natural landscape to reduce construction costs.
pg141_n0035: (iv) Good drainage, avoid flood-prone areas: Find an area with good drainage to prevent flooding and water-related issues.
pg141_n0037: (v) Easy manure disposal: Select a site where it is easy to dispose of poultry manure.
pg142_n0003: (b) Parasites and diseases in the area
pg142_n0005: Many parasites and diseases can harm poultry.
pg142_n0006: It is important to know which parasites and diseases are common in your area.
pg142_n0007: This will help you to prevent and control them.
pg142_n0008: For example, a farmer should know which diseases require vaccinations and when to give them.
pg142_n0009: They should also know about other ways to control parasites and diseases.
pg142_n0013: Finding reliable sources of high-quality poultry stock is important.
pg142_n0014: Look for a stock that is affordable and of good quality.
pg142_n0015: You can ask other poultry farmers about their experiences.
pg142_n0016: When ordering chicks, make sure that you do it well ahead of time.
pg142_n0017: When placing an order, you should say how many chicks you want, what kind of poultry, and when you want them.
pg142_n0018: Some hatcheries also sell older birds called growers, which can be a good option for poultry meant for egg production.
pg142_n0022: Before starting a poultry farm, you need to find out about the markets available in your area.
pg142_n0023: This will help you to decide how big your farm should be.
pg142_n0024: There are two types of markets for poultry products: open or free markets, and contracted or formal markets.
pg142_n0025: It is important to figure out how much you will be able to market.
pg142_n0026: This helps you to determine the size of your farm and how much you can produce.
pg142_n0030: When we talk about capital in a poultry farm, we mean all the things we need to make it work.
pg142_n0031: This includes buildings, equipment, and other things that help the farm to be productive.
pg142_n0032: We also need money for things such as paying workers and buying supplies, such as chicks and feed.
pg142_n0033: All of these things together are called capital.
pg142_n0034: There are different kinds of capital, for example, fixed capital for buildings and equipment, and operating capital for things we need every day.
pg142_n0035: We also need money to buy all of these things, and that is called liquid capital.
pg142_n0036: It is important to have a good balance of these different types of capital.
pg142_n0037: There are different ways to get the money we need, for example, saving up over time, borrowing from banks or other places, or getting grants or donations from people who want to help.
pg142_n0041: There are two ways to get feed for your birds.
pg142_n0042: One way is to make the feed yourself at home.
pg142_n0043: This means collecting different ingredients and mixing them following a formula.
pg142_n0044: It might be cheaper, but it takes a lot of work.
pg143_n0003: ingredients are only available at certain times of the year.
pg143_n0004: So, they might not always be easy to find.
pg143_n0005: Another way to get feed for your chickens is to buy it from companies that make chicken feeds.
pg143_n0006: You can buy it directly from the company or from stores that sell it.
pg143_n0007: Many different companies make chicken feeds, so you can choose the one that is better for your birds based on its reputation or with the help of poultry experts.
pg143_n0011: Poultry that are kept under intensive systems produce high amount of manure.
pg143_n0012: Depending on how many chickens you have, this can cause problems in the area around the farm.
pg143_n0013: For example, a bird that weighs 1.8 kg can produce 0.11 kg of manure every day, 0.80 kg every week, 3.5 kg every month, and 41.50 kg every year.
pg143_n0014: We need to take care of poultry manure in a way that is good for the environment.
pg143_n0015: There are different ways we can use to handle poultry manure in the right way.
pg143_n0016: We need to make sure that we choose the best option that helps the environment, plants, and animals on the farm.
pg143_n0017: The following are some of the ways to deal with poultry manure:
pg143_n0020: (i) Spreading: You can spread the poultry manure on fields where crops grow.
pg143_n0021: It can be used instead of artificial fertilisers.
pg143_n0022: The amount of manure you can spread depends on how good the soil is, but usually, you can spread about 4 - 15 tons of manure per hectare.
pg143_n0024: (ii) Composting: You can mix the poultry manure with other materials to make compost.
pg143_n0025: Compost is good for the soil and can help plants grow well.
pg143_n0027: (iii) Selling: Some people might want to buy your poultry manure.
pg143_n0028: They can use it to make natural fertilisers.
pg143_n0030: (iv) Feeding fish: You can put fresh poultry manure in ponds where fish live.
pg143_n0031: The manure will fertilise the pond.
pg143_n0033: (v) Feeding other animals: You can use processed chicken manure to feed animals such as cattle, goats, and sheep.
pg143_n0034: These animals have special stomachs that can handle it.
pg143_n0038: Infrastructures are important for poultry farming.
pg143_n0039: They include things such as roads, transportation, and access to markets.
pg143_n0040: These things help the poultry farm to run smoothly.
pg143_n0041: In places like Tanzania, urban and peri-urban areas have better infrastructures than rural areas.
pg143_n0042: That is why it is easier to have big poultry farms in
pg144_n0004: It is also important to have the poultry houses near a road or railway that goes to the main market.
pg144_n0005: This makes it easy to bring in inputs such as feeds for the poultry and take out products such as eggs and birds to sell.
pg144_n0006: Services for poultry farming include things such as water supply and electricity.
pg144_n0007: These services help the poultry farm to run smoothly.
pg144_n0008: It is important to have an alternative source of power in case of power off from public sources.
pg144_n0009: This is especially important for places such as the hatchery units or brooders.
pg144_n0010: It is also important to have enough clean and safe water for the poultry farm to work well.
pg144_n0014: We have to pay a close attention in making sure that everything happens at the right time, keep everything clean, and keep good records.
pg144_n0015: This needs someone who knows what he/she should do to make sure that everything happens the right way.
pg144_n0016: Therefore, as a poultry farmer, it is important to always be ready to learn how to take care of the poultry in the best way possible.

pg145_im003: Chapter Ten: General principles and practices of chicken production.
pg145_n0008: In this chapter, you will learn about the breeds and types of chickens.
pg145_n0009: You will also learn about general management in housing, feeding and health of chickens.
pg145_n0010: The competencies developed will enable you to carry out general management practices in chicken production enterprises.
pg145_n0013: “Lay the foundation for successful chicken production”
pg145_n0016: Different types of chickens have different characteristics, such as body size, growth rate, egg-laying ability, and resistance to diseases.
pg145_n0017: You need to know the characteristics of different chicken breeds to choose the most suitable breed for your farming goals and conditions.
pg145_n0018: Some chicken breeds are better suited for meat production, while others are known for their high egg production.
pg145_n0019: Understanding the types and breeds of chickens helps you to make informed decisions about breed selection, feeding requirements, and overall management practices.
pg145_n0020: It will also allow you to plan and implement appropriate housing and management systems based on the specific needs of the chicken breed you are working with.
pg145_n0022: Kinds of chickens can be grouped according to type.
pg145_n0023: Type of chicken is a term which describes the general shape and form as suited to a function of the bird.
pg145_n0024: There are four basic types of chickens which are egg-type, meat-type, dual-purpose chickens, that is, for both meat and eggs and ornamental chickens.
pg145_n0026: Egg-type chickens: This group involves chickens specifically developed for egg production.
pg145_n0027: They are usually light in weight compared to meat-type chickens.
pg145_n0028: They do not easily go broody, that is, they do not want to sit on their eggs to hatch them.
pg145_n0029: The egg-type chickens are called layers or eggers.
pg145_n0031: Meat-type chickens: This group specifies chickens developed for meat production.
pg145_n0032: They are heavier than egg-type chickens.
pg145_n0033: They do not tolerate the high ambient temperatures of the tropics as the egg-type chickens.
pg145_n0034: They only lay a few eggs.
pg146_n0003: However, in the commercial production of meat, these chickens are sold before they reach the stage of laying eggs.
pg146_n0004: The meat-type chickens are called broilers.
pg146_n0007: This group of chicken is developed to produce both eggs and meat.
pg146_n0008: This type of chicken is popular in the tropics.
pg146_n0009: They are of medium weight and they sometimes go broody.
pg146_n0012: This group involves chickens kept for their unique beauty in their appearance and they are not mainly used for egg or meat production.
pg146_n0013: They can be reared and then sold to earn money or kept in recreational gardens for show where money can be charged for the services provided.
pg146_n0014: However, ornamental chickens are not widespread in Tanzania.
pg146_n0015: Examples of ornamental chickens are Phoenix, Brahma, Polish, Orloff, Ayam, Silkie, and Dwarf and Long Crower chickens.
pg146_n0016: Figures 10.1 (a) and (b) show some ornamental chickens.

pg147_n0010: Chickens appear in different colours and sizes and other various traits or characteristics of each particular type.
pg147_n0011: A chicken breed is a group of chickens that share certain traits, for example, feather colour, egg colour, and type of comb.
pg147_n0012: A comb is the fleshy growth on the head of a chicken.
pg147_n0013: In most cases, breeds are named based on their origin but emphasis is put on developing them on important economic characteristics, for example, meat and egg quality and quantity.
pg147_n0014: There are exotic breeds (those originating in foreign countries) and indigenous breeds (those originating in local countries).
pg147_n0018: The exotic breeds of chicken are either pure breeds or hybrids.
pg147_n0019: A purebreed refers to offspring resulting from true breeding.
pg147_n0020: True breeding is a way to produce offspring that would carry the same phenotype as the parents.
pg147_n0021: Phenotype means observable characteristics that can easily be seen or measured.
pg147_n0022: The exotic purebreds are further grouped into heavy and light breeds.
pg147_n0023: The heavy breeds of chicken have generally heavy body weights and are suitable for meat production.
pg147_n0024: Heavy breeds provide a valuable carcass which is why they are more suitable for meat than egg production.
pg147_n0025: They include breeds such as New Hampshire, Rhode Island Red, Cornish, and White Plymouth Rock.
pg147_n0026: Light breeds are generally small in size and are early maturing.
pg147_n0027: They are mainly raised for egg production.
pg147_n0028: They include breeds such as White Leghorn and Ancona.
pg147_n0029: Due to their small size, light breeds are not very suitable for meat production.
pg147_n0030: Exotic purebred chickens are rare in poultry farming except in breeder farms.
pg147_n0034: Different pure breeds can be crossed to produce hybrids.
pg147_n0035: Such hybrids usually show increased fitness compared to their purebred parents.
pg147_n0036: The broiler hybrids are developed for certain intended fitness characteristics in meat production.
pg147_n0037: For example, heavy weight and fast growth, feed efficiency (increased body weight gain per unit of feed consumed), conformation (characteristic shape and form), hardness to living conditions, meat yield, reduced fat content and product uniformity.
pg147_n0038: Similarly, layer hybrids are developed for certain intended traits.
pg148_n0003: production, hardness to living conditions as well as improved eggshell quality and colour.
pg148_n0005: There are many kinds of hybrids.
pg148_n0006: The most common include light, medium and heavy hybrids.
pg148_n0007: The light and medium hybrids are for egg production purposes while heavy hybrids are for meat production.
pg148_n0008: Figures 10.2 (a) to (f) show examples of hybrids developed by crossing pure exotic breeds of chickens.

pg149_n0013: There are several indigenous breeds in Tanzania and other countries in Africa.
pg149_n0014: These breeds however, are genetically and phenotypically different.
pg149_n0015: That is, they neither have similar genes that control traits passed from one generation to the next nor observable characteristics that can easily be seen or measured.
pg149_n0016: Instead, they are groups of chickens that originate and fit more to a particular set of ecological conditions.
pg149_n0017: These chickens show some similar characteristics which make them different from other chickens of different ecological conditions.
pg149_n0018: Since chicken groups of such kinds originate from places with a given set of ecological conditions, they are termed as ecotypes rather than breeds.
pg149_n0019: Examples of local ecotypes found in Tanzania are Kuchi, Ching’wekwe, Singamagazi, Unguja and Pemba (refer to Figures 10.3 (a) to (d)).

pg150_n0003: Indigenous chickens are very good at surviving in our country.
pg150_n0004: They are strong and can tolerate different weather and diseases that are common in their areas.
pg150_n0005: They can also find food easily and are good at taking care of their young ones.
pg150_n0006: Because of these reasons, many small farmers prefer to keep indigenous chickens.
pg150_n0007: These chickens do not produce as many eggs or as much meat as exotic or commercial chicken breeds though the flavour of the eggs and meat is preferred.
pg150_n0009: Hybrids of local indigenous and exotic chickens
pg150_n0011: Since local indigenous ecotypes fit well with our local condition but they are low producers of meat and eggs, the development of hybrids of local ecotypes and exotic breeds becomes important.
pg150_n0012: Currently, there are some hybrids of this kind of crossing.
pg150_n0013: These include chickens such as Kuroiler, Tanbro and Sasso.
pg150_n0014: These kinds of hybrid grow fast and produce more eggs and meat than local indigenous ecotypes.
pg150_n0015: They also fit more to local conditions, for example, they can tolerate high ambient temperatures and diseases.

pg151_n0013: Chicken housing refers to the confinement of birds in a purpose-built enclosure.
pg151_n0014: The purpose of housing chickens is to keep them safe from very hot or very cold weather.
pg151_n0015: Housing chickens also keeps them safe from bad weather like rain or storms.
pg151_n0016: Housing also protects chickens from animals that might harm them, and people trying to steal them.
pg151_n0017: It also stops other animals such as rodents and wild birds from reaching them.
pg151_n0018: To achieve the purpose of housing, one needs to know the basic requirements of a chicken house and adhere to good design, proper location, positioning, suitable floor, walls and roof, living space, basic equipment, and proper farm layout or arrangement.
pg151_n0020: The basic requirements of the chicken house
pg151_n0022: A good chicken house needs to have enough space for the birds to live comfortably.
pg151_n0023: Chickens require an extremely good temperature to produce well.
pg151_n0024: Chicken’s requirement for the environmental temperature varies with age.
pg151_n0025: Chicks should be started at 35°C in the first week after being hatched.
pg151_n0026: The temperature is then gradually reduced to 20°C - 24°C by the fifth week.
pg151_n0027: Broilers reared at ambient temperatures below 18°C are heavier than similar stock reared within the 18 - 35°C range, but their feed utilisation will be less.
pg151_n0028: Laying poultry produces the greatest number of eggs and the largest sized eggs at 13 - 24°C.
pg151_n0029: Similarly, feed is best used by chickens when the temperature is between 21°C and 24°C.
pg151_n0030: When the environment gets hotter, chickens eat less and their behaviour changes.
pg151_n0031: Within the temperature range of 5 - 30°C, there is a reduction of about 1.6% in feed intake for every 10°C increase in ambient temperature.
pg151_n0032: When the temperature goes above 24°C, the number of eggs produced decreases and the eggs become smaller.
pg151_n0033: If the temperature keeps on increasing and reaches 38°C or higher, it can cause death.
pg151_n0034: When the weather is very hot and humid, chickens may be more likely to die because their bodies have a harder time struggling to cool down through breathing.
pg151_n0036: Poultry houses should also have enough airflow or ventilation.
pg151_n0037: Good ventilation in poultry houses is necessary for the removal of dust, ammonia and water vapour from the air and litter.
pg151_n0038: The living area in a chicken house should be dry and the light
pg152_n0004: The chicken house must be protected from vermin and wild birds.
pg152_n0005: The chicken house should also be well-arranged inside and should last for a long time.
pg152_n0009: Location is an important factor to think about when it comes to housing.
pg152_n0010: Here are some important things to think about when choosing a location.
pg152_n0011: Regardless of the type of house, all chicken houses need to be on land that drains well, protected from floods, and easy to get to and from the road.
pg152_n0012: The chicken house should also be set in a place where it is easy to find inputs such as chicks and feeds.
pg152_n0013: In addition, the chicken house should be located near a good market.
pg152_n0017: Chicken houses should be well-ventilated, reasonably cool in hot environments, and free from strong winds.
pg152_n0018: Curtains have to be provided to protect chickens against winds, especially during brooding.
pg152_n0019: In hotter areas, the long axis of the house should run from east to west.
pg152_n0020: This will prevent the direct sunshine over the birds.
pg152_n0021: In colder areas, it is desirable to construct houses facing south or southeast to get maximum sunlight.
pg152_n0022: The distance between two houses for birds of the same age group should be at least 18 m to allow proper ventilation.
pg152_n0023: However, the young stock house should be 45 to 100 m away from the houses having adult stocks to prevent diseases.
pg152_n0024: To avoid ventilation problems, the width of the house should not exceed 9 m in open-sided houses.
pg152_n0025: The height of the house depends upon the temperature of the place.
pg152_n0026: Generally, the height of the house should be 2.4 - 3 m from the foundation to the roof line.
pg152_n0027: When height is more it helps to reduce the inside temperature.
pg152_n0029: Floors and walls in chicken houses
pg152_n0031: The floor of the house should be moisture-proof, free from cracks, easily cleaned, rat proof and durable.
pg152_n0032: The different types of floors in use are all-litter floors, all-slate floors, slate and litter floors, wire and litter floors, and sloping wire floors.
pg152_n0033: The walls and partitions must be solid enough to support the roof and withstand heavy winds.
pg152_n0034: The wide variation is possible depending on the climatic conditions as well as the availability and cost of construction materials.
pg152_n0035: Every main and rear door of the chicken house should have a footbath with disinfectant for disease control.
pg153_n0005: The roofs of chicken houses must be waterproof.
pg153_n0006: Roof insulation keeps the building cool in a hot environment.
pg153_n0007: In areas that become very hot during the day, it is a good idea to paint your roof with a special kind of paint that reflects the sunlight, for example, aluminium paint.
pg153_n0008: An overhang of 0·9 m will help to prevent the rainwater from splashing inside the house.
pg153_n0009: The climatic conditions and age of birds will determine the extent of side openings.
pg153_n0010: Usually half to two-thirds area of the side walls is kept open in an open-sided house fitted with wire mesh.
pg153_n0011: In areas where the temperature is high and continuous, more than two-thirds of the side wall area may be left open for proper ventilation.
pg153_n0012: In brooder houses half of the area is left open, in grower and layer houses two-thirds is left open while a maximal ventilation is required in cage houses.
pg153_n0016: Floor space and equipment in the chicken house, vary with the system of rearing and the size of the birds.
pg153_n0017: In a free-range system, a chicken needs about 20 – 30 cm² of floor space in the house.
pg153_n0018: In a deep litter system, a minimum floor space of 30 cm² per broiler and 50 cm² per layer chicken is required.
pg153_n0019: However, in hot areas, the floor space may be increased to some extent by reducing the number of birds kept in a given unit of area.
pg153_n0020: In a slatted floor system, the stocking space in a house is 6 to 8 birds per square metre.
pg153_n0021: In the cage system, the recommended size of a cage for one bird is 30 cm × 45 cm × 45 cm.
pg153_n0022: The number of birds per cage varies from 1 to 4 depending on cage size, the size of the bird, and the farmer’s preference.
pg153_n0023: In semi-intensive systems particularly house and run, the living space in the house depends on environmental conditions.
pg153_n0024: However, the stocking density of 4 - 5 birds per square metre in a house can be used.
pg153_n0028: It is important to arrange the farm in a good way.
pg153_n0029: Livestock houses should be built in relation to places where feed is stored, where manure is disposed of, and other important facilities on the farm.
pg153_n0030: This will help in making sure that labour is used properly.
pg153_n0031: There should be sufficient space per animal for resting and well-arranged facilities such as feeding and watering troughs.
pg153_n0032: This will contribute to yield improvement of animals and makes the work of the operator easier.
pg153_n0033: The feed storerooms should be located near the animal houses.
pg153_n0034: Generally, feeds should be kept in the middle of the building where animals live and feed.
pg154_n0003: It is important to carefully plan the main path in the middle of the main chicken house.
pg154_n0004: This has to be done by considering the easiness of reaching feed stores and places for collecting eggs or broilers from where the birds live.
pg154_n0005: Likewise, there should be isolation rooms for arrival and sick chicken.
pg154_n0006: The isolation rooms should be positioned in a corner of the main house in a manner that the arrival and sick chickens cannot be reached by other chickens.
pg154_n0007: In addition, the quarantine sheds need to be placed at the entrance of the farm.
pg154_n0008: This makes it easier to separate new birds that are purchased from outside and those that come back from a market or other places where they might have been exposed to the risk of infection.
pg154_n0012: Chicken houses should be designed in a way that enables birds to easily be taken care of, and can produce without stress.
pg154_n0013: Chicken houses should also be designed to maintain a comfortable ambient temperature in the house by removing excessive heat and moisture produced by the birds.
pg154_n0014: There are two main types of chicken houses that poultry farmers commonly use.
pg154_n0015: These are closed and open-sided houses.
pg154_n0018: A closed house is a completely enclosed house with no windows.
pg154_n0020: Conditions inside the closed house are kept as close as possible to what birds need to be healthy and comfortable.
pg154_n0021: Extractor fans or ventilators are used to take out the air and bring in fresh air into the house through intake openings.
pg154_n0022: Artificial light is used to light up the interior of the house.
pg154_n0023: The width of the closed house is usually greater than 13 metres.
pg154_n0024: Closed houses are also called controlled environment houses.
pg154_n0025: This type of house is not commonly used in our country.
pg154_n0028: In our country, open-sided houses are the most common.
pg154_n0030: Usually, half to two-thirds area of the side walls are kept open in open-sided houses, but fitted with wire mesh.
pg154_n0031: In areas where temperature is continuously high, more than two-thirds of the side wall may be left open for proper ventilation.
pg154_n0032: Curtains are often used to prevent the house from getting too cold at night.
pg154_n0033: Open-sided houses rely on the free flow of air through the house for ventilation.
pg154_n0034: They work well in most places except in extremely cold temperatures.
pg154_n0035: They are also preferred because they are cheaper.
pg154_n0036: Generally, a chicken house should not be expensive, however, it should be strong, durable, comfortable and safe.
pg154_n0037: Figure 10.4 shows an example of an open-sided poultry house.
pg155_im002: Open-sided chicken house with wire-mesh sides, a low concrete wall, a wooden door, and a corrugated iron roof for ventilation.
pg155_n0003: Figure 10.4: Example of an open-sided chicken house
pg155_n0006: The basic construction requirements for an open-sided house are as follow:
pg155_n0008: (a) Widths: The width should not exceed 12.6 m.
pg155_n0009: The houses wider than this will not provide ample ventilation during hot weather.
pg155_n0011: (b) Heights: Most open-sided poultry houses have a stud that is 2.4 m long.
pg155_n0012: This represents the distance from the foundation or base of a building to the roofline or top.
pg155_n0013: Since it is always hot in most parts of Tanzania, it is recommended to increase the stud height of the house to 3 m.
pg155_n0014: The centre height should be 5.2 m.
pg155_n0016: (c) Lengths: Depending on the level of the land, you can choose any length that is convenient for you.
pg155_n0017: However, for small units, 10.3 m is recommended.
pg155_n0019: (d) Foundation: A solid and adequate foundation should support the building.
pg155_n0020: Concrete and other termite-proof materials should be used.
pg155_n0021: The evenness (how smooth and level) of the foundation determines the evenness of the completed building.
pg155_n0023: (e) Floor: Concrete or rammed earth floor can be used.
pg155_n0024: However, with disease-control programmes, the concrete or similar floor is mandatory.
pg155_n0025: Such a floor is also necessary when the soil is dense and can absorb and transfer water from the lower subsoil.
pg155_n0026: But, in certain areas where the soil is sandy, a concrete slab is not used when birds are placed on the floor.
pg156_n0003: (f) Walls: In hot (tropic) climate such as Tanzania, only the bottom 30 cm of both front and back sides, can be covered while the rest is left open with wire mesh.
pg156_n0004: Where cages are used, a roof over the cage may be adequate.
pg156_n0005: High-quality wire mesh for the sides is a good investment.
pg156_n0006: A fishing net can also be used instead of wire mesh, but it is difficult to clean and disinfect.
pg156_n0008: (g) The roof: The roof could be made from any roofing material.
pg156_n0009: The shape of the roof recommended is a gable roof with the pitch varying from ¼ - ⅓.
pg156_n0010: Insulation of the roof can be provided by using a thatch roof as this provides the best cooling effect in the house.
pg156_n0011: If thatch cannot be used, it is advisable to use aluminium sheets.
pg156_n0012: These sheets have the advantage of reflecting heat from the sun and are simple to take care of.
pg156_n0013: The roof sheets need to be thick enough and well attached to the frame so that they don’t get blown away by strong winds.
pg156_n0014: If galvanized iron sheets are used for roofing, they must be covered with palm branches or similar materials to reduce heat absorption.
pg156_n0015: In addition, if other materials such as fibre-cement plates, galvanized steel plates or tiles are used, it is advisable to paint the roof white to reduce heat absorption.
pg156_n0016: If the white paint is properly taken care of, it can make the building cooler by 3 to 8 degrees Celsius on hot days.
pg156_n0020: A good chicken house needs the right equipment for keeping birds.
pg156_n0021: The equipment will make it easy for birds to get food, water, or anything else they need.
pg156_n0022: The equipment in a chicken house depends on how the chickens are raised, kind and age of the chicken.
pg156_n0023: A well-constructed chicken house has to be equipped with feeders, drinkers, perches, nests, catching devices, broody coops, and other items considered necessary for production.
pg156_n0024: The equipment must be durable, fairly simple in construction, movable and easy to clean and disinfect.
pg156_n0026: Feeders and drinkers: Feeders and drinkers can be automated or filled by hand.
pg156_n0028: Feeders and drinkers should also be constructed in such a way that: (a) they are easy to fill; (b) they are easy to clean; (c) wastage of feed or water is minimised; (d) the birds cannot stand or roost in them and contaminate feed or water; (e) the birds can reach feed and water easily; (f) there is enough feeding or drinking space per bird; (g) feeders and drinkers are high enough that the birds cannot scratch litter in them.
pg156_n0029: Various designs of ready-made feeders and drinkers can be bought or made on a farm by using locally available resources.
pg156_n0030: Figures 10.5 (a) to (f) show some examples of chicken feeders while Figures 10.6 (a) to (e) show examples of drinkers.

pg159_n0003: Laying nests: The laying nests should be big enough, easy to clean and disinfect, dark, cool and well-ventilated especially in hot areas.
pg159_n0004: They also need to be placed in a convenient position.
pg159_n0005: It is also important to consider that hens prefer to have privacy when they lay their eggs.
pg159_n0006: Therefore, they like nests that are slightly dark inside.
pg159_n0007: Nests should be provided with a perch for easy entrance.
pg159_n0008: They are generally placed at a height of 10 – 15 cm from the floor to enable birds to jump into them easily.
pg159_n0009: Nests should be comfortable and safe by providing litter material on the nest floor and they should be properly constructed.
pg159_n0010: They must have a hip to prevent spillage of the litter material.
pg159_n0011: They must also have a slopped roof to avoid birds roosting on the nest roof.
pg159_n0012: There are individual and communal nests.
pg159_n0016: The size of an individual nest should be 31 cm length × 35 cm width × 35 cm height.
pg159_n0017: For every 4 hens, there should be 1 nest.
pg159_n0018: Individual nests are usually built in groups of 5 nests wide and 2 or 3 rows high.
pg159_n0019: These nests should have sloping roofs to prevent birds from sitting or sleeping on them.
pg159_n0020: The bottom part of these nests should be movable for easy cleaning.
pg159_n0021: Due to the hot weather in many areas of Tanzania, it is advisable to use wire mesh on the back side of the nests instead of solid material.
pg159_n0022: Figure 10.7 (a) shows an example of individual nests.

pg159_n0028: These are unpartitioned boxes of about 2.4 m long by 0.6 m wide with an opening at each end through which the birds enter and leave.
pg159_n0029: Each has a sloping cover that is hinged so that it may be opened for gathering the eggs.
pg159_n0030: The communal nest of 1.8 m length by 0.3 m width by 0.6 m height is enough for 50 hens (refer to Figure 10.8 (b).

pg160_n0008: Layer and dual-purpose chickens managed in systems other than cages have to preferably be equipped with perches.
pg160_n0009: Perches are horizontal wooden bars or poles in chicken houses that birds use to sleep or sit on.
pg160_n0010: Birds have a natural behaviour of roosting on higher places so perches provide them with the thing they like.
pg160_n0011: The most popular perches used are 5 cm by 8 cm or 5 cm by 10 cm pieces placed on the edge with upper corners rounded.
pg160_n0012: Each bird needs a perching space allowance of about 15 cm depending upon the breed.
pg160_n0013: The perches should be placed 20 – 25 cm apart.

pg161_n0006: Broody coops have bottoms made of wire mesh, which discourages chickens from sitting and being inactive.
pg161_n0010: The most carrying device in poultry farming is transport or carrying crates.
pg161_n0011: These crates are designed for holding and carrying chickens and other poultry birds.
pg161_n0012: The catching crates should be designed in such a way that they are durable, simple to put chickens in and take them out, and impossible for the bird to escape.
pg161_n0013: Their size depends on the size of the birds to be held.
pg161_n0014: They can be made of plastic, wood or any other suitable materials.
pg161_n0015: There are ready-made and on-farm-made crates using locally available resources.

pg162_n0022: The cost of feeds makes up 70 - 80% of the total expenses of raising chickens.
pg162_n0023: Chicken farmers should ensure that it is reasonable to spend those high costs.
pg162_n0024: An animal keeper always maintains feed costs low while maintaining the quantity and quality of products as high as possible.
pg162_n0025: Birds, like other animals, need balanced feed.
pg162_n0026: A balanced feed is one with enough energy, proteins, vitamins and minerals.
pg162_n0027: Birds also need to be provided with enough water all the time.
pg162_n0028: Moreover, chickens need to be fed with fodders.
pg162_n0029: Balanced feeds can, in the end, be packed in different forms and they are fed to chickens in different feeding methods.
pg162_n0030: Balanced ready-made chicken feeds can be bought from authorized distributors or made on the farm under the advice of livestock extension workers or chicken experts.
pg162_n0034: There are various forms of feed which are suitable for feeding chickens depending on the type of birds that are to be fed.
pg162_n0035: These include mashes, pellets, and crumbs.
pg162_n0037: Mash feeds: These feeds are made when feed ingredients are grounded into fine particles.
pg162_n0038: This is the commonest form that is fed to all poultry in our country but it is most suitable for layers.
pg162_n0039: Mashes are simple to make and they enhance the activity of the birds; birds take a longer time to feed and reduce boredom.
pg162_n0040: However, selective picking of bigger particles leaves some nutrients not eaten, hence encouraging deficiencies.
pg162_n0042: Pellet feeds: These are compounded balanced feeds, which after mixing are compressed into pellets (tablets-like) of different sizes.
pg163_n0003: due to their feeding habit of picking the big particles.
pg163_n0004: Pellet feeds are most suitable for broilers.
pg163_n0005: There is no chance of deficiencies with pellet feeds as every particle picked is balanced.
pg163_n0006: However, feeding pellet feeds may invite undesirable behaviour in birds.
pg163_n0007: This is because birds tend to feed fast and remain idle.
pg163_n0010: These feeds are produced when pellets are introduced to a cracker/pellets disintegrator to produce a product between mash and pellets.
pg163_n0011: They have the advantage of pellets because they are mostly fed to younger chicks.
pg163_n0012: It enables the chicks to get all nutrients that are in the ration.
pg163_n0013: It also reduces wastage and increases feed efficiency.
pg163_n0014: Figure 10.11 shows mash, crumble and pellet feed forms.
pg163_im002: Three forms of poultry feed arranged side by side: fine mash feed on the left, coarse crumble feed in the centre, and cylindrical pellet feed on the right.
pg163_n0020: Proper feeding of chickens helps them to grow fast.
pg163_n0021: Most feeding methods are more applicable to birds that are kept in confinement than those under free range.
pg163_n0022: The methods suggested for feeding birds include ad libitum, restricted and free choice feeding.
pg163_n0025: This means providing feed to an animal at all times.
pg163_n0026: Ad libitum feeding is done gradually to allow the animal to consume while increasing amounts of feed until it leaves behind at least 15% of the amount that had been offered.
pg163_n0027: Ad libitum feeding is commonly applied in fast-growing birds, for example, broilers.
pg164_n0003: Restricted feeding: In this method, the birds are fed a limited quantity of feed per day to meet the optimal body requirement.
pg164_n0004: It is commonly used to feed pullets of all types of production, layers and special-purpose birds, for example, the ones used for research.
pg164_n0006: Free choice feeding: This method involves providing different types of feedstuffs at all times and letting the chickens to choose what they need to eat.
pg164_n0007: Under this method, birds are usually given a choice among three types of feedstuffs.
pg164_n0008: These are (a) an energy source (e.g., maize, rice bran, sorghum or wheat); (b) a protein source (e.g., fish meal or oil seedcake meals); and (c) vitamins and minerals.
pg164_n0009: Through this method of feeding, birds can balance their diets well if each feedstuff is available in the feeder.
pg164_n0010: This method of feeding is commonly applied to game birds and indigenous chickens.
pg164_n0011: With this method, there is no labour required for mixing the feed.
pg164_n0015: Fresh fodders are green plant materials fed to animals such as chickens and others.
pg164_n0016: In chickens, fodders are used as extra food.
pg164_n0017: Fodders are important for chickens because they help them to grow strong and healthy.
pg164_n0018: They also help them to lay eggs that are better with strong yellow yolk.
pg164_n0019: Many types of fodder can be used for chickens.
pg164_n0020: One example is vegetable crop residues.
pg164_n0021: Another example is leguminous tree leaves.
pg164_n0022: These leaves are rich in nutrients and can be a great source of fodder for chickens.
pg164_n0024: If the natural sources of fodder are not available or not sufficient, we can make them by sprouting or growing them from grains (hydroponic fodder).
pg164_n0025: Sprouting grains into fodder is a great way to stretch your animal feed budget.
pg164_n0026: For example, 50 kg of whole grain can be transformed into as much as 300 kg of fodder simply by sprouting it.
pg164_n0027: Grains, for example, sorghum, finger millet, bulrush millet, wheat, barley, maize, and paddy are used.
pg164_n0028: These grains are grown in a nutrient-rich solution, not soil.
pg164_n0029: The grains are put in a tray or container for about a week to grow.
pg164_n0030: This fodder is full of vitamins, minerals, and other nutrients that chickens need.
pg164_n0031: Chickens will eat not only the sprouts but also the remaining seed residue from the fodder.
pg164_n0032: There is a great benefit of using this kind of fodder because it provides a continuous supply of nutritious feed for the chickens.
pg164_n0033: Growing this fodder can also help you to save money on chicken feed.
pg164_n0034: Figure 10.12 shows this kind of fodder.
pg164_im001: Ripe red tomatoes growing on the vine.
pg165_im002: Trays of grain at different stages of sprouting for hydroponic fodder, from soaked seeds to dense green shoots.
pg165_n0008: (i) Choose the right seeds: Sorghum, finger millet, bulrush millet, wheat and barley are good choices.
pg165_n0009: They are rich in nutrients for chickens.
pg165_n0011: (ii) Soak the seeds: Put seeds in a container such as a bucket.
pg165_n0015: (iii) Drain the water: After 8 hours, drain the water from the container.
pg165_n0017: (iv) Prepare the nutrient solution: You can buy a ready-made nutrient solution from a gardening store.
pg165_n0018: Alternatively, you can make your own.
pg165_n0019: You will need a water-soluble fertiliser (e.g., 20-20-20 or 24-8-16 NPK), which is available from the market.
pg165_n0020: Make sure you get the ones that have micronutrients included.
pg165_n0021: Add approximately 10 grams of this fertiliser per litre of water and mix them very well.
pg165_n0022: Add approximately 5 grams of magnesium sulphate per litre.
pg165_n0023: Stir the mixture thoroughly to ensure everything is well mixed.
pg165_n0025: (v) Spread the seeds: Spread the seeds evenly on a growing tray.
pg165_n0026: The tray should have small drain holes.
pg165_n0027: These holes allow excess water to drain away, preventing the roots of the plants from being submerged in water.
pg165_n0028: If the roots are submerged, they can’t breathe and the plants can become stressed or even die.
pg165_n0029: Winnowing baskets can be used as growing trays for hydroponic fodder because they are readily available.
pg165_n0030: They can be found in many places and they are a practical choice for this task.
pg166_n0003: (vi) Water the seeds: Use the nutrient solution to water the seeds 2 - 3 times a day.
pg166_n0004: The seeds should be kept moist all the time but not wet.
pg166_n0006: (vii) Grow the seeds: Put the tray in a warm place indoors.
pg166_n0008: The seeds will sprout into the grass.
pg166_n0010: (viii) Harvest the fodder: After 7 days, the fodder is ready.
pg166_n0011: It should be green and about 15 centimetres tall.
pg166_n0013: (ix) Feed the chickens: Give the fodder to the chickens.
pg166_n0014: You may spread it on plate feeders.
pg166_n0017: Always maintain a clean environment when growing hydroponic fodder.
pg166_n0018: This helps to ensure the safety and health of your chickens and the plants they eat.

pg166_n0038: Proper management of chicken health enables a poultry farmer to maximise production and profits.
pg166_n0039: For this to be achieved, poultry farmers should be able to identify healthy chickens from the sick ones.
pg166_n0040: This will enable a farmer to notice unhealthy chickens and find out the causes and solutions.
pg166_n0041: The following sections elaborate the meaning of animal health, conditions of healthy and unhealthy chickens including poultry vices, causes of poor or ill health in chickens, and general management of chicken health.
pg167_n0005: Health is a state of being in a good condition where all the body organs and systems are normal and functioning properly.
pg167_n0006: It is a freedom from diseases and abnormalities.
pg167_n0007: Any change from a normal state or any process which prevents an animal’s normal function is referred to as ill health.
pg167_n0009: Healthy and unhealthy conditions in chickens
pg167_n0011: Poultry farmers must observe birds closely to keep individual animals and flocks or herds in good health and productive.
pg167_n0012: When the animal is ill or falls sick, it shows some signs or behavioural deviation from the normal healthy animals.
pg167_n0013: The following are some signs and behaviours of a healthy chicken which a poultry farmer should be able to identify.
pg167_n0016: Eyes are bright (clear and shiny), clearly open, and free of discharge or swelling.
pg167_n0019: Both nostrils are clear and open, with no discharge from the nostrils.
pg167_n0022: Breathe with the mouth closed, except in very hot conditions.
pg167_n0025: The wings are carried close to the body in most breeds of chickens.
pg167_n0026: Few breeds have wings that point downward; therefore, you need to study breed characteristics to see what is normal for your breed.
pg167_n0027: The wings should not bend, hang down heavily or look twisted.
pg167_n0030: Feathers are evenly distributed with no missing large patches.
pg167_n0031: A healthy bird has its feathers smoothed down when it is active.
pg167_n0032: Hens kept with a cock often have bare patches on the back and the base of the neck near the back.
pg167_n0033: These patches are caused by scratching during mating and this is normal.
pg167_n0034: However, there are some differences with some kinds of chickens which have twisted or curled feathers, for example, Frizzle and Polish chickens.
pg167_n0037: The skin appears smooth and intact with no open sores or swelling.
pg167_n0040: A healthy chicken’s legs look smooth.
pg167_n0041: The scales are visible but sit relatively flat, like skin.
pg167_n0042: The three front toes of chicken point straight ahead, and the feet should not turn outward.
pg167_n0043: Feet should not be webbed (webbing is a skin connecting the toes), but rarely webbed feet show up as a genetic defect.
pg167_n0046: This is the opening from which the chicken passes out both faeces and eggs.
pg167_n0047: A healthy cloaca is clean, pinkish-red, moist and clean with no faeces stuck on it and no wounds or sores around it.
pg167_n0048: The vent should not protrude, or be bloody or dry.
pg168_n0003: Droppings or faeces: Healthy chicken excretes tightly packed droppings with white caps on them.
pg168_n0005: Mental state: A healthy chicken is quick to see and act, and will stay away from people it doesn’t know if it is in a place with light.
pg168_n0006: A chicken that is not moving or resisting to be held is likely to be sick.
pg168_n0007: When it is dark, chickens are calm and quiet, and this is normal.
pg168_n0009: Activity level: A healthy chicken is usually active during the day.
pg168_n0010: Some chickens are more easily scared and jumpy while others are relaxed but always active.
pg168_n0011: In very hot weather, all chickens are less active.
pg168_n0014: Normal growth or egg production: Healthy chickens should grow to weights that are right for their age.
pg168_n0015: If chickens are for eggs, they should lay as expected.
pg168_n0017: Other normal behaviours: Healthy chickens should show normal eating, drinking, walking and perching behaviour.
pg168_n0019: Note: Any unusual signs or behaviours in chickens indicate that they are not healthy.

pg168_n0027: Causes of poor health in chickens
pg168_n0029: Chickens can get sick for many reasons.
pg168_n0032: Poor feeding: If chickens don’t get enough good feed, they can get nutritional problems, for example, pecking each other or eating their eggs.
pg168_n0034: Poor housing, hygiene and biosecurity: If chickens live in dirty or unsafe places, they can get sick.
pg168_n0035: Biosecurity is about keeping people, animals, and plants safe from harmful germs and diseases.
pg168_n0036: If biosecurity is poor, germs can spread and make the chickens sick.
pg168_n0038: Injuries from poor handling: If chickens are treated badly or their houses are not well made, they can get hurt.
pg168_n0039: This can cause problems like broken bones or wounds.
pg169_n0003: Parasite infestation: Parasites are organisms that live in or outside another organism, called a host, and can harm it.
pg169_n0004: They can be external or internal.
pg169_n0005: External parasites, such as fleas, lice and mites, live on the chicken’s body.
pg169_n0006: Internal parasites, for example, roundworms, live inside the chicken’s body.
pg169_n0007: Parasites can cause problems in chickens.
pg169_n0008: They can compete with the chickens for food, make them lose their appetite, and cause them to get sick.
pg169_n0009: Figures 10.13 (a) to (d) show some chicken parasites.

pg169_n0019: Micro-organisms or pathogens: These are tiny organisms that can cause diseases.
pg169_n0020: Diseases happen when these harmful micro-organisms or pathogens enter a chicken’s body.
pg169_n0021: Examples of these pathogens are bacteria and viruses.
pg169_n0022: However, some diseases are caused by not getting enough nutrients from food, for example, vitamins.
pg169_n0023: Diseases often spread from one chicken to another, usually more so than from mother to chick.
pg169_n0028: Direct contact with an infected chicken;
pg169_n0031: Touching a litter that has been contaminated;
pg169_n0034: Breathing in tiny disease-carrying particles in the air; and
pg169_n0037: Eating feed or drinking water that has been in contact with infected animals or disease carriers such as insects and wild birds.

pg170_n0017: It is important to note the following:
pg170_n0019: (a) Parasites and diseases can cause problems for chickens, for example, discomfort, blood loss, and even death.
pg170_n0020: To prevent this, we must keep the chicken’s environment clean and use appropriate treatments recommended by a veterinarian.
pg171_n0003: (b) If you have used any drugs on your flock, make sure to follow the drug’s withdrawal period.
pg171_n0004: This is important to prevent the sale of products that contain residues of drugs.
pg171_n0005: The withdrawal period is the time after which the drug’s effects on the animals will no longer be detectable in their products.
pg171_n0006: It is important to follow this period to ensure the quality and safety of the products you sell to customers.
pg171_n0010: Chickens can also have bad habits (vices).
pg171_n0011: These are usually caused by poor management.
pg171_n0012: Some common bad habits in chickens include cannibalism, feather pecking and egg eating.
pg171_n0015: These are usually caused by stress.
pg171_n0016: Birds can peck each other, which can lead to death.
pg171_n0017: This can happen when birds are not well managed or when they are in conditions that are not part of their normal routine.
pg171_n0018: Figures 10.15 and 10.16 show cannibalism and feather pecking, respectively.
pg171_im002: White chickens with bloody wounds near the vent, showing cannibalism caused by severe pecking.
