pg171_n0023: To manage cannibalism and feather pecking in chickens, you can:
pg171_n0027: Give birds enough space based on their age, type, and care system.
pg171_n0030: Reduce light brightness by using dim lights or placing the building so that light doesn’t hit the long side.
pg171_n0033: Provide enough feeders and drinkers according to the recommended ratio to the floor space and birds.
pg171_n0036: Give birds the right amount of balanced feed according to their needs.
pg171_n0039: Use measures to control external parasites such as flies, lice, and mice.
pg171_n0042: Ventilate the houses to bring in fresh air and remove bad smells.
pg171_n0045: Keep birds busy by hanging up fodders such as vegetables or edible tree leaves.
pg171_n0048: Isolate birds that have been pecked to prevent further pecking or death then treat the pecked birds.
pg172_n0005: As a last resort, trim the birds’ beaks when other methods have failed.
pg172_n0006: But don’t trim the beaks of free-range birds as they need to pick food.
pg172_n0009: Birds can start eating their eggs if they find the broken or soft-shelled ones.
pg172_n0010: If this habit is not stopped, it can spread.
pg172_n0011: This habit shows that the chickens are not well looked after.
pg172_im002: Three hens pecking at a cracked egg on the ground, showing egg-eating behaviour in chickens.
pg172_n0017: There are several ways to prevent egg eating in chickens.
pg172_n0022: Give chickens enough good food and a safe place to live.
pg172_n0025: Keep the inside of the laying nest dark.
pg172_n0028: Improve feed quality and quantity, especially minerals to keep good quality egg shells.
pg172_n0031: Make sure no eggs should stay in the nests overnight after the last collection.
pg172_n0034: Provide ad libitum clean water to avoid thirst.
pg172_n0039: Management of parasites and diseases in chickens
pg172_n0041: Two approaches are applied in the management of parasites and diseases; preventive and curative.
pg172_n0042: While preventive ways focus on the control measures against the
pg173_n0003: parasite or disease-causing agents or their vectors, curative ways include the use of drugs and chemicals to treat the disease.
pg173_n0005: Preventive measures used to manage poultry parasites and diseases:
pg173_n0007: The preventive measures used in managing poultry parasites and diseases include vaccination, control of vectors, use of prophylactics, quarantine/isolation, sanitation, and proper nutrition.
pg173_n0008: These preventive measures are elaborated as follows:
pg173_n0012: Vaccination refers to the introduction of a vaccine into the animal body to protect from a specific disease.
pg173_n0013: A vaccine is a biological product which is administered to the animal body to stimulate the production of antibodies against specific diseases caused by micro-organisms.
pg173_n0014: There are various ways of administering vaccines to animals depending on the type of vaccine and manufacturer’s instruction.
pg173_n0015: All vaccines should be administered under technical advice from extension workers or qualified veterinarians.
pg173_n0017: It is important to follow the manufacturers’ instructions on the storage and administration of the vaccines.
pg173_n0018: Generally, vaccines should be stored at low temperatures of between 2°C and 8°C and they should not be exposed to direct sunlight.
pg173_n0019: It is required to treat water before providing vaccines through drinking water.
pg173_n0020: A teacher or livestock extension worker can assist with this.
pg173_n0021: Birds should be thoroughly observed to ensure that every bird has taken the vaccine within the allowed time limit.
pg173_n0022: Thereafter, drinkers should be thoroughly cleaned and refilled.
pg173_n0023: It is important not to give a vaccine to sick animals or those taking the medication until they are fully recovered.
pg173_n0024: At least 2 days should pass after their last dose.
pg173_n0025: Moreover, it is not recommended to mix water containing a vaccine with vitamin supplements.
pg173_n0029: This involves giving healthy animals drugs at regular intervals to avoid infection.
pg173_n0030: Chickens especially layers may be given coccidiostats either through feed or water where there is a high risk of coccidiosis.
pg173_n0031: This disease causes severe losses in young and growing chickens.
pg173_n0032: Coccidiostat is a substance that can be given to birds to stop or slow down the growth of the protozoa parasites that cause coccidiosis disease.
pg173_n0033: The administration of coccidiostat should commence in the third week as a continuous prophylactic programme.
pg173_n0034: However, to minimise the risk of resistance to a particular coccidiostat, it is common to use different coccidiostats in each production cycle or even within the same cycle.
pg173_n0035: Deworming with proper anthelmintics every 60 – 90 days is another form of prophylaxis against intestinal worms.
pg173_n0036: All prophylactic measures should be done under the supervision or advice of a qualified veterinarian.
pg174_n0005: During the outbreaks of highly infectious diseases such as avian influenza, the movements of birds and their by-products are restricted to avoid further spread of diseases to other areas.
pg174_n0006: Likewise, sick birds should be isolated from the healthy ones to avoid the spread of the disease.
pg174_n0010: This involves practices that prevent the spread of disease-causing agents.
pg174_n0011: The following are hygienic measures which can be practised to prevent parasites and diseases in poultry:
pg174_n0015: Practise an all-in all-out system to reduce the risk of contamination.
pg174_n0016: This system requires removing all birds from a room or building then cleaning and disinfecting it before bringing in a new batch.
pg174_n0019: Prevent people from entering the brooder house or poultry premises without permission.
pg174_n0022: Provide a room at the entrance that has a special dustbin to collect waste, a place to wash hands with soap and running water, and a place to change clothes and shoes.
pg174_n0023: Footbaths should also be used and managed properly.
pg174_n0026: Everyone must change shoes when entering or leaving a poultry house.
pg174_n0029: Clean the drinkers and disinfect them at least once a week.
pg174_n0035: Control vermin, flies and other external parasites.
pg174_n0039: Proper feeding of animals with adequate feeds in terms of quality and quantity helps to prevent nutritional deficiency diseases, for example, avitaminosis.
pg174_n0040: It also prevents animals from getting weak and generally poor growth and production.
pg174_n0044: Good design of chicken house provides the best internal conditions, for example, good ventilation.
pg174_n0045: This helps to reduce the chances of occurrence of some parasites and diseases hence keeping the birds healthy.
pg174_n0047: The curative approach to manage poultry parasites and diseases:
pg174_n0049: This approach involves practices such as:
pg174_n0053: Killing of external parasites by using pesticides:
pg174_n0054: This helps to control external parasites that may cause ill health in chickens.
pg174_n0057: Treating of sick birds by application of drugs and chemicals:
pg175_n0003: infectious diseases such as fowl typhoid and cholera and prevent the spread of such diseases.
pg175_n0007: Prepare a plan for maintaining the health of chickens in a small-scale chicken farm.
pg175_n0008: This could be at your school or home.
pg175_n0009: Your plan should include steps to ensure the chickens have enough space, receive the right amount of feed, and are protected from external and internal parasites.
pg175_n0010: It should also include ways to keep the chicken house clean and fresh, and how to keep the chickens busy and happy.

pg176_n0009: In this chapter, you will learn about the management of a Day-Old Chick (DOC) to 8th week, the management of layer chickens from the 9th week to the point of laying, and the management of layer chickens from the point of laying to final culling.
pg176_n0010: In addition, you will perform various husbandry practices in the management of layer chickens.
pg176_n0011: The competencies developed will enable you to carry out chicken egg production enterprises to employ yourself, employ others or be employed and generate profitable income.
pg176_n0015: “Ensuring a daily supply of eggs for income and home consumption”
pg176_n0019: These are special chickens that have been bred for laying of eggs.
pg176_n0020: They are good at laying eggs and can lay more eggs in a year than indigenous chickens.
pg176_n0021: To carry out profitable production of eggs, it is important to carefully plan and manage their housing, feeding, and health.
pg176_n0022: It also needs to carefully think about how to collect, handle, store, and sell eggs as well as by-products from layer chickens.
pg176_n0023: Advice can be sought from your teacher, livestock extension worker or any poultry expert during the planning and running of the enterprise.
pg176_n0024: This is because always new technologies are entering the layers and the poultry sector in general.
pg176_n0026: Management of layer chickens is done in three main stages: (a) Management of Day-Old Chick (DOC) to the 8th week; (b) Management from the 9th week to the point of laying; and (c) Management from the point of laying to culling.
pg176_n0027: The practices to adhere to in each of the stages are elaborated in the following sub-sections.
pg176_n0029: Management of layer chickens from day-old chick to 8th weeks
pg176_n0031: Management of DOC to 8th-week chickens will be elaborated regarding the preparation of brooding house and brooder, and management of required temperature, ventilation, lighting, humidity, feeding, stocking rate as well as disease and parasite management.
pg177_n0003: Preparation of brooding house and brooder
pg177_n0005: This stage involves a brooding period.
pg177_n0006: The brooding period is the time interval from hatching until the chicks no longer require some artificial heat.
pg177_n0007: The brooding period is the most important and difficult stage in the management of chickens.
pg177_n0008: In this stage, chicks are normally reared in the brooder houses that have been placed away from the other stock.
pg177_n0009: It is recommended to select a brooder that is easy to use, cheap, and gets the brooding done well.
pg177_n0010: Good management has also to be adhered to at the arrival of the chicks as well as the day-to-day management of temperature and comfort to chicks.
pg177_n0012: Preparation before the arrival of chicks:
pg177_n0014: The brooder should be ready at least 2 weeks before the arrival of chicks.
pg177_n0015: This includes thorough washing and disinfecting the brooder house as well as feed and water troughs and spreading clean, dry, soft and dust-free litter material at a depth of 5 cm.
pg177_n0016: If the number of chicks is not large and it is manageable, litter material is covered with pieces of paper.
pg177_n0017: This helps the chicks to identify food early.
pg177_n0018: The paper cover should have to be changed daily for 2 – 3 days or frequently as they get soiled with droppings.
pg177_n0019: If the number of chicks is large and a relatively large area is required for a brooder, spreading paper might not be practical.
pg177_n0020: In this case, a litter material sieved to reduce dust, spread evenly and compacted to a certain extent would be used.
pg177_n0021: Heat sources should be placed in a well-prepared brooder.
pg177_n0022: Feed and water should be placed in the troughs 12 hours before the arrival of chicks.
pg177_n0023: It is advisable to supplement chicks with proper vitamins and glucose through drinking water to enable them to overcome stresses due to transport and new environment.
pg177_n0024: A veterinarian can be consulted for advice.
pg177_n0028: On arrival, remove the chicks from the box immediately.
pg177_n0029: Separate the dead chicks and those with abnormalities and dispose them.
pg177_n0030: Count and weigh the newly arrived chicks, record each necessary data, and vaccinate them against Marek’s disease if they were not vaccinated in the hatchery.
pg177_n0031: To weigh chicks, pick a few and generalise the weight for the rest.
pg177_n0033: If the chicks’ navels are not dry enough, seek advice from a veterinarian to provide a proper solution.
pg177_n0034: The general characteristics of good chicks are as follow:
pg177_n0041: Alert and curious with clean, open and bright eyes; eyes should not be dull or closed.
pg177_n0044: Dry and well-closed navel; not open or with remains of yolk.
pg177_n0047: Active and move with an upright posture; not with bent legs.
pg177_n0050: Free from any other abnormality, for example, crooked beak and stiff or bent neck.
pg178_n0003: Management of temperature and comfort for chicks
pg178_n0005: It is necessary to heat the brooder for the required period.
pg178_n0006: The actual length of time depends on the outside weather conditions as well as the rate of feathering of the birds.
pg178_n0007: Heating of the brooder should be started 12 - 48 hours before the arrival of chicks.
pg178_n0008: During this time, heater should be regulated to achieve a temperature of about 35°C when measured 5 cm above the litter at the edge or at the border of the brooder.
pg178_n0009: This temperature is adequate for the chicks on the first day.
pg178_n0011: If possible, thermometers should be used before chicks are placed in the brooder.
pg178_n0012: After the first two days, thermometers may be removed.
pg178_n0013: As chicks grow older, the temperature is reduced at the rates you have already learnt.
pg178_n0014: One should be guided by the chick’s behaviour you have learnt in the previous Chapter (refer to Figures 9.11 (a) to (d)).
pg178_n0015: These will help to regulate the heat supply or take any corrective measures.
pg178_n0016: When the chicks are fully feathered, it is no longer necessary to provide heat.
pg178_n0017: Brooder heat may be increased beyond the guidelines if chicks appear chilled especially during stress created by vaccination or beak trimming.
pg178_n0018: This will help to keep birds comfortable at all times.
pg178_n0022: Ventilation means the circulation of fresh air through the enclosed space.
pg178_n0023: Good ventilation is important for the provision of oxygen and for removing ammonia gas, carbon dioxide gas and dust from the brooder.
pg178_n0024: It also eliminates the bacteria of air-borne diseases.
pg178_n0025: The movement of air in the brooding house must be controlled in such a way that even temperature and fresh air are maintained.
pg178_n0026: This helps to meet the best conditions required by the young chicks.
pg178_n0027: Chicks are susceptible to the cold and extreme wind (draughts) and therefore must be protected.
pg178_n0028: To achieve this, curtains must be hung down the length of the walls.
pg178_n0029: The size of the opening allowed to let fresh air in the brooder house without chilling the birds will depend on the weather.
pg178_n0030: As the chicks grow older, the curtains may be opened more during the warm hours of the day and kept closed during the hot hours of the day.
pg178_n0031: The common curtains used are those made up of plastic-like materials.
pg178_n0033: Management of lighting for layer chicks
pg178_n0035: Lighting is one of the important aspects that influences successful egg production.
pg178_n0036: It should be considered as a continuous process from the day old to the end of the laying cycle.
pg178_n0037: The programme used in lighting should be related to the growing period.
pg178_n0038: This is because day length directly influences sexual maturity hence influencing egg size, particularly in early production.
pg178_n0039: During the brooding period, provide 23 hours of light for the first 2 - 3 days then provide 22 hours of light up to the third week.
pg179_n0003: Thereafter, reduce the light by 2 hours every week until 12 hours of day length are reached on the 8th week.
pg179_n0004: Light brightness should be high enough to enable chicks to easily find feed and water.
pg179_n0005: After a few days, the brightness can be reduced.
pg179_n0006: The light lighting schedule recommended during this period is shown in Table 11.1.
pg179_n0007: Lighting requirements differ depending on breed, therefore, follow the lighting programme given by the chick distributor or poultry expert.
pg179_n0008: In the open-sided houses, which are commonly used in our country, it can, however, be difficult to control the light brightness.
pg179_n0010: Table 11.1: Lighting schedule during the brooding period
pg179_n0056: The best relative humidity for the chicks is between 70% and 80%.
pg179_n0057: High humidity prevents dehydration and cannibalism.
pg179_n0058: To maintain this high humidity in the first days, it may be necessary to place a pan filled with water near the heat source or spray water against the walls and or floors to increase humidity.
pg179_n0059: As birds grow, the extra humidity brought up by the droppings and breathing out air will need to be removed by good ventilation.
pg179_n0060: Wet litter may be the result of high humidity above the recommendation.
pg179_n0061: This may result in high chances of diseases such as coccidiosis.
pg179_n0063: Management of feeding for layer chicks
pg179_n0065: The chicks should be fed chick starter mash from day one up to the 28th day (4 weeks).
pg179_n0066: The chick mash contains high contents of protein, energy, minerals, vitamins and trace elements as additives.
pg179_n0067: One plate feeder can serve 65 – 70 chicks while a hopper chick feeder serves about 40 chicks.
pg179_n0068: The starter feeds should either be commercial
pg179_im001: Ripe red tomatoes hanging on the plant
pg180_n0004: feeds from the feed companies or homemade feeds using readily available materials to minimise feed costs.
pg180_n0005: Consult poultry experts to get a good formula for the feed you wish to make at the farm.
pg180_n0006: It is better to place some feed before the chicks on plate feeders (refer to Figure 10.5 (a)) or sheets of paper until the chicks learn to eat out of hopper feeders (refer to Figure 10.5 (b)).
pg180_n0007: It is advisable to arrange feeders and drinkers in separate rows.
pg180_n0008: To enable chicks reach feed and water points easily, rows for feeders should be alternated with those of drinkers (refer to Figure 9.9).
pg180_n0009: Ensure ample room for comfort, eating and drinking.
pg180_n0010: Provide well-placed feeders that will allow 7 - 12 cm per chick for up to 8 weeks.
pg180_n0011: Use appropriate feeders for chicks at different stages of chick growth.
pg180_n0013: Drinkers should preferably be placed on raised wire platforms or boards.
pg180_n0014: A water space allowance of 1.5 cm per chick for trough-type drinkers, one round automatic drinker for 70 -100 chicks or one nipple drinker per 20 chicks should be provided.
pg180_n0015: Drinkers should be adjusted to the shoulder height of the birds to prevent litter from scratching into the water.
pg180_n0016: Drinkers should be thoroughly cleaned and the water refilled frequently.
pg180_n0017: It is advisable to disinfect the drinkers weekly.
pg180_n0018: Table 11.2 shows the maximum and minimum feed allowance and weight in relation to the age of the chicks.
pg180_n0019: This can be used to make follow-up whether the chickens are doing well or not.

pg181_n0003: Management of stocking rate for layer chicks
pg181_n0005: During the brooding period, a stocking density of 50 chicks per square metre is recommended.
pg181_n0006: When housing density is increased, feeding space must also be increased.
pg181_n0007: This is because as the chicks grow, the floor space allowance becomes small.
pg181_n0008: It is recommended to start with a floor space allowance of 64 cm² per chick during the first week and increase this allowance by 64 cm² per chick weekly until the birds are 5 - 6 weeks old.
pg181_n0010: Management of parasites and diseases for layer chicks
pg181_n0012: Follow all measures you have learnt in the previous chapter to prevent chicks from parasites and diseases.
pg181_n0013: Where diseases arise, treat the chicks immediately with the advice of a veterinarian.
pg181_n0014: Chicks must be vaccinated correctly and on schedule against Newcastle, Infectious Bursal disease (Gumboro) and Fowl pox.
pg181_n0015: The first vaccination against Marek’s disease is done at the hatchery and the rest on the farm, if necessary.
pg181_n0016: A sample of the vaccination schedule is shown in Table 11.3.
pg181_n0047: Drinking water, oral drenching or eye drop
pg181_n0061: Drinking water, oral drenching or eye drop
pg181_n0082: Drinking water, oral drenching or eye drop
pg182_n0003: Chicks may be given coccidiostats either through feed or water where there is a high risk of coccidiosis.
pg182_n0004: Start it in the third week as a continuous prophylactic programme.
pg182_n0005: Deworm the chicks with proper anthelmintics every 60 – 90 days to prevent intestinal worms.
pg182_n0006: All of these measures should be done under the advice of a qualified veterinarian.
pg182_n0007: Moreover, follow all the hygienic measures you have learnt in the previous chapter.

pg182_n0019: Management of layer chickens from the 9th week to the point of laying
pg182_n0021: This stage is known as the growing period and the chickens in this stage are called pullets or growers.
pg182_n0022: The management of growers greatly determines the performance in the laying stage.
pg182_n0023: Therefore, ensure good management of growers in aspects of housing, stocking rate, feeding, lighting, as well as parasite and disease management.
pg182_n0024: Other aspects of grower management include culling and beak trimming.
pg182_n0028: In large poultry farms, growers have to be transferred from the brooding house to the growing house at the age of 4 – 6 weeks.
pg182_n0029: However, in small and medium poultry farms, the common practice is to use the same house for brooding and growing pullets.
pg182_n0030: The average for birds on litter floors is 8 - 10 birds per square metre.
pg182_n0031: The house should have good ventilation.
pg182_n0032: A favourable temperature of about 24°C has also to be maintained.
pg182_n0033: If layers are later to be reared in a battery cage system, pullets must be transferred to cages at 16 weeks of age.
pg182_n0035: During the growing period, litter should contain between 20 and 30% moisture.
pg182_n0036: This moisture content is important for better feathering, improved feed use, normal growth, reduced ammonia level in the house and control of some diseases, for example, coccidiosis.
pg182_n0037: The condition of the litter can be determined by holding it.
pg183_n0003: Pick up a handful of litter and squeeze it tightly then open the hand.
pg183_n0004: If the condition of the litter is alright, crevices will form in the compressed material.
pg183_n0005: It will not form a cohesive ball or fall away in a pile.
pg183_n0006: If possible, special devices can be used for determining the moisture percentage in the litter.
pg183_n0007: Pullets which are later intended to be raised in deep litter-laying houses have to be provided with properly placed perches.
pg183_n0011: At the growing stage, the feed is changed from chick starter to grower mash until the chickens start laying by 3%.
pg183_n0012: Grower mash is poor in energy and low in protein compared to chick mash.
pg183_n0013: This aims to control the growth rate of the growers.

pg183_n0016: The daily feed allowance is provided twice a day to control selection and encourage feed intake.
pg183_n0017: This should be done at the same time every day.
pg183_n0018: They should be given 60% of their feed in the morning and 40% in the afternoon.
pg183_n0019: Sick birds and those which have just undergone vaccination or beak trimming should be fed without restriction until they feel better.

pg184_n0003: Follow-up of pullet growth progress should be done.

pg184_n0005: If on weekly weighing the birds are too heavy then the daily feed allowance should be reduced.
pg184_n0006: If pullets are too light, the daily allowance should be increased.
pg184_n0007: Pullets should be provided with vitamin supplements after weekly weight measurements to help them overcome stress.
pg184_n0008: Changing of type of feed must be done by introducing new feed slowly while reducing the former.
pg184_n0009: For example, changing from chick starter to grower mash can be done as follows:

pg184_n0020: Pullets need to be provided with enough space to reach the feed.
pg184_n0021: Where restricted feeding is practised, enough feeders must be provided.
pg184_n0022: This helps all birds to eat at the same time when the feed is provided.
pg184_n0023: When feeding space is inadequate, the aggressive birds would eat more feed than the docile ones.
pg184_n0024: The height of the feeder should be adjusted in such a way that the bottom of the trough is at an even level with the backs of the birds.
pg184_n0025: When the level is lower, birds peck out more feed which is wastage.
pg184_n0027: In addition, pullets should be provided with water all the time.
pg184_n0028: An adequate number of drinkers should be provided and arranged properly in the pullet house.
pg184_n0029: A 10-litre round plastic drinker can serve up to 50 pullets.
pg184_n0030: The water requirement for pullets is twice as much as feed intake, and even more for temperatures above 21.5°C.
pg184_n0031: Drinkers should accordingly be adjusted as you have already learnt (in chick management).
pg184_n0032: Drinkers should thoroughly be cleaned and the water refilled frequently.
pg184_n0036: Growers are raised such that they don’t get extra light until 13 weeks of age.
pg184_n0037: This is done to control or set sexual maturity to the intended period.
pg184_n0038: After 13 weeks, light is gradually increased to 16 hours per day (refer to Table 11.5).
pg184_n0039: This encourages sexual maturity and sets the point of laying at 17 - 18 weeks.
pg184_n0040: A 3-watt/m<math><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math> light brightness is enough for this purpose.
pg184_n0041: Too bright light is not recommended.
pg184_n0042: You have to determine daylight for your local area to use artificial light to complete the required light schedule, if necessary.
pg184_n0043: Light (either natural or artificial), affects the pituitary gland at the base of the brain, and the stimulation causes mature pullets to begin the production of eggs.

pg185_n0083: Parasite and disease management in layer growers
pg185_n0085: The hygienic measures you have learnt in previous sections should be observed throughout the growing of the birds.
pg185_n0086: Continue with the vaccination programme required in the growing stage.
pg185_n0087: These include the Newcastle vaccine given every 75 – 90 days and the Fowl pox vaccine administered on the 10th week of age.
pg185_n0088: The use of prophylactics to control parasites and diseases should be continued during the growing period with the advice of a qualified veterinarian.
pg185_n0089: Likewise, regular deworming every 60 - 90 days by using proper anthelmintics should be continued with the advice of a qualified veterinarian.
pg185_n0090: Proper litter management should be observed, for example, removing wet spots around the drinkers and replacing them with clean dry litter to reduce the build-up of coccidiosis disease-causing agents.
pg185_n0091: This has to be done together with efforts to reduce water spillage from drinkers.
pg185_n0095: This is an act of reducing the beak of a bird by a properly trained person.
pg185_n0096: It is also termed as debeaking.
pg185_n0097: It is done to avoid egg eating, cannibalism, and other vices.
pg185_n0098: It is also done to avoid spilling the feeds from the feeders.
pg185_n0099: It can be done using an electric debeaker or manual debeaker (refer to Figures 11.1 (a) and (b)).
pg185_n0100: Usually, less than a third of the upper beak is trimmed.

pg186_n0008: In case of overgrowth, the debeaking exercise has to be conducted.
pg186_n0009: It is advisable to trim beaks when birds are about 10 – 12 weeks of age, that is, before laying.
pg186_n0010: Beak trimming at this age causes less stress to birds and beaks will not regrow much.

pg186_n0020: They may harbour and transmit diseases, they occupy spaces which can be used by good layers, and they consume feeds causing high feed costs unnecessarily.
pg186_n0021: Therefore, weekly culling should be done on inferior, crippled, injured and deformed layers.

pg188_n0005: Management of layer chickens from the point of laying to final culling
pg188_n0007: Birds are placed in a laying house just before the onset of the laying period.
pg188_n0008: Laying starts at the age of 17 - 20 weeks.
pg188_n0009: Laying lasts for 12 to 14 months for optimal production.
pg188_n0010: During this period, the important management aspects that should be observed are feeding, provision of water, ventilation, parasites and disease management.
pg188_n0011: It also involves adhering to hygiene and biosecurity measures as discussed in previous chapters.
pg188_n0012: In the case of the cage system, the birds are introduced to the cages a few days before the onset of the laying period.
pg188_n0013: This is to make them familiarize themselves with the new confinement.
pg188_n0015: The housing of mature layer chickens
pg188_n0017: Continue following the housing management aspects you have already learnt especially maintenance of cleanliness.
pg188_n0018: Also, provide the chickens with laying nests, proper living space as well as lighting and ventilation.
pg188_n0021: Laying boxes are also termed as laying nests.
pg188_n0022: They are to be placed in the laying house well before the hens are brought in, preferably in 16th week.
pg188_n0023: The nest boxes should be provided with plenty of good clean litter such as wood shavings or other nesting materials to avoid cracking of eggs.
pg188_n0024: They should also be placed at relatively lower heights compared to perches.
pg188_n0025: This will discourage chickens from using them to roost and also preventing chickens and eggs from becoming dirty.
pg188_n0027: The stocking rate for mature layer chickens:
pg188_n0028: At this stage, the stocking rate should be maintained at 4 - 5 birds per m² in a deep litter system.
pg188_n0029: In the case of battery cages, it is better not to keep more than 12 birds per cage.
pg188_n0030: Typically, you can keep 2 – 10 hens per cage, which can be equated to 18 hens per m².
pg188_n0032: Lighting and ventilation for mature layer chickens:
pg188_n0033: For optimal laying, layers should be provided with lighting for 16 hours daily up to the final culling.
pg188_n0034: Therefore, layers should be provided with artificial light for some hours.
pg188_n0035: The hours of artificial light should be determined by the length of daylight in a given area.
pg188_n0036: Likewise, the houses for laying birds should be well-ventilated to allow air circulation.
pg189_n0005: Feed the birds twice a day using appropriate feed and feeders placed at a distance to allow free movement in case of a deep litter system.
pg189_n0006: A laying bird requires to be fed an appropriate amount of layers mash per day depending on the heaviness of the breed.
pg189_n0007: Light breeds (110 – 115 g/birds/day), medium breeds (120 g/bird/day), and heavy breeds (130 – 140 g/bird/day).
pg189_n0008: Layers should also be provided with cool and clean water throughout the day (ad libitum).
pg189_n0009: Check if water consumption is normal because if there is any problem with the flock, consumption is reduced.
pg189_n0013: During this period, there are two kinds of culling.
pg189_n0014: These are the culling of non-laying birds after the laying peak and the culling of the laying flock after the economic laying is completed.
pg189_n0016: Culling of non-laying birds after the laying peak:
pg189_n0017: Culling of non-laying birds involves identifying and removing non-laying birds from the flock.
pg189_n0018: Properly reared layers reach the laying peak one month after laying begins, however, it may take up to 2 months when birds are not well maintained.
pg189_n0019: Peak can be around 24 weeks of age when laying is 90% or more.
pg189_n0020: There are several characteristics which can be used to identify non-laying hens from the laying ones.
pg189_n0021: The identification exercise for this purpose has to be carried out by an experienced poultry expert.
pg189_n0022: It is also advisable to isolate the identified non-laying birds for some days.
pg189_n0023: This helps the poultry farmer to check if those birds are truly not laying eggs.
pg189_n0024: The culling exercise can disturb the flock thereby lowering egg production.
pg189_n0025: To minimise this negative effect on the flock, culling exercises should be practised at night.
pg189_n0027: Culling of the laying flock after the economic laying is completed:
pg189_n0028: From the 24th week of age, well-managed layers are expected to lay productively for 12 – 14 months.
pg189_n0029: After this period, laying will have dropped to 50%.
pg189_n0030: At this stage, it is no longer economical to continue keeping the birds.
pg189_n0031: Unless the egg prices are very high or you feed a very cheap feed, you should cull them and replace the flock.
pg189_n0032: The economic laying is 60% or above.
pg189_n0033: The culling processes may start from the 10th month of the laying period.
pg189_n0034: This will allow the elimination of non-productive chickens and reducing the management of non-laying hens.

pg191_n0003: Handling and value addition of table eggs
pg191_n0005: Handling and adding value to table eggs involves several important aspects.
pg191_n0006: First, eggs are collected from egg-laying hens.
pg191_n0007: Egg producers should follow local regulations and practices.
pg191_n0008: Next, eggs are inspected for quality and defects.
pg191_n0009: Grading is done based on quality, size, and weight.
pg191_n0010: Eggs are then carefully packaged in cartons or trays, and labelled with relevant information.
pg191_n0011: Proper storage is crucial to maintain the freshness and quality of the eggs, depending on the desired storage duration.
pg191_n0012: It is important to handle eggs safely to prevent foodborne illnesses.
pg191_n0015: In the poultry farm/unit, it is advised to collect eggs from the laying house at least twice a day (early morning and late afternoon).
pg191_n0016: This practice helps to prevent dirtying and breakage of eggs.
pg191_n0017: It also reduces the chances of contamination and egg eating.
pg191_n0020: Inspection of eggs is done to identify and remove dirty eggs, wrinkled shells and cracked the ones from the normal ones (refer to Figures 11.5 (a) to (d)).
pg191_im002_seg001_v1_crop_v1: Normal white egg with a smooth, clean shell.
pg191_im002_seg002_v1_crop_v1: Normal brown egg with a smooth, unbroken shell.
pg191_im003: White egg in a tray with visible shell cracks.
pg191_im004: Several wrinkled eggs with rough, uneven shells.
pg191_im005: Dirty eggs in a tray with stained and soiled shells.
pg192_n0003: If it is necessary to clean dirty/soiled eggs, a piece of cloth, soaked in warm water can be used to wipe gently the surface of the egg shells.
pg192_n0004: However, as much as it is possible, the need for cleaning should be minimal.
pg192_n0005: This means it is easier to maintain a clean environment where eggs are to be laid than to clean soiled eggs.
pg192_n0006: This can be achieved by cleaning the nest boxes and by keeping a supply of fresh bedding as often as possible.
pg192_n0007: Cleanliness of eggs can also be achieved by placing perches higher than the nest boxes.
pg192_n0008: This is because chickens like to roost in the highest part of the house that they can access.
pg192_n0009: Therefore, perches being higher than nest boxes will discourage them from roosting in and soiling their boxes.
pg192_n0012: Grading is a practice adopted in places where eggs are sold by class.
pg192_n0013: Eggs are classified by weight and in some markets, the shell colour is added to the value.
pg192_n0014: In this case, brown eggs are preferred to the white ones.
pg192_n0015: You can grade your eggs according to size and colour if the market demands so.
pg192_n0018: There are many ways of packaging eggs for the market.
pg192_n0019: In all forms of packaging, the principal requirement is to ensure that the eggs remain wholesome throughout the transit to the market, and when in shelves in the market.
pg192_n0020: It is recommended that eggs should be packed in special egg trays such as those shown in Figures 11.6 (a) to (d).
pg192_n0021: When eggs are packed for the formal market, the package should indicate the following:
pg192_n0031: Number of eggs inside the carton; and
pg192_n0034: Name of source (farm name and address).
pg192_im002_seg001_v1_crop1: Open six-egg carton with six brown eggs arranged in a moulded paper tray.
pg192_im002_seg002_v1: Closed moulded paper carton for packaging six eggs.
pg192_im003: Open ten-egg carton with ten white eggs in a moulded paper tray.
pg193_im002: Open carton containing 12 white eggs in a 12-egg package.
pg193_im003: Tray containing 30 white eggs arranged in a 30-egg package.
pg193_n0007: Eggs going to the market must have acceptable shapes and sizes.
pg193_n0008: An acceptable shape is that of a pear shape, clearly showing the broad and narrow ends of the egg (refer to Figure 11.5(a)).
pg193_n0009: When stacking eggs in trays, the broad end should always be uppermost.
pg193_n0010: This allows for the air cell to remain at the top side.
pg193_n0011: In addition, the narrow tip is usually thicker and stronger and it helps in supporting the weight of the egg.
pg193_n0015: The egg storage room or area should be clean, free of strong smells and away from rodents.
pg193_n0016: Eggs can be maintained in good condition at a temperature of 10°C or lower.
pg193_n0017: However, the exact storage condition will depend on the length of storage required.
pg193_n0018: For less than 7 days, table eggs can be stored in a cool room where temperatures do not exceed 20°C.
pg193_n0019: When the temperature in the egg storage room or area is above 20°C, serious loss of egg quality and weight occurs.
pg193_n0020: For 6 – 8 weeks, table eggs should be kept in temperatures around 8 - 10°C and a relative humidity of 85%.
pg193_n0024: Table eggs are sold for direct human consumption or used in cooking and baking.
pg193_n0025: Before starting production, it is important to identify the market for the eggs thoroughly.
pg193_n0026: To achieve this, you should search for important information which will enable you to make informed decisions about the marketing of your table eggs.
pg193_n0027: The following are some key aspects you will need to work on:
pg193_n0031: You should be familiar with different middlemen involved in the egg business.
pg193_n0032: Marketing middlemen are like helpers who connect egg producers to people who want to buy eggs.
pg193_n0033: They can be wholesalers, retailers, agents, or brokers.
pg193_n0034: Wholesalers buy eggs in large quantities from producers and sell them in bulk to retailers.
pg193_n0035: Retailers sell eggs in smaller quantities to consumers.
pg193_n0036: Middlemen store and transport eggs, promote them, and make it easier for people to buy eggs.
pg194_n0003: They also help producers to understand what people want and make decisions about selling eggs.
pg194_n0004: Understanding these middlemen will help you to identify potential buyers and distribution channels for your table eggs.
pg194_n0007: When selling table eggs, you need to know where and how to sell them.
pg194_n0008: This includes selling at local markets or to businesses that sell eggs to shops, restaurants, and hotels.
pg194_n0009: It is also important to make sure that the eggs are of good quality, stored properly, packaged and labelled correctly.
pg194_n0010: Some markets may require eggs of a specific grade.
pg194_n0013: When selling table eggs, it is important to understand what customers want.
pg194_n0014: This can be done through market research, which involves asking questions or observing people to learn about their preferences and trends.
pg194_n0015: For example, you can ask people how much they are willing to pay for eggs, what kind of packaging they like, and who they think the target market for eggs is.
pg194_n0016: By understanding what customers like, you can make your marketing strategies better.
pg194_n0019: Marketing strategies help business people to promote table eggs effectively.
pg194_n0020: Here are some simple explanations of key marketing strategies you can use:
pg194_n0025: This means finding something special about your eggs that makes them different from others.
pg194_n0026: It could be the way they are produced or their special qualities.
pg194_n0027: For example, if your eggs come from free-range chickens or organic eggs, you can highlight that as your unique selling proposition.
pg194_n0030: Creating a strong brand identity for your eggs:
pg194_n0031: Creating a strong brand identity means giving your eggs a recognisable and memorable image.
pg194_n0032: This can include a logo, packaging design, and a catchy name.
pg194_n0033: When people see your brand, they should instantly know it is your eggs.
pg194_n0037: This involves using digital platforms such as social media to promote your eggs.
pg194_n0038: You can create a social media marketing platform(s) where people can learn about your eggs and place orders.
pg194_n0039: Social media platforms such as Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook can help you reach a wider audience.
pg194_n0042: Participating in local markets and events:
pg194_n0043: Participating in local markets and events allows you to showcase and sell your eggs directly to customers.
pg194_n0044: It is a great way to connect with the community and build relationships with customers.
pg194_n0048: Partnering with local businesses or restaurants can help you expand your reach.
pg194_n0049: For example, you can supply your eggs to local bakeries, restaurants or street food vendors, and they can use them in their recipes.
pg194_n0050: In this way, more people will get to taste your eggs.
pg195_n0003: (f) Building good customer relationships and service: Building good relationships with customers and providing excellent customer service is crucial for long-term success.
pg195_n0004: This means being friendly, responsive, and attentive to customer needs.
pg195_n0005: Happy customers are more likely to come back and recommend your eggs to others.

pg195_n0009: Record keeping is a process by which information is systematically collected, organised and stored.
pg195_n0010: Layer chicken production can be a highly competitive business which involves high capital for investment and high risks as well.
pg195_n0011: For the success of the enterprise, as the owner, you have to record all the farming activities from the beginning to the end of the laying cycle and do some analysis.
pg195_n0012: This will enable you to determine how your enterprise is performing, for example, to identify problems and solve them before it is too late.
pg195_n0013: It also helps you to control your cash and plan for the future.
pg195_n0014: Records for aspects such as mortality, egg production, feed consumption, growth rate, treatments or medication, expenditures and revenues must be kept daily.
pg195_n0018: There is a wide range of information required to be kept in layer production.

pg199_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn about the management of broiler chickens from DOC to slaughter point and handling, value addition and marketing of broiler chicken products.
pg199_n0011: You will also perform various husbandry practices in the production of broiler chickens.
pg199_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to carry out broiler chicken production enterprises to employ yourself, employ others or be employed and generate profitable income.
pg199_n0015: “The bird that produces a kilogram of the best meat in one month”
pg199_n0017: Management of broiler chickens from DOC to slaughter point
pg199_n0019: Chickens that are raised specifically for meat are termed broilers.
pg199_n0020: Commercial broilers are preferably raised from day one up to 3 - 8 weeks of age when they attain market weight (1.5 - 2 kg).
pg199_n0021: The type of chicken breed you should keep depends on your area’s demand and the availability of the DOC.
pg199_n0022: The weight of the chicken you want to sell should also be based on market demand.
pg199_n0023: The larger the chicken, the more it can be sold, as it provides more meat.
pg199_n0025: Management of brooder for broiler chickens
pg199_n0027: Prepare the brooding house for the DOC well before the arrival of the chicks in a similar way as that of raising layer chicks.
pg199_n0028: During the rearing period, provide 23 hours of light and 1 hour of darkness so that they are not stressed in case of power failure.
pg199_n0029: The preferred stocking rate is 10 - 12 birds per m2 for the birds expected to grow to about 1.5 - 2.5 kg market weight.
pg199_n0030: The birds are fed ad libitum throughout the rearing period.
pg200_n0005: Broilers can be fed by using one of these two programmes:
pg200_n0010: Three feed types feeding schedule: This schedule involves feeding the birds with three types of feeds at different stages.
pg200_n0011: These are broiler starter crumbles or mash, broiler grower pellets or mash and broiler finisher pellets or mash.
pg200_n0012: These feeds have to be fed as follow:
pg200_n0016: Broiler starter crumble/mash from day one up to day 14 (2 weeks).
pg200_n0019: Broiler grower pellet/mash from week three to week four.
pg200_n0022: Broiler finisher pellet/mash from week 5 to marketing weight.
pg200_n0026: Two feed types feeding schedule: This schedule involves feeding the birds with two types of feeds.
pg200_n0027: These are broiler starter crumbles and broiler finisher pellets/mash.
pg200_n0028: These feeds have to be fed as follow:
pg200_n0032: Broiler starter crumble from day one up to day 21, and
pg200_n0035: Finisher pellets from day 22 up to market point.
pg200_n0037: Such feeds may be either commercial feeds from the feed companies or homemade feeds using local ingredients/materials available by using local mixing methods to minimise feed costs.
pg200_n0038: But, make sure you get assistance from a feed expert to get a good formula for the feed you wish to formulate.
pg200_n0039: Provide vitamins and minerals to the chickens to avoid nutritional disorders.
pg200_n0041: Each feeding schedule has its advantages and challenges.
pg200_n0042: The first schedule (starter, grower, and finisher type of feed) ensures a balanced growth and development of the chickens, but it can be more expensive.
pg200_n0043: The second schedule (starter and finisher without grower type of feed) can be less expensive, but it might not provide the same level of nutrients for the chickens to grow and develop properly.
pg200_n0047: Birds should be provided with the least amount of floor space necessary to the greatest return on investment.
pg200_n0048: The larger birds require more floor space than the smaller ones.
pg200_n0049: The optimum stocking rates vary with the size of the bird to be marketed.
pg200_n0050: For example, if the farmer is to sell small-sized birds of 1.4 kg in weight, there is a possibility of raising more birds in a unit area than raising large birds of 2.3 Kg.

pg203_n0004: Slaughtering is done by cutting off the head either partially or fully severed from the neck.
pg203_n0005: It is a good practice to hold the chicken in a slaughtering cone with the head hanging out from the narrow end of the cone (refer to Figure 12.1).
pg203_n0006: The cone helps a chicken from struggling violently after slaughtering.
pg203_n0007: The person slaughtering the chicken grabs the head of the chicken while firmly pressing his thumb at the point between the head and the neck.

pg203_n0009: The chicken is left in the killing cone for at least 5 minutes for thorough bleeding.

pg203_n0016: First, you put the chicken in hot water.
pg203_n0018: Then, you take off the feathers.

pg203_n0023: The other way is wet plucking where you use hot water before taking off the feathers.
pg203_n0024: After all the feathers are off, you take out the internal organs and the legs.
pg203_n0025: Then, you wash the chicken well.

pg209_im003: Chapter Thirteen: Management of indigenous and dual-purpose hybrid chickens.
pg209_n0006: Management of indigenous and dual-purpose hybrid chickens
pg209_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn about the specific management of indigenous and dual-purpose hybrid chickens.
pg209_n0011: You will also perform various husbandry practices in the production of indigenous and dual-purpose chickens.
pg209_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to carry out indigenous and dual-purpose hybrid chicken production enterprises to employ yourself, employ others or be employed and generate profitable income.
pg209_n0015: “Thriving under poor conditions yet providing you with meat and eggs”
pg209_n0019: Indigenous chickens produce both eggs and meat.
pg209_n0020: These chickens do well in their natural environment because they can adapt easily.
pg209_n0021: They need basic care such as proper housing and feeding.
pg209_n0022: It is important to check on them regularly to manage breeding or mating as well as parasites and diseases.
pg209_n0023: Indigenous chicken farming helps the local economy by creating opportunities for farmers and the community to earn money.
pg209_n0027: Indigenous chickens need a good house to live in, just like other chickens.
pg209_n0028: The house should be in a good location, have the right size, and be made of the right materials.
pg209_n0029: It is important to make a good plan or design for the house.

pg210_n0048: Outline the lessons you have learnt from this activity.
pg210_n0050: Although most households keep indigenous chickens in free range, the most convenient system to raise indigenous chickens is a semi-intensive system.
pg210_n0051: This means having a small house for them to sleep in at night, and a space for them to run around during the day.
pg210_n0052: A square metre can accommodate 8 chickens.
pg210_n0053: If the house is provided with perches, a square metre can accommodate more chickens.
pg210_n0054: An ideal house for indigenous chickens should be constructed on well-drained soils if it is not to be lifted off the ground.
pg210_n0055: The house should have open sides with solid walls that cover about one-third of the wall.
pg210_n0056: It should have good ventilation but protect the chickens from strong winds.
pg210_n0057: The roof should be strong to prevent rain from entering the house.
pg210_n0058: Lastly, the house should be designed to keep vermin and predators out.
pg210_n0059: It is advisable to use locally available construction materials.
pg210_n0060: The house should be provided with properly managed laying nests and perches.
pg210_n0061: Make sure there is some good grass in the runs for chickens to eat.
pg211_n0005: These chickens need to search for their food and water.
pg211_n0006: In this way, chickens can meet some of their daily needs.
pg211_n0007: However, they can only meet one-third of their daily requirements.
pg211_n0008: As a result, they grow slowly and produce less meat and eggs.
pg211_n0009: Supplementing with a balanced ration helps them to grow faster and produce more.
pg211_n0010: Indigenous chickens also require clean water all day for their health.
pg211_n0014: Under the guidance of your teacher/livestock expert, formulate a simple rations to supplement local indigenous chickens in your school.
pg211_n0015: (Consider the resources available in your environment)
pg211_n0017: Make a list of ways that can be used to give extra feed to the local chickens in a sustainable manner.
pg211_n0021: Outline the lessons you have learnt from this activity.
pg211_n0023: Chicken farmers should give adequate feed to the birds to make them healthier.
pg211_n0024: The indigenous chickens need to have adequate feed every day.
pg211_n0025: One can plan better feeding programmes.
pg211_n0026: Use the available resources on the farm to make simple rations for the birds.
pg211_n0027: If pulse and cereal grains are grown together on the farms, one can make extra rations for the birds.
pg211_n0028: For example, sorghum, maize, and millet can provide energy, while pigeon peas and cowpeas can provide protein for the birds.
pg211_n0029: In areas where paddy or maize is grown, by-products such as brans for the bird’s rations can be used.
pg211_n0030: Another way to give extra feed, especially protein to the chickens, is by growing earthworms, edible larvae, and insects such as ants and cockroaches.
pg211_n0031: You can feed these to the chickens together with cereal grains or cereal by-products.
pg211_n0032: Indigenous chickens can also be given good food leftovers from the farmers’ meals.
pg211_n0034: Parasite and disease management in indigenous chickens
pg211_n0036: Indigenous chickens are tough and can resist many parasites and diseases.
pg211_n0037: However, if not cared for, they can still fall sick, especially when searching for food.
pg211_n0038: For example, Newcastle disease can kill more than 60% of chickens in the dry seasons.
pg211_n0039: Parasites do not usually kill the chickens, but they can lower their productivity.
pg211_n0045: find out the common parasites and diseases that can attack indigenous chickens.
pg212_n0004: (b) Identify measures that can be taken to manage or prevent them.
pg212_n0005: These measures should be sustainable, meaning that they are effective, affordable and can be used over a long period.
pg212_n0006: Consider factors such as the chicken’s environment, feeds and feeding, and routine care when coming up with these measures.
pg212_n0008: 2. Based on your findings in tasks 1 and 2, write down a plan to manage parasites and diseases for your indigenous chickens.
pg212_n0009: Explain why you chose the measures in your plan and how they can help to manage or prevent the parasites and diseases you identified.
pg212_n0011: 3. Reflect on what you have learnt from this activity and how you can apply them in the future.
pg212_n0014: The more you understand about parasite and disease management in indigenous chickens, the better you can care for these chickens.
pg212_n0015: If you provide good housing and food for the chickens, they can be healthier.
pg212_n0016: Most importantly, you can protect them from deadly diseases, for example, Newcastle and Fowl pox by giving them vaccines.
pg212_n0017: These vaccines have been shown to work well against viral diseases.
pg212_n0018: It is also advisable to deworm all the chickens.
pg212_n0019: This can reduce problems caused by intestinal parasites and diseases.
pg212_n0020: Also, it can improve the chickens’ performance.
pg212_n0021: You can control external parasites such as mites and fleas with proper pesticides.
pg212_n0022: To get rid of these parasites, you should also spray the chicken house, especially hidden spots.
pg212_n0023: You can control diseases in other ways too.
pg212_n0024: You could buy healthy flocks from clean farms, keep high hygiene standards, avoid using contaminated or mouldy feeds, dispose of dead birds properly, and treat sick birds early.
pg212_n0028: A good breeding plan can help to improve the meat and egg quality of indigenous chickens.
pg212_n0029: Breeding is a complex process that requires specialised knowledge and skills.
pg212_n0030: In this section, you will focus on the basic process of mating hens and cocks, and managing the incubation of eggs.
pg212_n0032: Mating of indigenous chickens: It is advisable to use the best cocks and hens for the production of eggs for the next group of chicks, based on what the farmer wants to achieve. The farmer should have at least one cock for every ten hens. In this way, most of the eggs will be fertilised and thus will be able to hatch into chicks.
pg212_n0034: Indigenous chickens take about 7 to 8 months to grow and be ready for meat.
pg212_n0035: They lay about 40 to 60 eggs in a year.
pg212_n0036: If new traits from foreign breeds are introduced into the flock, the local chickens’ performance can double.
pg212_n0037: To get more and better eggs and
pg213_n0003: meat, you can use exotic cocks to mate with the local hens.
pg213_n0004: For better egg production, egg production breeds such as White Leghorn and Ancona can be crossed with the indigenous hens.
pg213_n0005: For better meat production, meat breeds, for example, Cornish and New Hampshire can be used.
pg213_n0006: Crossbreds which are the resulting offspring are always better than the original parents in terms of egg production or meat quantity.
pg213_n0007: When new cocks are used, the local cocks should be kept under control.
pg213_n0011: Fertilised eggs can be incubated by a broody hen or egg incubators.
pg213_n0012: Chicken eggs take 21 days to hatch into chicks.
pg213_n0013: The eggs used for hatching should be fresh and not more than ten days from when it was hatched.
pg213_n0014: They should be stored in a cool place where the temperature does not exceed 20oC.
pg213_n0015: If the temperature is higher than 20oC, the eggs should not be stored for more than five days before being incubated.
pg213_n0017: To incubate chicken eggs successfully, it is important to use eggs that are of normal size and shape for the type of chicken involved.
pg213_n0018: The shell of the egg should be undamaged, with no scratches or cracks.
pg213_n0019: If the shell is cracked, the egg might lose moisture which could cause the developing chick to die before it hatches.
pg213_n0020: It could also let in germs which later make the chick unhealthy or even cause it to die before it hatches.
pg213_n0022: About a week after incubation starts, you need to check whether the eggs are fertile or not.
pg213_n0023: This means to check if eggs have a chick growing inside.
pg213_n0024: You can do this by using a method called candling.
pg213_n0025: Candling is when you hold the egg up to a bright light in a dark room.
pg213_n0026: To see if the egg is fertilised, shine a light on it in a dark room.
pg213_n0027: If the egg is fertilised, you will see a dark spot in the middle with lines like a spider’s web around it.
pg213_n0028: If the egg is not fertilised, you will only see the shadow of the yellow part of the egg called the yolk, and no spider-web lines (refer to Figure 13.1 (a) and (b)).

pg214_n0033: Eggs from indigenous chickens are collected and kept on clean trays.
pg214_n0034: If trays are not available, they can be collected in baskets or plastic containers which let air pass through.
pg214_n0035: If required, the eggs are graded based on external quality factors such as shape, texture and size.
pg214_n0036: Once graded, eggs should be stored properly to maintain their quality.
pg214_n0037: Eggs should be properly packed and distributed to customers.
pg214_n0038: For meat, chickens should be sold alive or slaughtered at the appropriate age depending on the needs of the market.
pg214_n0039: The meat is then processed and packaged for distribution and sale.
pg214_n0040: Since indigenous chickens have no uniform characteristics as exotic broilers, it is better to sell them alive or as whole chickens.
pg214_n0041: All measures to meet customers’ needs, quality of the product and safety should be properly observed.
pg214_n0045: Keeping records is very important in indigenous chicken production.
pg214_n0046: Just like with other chickens, it is necessary to keep proper records.

pg216_n0039: This section deals with chickens which are crossbreds between indigenous chickens and superior cocks for meat or egg production and dual-purpose hybrids.
pg216_n0040: These chickens are specifically designed to be suitable for both meat and egg production.
pg217_n0003: These chickens can be raised in normal environments just like indigenous chickens.
pg217_n0004: These chickens can be reared in all systems of poultry farming, that is, intensive, semi-intensive, and extensive or free-range.
pg217_n0005: Examples of dual-purpose hybrid chickens are as follow:
pg217_n0007: (a) Sasso: This is a hybrid chicken that is a crossbreed between indigenous hens and a superior meat cock.
pg217_n0008: Sasso can be reared for meat and egg production.
pg217_n0009: If reared for meat and given fattening feed, they can weigh more than 2.5 kg within 70 - 90 days.
pg217_n0010: If reared for eggs, they start laying eggs at the age of 20 weeks and can lay up to 240 eggs throughout their laying period.
pg217_n0012: (b) Kuroiler: These are hybrid chickens bred after crossing indigenous hens and a superior egg-laying cock.
pg217_n0013: Kuroiler is also reared for meat and eggs.
pg217_n0014: If reared for eggs, these chickens can lay 190 – 250 eggs within 30 months.
pg217_n0015: Kuroiler starts laying eggs at just 5 months, unlike the local chickens which start laying eggs at 6 months.
pg217_n0016: Kuroiler lays for 2 years if well taken care of.
pg217_n0017: Kuroilers are also good for meat because the cocks can reach a weight of up to 5 kg and the hens can reach between 3.5 to 4 kg.
pg217_n0019: (c) Tanbro: These chickens grow quickly and have large bodies compared to local chickens, making them very good for meat.
pg217_n0020: If reared for eggs, these chickens can lay 180 - 220 eggs within 81 weeks.
pg217_n0021: Tanbro starts laying eggs at 19 - 21 weeks of age.
pg217_n0022: Tanbro is also good for meat because the pullets can reach a weight of up to 1.5 kg within 7 weeks and 2 kg within 9 weeks and the cocks can reach 4 kg if well cared for.
pg217_n0023: These have good disease resistance compared to meat or egg chickens.
pg217_n0025: In Tanzania, there are several kinds of dual-purpose hybrid chickens.
pg217_n0026: Whichever you choose to raise depends on what you want to achieve and what the people in your area need.
pg217_n0027: To choose the right hybrid, you should think about where you live and what type of chicken people like.
pg217_n0028: It is advisable to ask livestock extension workers and/or experienced poultry farmers for opinions.
pg217_n0030: Looking after dual-purpose hybrid chickens is not much different from taking care of other types of chickens.
pg217_n0031: The main difference is in feeding them.
pg217_n0032: This depends on whether you are raising them for their meat or eggs.
pg217_n0033: The feeding schedule when raised for meat is as follows:
pg217_n0035: (a) From day 1 to 18, or until they weigh 400 grams, give them broiler starter crumble.
pg217_n0036: If they reach 400 grams before day 18, start feeding broiler grower pellets.
pg218_n0005: From day 19 to 35, feed them broiler grower pellets.
pg218_n0008: From day 36 until they are sold, feed them broiler finisher pellets.
pg218_n0010: The feeding schedule for dual-purpose hybrid chickens raised for eggs is as follows:
pg218_n0014: For the first 2 weeks, feed them with broiler starter crumble.
pg218_n0017: From 2 to 10 weeks, switch to layer starter mash.
pg218_n0020: From 10 to 4 months, feed them with layer grower mash.
pg218_n0021: This is a period when the chickens start laying.
pg218_n0024: At 5 months, feed them with a complete layer mash until final culling.
pg218_n0028: It is important to monitor the bird’s health and adjust the feeding schedule as needed.
pg218_n0029: Sometimes, commercial dual-purpose chicken feed is available and cheaper.
pg218_n0030: This can reduce your cost of production.

pg220_n0009: In this chapter, you will learn about the general importance of duck production, breeds of ducks as well as management of ducks with respect to housing, feeding, parasites and diseases, mating/breeding, handling and marketing of duck products.
pg220_n0010: The competencies developed will enable you to carry out duck production enterprises to employ yourself or be employed and generate profitable income.
pg220_n0013: “Enhances farm diversity, provides valuable eggs, meat, and can be used as natural pest controller”

pg220_n0019: Ducks have broad bills, which are large and flat beaks that help them eat aquatic foods.
pg220_n0020: They also have webbed feet, which are feet with skin between the toes that make it easier for them to swim and walk on water.
pg220_n0021: Raising ducks is known as duck farming or duck production.
pg220_n0022: As you start to learn about this, think about how ducks might influence your life, your family, your school, or your whole local area.
pg220_n0023: Remember, as you explore this topic, keep asking questions and enjoy finding out new things about ducks.

pg220_n0027: Ducks are often kept for their eggs and meat.
pg220_n0028: If they are raised in a free-range system with minimal feed, they can weigh about 1.8 kg and lay 60 to 80 eggs a
pg221_n0004: Some duck breeds, including local ones, can weigh over 2.95 kg.
pg221_n0005: Under an intensive system, some ducks can lay up to 300 eggs a year.
pg221_n0006: Adult male ducks, or drakes, can weigh about 2 kg.
pg221_n0007: If they are from improved breeds and they are well-cared for, they can grow to weigh 4.5 kg and females or hens can weigh 3.5 kg.
pg221_n0008: In an integrated system, ducks can be raised with fish.
pg221_n0009: This helps to increase fish production, improve fish quality, and reduce feed costs for ducks.
pg221_n0010: It also boosts farmers’ output and income.
pg221_n0011: However, a problem is that ducks can eat small fish, which weigh less than 4 grams.
pg221_n0012: Despite this challenge, the benefits of this system are greater than the problems.
pg221_n0013: Ducks can survive in tough conditions and diseases.
pg221_n0014: They eat less because they can eat forage like ruminants.
pg221_n0015: Ducks live longer and are profitable.
pg221_n0016: They need affordable housing, thus, they can be raised for food or saleable products with low costs.
pg221_n0020: Several duck breeds that are suitable for warm climates and thrive in tropical environments are also suitable for Tanzania.
pg221_n0021: The following are some duck breeds that are suitable for tropical conditions including Tanzania:
pg221_n0026: These ducks stand up straight and have a unique way of running.
pg221_n0027: They are excellent foragers (eating grasses) and hence can adapt well to free-range conditions.

pg222_n0005: These ducks are known for their high egg production.
pg222_n0006: They are a lightweight breed that can adapt well to various climates.

pg222_n0014: These ducks are popular for meat production.

pg222_n0021: It is important to note that while these duck breeds are suitable for tropical conditions, proper care and management are still necessary to ensure their health and well-being.
pg222_n0022: Providing proper housing, clean water, and proper feeding and mating or breeding are essential for raising ducks.

pg223_n0016: Looking after ducks is like looking after chickens.
pg223_n0018: We need to think about housing and feeding them.
pg223_n0019: We also need to think about managing their mating and incubation as well as keeping them healthy.
pg223_n0020: Each of the following subsections will help you to take care of your ducks properly.
pg223_n0025: They need shelter and they don’t like wind or excessive sunlight.
pg223_n0026: When resting, they require a dry and sheltered nesting place.
pg223_n0027: Providing ducks with housing is important to protect them from harsh weather conditions, predators and to facilitate egg collection.
pg223_n0028: Here are some key points to consider when providing housing for ducks:
pg223_n0031: (a) Ducks can be housed in a conventional house or a simple shed made from locally available resources.
pg223_n0033: (b) The housing should protect ducks from wind, rain, and sun.
pg223_n0034: It should have adequate room ventilation and a dry bed.
pg223_n0036: (c) Normally, ducks lay eggs at night or in the morning usually between 6:00 a.m to noon, so housing prevents losses from predators and it makes egg collection easier.
pg223_n0038: (d) If possible, using a free-range system where ducks are allowed to disperse or keeping only one flock can save on feeding and penning costs.
pg223_n0040: (e) The recommended space for free-ranging ducks is approximately 0.5 hectares per 100 ducks.
pg223_n0042: (f) The size of the entrance should be large enough for the biggest duck to enter the housing smoothly.
pg223_n0044: (g) If ducks are allowed to range freely, it is important to rotate enclosed ranges, offer shade and shelter from bad weather, and avoid confining them for too long during daylight hours.
pg224_n0005: Provide adequate space for ducks to get feed and drinking water.
pg224_n0008: If ducks are for egg production, the house should be provided with lighting for about 14 hours to stimulate egg production.
pg224_n0012: In an intensive system, each duck requires a floor space of 3,710 - 4,650 cm².
pg224_n0013: In battery cages, the floor space can be reduced to 1,350 cm² per duck.
pg224_n0014: In a semi-intensive system, ducks need a floor space of 2,790 cm² in the night shelter and 929 - 1,395 cm² as an outside run.
pg224_n0015: Layer ducks should be provided with laying nest boxes.
pg224_n0016: A nest box measuring 30 cm wide, 45 cm deep, and 30 cm high is sufficient.
pg224_n0017: One nest box should be provided for every 3 ducks.
pg224_n0019: Where ducks are reared in a semi-intensive system, the run can be provided with a pool.
pg224_n0020: Apart from drinking, ducks need water for bathing and entertainment.
pg224_n0021: Naturally, ducks enjoy swimming and splashing around in the water.
pg224_n0022: They can even dive underwater to find food.
pg224_n0023: It is recommended to wait until ducklings (young ducks) are at least 5 - 6 weeks old before introducing them to water.
pg224_n0024: This allows ducklings to grow larger, develop their feathers, and handle changes in temperature better.
pg224_n0026: To manage a water pool in duck farming, it needs to provide sufficient water space and maintain water quality.
pg224_n0027: Ensure the duck’s water pool remains clean and free from contaminants by regular cleaning and changing the water.
pg224_n0031: Ducks should be fed a balanced diet that includes carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, and minerals.
pg224_n0032: Ducks can be fed with locally available feeds or commercial feeds prepared by authorised distributors.
pg224_n0033: Ducklings should be fed a starter diet from hatching to 4 weeks of age and then switched to a grower feed after 2 weeks.
pg224_n0034: These feeds can be in the form of mash, crumble, or pellet.
pg224_n0035: If special duck feeds are not available, standard poultry feeds can be used.
pg224_n0036: Wet mash is commonly used and should be fed as a wet mash.
pg224_n0038: If ducklings are brooded artificially, they should be fed as soon as they are placed in the brooder.
pg224_n0039: However, it is important not to feed ducks on poultry feed that contains a coccidiostat as it can be harmful to ducklings.
pg224_n0040: Ducks can be switched to grower feed at 5 weeks of age, and this feed should be used until the ducks reach sexual maturity at 24 weeks of age.
pg224_n0041: During the development stage (8 - 24 weeks), a duck should be fed 150 grams per day.
pg224_n0042: If wet mash is used, it should be mixed with 40% water and
pg225_n0003: fed as 115 grams of wet feed in the morning and evening.
pg225_n0004: Two weeks before laying, the daily ration should be increased to 220 grams per day if feeding dry mash, and to 330 grams per day if feeding wet mash.
pg225_n0005: Ducklings should be provided with grit regularly, especially if they are not foraging for their food.
pg225_n0006: Feeding grits allows ducklings to regulate their intake and it ensures proper digestion.
pg225_n0008: During the laying period (25 - 66 weeks), the feed intake of ducks should be increased to 325 grams per day if using dry mash, and to 485 grams per day if using wet mash.
pg225_n0009: The 50% egg-laying stage is expected to be reached at around 25 - 26 weeks of age.
pg225_n0010: From this stage onwards, ducks should be given a minimum of 0.5 kg of feed per duck per day.
pg225_n0011: Any type of feeder that can be used for feeding chickens can also be used for feeding ducks.
pg225_n0012: Layer ducks reared in an intensive system are fed twice a day, in the morning and evening.
pg225_n0013: They should be fed an amount that can be finished in about 10 - 15 minutes.
pg225_n0014: Layer ducks can be fed with either mash or pellets, but wet mash is preferred.
pg225_n0015: For feeding, one long feeder can be used by 20 ducks and one round feeder can be used by 10 - 15 ducks.
pg225_n0016: In addition to proper nutrition, providing ducks with grit is important for their digestion and overall health.
pg225_n0018: Clean water is essential for ducks, and it should be provided in standing troughs with wire mesh to prevent ducks from wetting their bodies.
pg225_n0019: Drinkers should be arranged so that ducks can submerge their bills in the water and clear their nostrils by squirting water through them.
pg225_n0020: Cleanliness of feeders and waterers should be maintained to ensure flock health.
pg225_n0022: Feeding of ducks in integrated farming:
pg225_n0023: Ducks fit well in integrated farming systems such as duck-cum-fish farming.
pg225_n0024: In these systems, ducks get most of their feed from the pond, which includes aquatic weeds, insects, larvae, and earthworms.
pg225_n0025: At the same time, fish can use waste from duck droppings and feed particles that fall into the pond.
pg225_n0026: When ducks are allowed to roam freely over the pond surface, their droppings fertilise the pond, stimulating the growth of natural foods for both fish and ducks.
pg225_n0028: Mating and incubation management in ducks
pg225_n0030: Male ducks, known as drakes, can serve six female ducks.
pg225_n0031: However, if the farmer needs more fertile eggs, then one drake should serve only four ducks.
pg225_n0032: Ducks usually start laying eggs when they are around 5 - 6 months old.
pg225_n0033: The highest egg production occurs about 5 - 6 weeks after they start laying.
pg225_n0034: To induce high egg production, ducks need a lighting period of 14 hours.
pg226_n0003: Duck eggs can be incubated naturally or artificially.
pg226_n0004: Commercial duck breeds cannot incubate their eggs because they are non-broody.
pg226_n0005: For natural incubation, good broody chickens and ducks are chosen and used for hatching duck eggs.
pg226_n0006: Duck eggs, except some few breeds take 28 days to hatch.
pg226_n0007: On day 10 or 11, candling is usually done to check for development.
pg226_n0009: Parasite and disease management in ducks
pg226_n0011: Ducks are known to be hard against parasites and diseases.
pg226_n0012: However, several parasites can affect them.
pg226_n0013: Lice, mites, fleas, flukes and roundworms are examples of parasites that can infest ducks.
pg226_n0014: Flukes are flatworms that can infect the liver, gallbladder, and intestine of ducks.
pg226_n0015: The symptoms of fluke infection include weight loss, anaemia, and jaundice.
pg226_n0016: Roundworms can infect the intestines of ducks causing weight loss, diarrhoea, and anaemia.
pg226_n0017: Duck lice are small insects that feed on the feathers and skin of ducks causing irritation and potential secondary infections.
pg226_n0018: Practical ways of managing parasites in ducks include the following:
pg226_n0022: Practise good hygiene by washing hands thoroughly before and after handling ducks and keeping their food and water clean;
pg226_n0025: Regularly inspect ducks for signs of parasites, such as weight loss, lethargy, and diarrhoea;
pg226_n0028: Use approved pesticides, such as powders or sprays, to treat external parasites such as fleas, mites, and lice;
pg226_n0031: Clean the duck houses and runs thoroughly to prevent re-infestation;
pg226_n0034: Deworm ducks regularly to prevent intestinal worms; and
pg226_n0037: Quarantine new birds to prevent the spread of external parasites to the entire flock.
pg226_n0039: Likewise, diseases such as duck viral enteritis, avian influenza, duck plague, and fowl cholera can affect ducks.
pg226_n0040: Generally, diseases in ducks can be managed through the following ways:
pg226_n0044: Vaccinating ducks against common viral diseases with the advice of a veterinarian or poultry experts.
pg226_n0047: Providing ducks with clean and hygienic housing conditions.
pg226_n0050: Ensuring balanced feeds and proper nutrition for ducks to prevent nutritional disorders.
pg226_n0053: Regular monitoring of duck health and early detection of symptoms.
pg226_n0056: Isolating sick ducks to prevent the spread of diseases.
