pg227_n0036: Handling, value addition and marketing of duck products
pg227_n0038: Duck products, for example, meat and eggs, are important for the farmers as well as the country’s economy.
pg227_n0039: People buy these duck products to cook delicious meals.
pg227_n0040: Selling ducks or duck products helps farmers to earn money.
pg227_n0041: For farmers to earn profitable income, duck eggs and meat should be properly handled and marketed at a reasonable price.
pg228_n0003: Handling, value addition and marketing of duck eggs
pg228_n0005: This sub-section provides a brief overview of duck egg collection, handling, processing, storage, and marketing.
pg228_n0006: For more detailed information and specific regulations, it is important to seek more information and advice from poultry extension workers or experts.
pg228_n0009: Collect duck eggs at least twice a day (early morning and late afternoon) to ensure freshness.
pg228_n0010: Handle them carefully to avoid cracking or damaging the shells.
pg228_n0011: Use clean containers to collect the eggs.
pg228_n0014: Handle the eggs with clean hands to prevent contamination.
pg228_n0015: Clean the eggs by gently wiping off any dirt.
pg228_n0016: Do not wash the eggs as it can remove the protective coating.
pg228_n0019: Grade the duck eggs based on their size and quality.
pg228_n0020: Use appropriate packaging materials to protect the eggs during transportation.
pg228_n0021: Label the packages with relevant information for wholesalers, retailers, and consumers.
pg228_n0022: Follow hygiene and biosecurity practices to ensure that the eggs are not contaminated during processing.
pg228_n0025: Use clean containers to store the eggs in a cool and dry place to maintain freshness.
pg228_n0026: Also, keep them away from contaminants and predators.
pg228_n0027: Follow storage guidelines to ensure that the eggs are safe for consumption.
pg228_n0028: Regularly check for any damaged or spoiled eggs and discard them.
pg228_n0031: Assess market requirements and choose appropriate marketing channels.
pg228_n0032: Work with collectors, assembly merchants, wholesalers, and retailers in the marketing process.
pg228_n0033: Consider factors such as market demand, intermediaries available, and costs involved.
pg228_n0034: Follow regulations and guidelines for packaging, labelling, and transportation of duck eggs.
pg228_n0036: Handling, value addition and marketing of duck meat
pg228_n0038: This section provides a brief overview of duck meat handling, slaughtering, and marketing.
pg228_n0039: For more detailed information and specific regulations, it is important to seek more information and advice from poultry extension workers or experts.
pg229_n0003: Duck meat handling and value addition:
pg229_n0004: Ensure that ducks are slaughtered and processed in a clean and hygienic environment to maintain meat safety and quality.
pg229_n0009: Fast the ducks for 12 - 24 hours before slaughter to empty their digestive system.
pg229_n0012: Pluck the ducks to remove feathers after slaughter.
pg229_n0016: Take out the internal organs and the legs.
pg229_n0018: Leave it as a whole carcass or cut it into specific cuts depending on your market preference.
pg229_n0019: After it cools down, it is ready to be packaged.
pg229_n0022: Package it for sale at the butchery.
pg229_n0023: Wrap each whole duck carcasses or cuts in thin-layer polythene or any other materials that are not corrosive to meat.
pg229_n0024: Label the package properly to provide information about the product, including its origin, production method, and handling instructions.
pg229_n0027: Store the packaged duck carcass in the freezer ready for sale.
pg229_n0029: Marketing of live ducks and duck meat:
pg229_n0030: The marketing of live ducks and duck meat is subject to regulations governed by various regulatory bodies to ensure food safety and quality.
pg229_n0031: You may not know all these, but livestock extension workers or poultry experts can advise you about the regulations.
pg229_n0032: The marketing process may involve various stakeholders such as farmers, processors, distributors, and retailers.
pg229_n0033: Cold storage and transportation facilities should be used to maintain the quality and freshness of the duck meat during marketing.
pg229_n0034: Where live ducks are sold, they have to be handled and transported properly.
pg229_n0036: Record keeping and Management in ducks
pg229_n0038: Maintaining accurate and detailed records is important for tracking the performance, health, and production of ducks.
pg229_n0039: Records should include information on mating/breeding, feeding, health treatments, egg production, and sales.
pg229_n0040: Digital tools can be used for record-keeping processes and to improve data management.

pg010_n0014_easy_read: Agriculture is another word for farming.
pg010_n0015_easy_read: It means growing and harvesting crops, and taking care of animals.
pg010_n0016_easy_read:
This work includes:
- caring for crop plants
- collecting crops
- preparing crops for use
- keeping crops safe in storage
- selling crops
pg010_n0017_easy_read:
It also includes taking care of animals such as:
- cattle
- chickens
- bees
- fish
pg010_n0018_easy_read: The main aim of agriculture is to produce food.
pg010_n0019_easy_read:
This is important because it helps feed more people around the world.
It also helps to make sure everyone has enough to eat.
pg010_n0021_easy_read: Agriculture is a mix of science and art.
pg010_n0022_easy_read: Scientists use science to improve farming.
pg010_n0023_easy_read:
Scientists create new ideas and technologies.
For example, they use special methods to improve crops and animals.
pg010_n0024_easy_read: This means scientists can develop better crop varieties and animal breeds.
pg010_n0025_easy_read:
Scientists also use Chemistry to make fertilisers.
Fertilisers help plants grow better by giving them the nutrients they need.
pg010_n0026_easy_read: In the same way, scientists use Biology and Chemistry to control crop pests and diseases.
pg010_n0027_easy_read: This means scientists use knowledge about living things and Chemistry to manage and prevent diseases and harmful insects that can harm crops and animals.
pg010_n0029_easy_read: Farming is not only about science.
pg010_n0030_easy_read: It also uses our hands and our brains.
pg010_n0031_easy_read: This is called the art of farming.
pg010_n0032_easy_read: For example, when we do physical work on the farm, such as building structures or using tools, we are practising the art of farming.
pg010_n0033_easy_read: We also use our brains to make important decisions.
pg010_n0034_easy_read:
We decide:
- what crops to grow
- what animals to raise
- how much to grow
- how to do it
pg010_n0035_easy_read: We also think about when and where to
pg011_n0003_easy_read: Buy the things we need for farming, for example seeds and tools. Also find where to sell our products.
pg011_n0004_easy_read: So, farming is also an art. We use our hands and our brains to help crops and animals grow well.
pg011_n0008_easy_read: How does agriculture help to produce food?
pg011_n0010_easy_read: In what ways do scientists use science to improve farming?
pg011_n0012_easy_read: How does the art of farming help crop and animal farming to succeed?
pg011_n0016_easy_read: You have learnt that agriculture is both an art and a science.
pg011_n0017_easy_read: Agriculture includes different activities from the start to the end of producing animal and crop products.
pg011_n0018_easy_read: To do these activities well, we need to study specific fields of agriculture.
pg011_n0019_easy_read: These fields are also called branches of agriculture.
pg011_n0020_easy_read: Agriculture is divided into 5 main branches, as shown in Figure 1.2.
pg011_n0031_easy_read: Crop production includes different activities, from planting seeds to selling the crops.
pg012_n0005_easy_read: Taking care of crop plants by giving them water and nutrients.
pg012_n0008_easy_read: Protecting the plants from pests and diseases.
pg012_n0011_easy_read: Harvesting the produce when it is ready.
pg012_n0014_easy_read: Handling and processing the harvested produce.
pg012_n0022_easy_read: All these activities together form the crop production value chain.
pg012_n0023_easy_read: It is important to do each activity well to make sure the produce is of good quality and the crop yield is high.
pg012_n0024_easy_read: Different types of crops can be grown for different uses.
pg012_n0025_easy_read:
Some examples are:
- cereals
- pulses
- oil crops
- horticultural crops
- aquatic crops such as seaweed and Azolla
pg012_n0029_easy_read: Animal production includes different activities, from raising animals to selling the animals or their products.
pg012_n0043_easy_read: Helping the animals to produce their young ones.
pg012_n0049_easy_read: Handling and processing animals and their products.
pg012_n0057_easy_read: All these activities together form the animal production value chain.
pg012_n0058_easy_read: It is important to do each activity well to make sure the yield is as high as possible and the products are of good quality.
pg012_n0059_easy_read:
Many different types of animals can be raised, such as:
- cattle
- sheep
- goats
- pigs
- poultry
- fish
pg012_n0060_easy_read: When we raise livestock, we get different animal products such as meat, milk, eggs, and honey.
pg012_n0061_easy_read: It is important to plan well and use good animal production practices to meet the demand for animal products.
pg012_n0065_easy_read: Soil Science is a part of Agriculture that studies soil.
pg012_n0066_easy_read: It involves studying the physical, chemical, and biological properties of soil.
pg012_n0067_easy_read: By learning soil science, we can manage soil better for growing different crops, including animal feeds.
pg012_n0068_easy_read: Soil is important because it gives plants a place to grow and gives them nutrients.
pg012_n0069_easy_read: Soil also helps to filter and store water. Soil is also a home for many organisms.
pg012_n0070_easy_read: Understanding soil helps farmers make good decisions about how to manage their land and improve their crops.
pg013_n0005_easy_read:
Agricultural engineering uses science and technology to make:
- tools
- equipment
- machines
- other farm structures
pg013_n0006_easy_read: Agricultural engineering helps to solve problems and make farming better.
pg013_n0007_easy_read:
Agricultural engineers design:
- irrigation systems to supply water to crops
- machines for land preparation
- machines for planting
- machines for harvesting
pg013_n0008_easy_read: In short, agricultural engineering uses science and technology to improve efficiency, productivity, and quality in farming.
pg013_n0012_easy_read: Agricultural economics is about managing resources to make profit.
pg013_n0013_easy_read:
Farming uses resources such as:
- land
- capital
- workers
- business skills
pg013_n0014_easy_read: These resources are also called factors of production.
pg013_n0015_easy_read: Farmers need to use these resources wisely to reduce production costs and increase income.
pg013_n0016_easy_read:
Farmers do this by:
- planning well
- increasing yields
- reducing costs
- finding the best prices for products
pg013_n0017_easy_read: Research in agricultural economics helps people find ways to improve productivity and make farming more profitable.
pg013_n0024_easy_read: Why is it important to do well in each basic activity in crop and animal production?
pg013_n0027_easy_read: How can soil science help farmers improve crop yields?
pg013_n0030_easy_read: Why is agricultural engineering important in modern farming?
pg013_n0033_easy_read: How can agricultural economics help farmers reduce costs and increase income?
pg013_n0037_easy_read:
Agriculture provides:
- food
- raw materials for industries
- medicinal products
- career opportunities
- business opportunities
- recreation opportunities
- foreign exchange
pg013_n0038_easy_read: Agriculture affects many parts of the lives of Tanzanians.
pg013_n0039_easy_read: Agriculture is a key part of Tanzania’s economy.
pg013_n0040_easy_read: Agriculture provides livelihoods to about 65.6 % of the population, directly or indirectly.
pg013_n0044_easy_read: Farming in Tanzania is important for feeding the nation.
pg013_n0045_easy_read:
Tanzania produces many crops, such as:
- cereals
- pulses
- different types of fruits
- different types of vegetables
pg013_n0046_easy_read:
Farming also provides animal products such as:
- meat
- milk
- eggs
pg013_n0048_easy_read: If there is not enough food, people will starve and become weak.
pg013_n0049_easy_read: So, agriculture is a back-up that helps make sure we always have enough food to meet our dietary needs and keep us strong.
pg014_n0005_easy_read: Agriculture is important for industries in Tanzania because it provides raw materials.
pg014_n0006_easy_read:
For example:
- Cotton is used in textile industries.
- Cattle provide hides.
- Goats and sheep provide skins for leather industries.
pg014_n0007_easy_read: Other crops are also important in food processing industries.
pg014_n0008_easy_read:
For example:
- Maize is used to make maize flour.
- Fruits are used to make fruit juices.
- Vegetables are used to make canned products.
pg014_n0009_easy_read: Also, agriculture provides raw materials for the chemical industry.
pg014_n0010_easy_read: These raw materials are used to make fertilisers and pesticides. Fertilisers and pesticides are important for the country's agriculture sector.
pg014_n0011_easy_read: So, agriculture is not only about producing food.
pg014_n0012_easy_read: Agriculture also supports other industries. It does this by providing the raw materials they need to work.
pg014_n0016_easy_read: Agriculture creates many business and job opportunities.
pg014_n0017_easy_read: These opportunities are not only in farming. They are also in related areas.
pg014_n0018_easy_read: For example, people can work in food processing and marketing.
pg014_n0019_easy_read: Processing means changing raw agricultural products into something else.
pg014_n0020_easy_read: For example, maize can be processed into maize flour.
pg014_n0021_easy_read: Marketing means selling these products to customers.

pg020_n0023_easy_read: Mineral matter, such as sand, silt and clay, forms the main solid particles in soil.
pg020_n0024_easy_read: Mineral matter also gives plants the mineral nutrients they need to grow.
pg020_n0025_easy_read:
These nutrients include:
- nitrogen
- phosphorus
- potassium
- others

These nutrients help to make the soil fertile. This is good for growing crops.
pg020_n0026_easy_read: Mineral nutrients in the soil may come from weathering of rocks over a long time. They may also come from adding fertilisers to the soil.
pg020_n0027_easy_read: Weathering breaks down rocks and releases minerals into the soil.
pg020_n0028_easy_read: It is important to understand and manage the mineral content in soil for successful farming.
pg020_n0029_easy_read: This knowledge helps farmers know if the soil is suitable for different plants. It also helps farmers decide how to add more minerals to the soil.
pg020_n0032_easy_read: When plants and animals die, their remains break down. They release nutrients and humus into the soil.
pg020_n0033_easy_read:
These nutrients include:
- carbon
- nitrogen
- phosphorus
- others
pg020_n0034_easy_read: These nutrients are like food in the soil. Plants need them to grow well.
pg020_n0035_easy_read: Humus is a dark substance. It easily breaks into small pieces or crumbs.
pg020_n0036_easy_read: Humus helps to improve the structure of the soil. This makes it easier for plant roots to grow and get water and nutrients.
pg020_n0037_easy_read: Humus also helps the soil hold moisture. This is important for plants during dry periods.
pg020_n0039_easy_read:
Farmers can improve the soil's organic matter by adding:
- animal manure
- compost
pg020_n0040_easy_read: This makes the soil fertile and healthy. This is good for growing crops.
pg020_n0041_easy_read: Organic matter and humus in the soil are important. They keep the soil fertile, support plant growth, and help crop farming to succeed.
pg020_n0044_easy_read: The soil has living things, including plants and animals.
pg020_n0045_easy_read:
Some soil organisms are big enough to see easily, for example:
- earthworms
- insects
pg020_n0047_easy_read: Other soil organisms, such as bacteria and some fungi, are very small. You can only see them with a microscope.
pg020_n0049_easy_read: Soil organisms eat the remains of plants and animals.
pg020_n0050_easy_read: When soil organisms eat the remains of plants and animals, they break them
pg021_n0003_easy_read: break down and release nutrients and humus.
pg021_n0004_easy_read: Soil organisms can be divided into 2 groups: beneficial organisms and harmful organisms.
pg021_n0005_easy_read: Beneficial soil organisms help to keep the soil healthy. They also help plants grow well.
pg021_n0006_easy_read:

- applying compost
- applying animal manure
- using mulch
- using cover crops
- rotating crops
pg021_n0007_easy_read: On the other hand, harmful soil organisms affect plant growth.
pg021_n0011_easy_read: Water in the soil is found in small spaces.
pg021_n0012_easy_read: Soil water can come from rain or from irrigation by farmers.
pg021_n0013_easy_read: This water has dissolved mineral nutrients in it.
pg021_n0014_easy_read: When water and minerals mix, this is called soil solution.
pg021_n0015_easy_read: Soil water is important because it helps dissolve mineral nutrients in the soil. It also carries them to plant roots.
pg021_n0016_easy_read: Soil water also gives water to living things in the soil.
pg021_n0017_easy_read: Farmers can keep the right amount of soil water through irrigation and drainage.
pg021_n0018_easy_read:
Farmers can also use methods to prevent or reduce water loss from the soil, for example:
- adding organic manures
- using dry grass mulch
- practising conservation agriculture by planting shed trees on the farm

pg022_n0010_easy_read: Soil air moves between the soil and the atmosphere.
pg022_n0011_easy_read: Soil air is important for plant growth.

Plants need oxygen from the soil air.
Their roots use it to breathe, or respire, and grow.
pg022_n0013_easy_read: Soil organisms also need air to survive.
pg022_n0014_easy_read: Soil organisms breathe in soil air to stay alive.
pg022_n0015_easy_read: Farmers need to keep soil air healthy.

pg022_n0024_easy_read:
Do not overwater the soil.
Water can fill all the pore spaces and push out the air.
pg022_n0027_easy_read:
Be careful when using chemicals or fertilisers.
Some can harm soil organisms and affect air quality.

pg023_n0022_easy_read: When you dig a vertical section through the soil, you can see different layers.
pg023_n0023_easy_read: This vertical section is called a soil profile.
pg023_n0024_easy_read: The layers in the soil profile are called soil horizons.
pg023_n0025_easy_read: They are called horizons because they spread from side to side.
pg023_n0026_easy_read: There are 4 major horizons in a soil profile in undisturbed soils.
pg023_n0027_easy_read:
These are horizons:
- O
- A
- B
- C
Refer to Figure 2.2.
pg024_n0003_easy_read: O horizon: This is the top layer. It is also called the organic horizon.
pg024_n0004_easy_read: The O horizon has a lot of decomposed organic matter, such as leaves and plant remains.
pg024_n0005_easy_read: The O horizon has a dark colour. It is also rich in nutrients.
pg024_n0007_easy_read: A horizon: This is also called topsoil.
pg024_n0008_easy_read: Most plant roots grow in the A horizon.
pg024_n0009_easy_read: The A horizon is usually darker in colour because it has more organic matter than the horizons below it.
pg024_n0010_easy_read:
Horizon A is important for plant nutrients because it contains:
- organic matter
- minerals
- micro-organisms
pg024_n0011_easy_read: However, Horizon A is marked by eluviation.
pg024_n0012_easy_read: Eluviation is the process where water washes soluble minerals and organic matter out of the upper soil horizons and deposits them in lower horizons.
pg024_n0014_easy_read: B horizon: This is also called subsoil.
pg024_n0015_easy_read: The B horizon collects minerals and nutrients washed from the upper layers. For this reason, it is called the illuvial horizon.
pg024_n0016_easy_read: Horizon B is denser and less fertile than Horizon A.
pg024_n0018_easy_read: C horizon: The C horizon is the parent material horizon.
pg024_n0019_easy_read: The C horizon is made of weathered rock fragments. It does not have the organic matter and nutrients found in the upper horizons.
pg024_n0021_easy_read: R: This is not considered a horizon. It means bedrock.
pg024_n0022_easy_read: It is a layer of hard bedrock at the bottom of all soil profiles.
pg024_n0023_easy_read: It is the solid rock from which soil is formed.
pg024_n0024_easy_read: It is made of materials that have not changed since they were formed.
pg024_n0026_easy_read:
In fields, the usual soil profile has:
- Horizon A
- Horizon B
- Horizon C
pg024_n0027_easy_read: In forests, there is an extra O horizon above Horizons A and B.
pg024_n0028_easy_read: Not every soil profile has all horizons, especially when the soil is disturbed.
pg024_n0029_easy_read: The presence and features of each horizon depend on the location and how the soil formed.

pg025_n0011_easy_read: Agricultural soil has some properties that affect plant growth.
pg025_n0012_easy_read:
These properties include:
- texture
- structure
- porosity
- soil pH
- fertility
- living organisms in the soil
pg025_n0013_easy_read:
These properties can be grouped into:
- physical soil properties
- chemical soil properties
- biological soil properties
pg025_n0014_easy_read: In the next sections, we will learn about these properties.
pg025_n0018_easy_read: The physical properties of soil are the features of soil that you can see, observe, and measure without changing what the soil is made of.
pg025_n0019_easy_read:
These physical properties include:
- the feel of the soil. This is soil texture.
- how the soil particles are packed or arranged. This is soil structure.
- how much space is between and inside the soil particles. This is soil porosity.
pg025_n0020_easy_read:
The physical properties of soil are important because they affect:
- how water moves through the soil
- how air moves through the soil
- how plants grow
pg025_n0021_easy_read: In general, the physical properties of soil show how well the soil can give plants and other organisms the right conditions to grow well.
pg025_n0025_easy_read:
Soil is made of solid mineral particles:
- sand
- silt
- clay
pg025_n0026_easy_read: Sand particles are the largest. Their diameter is from 0.05 mm to 2 mm.
pg025_n0027_easy_read: Silt particles are smaller than sand but larger than clay. Their diameter is between 0.002 mm and 0.05 mm.
pg025_n0028_easy_read: Clay particles are the smallest. Their diameter is less than 0.002 mm.
pg025_n0029_easy_read: Solid soil particles that are more than 2 mm in diameter are called stones and gravels.
pg025_n0030_easy_read: Soil texture means the relative amount of sand, silt, and clay particles in the soil.
pg025_n0031_easy_read: Soil texture can also mean how coarse or fine the soil feels. This depends on the relative amounts of sand, silt, and clay.
pg026_n0004_easy_read: The 3 main types of soil texture are sand, silt, and clay.
pg026_n0005_easy_read: Loamy soil is soil with a balanced mix of sand, silt, clay, and organic matter.
pg026_n0007_easy_read: When we want to grow crops, we need to look at the type of soil we have.
pg026_n0008_easy_read: We can group soil into 4 main types: clayey, silty, sandy, and loamy.
pg026_n0009_easy_read: The size of the soil particles causes these differences.
pg026_n0010_easy_read: Clay is very small. Silt is medium. Sand is large.
pg026_n0011_easy_read: Some types of soil are good for growing crops on their own. Adding manure or fertilisers can make the soil better for growing crops.
pg026_n0012_easy_read: Soil can change over time. So it is important to check it often and take care of it.

pg027_n0032_easy_read: You can determine soil texture by using laboratory analysis or by using simple methods in the field, such as the feel method.
pg027_n0033_easy_read: Usually, laboratory analysis of soil texture costs a lot and takes time. Feeling soil texture by hand is cheap, quick, and accurate.
pg027_n0034_easy_read:
Soils are divided into 3 main texture groups:
- coarse-textured soils
- medium-textured soils
- fine-textured soils
pg027_n0035_easy_read: The term coarse-textured usually means soils with mostly sand.
pg027_n0036_easy_read: Fine-textured soils are soils with mostly clay. Medium-textured soils are a more balanced mix of sand, silt, and clay particles.
pg027_n0037_easy_read: Medium-textured soils are also called loam soils.
pg027_n0039_easy_read: Determining soil texture by the feel method:
pg027_n0040_easy_read: This method helps you determine the soil textural class in the field. You use simple field tests and feel the parts of the soil by hand.
pg027_n0041_easy_read: The soil sample must be moist or slightly wet.
pg027_n0042_easy_read: Remove gravel and other parts that are more than 2 mm wide.
pg027_n0044_easy_read: Procedure for determining soil texture by the feel method
pg027_n0047_easy_read: Step 1: Take a handful of soil.
pg027_n0048_easy_read: If the soil is dry, add a little water. Squeeze the soil in your palm to check if it forms a ball. Refer to Figure 2.4. Then go to step 2.
pg027_n0049_easy_read: If the moist soil does not form a ball, the soil is sand.
pg027_n0054_easy_read: If the moist soil stays in a ball when you open your hand, bounce the ball in your hand.
pg027_n0055_easy_read: If the ball breaks when it hits the hand, the soil is loamy sand.
pg027_n0056_easy_read: If the ball does not break, go to step 3.
pg028_n0003_easy_read:
Step 3: Check if the moist soil forms a ribbon when you press a soil ball between your thumb and forefinger.
See Figure 2.5.
pg028_n0004_easy_read: Also, check how long the ribbon is when you roll it between your palms or on a flat table.
pg028_n0006_easy_read:
If you start with dry clay, give the clay time to become moist.
Also make sure the "gritty" particles are not stuck together.
pg028_n0008_easy_read: Figure 2.5: Forming a ribbon from the soil ball
pg028_n0010_easy_read: The idea behind forming ribbons is about the cohesion between clay particles.
pg028_n0011_easy_read:
Clay is sticky when it is moist.
So, the ribbon length matches the amount of clay in the soil.
pg028_n0016_easy_read: less than 2.5 cm, the general soil texture category is loam.
pg028_n0019_easy_read: between 2.5 cm and 5 cm, the general soil texture category is clay loam.
pg028_n0022_easy_read: greater than 5 cm, the general soil texture category is clay.
pg028_n0024_easy_read: After you find the general category by clay content, go to step 4.
pg028_n0026_easy_read: Step 4: After the ribbon test, find the modifier if it is needed.
pg028_n0027_easy_read: Add water to a small amount of soil in the palm of your hand until it becomes a muddy puddle.
pg028_n0028_easy_read:
Rub the muddy puddle against your palm.
See Figure 2.6.
pg028_n0029_easy_read: Feel the sample as you work it in your hand.
pg028_n0031_easy_read: Figure 2.6: Feeling the soil texture in the palm
pg028_n0037_easy_read:
If grittiness is stronger, add the modifier "sandy" to the general category from step 3.
For example:
- sandy loam
- sandy clay loam
- sandy clay
pg028_n0040_easy_read:
If grittiness is not stronger, but smoothness is stronger, add the modifier silt.
For example:
- silt loam
- silty clay loam
- silty clay
pg028_n0041_easy_read:
Silt is not sticky.
But it is smooth like:
- flour
- foundation make-up
- talcum powder

pg029_n0014_easy_read:
Soil is made of sand, silt, or clay particles.
These particles join together to form groups called soil aggregates.
Refer to Figure 2.7.
pg029_n0015_easy_read:
Soil aggregates can be:
- sandy
- silty
- clayey
- loamy
pg029_n0016_easy_read: A soil aggregate is like a basket with different types of soil particles.
pg029_n0017_easy_read: Soil structure is how soil particles are arranged in an aggregate.
pg029_n0018_easy_read: The way soil particles are arranged in an aggregate can affect the spaces between and inside the soil aggregates.
pg029_n0023_easy_read: Well-structured soil has a network of tiny spaces.
pg029_n0024_easy_read: These spaces are between the soil aggregates and inside the soil aggregates.
pg029_n0025_easy_read: This network lets water and air move around.
pg029_n0026_easy_read:
Soil structure helps water and air move easily.
It is like air moving through doors and windows in a house.
pg029_n0027_easy_read: In farming, soil structure is important because it helps plants grow strong and healthy.
pg029_n0028_easy_read: Soil structure also stops the soil from being washed away when it rains or when wind blows.
pg029_n0030_easy_read: Poor farming practices can damage soil structure.
pg029_n0031_easy_read: For example, big and very heavy machines can squash the soil if people use them too much.
pg029_n0032_easy_read: If we give the soil too much water or too many chemical fertilisers, this can also damage the soil structure.
pg029_n0033_easy_read: But we can protect soil structure in many ways.
pg029_n0034_easy_read: One way is to change the type of crop we grow each season.
pg029_n0036_easy_read:
Crop rotation means growing a different type of crop on the same piece of land each year or each growing season, using a set pattern.
Refer to Figure 2.8.
pg029_n0037_easy_read: Another way is to use organic fertilisers instead of inorganic fertilisers.
pg029_n0038_easy_read:
These are some recommended cultural practices.
They help improve soil structure and make it suitable for crop production.

pg030_n0028_easy_read: Soil pore spaces, also called soil porosity, are open spaces between and inside soil aggregates.
pg030_n0029_easy_read: These spaces usually contain water and air.
pg030_n0030_easy_read: Everything in the soil that is not solid is in these pore spaces.
pg030_n0031_easy_read: There are 2 types of pores by size: macro pores and micro pores (Figure 2.9 (a) and (b)).
pg030_n0035_easy_read: Figure 2.9 (a): Pore spaces in loosely arranged sand particles
pg030_n0040_easy_read: Figure 2.9 (b): Pore spaces in grouped clay particles
pg030_n0042_easy_read: When soil is porous, it can hold more water and nutrients.
pg030_n0043_easy_read: This is important for plant growth. It helps plants absorb water and nutrients from the soil.
pg030_n0044_easy_read: Without enough porosity, water and nutrients cannot enter the soil well. This leads to poor plant growth and poor plant health.
pg030_n0045_easy_read: Also, soil porosity affects airflow in the soil.
pg030_n0046_easy_read: This is important because it allows gases to move. These gases are important for the life of plants and soil organisms.
pg030_n0047_easy_read: If soil is compacted or has low
pg031_n0003_easy_read:
If soil has low porosity, air cannot move through it well.
This can lead to poor plant growth and poor plant health.
pg031_n0004_easy_read: These soil properties can affect the amount of pore spaces in the soil.
pg031_n0005_easy_read:
These are:
- soil texture
- soil structure
- organic matter
- soil compaction
pg031_n0009_easy_read: Soil texture: Different types of soil have different amounts of pore spaces.
pg031_n0010_easy_read:
For example, sandy soil has big particles.
It has more pore spaces than clay soil.
Clay soil has small particles.
pg031_n0013_easy_read: Soil structure: The way soil particles stick together can change the amount of pore spaces.
pg031_n0014_easy_read: Loosely packed soil has more pore spaces than tightly packed soil.
pg031_n0017_easy_read: Organic matter: Soil with a lot of organic matter, for example leaves, has more pore spaces.
pg031_n0018_easy_read: This happens because the soil forms well-aggregated structures.
pg031_n0021_easy_read:
Soil compaction: When soil is pressed down a lot, it can have fewer pore spaces.
For example, this can happen when people walk on wet soil or when machines are used on wet soil.

pg031_n0042_easy_read: Soil helps plants grow because it provides essential nutrients.
pg031_n0043_easy_read:
The chemical properties of soil affect its fertility and nutrient content.
These properties include:
- the presence of different elements
- how available these elements are
- the soil reaction
pg031_n0044_easy_read: Understanding the chemical properties of soil is like understanding the nutrition facts on a food label.
pg031_n0045_easy_read: It helps us know what is good for plants and what is not good for plants.
pg031_n0046_easy_read:
Nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) are the main macronutrients.
Plants need them in large quantities.
People commonly provide them as inorganic fertilisers.
pg031_n0047_easy_read: Calcium (Ca), Magnesium (Mg), and sulphur (S) are secondary macronutrients.
pg031_n0048_easy_read: Micronutrients are needed in small quantities.
pg031_n0049_easy_read:
These include:
- iron (Fe)
- manganese (Mn)
- zinc (Zn)
- boron (B)
- copper (Cu)
- molybdenum (Mo)
- chlorine (Cl)
pg031_n0050_easy_read: Table 2.2 shows the basic functions of mineral nutrients in crop plants and the signs of nutrient deficiency.
pg032_n0016_easy_read: Nitrogen helps leaves and stems to grow. It gives plants their green colour, called chlorophyll.
pg032_n0018_easy_read: Plants may look yellow. They may grow slowly.
pg032_n0023_easy_read: Phosphorus helps roots to develop. It helps flowering and seed formation.
pg032_n0025_easy_read: Leaves may be dark green or purple. Roots may not develop well. Flowering and seed formation may be poor.
pg032_n0030_easy_read: Potassium helps plants resist disease. It also helps plants use water.
pg032_n0032_easy_read: Leaves may be yellow at the edges. Plants may get diseases more easily.
pg032_n0037_easy_read: Calcium helps roots and leaves to grow. It also helps form cell walls.
pg032_n0039_easy_read: Leaves may have dead spots. Leaves may also curl.
pg032_n0044_easy_read: Magnesium is important for photosynthesis. It helps to make chlorophyll.
pg032_n0046_easy_read: The area between the leaf veins may turn yellow.
pg032_n0053_easy_read: Plants may be pale or small.
pg032_n0058_easy_read: Iron helps to form chlorophyll for photosynthesis.
pg032_n0060_easy_read: Leaves may be yellow with green veins.
pg032_n0074_easy_read: The area between the leaf veins may turn yellow. The distance between leaves on stems may be reduced. This is called short internodes.
pg032_n0079_easy_read: Boron helps in plant growth and development.
pg032_n0081_easy_read: The terminal growing points may die. Growth may be stunted. Fruits or vegetables may be malformed or discoloured.
pg032_n0086_easy_read: Copper is important for seed production.
pg032_n0088_easy_read: Leaves may become dark and curled.
pg032_n0095_easy_read: Leaves may be pale. The leaf edges may have fringes.
pg032_n0102_easy_read: Leaves may wilt. Leaves may turn yellowish-brown. Roots may not develop well.
pg033_n0005_easy_read: Soil reaction, also called soil pH, measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is.
pg033_n0006_easy_read: Soil pH ranges from about 0 to 14.
pg033_n0007_easy_read:
Soils with pH below 7 are acidic soils.
Soils with pH about 7 are neutral soils.
Soils with pH above 7 are alkaline soils.
pg033_n0008_easy_read: People usually show soil pH on a pH scale, as shown in Figure 2.10.
pg033_n0009_easy_read: Soil pH affects how plants get nutrients and how the nutrients react with each other.
pg033_n0010_easy_read: The suitable pH range for most plants is 5.5 to 7.0.
pg033_n0015_easy_read: In acidic soils, the availability of nutrients changes.
pg033_n0016_easy_read:
For example:
- Aluminium and manganese can become more available.
- Aluminium and manganese can also become more toxic to plants.
- Calcium becomes less available.
- Phosphorus becomes less available.
- Magnesium becomes less available.
pg033_n0017_easy_read: When this happens, you can see some signs in plants.
pg033_n0018_easy_read:
These signs include:
- stunted growth
- yellowing of leaves
- poor fruit development
pg033_n0019_easy_read:
To manage acidic soil, you can add materials called lime to the soil.
This increases soil pH and makes the soil more alkaline.
pg033_n0022_easy_read: In alkaline soils, the availability of nutrients also changes.
pg033_n0023_easy_read: For example, phosphorus and most micronutrients become less available.
pg033_n0024_easy_read: When this happens, you can see some signs in plants.
pg033_n0025_easy_read:
These signs include:
- stunted growth
- yellowing leaves
- poor fruit development
pg033_n0026_easy_read: To manage alkaline soil, you can add acidifying materials to lower soil pH.
pg033_n0030_easy_read: The availability of nutrients in the soil is affected by more than acidity or alkalinity.
pg033_n0031_easy_read: The amount of organic matter in the soil and the soil texture can also affect it.
pg033_n0033_easy_read: Look for signs such as slow growth or yellow leaves.
pg033_n0034_easy_read: This could mean the plants need more nutrients.
pg033_n0035_easy_read: If possible, consult soil scientists for soil testing.
pg033_n0036_easy_read:
Soil testing results will give information about the soil's nutrient content and pH.
The results will also suggest the management actions needed if the conditions are not suitable for plant growth.

pg034_n0020_easy_read: Soil has both macro-organisms and micro-organisms.
pg034_n0021_easy_read:
Macro-organisms are living things that people can see with the naked eye.
Examples are:
- earthworms
- beetles
- other insects
pg034_n0022_easy_read: Micro-organisms are very small living things. We cannot see them without a microscope.
pg034_n0024_easy_read: Macro-organisms, such as earthworms, help to break down dead plants and animals in the soil.
pg034_n0025_easy_read: As macro-organisms move through the soil, they make channels. These channels let air and water move through the soil. This is important for plant roots to grow.
pg034_n0026_easy_read: Micro-organisms play an even bigger part in soil health and crop production.
pg034_n0027_easy_read: For example, some bacteria take nitrogen from the air and change it into a form that plants can use for growth.
pg034_n0028_easy_read: This process is called nitrogen fixation.
pg034_n0029_easy_read: Fungi are also a type of micro-organism.
pg034_n0030_easy_read: Some fungi have a helpful relationship with plant roots. The fungi help the plant to take in water and nutrients.
pg034_n0031_easy_read: In return, the plant gives sugars to the fungi.
pg034_n0032_easy_read: So, both macro-organisms and micro-organisms are very important for soil health and for growing crops.
pg034_n0033_easy_read:
They help to:
- break down organic matter
- improve soil structure
- give plants the nutrients they need to grow
pg034_n0034_easy_read:
To improve the biological properties of soil, farmers can use practices that keep soil safe for soil organisms.
Examples are:
- reducing tillage
- using organic matter
pg034_n0038_easy_read: Soil is a home for micro-organisms, also called microbes.
pg034_n0039_easy_read: Some of these microbes help plants to grow, but others can harm plants. Nematodes are one example.
pg034_n0040_easy_read: These harmful microbes can enter plants through roots and stems. They cause damage and stop the flow of water and nutrients.
pg034_n0041_easy_read: Some harmful microbes can also enter plants through leaves and cause diseases.
pg035_n0003_easy_read: Before planting a crop, we must check the soil for harmful microbes.
pg035_n0004_easy_read: If we do not check, these harmful microbes can damage our crops.
pg035_n0005_easy_read: It is also important to know that managing these harmful microbes can be difficult.
pg035_n0006_easy_read: This takes time and effort. We may not see results at once.
pg035_n0007_easy_read: But if we manage the harmful microbes well, our crops can stay healthy.

pg035_n0016_easy_read: People use soil to grow crops.
pg035_n0017_easy_read: Soil is like a home for a plant.
pg035_n0018_easy_read: Plants need some things from soil to grow well.
pg035_n0019_easy_read:
These things include:
- enough nutrients
- suitable soil pH
- good micro-organisms in the soil
pg035_n0020_easy_read: However, not all soil is good for growing crops.
pg035_n0021_easy_read: Some soil does not have the important nutrients that plants need.
pg035_n0022_easy_read:
Some soil has:
- harmful bacteria
- fungi
- nematodes
pg035_n0023_easy_read: Some soil is too acidic or too alkaline.
pg035_n0024_easy_read: Some soil has harmful substances because of pollution.
pg035_n0025_easy_read: These things can make the soil unhealthy.
pg035_n0027_easy_read: Taking care of soil health is very important in farming.
pg035_n0028_easy_read: Healthy soil supports life and helps it continue.
pg035_n0029_easy_read: Healthy soil is like the human body. The human body needs nutrients, water, and a healthy environment to stay well.
pg035_n0030_easy_read: Soil needs these things to grow plants and support other organisms.
pg035_n0031_easy_read:
Healthy soil has:
- living things such as bacteria and worms
- non-living particles such as minerals and organic matter
pg035_n0032_easy_read: These parts work together to keep the soil healthy.
pg035_n0033_easy_read: Healthy soil helps plants grow well.
pg035_n0034_easy_read: Healthy soil gives plants the right nutrients. It supports their roots. It also helps plants get water and air when they need them.
pg035_n0036_easy_read: Just as we take care of our health, farmers need to take care of their soil health.
pg035_n0037_easy_read: Farmers can do this in different ways.
pg035_n0038_easy_read: For example, farmers can add organic matter. This feeds the micro-organisms in the soil.
pg035_n0039_easy_read: Farmers can also use methods such as crop rotation.
pg035_n0040_easy_read: Crop rotation helps to keep soil healthy. Different crops use different nutrients from the soil.
pg035_n0041_easy_read: Crop rotation also helps to control pests and diseases. It also helps the soil hold water better. This is important for keeping plants healthy.

pg037_n0016_easy_read: "Nourishes our health, beautifies our gardens, and promotes biodiversity"
pg037_n0020_easy_read:
Horticulture is part of agriculture.
It uses art and science to grow and manage:
- vegetables (olericulture)
- fruits (pomology)
- ornamental plants (floriculture)
- spice crops
pg037_n0021_easy_read:
Horticulture also includes work after harvest.
This work includes:
- handling crops
- processing crops
- packaging crops
This work helps crops last longer.
It also makes crops more available and more profitable.
pg037_n0022_easy_read:
Landscaping is also part of horticulture.
Landscaping makes places look beautiful by using different garden designs and materials.
pg037_n0023_easy_read:
Most horticultural products are sold or eaten fresh.
These products include:
- fruits
- vegetables
- some spices
pg037_n0030_easy_read:
Provide nutritious food:
Vegetables, fruits, and spices are the main source of vitamins and minerals.
These nutrients help our bodies stay healthy.
pg037_n0031_easy_read:
Spices also improve the flavour of food.
They also have some medicinal uses for our health.
pg037_n0035_easy_read:
Provide income:
When farmers grow horticultural crops for sale, they can earn money for their day-to-day needs.
pg037_n0036_easy_read:
This also helps farmers save money for emergencies.
It also helps farmers invest more money to earn more money.
pg037_n0037_easy_read:
Farmers can also sell horticultural crops to foreign countries.
This brings in foreign income.
pg038_n0003_easy_read:
(c) Provide employment:
Producing horticultural crops involves many activities.
These activities happen from the start of production to final use in the value chain.
pg038_n0004_easy_read: This creates jobs for the people who do those activities.
pg038_n0006_easy_read:
(d) Stimulate industrial growth:
Most horticultural crops provide raw materials for processing and value addition in industries, including beverage industries.
pg038_n0008_easy_read:
(e) Provide business opportunities:
There are many chances to start a business in the horticultural industry.
pg038_n0009_easy_read: You can do this by working directly with businesses in the crop production process.
pg038_n0010_easy_read: This is possible if there are people who want to buy the produce and its by-products.
pg038_n0011_easy_read: You can also start a business that helps the main horticultural businesses work better.
pg038_n0012_easy_read:
You can find a business opportunity in horticultural crops by:
- finding the problems that people have in the crop value chain
- coming up with solutions that can help a person earn money
pg038_n0014_easy_read:
(f) Conserve soil:
Besides making the environment look beautiful, crops such as ornamental shrubs and grasses in the landscape give the soil enough cover.
pg038_n0015_easy_read: This protects the soil from erosion by wind and water.

Ornamental crops make the environment beautiful.

In this chapter, you will learn the basic principles and practices of vegetable production.
You will learn about:
- planning vegetable production
- preparing the land
- sowing or planting
- managing water, nutrients, and pests
- harvesting and postharvest practices
pg054_n0011_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you combine scientific knowledge, farming techniques, and sustainable approaches to produce vegetables.
pg054_n0012_easy_read: This will help you earn money and have food at home.
pg054_n0015_easy_read: Lays the foundation for successful horticultural farming
pg054_n0019_easy_read: When you grow vegetables, it is important to remember a few things.
pg054_n0020_easy_read:
Most vegetables spoil quickly.
Most vegetables are also bulky.
Some vegetables grow only in certain seasons.
pg054_n0021_easy_read:
Vegetables also need resources to grow.
Pests and diseases can also affect vegetables.
pg054_n0022_easy_read: Sometimes it is not easy to know how much to produce because the market can change.
pg054_n0023_easy_read: So, to make a plan for growing vegetables, we need to think about:
pg054_n0027_easy_read: What do you want to achieve in vegetable production?
pg054_n0030_easy_read: What resources do you need for vegetable production?
pg054_n0033_easy_read: Which types of vegetables can you produce with the resources you have?
pg054_n0036_easy_read: How do you look after the vegetables to make sure they grow well?
pg054_n0039_easy_read: If you are growing more than 1 type of vegetable, or if you are growing vegetables and keeping animals, it is important to think about how they can be grown or kept together.
pg054_n0043_easy_read: Setting goals for vegetable production is an important step for successful production.
pg054_n0044_easy_read: Is the goal to earn money, to get food, or for other reasons?
pg054_n0045_easy_read: Also think about how much time and money you can invest in vegetable production.
pg054_n0046_easy_read: Make sure your goals are clear, specific, and achievable.
pg055_n0005_easy_read: Starting a vegetable business needs several resources.
pg055_n0006_easy_read: The resources you need can change based on where you are and the vegetables you want to grow.
pg055_n0007_easy_read: It is important to think carefully about each resource before you start your vegetable business.
pg055_n0012_easy_read:
Land: You need to know:
- where you will grow your vegetables
- how much land you have
- the type of vegetable to grow
pg055_n0015_easy_read: Climate: You need to know if the horticultural crop you want to grow suits the climate of the area.
pg055_n0018_easy_read: Water: You need to know where you will get water and how much it will cost.
pg055_n0019_easy_read: You also need to know if this water is suitable for your vegetables.
pg055_n0022_easy_read: Structures: You need to know the structures you need, such as buildings and fences.
pg055_n0023_easy_read: You also need to know how much it costs to keep the structures in good condition.
pg055_n0026_easy_read: Tools and equipment: You need to know the tools and equipment you need to use in your vegetable business.
pg055_n0027_easy_read: You also need to know if you need to rent or borrow tools and equipment, and estimate the cost.
pg055_n0030_easy_read: Money for capital: You need to know how much money you have to start your business.
pg055_n0031_easy_read: You also need to identify the source of money for starting and running the business.
pg055_n0034_easy_read:
Management skills: You need to know how to:
- keep records
- manage people
- prepare your budget
pg055_n0037_easy_read: Labour: You need to know how many people your vegetable business needs.
pg055_n0038_easy_read: You also need to know if you can use family labour or hired labour.
pg055_n0041_easy_read:
Market and marketing: You need to know:
- where your customers are
- how you will take your vegetables to them
- whether customers will collect the vegetables directly from your farm
pg055_n0042_easy_read: You also need to decide on a selling price that is reasonable and profitable.
pg055_n0046_easy_read: Plan your vegetable businesses using the resources you have.
pg055_n0047_easy_read: These resources include the water, land, money, and equipment you have.
pg055_n0048_easy_read: Compare your resources with the needs of each crop.
pg055_n0049_easy_read: If a crop needs a lot of sun and you have a lot of sun, that is good.
pg055_n0050_easy_read: If a crop needs rich soil and you have poor soil, you may need to apply fertilisers.
pg055_n0051_easy_read: If you are not sure, ask a local farmer or an expert.
pg055_n0052_easy_read: A local farmer or an expert can give you good advice based on their expertise and experience.
pg055_n0053_easy_read:
Use resources such as:
- books
- the internet
- local libraries
to learn more.
pg055_n0054_easy_read: Several websites and books can help you understand which crops grow well together and which crops suit your resources.
pg056_n0005_easy_read: You should also think about these things when you plan vegetable crop production:
pg056_n0009_easy_read: Crop rotation: If you plan to grow different crops in rotation, you should know how the crops affect each other.
pg056_n0010_easy_read:
Some crops can help other crops grow.
Some crops can harm other crops.
pg056_n0013_easy_read:
Pests and diseases: Learn about common pests and diseases that can harm your crop.
Examples are:
- insects
- birds
- wild animals
- domestic animals
- weeds
- diseases
Learn how to manage them.
pg056_n0016_easy_read: Harvesting: You need to know when to harvest your crops and how to harvest them.
pg056_n0019_easy_read: Risks: Each crop has its own risks.
pg056_n0020_easy_read:
Identify the risks.
Think early about how to reduce them.
pg056_n0022_easy_read: If you think about all these things, you can grow your vegetable crops successfully.
pg056_n0026_easy_read: If you want to grow more than 1 type of crop, think about how the crops fit together.
pg056_n0027_easy_read: For example, you might have enough people to help with 1 crop.
pg056_n0028_easy_read: But if you choose another crop that also needs a lot of labour, you might not have enough people to help.
pg056_n0029_easy_read: It is important to do all activities on time and in the right way.
pg056_n0030_easy_read:
In this case, you will need to prepare a chart.
The chart should show the labour needed for each crop at the right time.
pg056_n0031_easy_read: If you want to keep animals and grow vegetables, think about how they can stay together.
pg056_n0032_easy_read: This is because some animals and crops do not mix well.
pg056_n0033_easy_read: For example, free-range chickens can destroy some vegetables, such as amaranth.
pg056_n0034_easy_read: However, free-range chickens do not cause trouble for cassava production.
pg056_n0035_easy_read: Fencing can help separate the 2 enterprises.
pg056_n0039_easy_read: There are different ways to take part in the vegetable industry.
pg056_n0044_easy_read:
Production of traditional vegetables: This means growing vegetables such as:
- nightshade
- pumpkin leaves
- amaranth
- sweet potato leaves
pg056_n0047_easy_read: Organic vegetable production enterprises: This means growing vegetables without using synthetic or industrial fertilisers and pesticides.
pg056_n0050_easy_read: Conventional vegetable production enterprises: This means growing vegetables using synthetic inputs such as fertilisers and pesticides.
pg056_n0053_easy_read: Retail marketing of vegetables: This means selling vegetables in small portions.
pg057_n0005_easy_read: Wholesale marketing of vegetables: This means selling vegetables in large amounts.
pg057_n0008_easy_read:
Leafy vegetable production: This means growing vegetables that people eat for their leaves, such as:
- amaranth
- Chinese cabbage
- cowpea leaves
pg057_n0011_easy_read:
Fruit vegetable production: This means growing vegetables that are grouped as fruits, such as:
- tomato
- pepper
- eggplant
- cucumber
pg057_n0014_easy_read:
Root vegetable production: This means growing vegetables that are grouped as roots, such as:
- carrot
- beetroot
- bulb onion
pg057_n0017_easy_read: Assorted vegetable production: This means growing a mix of several vegetables.

pg058_n0008_easy_read: The next step is to prepare the land for planting.

This has several steps:

In vegetable production, 3 types of seedbeds are commonly used.
The type depends on:
- the production season
- the type of irrigation
- the condition of the field
pg058_n0015_easy_read:
These are:
- raised seedbed
- sunken seedbed
- flat seedbed
pg058_n0018_easy_read: Raised beds are good for clayey soils or areas with poor drainage.
pg058_n0019_easy_read: Raised beds are also useful for irrigated crops where water flows down the furrows between the beds.
pg058_n0020_easy_read:
Raised beds are usually 100 cm wide and 10 - 30 cm high.
The best height depends on the soil texture and moisture.
pg058_n0021_easy_read:
People can make raised beds with hand tools on small to medium farms.
People can make them with machines on large farms.
pg058_n0022_easy_read:
Raised beds have 2 advantages:
- better drainage
- easier access for hand work such as weeding
pg058_n0023_easy_read: Figures 4.1 (a) and (b) show examples of raised beds.
pg058_n0024_easy_read: The beds in Figure 4.1 (a) are best for areas with high rainfall.
pg058_n0025_easy_read:
The beds in Figure 4.1 (b) have a lip on all 4 sides.
This lip helps stop water from running off, especially in drier conditions.
pg058_n0028_easy_read: Figure 4.1 (a): Raised beds without a lip around
pg058_n0030_easy_read: Figure 4.1 (b): Raised beds with lips around
pg058_n0033_easy_read:
Sunken seedbeds are about 100 cm wide.
People make them by removing soil to 10 - 20 cm below the surrounding soil level.
pg058_n0034_easy_read:
This helps sunken seedbeds to conserve water.
They do not have exposed sides where moisture can be lost.
pg059_n0003_easy_read: in dry regions or during dry seasons.
pg059_n0004_easy_read: The main problem with sunken beds is that they lose some topsoil when people make them.
pg059_n0005_easy_read: People do this by removing soil from the bed area and putting it on the paths around the beds.
pg059_n0006_easy_read: Figure 4.2 shows examples of sunken beds.
pg059_n0011_easy_read: Flatbeds are seedbeds made by levelling the area where people will plant.
pg059_n0012_easy_read: People use flatbeds where there is enough water and there are no drainage problems.
pg059_n0013_easy_read:
In some areas, people first plant crops on a flatbed.
Then, as the season goes on, they throw soil into the crop row to make a mound around the plants.
pg059_n0014_easy_read: This process is called ‘hilling up’ or ‘earthing up’.
pg059_n0015_easy_read:
People also do this to:
- control weeds in the row
- support the plants
- improve drainage
pg059_n0016_easy_read: For tuber crops, hilling up keeps the growing tubers covered with soil.

pg060_n0031_easy_read: Germination is when a seed starts to grow into a plant.
pg060_n0032_easy_read: This is an important step in planting.
pg060_n0033_easy_read: Before we plant crops, we need to check if the seeds can germinate.
pg060_n0034_easy_read: We do this by using a germination test.
pg060_n0035_easy_read: This test helps us know if the seeds are alive and ready to grow.
pg060_n0036_easy_read: To do a germination test, follow these steps:
pg060_n0046_easy_read: Get some sand and put it in a container, such as a bucket or a plate.
pg060_n0049_easy_read: Put the seeds in the sand.
pg060_n0050_easy_read: If the container is small, you may need more than 1 container.
pg060_n0053_easy_read: Add water to the sand to make the seeds moist.
pg060_n0056_easy_read: Keep watering the seeds so they stay moist, but not too wet, until they germinate.
pg060_n0057_easy_read: The amount of water depends on how moist the sand is.
pg060_n0060_easy_read: When the seeds start to grow, count them.
pg060_n0061_easy_read: The number of seeds that germinate shows how many seeds grew out of the 100 seeds you planted.
pg060_n0062_easy_read: For example, if 96 out of 100 seeds grew, it means 96% of the seeds germinated.
pg060_n0064_easy_read: The germination percentage helps us know how good the seeds are at germinating.
pg060_n0065_easy_read: It helps us choose the best seeds to buy.
pg060_n0066_easy_read: Seeds are good if they have a high germination percentage, about 95% or more.
pg061_n0003_easy_read: The germination percentage is usually on the packet of certified seeds.
pg061_n0004_easy_read: If seeds have a low germination percentage, you need to sow more seeds to get the required number of plants.
pg061_n0008_easy_read: When planting vegetables, it is important to choose the right planting materials.
pg061_n0009_easy_read: Here are some things to consider:
pg061_n0013_easy_read:
Suitability of the planting material to ecological conditions:
Choose planting materials that grow well in your area's climate and soil.
pg061_n0016_easy_read:
Purity of the planting materials:
Use high-quality seeds or seedlings that are free from contaminants.
pg061_n0019_easy_read:
Germination capacity:
Look for planting materials with a high germination rate. This means they are more likely to sprout and grow.
pg061_n0022_easy_read:
Disease resistance:
Choose planting materials that resist common diseases in your area. This helps plants stay healthy.
pg061_n0025_easy_read:
Certified planting materials:
Choose certified seeds or seedlings. They have been tested and shown to be safe and reliable.
pg061_n0029_easy_read: Proper spacing in vegetable production is important for good plant growth.
pg061_n0030_easy_read: Each plant needs space for its roots and leaves to spread. Each plant also needs enough air.
pg061_n0031_easy_read:
Proper spacing helps plants get enough:
- sunlight
- nutrients
- air
These are necessary for plant growth and development.
pg061_n0032_easy_read: Farmers should follow the recommended spacing. Farmers can ask a nearby agricultural extension worker for help.
pg061_n0033_easy_read:
Before planting, measure and mark the recommended spacing between plants. Use:
- tape measures or a ruler
- strings
- pegs
pg061_n0034_easy_read: As plants grow, check their spacing regularly. Do thinning or gap-filling where necessary.
pg061_n0035_easy_read: This will help you get bigger and healthier plants, with higher yields.
pg061_n0039_easy_read:
There are 2 main methods of planting vegetables:
- direct seeding
- transplanting
pg061_n0041_easy_read:
(a) Direct seeding (sowing):
This means you put the vegetable seed straight into the garden. The seed starts growing there and stays there until harvesting.
pg061_n0042_easy_read: Direct seeding costs less. It also reduces the risk of transplant shock.
pg061_n0043_easy_read:
There are 3 common methods of direct seeding:
- broadcasting
- drilling
- dibbling
pg062_n0005_easy_read: (i) Broadcasting: Scatter seeds thinly and evenly over the area.
pg062_n0006_easy_read: When you broadcast vegetable seeds, you can mix the seeds with the same amount of sand, in a 1 to 1 ratio. This stops the seeds from sticking together and helps you spread them more evenly.
pg062_n0007_easy_read: This method is best for crops such as amaranth and lettuce. Their seeds are small and light.
pg062_n0008_easy_read: These plants have shallow roots. You can thin them out easily later if needed.
pg062_n0010_easy_read: (ii) Drilling: Make a shallow furrow in the soil. Then drop the seeds thinly in the furrow.
pg062_n0011_easy_read: This method is best for vegetables like carrots. Carrot seeds are small, and the plants need close spacing.
pg062_n0012_easy_read: With drilling, the space between rows is known. But the space between plants in the same row is not clear.
pg062_n0013_easy_read: People also commonly use this method when sowing onion or tomato seeds in the nursery seed-bed.
pg062_n0015_easy_read:
(iii) Direct row planting: This method is best for crops that need space, for example:
- green beans
- common peas
- okra
pg062_n0016_easy_read: These crops are large. They need space for the best growth.
pg062_n0017_easy_read: The space between rows is known. The space between plants in each row is also known.
pg062_n0019_easy_read: (b) Transplanting: Start seeds in a controlled area called a nursery. Let them grow and become stronger. Then move the seedlings to the garden at the right time.
pg062_n0020_easy_read:
Some vegetables that grow best by transplanting are:
- tomatoes
- peppers
- onions
pg062_n0024_easy_read: Planting vegetables at the right time is important. It helps the vegetables grow well and helps farmers sell them when prices are high.
pg062_n0025_easy_read: Planting on time helps farmers get the best yield from their land.
pg062_n0026_easy_read: If farmers plant vegetables too early or too late, the vegetables may not grow well. Farmers may also get a low yield.
pg062_n0027_easy_read: To sell vegetables when prices are high, farmers need to plant them at the right time.
pg062_n0028_easy_read: This can be difficult because it depends on the weather and the soil type.
pg062_n0029_easy_read: Experienced farmers, teachers, or agricultural extension workers can advise on the best planting times.
pg062_n0030_easy_read: The goal is to plant vegetables at a time when they will grow better and be ready for harvest when prices are high.
pg062_n0031_easy_read: This will help farmers earn more money from their crops.

pg063_n0031_easy_read: Soil is a natural material where plants grow and get nutrients.
pg063_n0032_easy_read: Sometimes, however, soil becomes unhealthy or infertile.
pg063_n0033_easy_read: The following subsections discuss the causes of loss of soil fertility. They also discuss how organic and inorganic fertilisers help to maintain soil fertility.
pg063_n0037_easy_read: There are several causes of soil fertility loss or depletion. Some of them are discussed here.
pg063_n0040_easy_read: Soil erosion happens when moving wind or water removes the topsoil from the land.
pg063_n0041_easy_read: This can happen when there is a lot of rainfall or when the land has no vegetation cover.
pg063_n0042_easy_read: When soil erosion happens, nutrients in the soil can be washed away. This makes the soil infertile.
pg063_n0043_easy_read: To stop this, we can plant trees and other vegetation. This helps protect the soil from being washed or blown away.
pg063_n0044_easy_read: We can also use contour farming in sloping areas to reduce soil erosion (refer to Figure 4.4).
pg064_n0006_easy_read: Water logging happens when too much water stays in the soil for a long time.
pg064_n0007_easy_read: When water logging happens, the air in the soil is pushed out. This makes it hard for plant roots to breathe.
pg064_n0008_easy_read: To solve this problem, we can improve soil drainage. We can add organic matter or make channels for extra water to flow out.
pg064_n0011_easy_read: Leaching is when water washes nutrients down through the soil.
pg064_n0012_easy_read: This happens when it rains a lot or when we use irrigation.
pg064_n0013_easy_read: The nutrients move down in the soil, away from the plant roots.
pg064_n0014_easy_read: This means the plant cannot get the nutrients it needs.
pg064_n0015_easy_read: This is a problem because plants need these nutrients to grow.
pg064_n0016_easy_read: To stop this, we can use mulch or cover crops. They slow down water movement and reduce nutrient loss.
pg064_n0017_easy_read: We should also replace the lost nutrients by adding organic manure or inorganic fertilisers to the soil.

pg064_n0025_easy_read: This leaves the ground open to water and wind. This can cause the land to erode.
pg064_n0026_easy_read: This erosion can make the land less fertile and harder to farm.
pg064_n0027_easy_read:
Plants and soil contain important nutrients such as:
- carbon
- nitrogen
- phosphorus
- sulphur
pg064_n0028_easy_read: When these nutrients are burned, they are destroyed. Then they cannot help plants to grow well.

pg065_n0003_easy_read: The soil can be washed away by water and wind. This causes more erosion and loss of fertility.

pg065_n0009_easy_read: When crops grow on the same land all the time, they can reduce nutrients in the soil.
pg065_n0011_easy_read: Grazing can also reduce nutrients in the soil, especially when animals graze too much.
pg065_n0012_easy_read: To deal with this, we can practise crop rotation or use rotational grazing.
pg065_n0013_easy_read: This helps to keep a balance of nutrients in the soil.

pg065_n0018_easy_read: Using acid-forming or alkali-forming fertilisers for a long time can change soil pH.
pg065_n0019_easy_read: Acidic fertilisers can lower soil pH.
pg065_n0020_easy_read: Lower soil pH can affect plant growth.
pg065_n0021_easy_read: Alkaline fertilisers can raise soil pH.
pg065_n0022_easy_read: Higher soil pH can also affect plant growth.
pg065_n0023_easy_read: Changes in soil pH can affect soil micro-organisms and available nutrients.
pg065_n0024_easy_read: To avoid a lower pH, do not use too much acidic fertilisers.
pg065_n0025_easy_read: To avoid a higher pH, do not use too much alkaline fertilisers.
pg065_n0026_easy_read: Always check the soil pH before adding fertilisers.
pg065_n0027_easy_read: You can test the soil at home with a pH meter.
pg065_n0028_easy_read: You can also ask a crop extension worker for advice on choosing fertilisers.
pg065_n0029_easy_read: This will help keep the soil pH balanced for plant growth.
pg065_n0033_easy_read: Weeds are plants that grow where they are not needed.
pg065_n0034_easy_read: When we pull out weeds, we lose the nutrients that the weeds took from the soil.
pg065_n0035_easy_read: It is better to let the weeds decompose into humus in the field.
pg065_n0036_easy_read: But when weeds cause problems, we should remove them.
pg065_n0037_easy_read: To improve weed control and manage soil fertility, we can do the following:
pg065_n0041_easy_read: Removed weeds can be composted. This means they are left to decompose naturally.
pg065_n0042_easy_read: This process changes the weeds into nutrient-rich compost. The compost can be used to enrich the soil.

pg065_n0048_easy_read: Crop rotation also helps keep nutrients in the soil at a good level.

This is done by growing crops with different nutrient needs:
- crops with higher nutrient needs (heavy feeders)
- crops with lower nutrient needs (light feeders)
pg066_n0003_easy_read: By growing different types of crops, we keep soil nutrients balanced.
pg066_n0004_easy_read: Also, by changing crops with deep roots and crops with shallow roots, we make sure nutrients in all parts of the soil are used.
pg066_n0005_easy_read: Shallow-rooted crops take nutrients from the topsoil. Deep-rooted crops take nutrients from the lower soil.
pg066_n0006_easy_read: Legumes and rest periods in crop rotation also help to keep the soil fertile.
pg066_n0007_easy_read: This is because legumes and rest periods add more nutrients to the soil.
pg066_n0008_easy_read: So, crop rotation is a good way to reduce weeds and keep our soil healthy and productive.

pg066_n0022_easy_read: Too much salt can make the soil lose its fertility.

pg066_n0024_easy_read: Salts can also change the soil’s pH level.

pg067_n0008_easy_read: Volatilization is when nutrients in the soil change into gas and go up into the air instead of staying in the soil to feed plants.
pg067_n0009_easy_read:
The nutrients most often lost through volatilization, especially in hot weather, are:
- nitrogen
- sulphur
- phosphorus, in smaller amounts
pg067_n0010_easy_read: To stop this, put nitrogen and sulphur fertilisers into the soil instead of leaving them on top of the soil.
pg067_n0011_easy_read: Also, do not apply fertilisers in hot, dry conditions, because volatilization is more likely then.

pg067_n0022_easy_read: Organic fertilisers are materials from plants and animals that carry nutrients. They are also called manures or natural manures.

pg067_n0024_easy_read:
They add nutrients to the soil that plants need to grow, such as:

pg067_n0026_easy_read: There are different types of organic fertilisers, including manures.
pg067_n0027_easy_read:
Examples of manures are:

pg067_n0029_easy_read: It is important to store farmyard manure properly so that nutrients do not get lost.
pg067_n0030_easy_read: You can use farmyard manure in fields after it has decomposed well.
pg067_n0031_easy_read: Compost is made from organic materials or waste.

- the pile becomes smaller

pg069_n0026_easy_read: Water in the soil helps plants grow and stay healthy.
pg069_n0028_easy_read: Transpiration is when water turns into water vapour and leaves the plant through the leaves.
pg069_n0029_easy_read: Water also leaves the soil through a process called evaporation.
pg069_n0030_easy_read: The loss of water from both the soil and plants is called evapotranspiration.
pg069_n0031_easy_read: If we do not add water to the soil, plants can die.
pg069_n0033_easy_read: Different plants need different amounts of water.
pg069_n0034_easy_read: Some plants can tolerate a lot of water, and some cannot.
pg069_n0035_easy_read: Also, the amount of water a plant needs depends on its stage of growth and the weather.
pg069_n0036_easy_read: We can check how much water is in the soil by feeling it and looking at it.
pg069_n0037_easy_read: You can do this by squeezing a soil sample and checking how it feels and looks.
pg069_n0038_easy_read: If plants get too little water, they start to wilt and their leaves turn brown.
pg069_n0039_easy_read: If plants get too much water, their leaves can become soft and limp. They can also start to wilt because the roots cannot get enough air and diseases can attack them.
pg069_n0041_easy_read: Some stages of plant growth are more sensitive to lack of water.
pg069_n0042_easy_read: If we do not give plants enough water during these stages, the yield and quality of the produce are badly affected.
pg069_n0043_easy_read:
We can keep moisture in the soil by:
- applying compost or manure on the soil
- placing mulch on the soil
- practising crop rotation
pg069_n0044_easy_read: This helps to reduce how often we need to water or irrigate the crop.

pg072_n0019_easy_read: Choosing the right irrigation method for vegetable crops depends on several factors:
pg072_n0023_easy_read: The type of soil: Some irrigation methods work better with some types of soil.
pg072_n0024_easy_read: For example, furrow irrigation is not good for sandy soil because it can cause soil erosion and loss of plant nutrients.
pg072_n0027_easy_read: The shape of the land: If the land is flat, a method that spreads water evenly may be best.
pg072_n0028_easy_read: If the land is hilly, a method that can take water to the top of the hills may be better.
pg072_n0031_easy_read: The weather: In areas with a lot of rain, you may not need to water your plants as much.
pg072_n0032_easy_read: In areas with little rain, you may need to water your plants more.
pg072_n0035_easy_read: The type of crops: Some crops need more water than others.
pg072_n0036_easy_read: For example, tomatoes need more water than lettuce.
pg072_n0039_easy_read: The amount and quality of water: If you have a small amount of clean water, drip irrigation may be a good choice.
pg072_n0040_easy_read: Dirty or salty water can block drip lines and drippers. So, it is not good for drip irrigation.
pg072_n0041_easy_read: A small amount of water cannot support furrow irrigation.
pg072_n0044_easy_read: The costs and benefits: Some methods of watering plants can be expensive but use water in an economical way.
pg072_n0045_easy_read: Other methods may be cheaper but not economical.
pg072_n0048_easy_read: The amount of work: Some methods need a lot of work to set up and maintain.
pg073_n0003_easy_read: Other methods are easier to set up and maintain.
pg073_n0004_easy_read:
(h) Level of technology and capital:
Some methods need a lot of technology and money to set up.
pg073_n0005_easy_read: Other methods are simpler and cheaper to set up.
pg073_n0007_easy_read: So, you need to think about each of these factors when choosing the best irrigation method for your vegetable crops.
