pg073_n0040_easy_read: A crop pest is any living thing that harms plants.
pg073_n0041_easy_read:
Crop pests can be:
- insects
- animals
- weeds
- bacteria
- fungi
- viruses
pg073_n0042_easy_read: It is important to understand crop pests because they can badly damage our plants.
pg073_n0043_easy_read: Pests can harm crops in the field and after storage.
pg073_n0044_easy_read: This is how pests can damage our crops:
pg074_n0005_easy_read: They eat plant leaves and stems. This slows plant growth.
pg074_n0006_easy_read: This can make plants produce less. The damaged part of the plant cannot do important life processes well.
pg074_n0009_easy_read: Some pests, such as nematodes and moles, damage plant roots. This makes the plants wilt and die.
pg074_n0012_easy_read: Some pests, for example squirrels and rats, dig up seeds. This means there are fewer plants in each unit area.
pg074_n0015_easy_read: Insects like thrips can damage flowers and fruits. This lowers their quality.
pg074_n0018_easy_read: Some pests suck plant sap. This makes the plant grow slowly and become deformed.
pg074_n0021_easy_read: Pests such as diseases make crop plants unhealthy. They may also cause the plant to die.
pg074_n0024_easy_read: Crop pests can increase the cost of farming. We need to spend money to control them, for example by buying pesticides.
pg074_n0027_easy_read:
Pests such as weeds compete with vegetable crops for:
- nutrients
- water
- light
This reduces the quality and yield of the produce.
pg074_n0029_easy_read: We can manage crop pests in different ways.
pg074_n0030_easy_read:
We can use:
- cultural farming practices
- physical or mechanical methods
- biological methods
- chemical methods
- a combination of methods called Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
pg074_n0034_easy_read: Cultural pest management protects plants from pests by using good farming practices.
pg074_n0035_easy_read: We do this by changing the environment where the pest lives.
pg074_n0036_easy_read:
For example, we can change:
- the amount of sunlight
- the temperature
- the soil's pH level
pg074_n0037_easy_read:
This includes:
- using resistant varieties
- planting and weeding at the right time
- keeping the field and the area around it clean
- using mulching materials
- removing diseased plants
- crop rotation
pg074_n0038_easy_read: This method helps stop pests from becoming too many and damaging our crop plants.
pg074_n0039_easy_read: It makes the farming system stronger. It also reduces the need for chemical pesticides.
pg074_n0043_easy_read: These methods use physical or mechanical ways to kill pests. They also create barriers to stop pests from reaching the crops they attack.
pg074_n0044_easy_read:
The methods include:
- hand picking
- trapping and killing
- flooding and overhead irrigation
- physical barriers
- proper drying before storage
- use of lethal temperature
pg074_n0048_easy_read: This method uses living organisms to control pests. These organisms are natural predators that eat other organisms.
pg074_n0049_easy_read: The natural predators can be birds and insects.
pg075_n0003_easy_read: Biological pest management is better than using chemical pesticides because it helps to keep the farm ecosystem balanced.
pg075_n0004_easy_read: Farmers often bring good natural predators into the farm.
pg075_n0005_easy_read:
Examples are:
- parasitic wasps that prey on whitefly and mealy bugs
- ladybird beetle that preys on aphids
- praying mantis that preys on the giant looper
- weaver ants that prey on white scales
- chicken that preys on stainers
- chameleons that prey on most insects
- cats that prey on rats, mice, and moles
- wasps and poultry that prey on bollworms
pg075_n0006_easy_read: When a farm has a good environment, it helps these good creatures, called predators, to live there.
pg075_n0007_easy_read: In this way, the farm ecosystem helps to control pests.
pg075_n0009_easy_read: When farmers use biological pest management, they help to keep the environment healthy and sustainable.
pg075_n0010_easy_read: However, biological pest management needs careful planning and management.
pg075_n0011_easy_read: The farmer needs to introduce or keep the right good creatures. The farmer must also make sure these creatures have the conditions they need to stay alive and do well.
pg075_n0012_easy_read: Biological pest management controls pests and keeps the farm environment healthy and balanced.
pg075_n0013_easy_read: However, this process can be slow in some cases.
pg075_n0017_easy_read: Chemical pest control is a way of controlling pests by using chemicals, also called pesticides.
pg075_n0018_easy_read:
These chemicals come in different forms:
- powders
- liquids
- gases
pg075_n0019_easy_read: People can spray, dust, or fumigate them onto soil and crop plants.
pg075_n0020_easy_read:
People group pesticides by:
- their formulation
- the type of pest they target
- how they work
pg075_n0021_easy_read:
Some pesticides are made to kill specific pests. For example:
- insecticides kill insect pests
- nematicides kill nematodes
- rodenticides kill rodents
- fungicides kill fungi
- bactericides kill bacteria
- herbicides kill weeds
pg075_n0022_easy_read: Pesticides can also be synthetic or bio-pesticides.
pg075_n0023_easy_read: It is recommended to use bio-pesticides. These are pesticides that come from animal and plant by-products.
pg075_n0026_easy_read: When you use pesticides to control pests, consider these factors:
pg075_n0030_easy_read: Know the target pest. It is important to know what kind of pest you are dealing with.
pg075_n0034_easy_read: Choose the right pesticide. Not all pesticides work in the same way.
pg075_n0035_easy_read: Choose one that is known to work well against the target pest.
pg075_n0038_easy_read: Rotate different pesticides. Sometimes pests get used to a certain pesticide, so the pesticide no longer works well on the target pest.
pg075_n0039_easy_read: In this case, you should try a different pesticide.
pg075_n0042_easy_read: Choose the right time. The best time to use a pesticide is when pests are most likely to be harmed by the pesticide.
pg075_n0043_easy_read: It is recommended to start using pesticide
pg076_n0003_easy_read: Use this only when the number of pests is high enough to cause economic loss.
pg076_n0004_easy_read:
Do not use pesticides when rain is about to fall.
Rain can wash away the chemical.
pg076_n0008_easy_read:
Use the right amount.
Too much pesticide can be harmful.
Too little pesticide may not work.
pg076_n0009_easy_read: Make sure you use the right amount.
pg076_n0012_easy_read:
Monitoring:
After using the pesticides, keep watching to see if they worked.
pg076_n0015_easy_read:
Pesticides are toxic chemicals.
Handle them with care.
pg076_n0016_easy_read: So, when you use pesticides, take these precautions:
pg076_n0020_easy_read:
Always check the expiry date.
Read the instructions carefully.
pg076_n0023_easy_read:
Wear protective gear, such as:
- masks
- gloves
- field boots
pg076_n0026_easy_read: Do not breathe in the pesticide.
pg076_n0029_easy_read: Do not let the pesticide touch your food or water.
pg076_n0032_easy_read: Wash your hands and clothes after handling pesticides.
pg076_n0035_easy_read: Do not smoke or eat while using pesticides.
pg076_n0038_easy_read: Clean the spraying equipment after use.
pg076_n0041_easy_read:
Store the chemicals in a safe place.
Keep them out of reach of children and animals.
pg076_n0044_easy_read: Do not throw leftover containers in gardens.
pg076_n0047_easy_read:
Always wait for the recommended time before harvesting a treated crop.
This is called the withdrawal period.
pg076_n0050_easy_read: Keep a record of the dates and all the chemicals you use.
pg076_n0051_easy_read: This record helps you know when to harvest your crops.
pg076_n0053_easy_read:
Chemical pest control is faster and easier to predict than other methods.
But it can be expensive.
It can also harm people, animals, and the environment.
pg076_n0054_easy_read:
So, use these chemicals safely and responsibly.
Think about their effects on the environment and other helpful organisms.
pg076_n0057_easy_read:
Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is a way to control pests.
It uses a mix of pest control methods, such as:
- cultural control
- biological control
- physical control
- chemical control
pg076_n0058_easy_read: These methods are chosen using information about pests and how pests interact with the environment.
pg076_n0059_easy_read: Follow these steps when using IPM:
pg076_n0063_easy_read:
Choose pest control methods that are safe for:
- crops
- soil
- air
- water
- people
pg076_n0066_easy_read:
Use the differences between crops and pests.
This gives crops an advantage over pests.
pg077_n0005_easy_read: Try to reduce how long pests survive in the soil.
pg077_n0008_easy_read: Use weed control methods to stop weeds from growing.
pg077_n0011_easy_read: Make pest control methods flexible so they can fit different seasons.
pg077_n0014_easy_read: Use different methods together to suppress, block, or repel the pests.
pg077_n0016_easy_read: When you use integrated pest management, start with the least harmful methods.
pg077_n0017_easy_read:
These methods include:
- prevention or cultural practices
- physical control methods
- biological control methods
pg077_n0018_easy_read: If these methods do not work, consider using non-native predators.
pg077_n0019_easy_read:
Use chemical control methods only when necessary.
Always start with naturally occurring materials.
pg077_n0020_easy_read: Here are some strategies for using integrated pest management in vegetables:
pg077_n0025_easy_read: This can reduce the need for pesticides.
pg077_n0028_easy_read: Rotate your crops to stop pests from building up in the soil.
pg077_n0029_easy_read: You can do this by planting different types of vegetables in the same area each year.
pg077_n0032_easy_read: Use biological control agents such as ladybird beetles and parasitic wasps to control pests.
pg077_n0033_easy_read: These natural enemies can help keep pests under control.

pg077_n0037_easy_read: This can help prevent pests from growing.

Harvesting is the process of removing the whole plant, or the useful parts of the plant, after it is mature.
People do this for eating, selling, storing, or processing.
pg078_n0028_easy_read: The harvested part or the whole plant must reach the right stage of maturity before harvest.
pg078_n0029_easy_read:
So, it is important to know the maturity signs for different vegetable crops.
Harvesting too early or too late lowers the quality of the produce and shortens its shelf life.
pg078_n0030_easy_read: The harvesting method depends on the type of vegetable crop.
pg078_n0031_easy_read:
Harvest properly.
Do not damage the plant or the produce.
pg078_n0035_easy_read: Postharvest practices in vegetable crops are the processes that happen after vegetables are harvested.
pg078_n0036_easy_read: These practices help to make vegetables ready to eat, easy to handle, and able to last longer.
pg078_n0037_easy_read:
These practices depend on:
- the type of vegetables
- how we want to use them
- when we want to use them
pg078_n0038_easy_read:
For most vegetables, these practices may include:
- cooling
- cleaning
- sorting and grading
- packaging
- storing
- transporting
pg078_n0039_easy_read:
We can also use special treatments to keep vegetables fresh and good to eat for longer.
These treatments include:
- refrigeration
- heat treatment
- modified atmosphere packaging
pg078_n0040_easy_read: Figure 4.7 shows a summary of postharvest practices in vegetables.
pg079_n0003_easy_read: Figure 4.7: Practices after harvest for vegetables
pg079_n0006_easy_read: Precooling is a way to remove heat quickly after harvesting vegetables.
pg079_n0007_easy_read: This is important because heat can make vegetables spoil faster.
pg079_n0008_easy_read: Precooling helps to remove field heat from vegetables after harvest.
pg079_n0009_easy_read: It also helps to stop vegetables from losing water and from spoiling.
pg079_n0010_easy_read: In this way, vegetables can stay fresh for a long time and keep their taste.
pg079_n0011_easy_read: You can do precooling by putting vegetables in a cool place, such as a refrigerator or a cool room.
pg079_n0012_easy_read:
If refrigerators or cool rooms are not available, put the vegetables in:
- a cool shaded area
- a charcoal evaporative cooler
- a zero energy cooling chamber
pg079_n0015_easy_read: Farmers and other people who handle vegetables need to clean or disinfect properly.
pg079_n0016_easy_read: This is important to prevent diseases and food-related illnesses that can pass to people who eat the vegetables.
pg079_n0019_easy_read:
When we sort vegetables, we remove the ones that are:
- spoiled
- damaged
- diseased
pg079_n0020_easy_read: This is important because it stops the production of a harmful gas called ethylene. It also prevents contamination that can affect other vegetables.
pg079_n0021_easy_read:
Grading means organising vegetables by features such as:
- colour
- size
- shape
- how ripe they are
- how mature they are
pg079_n0022_easy_read: Grading helps us to identify and handle vegetables easily by using common features.
pg079_n0025_easy_read: Packaging vegetables means protecting them from harm.
pg079_n0026_easy_read: We put vegetables in boxes or bags to keep them safe from damage.
pg079_n0027_easy_read: This also helps us to carry or handle the vegetables easily.
pg079_n0028_easy_read: However, if we use the wrong packaging materials, the vegetables can get damaged. This can lead to losses.
pg079_n0029_easy_read:
In Tanzania, we often use these materials for packaging:
- wooden crates
- cardboard boxes
- woven palm baskets
- plastic crates
- nylon sacks
- jute sacks
- polythene bags
pg079_n0030_easy_read: However, some of these materials may not protect the vegetables well.
pg080_n0003_easy_read:
The packaging material should let the vegetables breathe.
This helps to stop them from getting too hot.
pg080_n0004_easy_read:
Good packaging material should be smooth.
It should not be too tall or too large.
If it is too tall or too large, it can put too much pressure on the vegetables at the bottom of the pack.
pg080_n0005_easy_read:
This pressure can injure the inside of the vegetables.
This can lower the quality of the vegetables after harvest.
pg080_n0008_easy_read: Storing vegetables is important because it keeps them fresh for a long time.
pg080_n0009_easy_read: However, some vegetables are hard to keep fresh for a long time.
pg080_n0010_easy_read:
For short-term storage, we can keep vegetables at room temperature if there is good airflow.
This stops the vegetables from getting too hot.
pg080_n0011_easy_read: For longer-term storage, we can keep vegetables at cooler temperatures and high humidity.
pg080_n0012_easy_read:
We can also use a charcoal evaporative cooler or a zero-energy cooling chamber to keep vegetables fresh.
Refer to Figure 4.8 (a) and (b).
pg080_n0013_easy_read: So, to stop many harvested vegetables from spoiling, we need to find and use good storage methods.
pg080_n0016_easy_read: Figure 4.8 (a): Section of a charcoal cooler
pg080_n0022_easy_read:
Transporting vegetables to the market needs special transport.
The transport must keep the vegetables cool and safe.
pg080_n0026_easy_read: Processing vegetables is a way to make them last longer.
pg080_n0027_easy_read:
We can do this by:
- canning
- drying
- freezing
pg080_n0028_easy_read:
You can choose where to process the produce.
This depends on the size of the produce and the level of technology.
You can process it in a large factory or in a small backyard.
pg080_n0029_easy_read: To learn more, you can ask your local crop or food processing experts.
pg080_n0032_easy_read: We need to sell our vegetables in a way that reduces losses as much as possible and gives a reasonably good price.

pg082_n0016_easy_read: Amaranth is a vegetable crop that grows fast. People can grow it all year round in Tanzania.
pg082_n0017_easy_read: People can grow amaranth for its leaves or its seeds.
pg082_n0018_easy_read: Amaranth is easy to grow. It gives quick returns and needs only a few simple things.
pg082_n0019_easy_read:
Amaranth is rich in:
- vitamins A, B, and C
- minerals such as calcium and iron
pg082_n0020_easy_read: Some amaranth grains also have a lot of protein.
pg082_n0021_easy_read: You can eat amaranth by itself or mix it with other vegetables.
pg082_n0022_easy_read: Amaranth can grow in many different soil and weather conditions.
pg082_n0023_easy_read: Farmers can also earn money by selling amaranth leaves or grains.
pg082_n0024_easy_read: Figure 5.1 shows leafy amaranth. Figure 5.2 shows grain amaranth.
pg083_n0009_easy_read:

pg083_n0032_easy_read: Amaranth grows well in different types of soil.
pg083_n0033_easy_read:
However, amaranth grows best in well-drained soil, such as:
- loamy soil
- sandy loamy soil
- silty loamy soil
This soil should be rich in organic matter.
pg083_n0034_easy_read: A pH level between 4.5 and 7.5 is suitable for amaranth.
pg083_n0035_easy_read: Amaranth grows well in hot and humid weather.
pg083_n0036_easy_read: The best temperature for amaranth is between 18 and 25 degrees Celsius.
pg083_n0037_easy_read: Amaranth does not grow well in waterlogged conditions.
pg083_n0038_easy_read: If free-range animals are around, put a fence around the place.
pg084_n0005_easy_read: To prepare a seedbed for amaranth, follow these steps:
pg084_n0009_easy_read: Clear the site. Then plough it to a depth of at least 25 centimetres.
pg084_n0010_easy_read: After that, harrow and level the soil to make a fine tilth.
pg084_n0013_easy_read: Remove weeds and debris. This helps to reduce competition for resources.
pg084_n0016_easy_read:
Apply well-decomposed farmyard manure at fine ploughing.
Use about:
- 25 tons per 1 hectare
- 2 kg per 1 m²
pg084_n0019_easy_read: Use sunken beds in dry seasons when water is not enough. Use raised beds in very wet or rainy seasons.
pg084_n0022_easy_read: Level the seed beds well. Do not leave low patches on the surface. This helps to prevent damping off diseases.
pg084_n0026_easy_read: Amaranth seeds have many types. Each type has its own features.
pg084_n0027_easy_read: Some types are good for grain. Other types are better for leafy vegetables.
pg084_n0028_easy_read:
Buy high-quality seeds from trusted sellers. For example:
- research centres
- registered seed distributors
pg084_n0029_easy_read: If you cannot find registered seed sellers, you can buy seeds from local markets or grow your own seeds at home.
pg084_n0030_easy_read: Before you use the seeds, check their germination rate.
pg084_n0031_easy_read: Amaranth seeds are very small. So, during sowing, people usually mix them with sand to make them easier to handle.
pg084_n0032_easy_read: The common ratio is 1 gram of seed to 100 grams of sand.
pg084_n0033_easy_read: People usually sow amaranth seeds directly into the soil.
pg084_n0034_easy_read: Sometimes, people first grow amaranth in a nursery. Later, they transplant it to the main field.
pg084_n0035_easy_read: However, this method is not practical for large fields.
pg084_n0037_easy_read: You can sow seeds directly in the field by broadcasting. You can also sow them in rows by the drilling method.
pg084_n0038_easy_read: In the broadcasting method, spread the seeds mixed with sand thinly and evenly over the seed bed.
pg084_n0039_easy_read: To sow by the drilling method, follow these steps:
pg084_n0043_easy_read: Make furrows that are 0.5 to 1.0 cm deep.
pg084_n0044_easy_read: Drill the seeds mixed with sand into the furrows. Then lightly cover the seeds with soil.
pg084_n0047_easy_read: If you grow amaranth for uprooting, keep the furrows 15 - 20 cm apart.
pg084_n0048_easy_read: For amaranth picked piece by piece, space the furrows 30 cm apart.
pg084_n0049_easy_read: After planting, thin out the plants. Keep 15 cm between each plant.
pg084_n0052_easy_read: Water the bed gently to keep the field moist.
pg084_n0053_easy_read: The amount of water in the soil will show how much and how often to irrigate.
pg084_n0055_easy_read: If you follow the spacing properly, you will need about 2 - 2.5 kg of seeds per
pg085_n0003_easy_read:
Per hectare.
This is the same as 0.5 g of seeds per square metre of a bed.
pg085_n0004_easy_read: Usually, seeds take about 3 days from sowing to germination.
pg085_n0008_easy_read: Amaranth needs a lot of nutrients.
pg085_n0009_easy_read: You can use organic or synthetic fertilisers, depending on what the plant needs.
pg085_n0010_easy_read: If you want to harvest the whole amaranth plant, improve the soil fertility before planting.
pg085_n0011_easy_read: You can do this by adding about 20 - 25 tons of well-decomposed manure per hectare (2 - 2.5 kg per m²) at the ploughing stage.
pg085_n0012_easy_read:
You can also use chemical fertilisers at planting, such as:
- Nitrogen
- Phosphorous
- Potash (NPK)
pg085_n0014_easy_read:
Also, you can spray the crop with 1% urea or diluted cow urine after every harvest.
This can help the plants grow more and produce more.
pg085_n0018_easy_read: Amaranth needs a steady amount of water, especially during germination and early growth.
pg085_n0019_easy_read:
Water the plants regularly.
Do not use too much water because too much water can cause a disease called damping off.
pg085_n0020_easy_read: It is better to water the plants when the air is cooler, such as in the morning or evening.
pg085_n0021_easy_read:
There are several ways to water amaranth plants:
- watering through furrows
- overhead watering
- basin irrigation
- using a watering can, especially for small-scale or home gardens
pg085_n0025_easy_read: Use practices to reduce weeds and weed seeds before sowing.
pg085_n0026_easy_read: This may include deep ploughing to kill both annual and perennial weeds.
pg085_n0027_easy_read: You can apply non-selective systematic herbicides before ploughing to kill weeds such as nut grass.
pg085_n0028_easy_read:
Irrigating ploughed land before sowing will make new weeds grow.
You will need to remove the new weeds before sowing.
pg085_n0029_easy_read:
You can use other practices after the crop has been established, for example:
- hand pulling
- weeding
pg085_n0033_easy_read: You can harvest amaranth shortly after planting.
pg085_n0034_easy_read: This means you must deal with pest problems early, even before sowing.

pg086_n0009_easy_read: Figure 5.3 (d): Damage from leaf webber larvae
pg086_n0026_easy_read: Aphids suck sap from the plant.
pg086_n0028_easy_read:
The leaves curl.
The plants become stunted.
pg086_n0035_easy_read: Stem weevils make holes inside the plant stem.
pg086_n0037_easy_read: There are galls on the stems.
pg086_n0044_easy_read: The larvae chew the leaves between the veins.
pg086_n0046_easy_read:
The leaves look white and silky.
There are brown deposits that look like sawdust.
pg086_n0053_easy_read: Spider mites suck sap from the plant.
pg086_n0055_easy_read:
There are yellow or white spots on the leaves.
There are ball-like masses.
pg087_n0016_easy_read: The stem rots. Brown-black marks appear at the base of the stem.
pg087_n0018_easy_read:
Do the following:
- Level the land.
- Prepare the soil well.
- Avoid too much water.
- Do not plant too closely.
pg087_n0023_easy_read: White spots appear on the leaves.
pg087_n0025_easy_read:
Do the following:
- Avoid planting in the rainy season.
- Avoid overhead irrigation.
pg087_n0030_easy_read: White, hairy, silk-like threads appear. The tips are black.
pg087_n0032_easy_read: Do not let water soak the stems and leaves.

pg090_n0034_easy_read: Chinese cabbage grows well in temperatures of 15 - 22oC.
pg090_n0035_easy_read: If the weather gets colder, the cabbage will start to flower and stop making leaves.
pg090_n0036_easy_read: Chinese cabbage grows best at heights of 500 – 1500 m above sea level.
pg090_n0037_easy_read: When you choose a site, look for a sunny area with good drainage.
pg090_n0038_easy_read: Make sure there is a reliable source of water for irrigation.
pg090_n0039_easy_read: Avoid areas where water can collect and cause waterlogging.
pg090_n0043_easy_read: To prepare the soil for Chinese cabbage, first dig up the soil.
pg090_n0044_easy_read: After that, remove all weeds and other unwanted things.
pg090_n0045_easy_read: Then make the dug soil smooth with a harrow or rake.
pg090_n0046_easy_read: The next step is to add well-decomposed manure to the soil.
pg090_n0047_easy_read: This manure can come from farm animals or compost.
pg090_n0048_easy_read: Use about 1 bucket of 20 litres of manure for every square metre of soil.
pg090_n0053_easy_read:
The seeds should be:
- clean
- strong
- free from mould
pg090_n0054_easy_read:
Avoid seeds that have:
- spots
- cracks
- discolouration
pg090_n0055_easy_read: Larger seeds usually grow into stronger plants.
pg090_n0056_easy_read: Choose the type that is most in demand.
pg091_n0004_easy_read: You can sow Chinese cabbage seeds directly in the seedbed.
pg091_n0005_easy_read: You can also sow Chinese cabbage seeds first in a nursery. Then transplant them to the seedbed.
pg091_n0006_easy_read: An average of 5 – 6 kg of seeds for direct sowing and 1.2 – 1.7 kg of seeds for transplanting is enough for 1 hectare.
pg091_n0009_easy_read: You can sow Chinese cabbage seeds directly in the field by using the dibbling method.
pg091_n0010_easy_read:
Put 2 - 3 seeds in each hole.
Leave 25 - 35 cm between holes.
Leave 30 - 40 cm between rows.
pg091_n0011_easy_read: The spacing depends on the type of Chinese cabbage.
pg091_n0012_easy_read: Keep the seedbed moist by watering it.
pg091_n0013_easy_read: When the seedlings are about 6 - 10 cm tall, remove some seedlings. Leave only 1 plant in each hole.
pg091_n0014_easy_read: Also, fill the gaps where the seeds did not grow.
pg091_n0017_easy_read: First, prepare the nursery bed well.
pg091_n0018_easy_read: Make shallow furrows about 25 - 30 cm apart.
pg091_n0019_easy_read: Sow the seeds thinly in the furrows. Then cover them with a thin layer of soil.
pg091_n0020_easy_read: Water the nursery lightly. Then cover it with dry grass mulch to keep the soil moist.
pg091_n0022_easy_read: When the seedlings start to grow, remove the grass cover.
pg091_n0023_easy_read: Put a partial shade about 60 - 100 cm high. This protects the seedlings from strong sunlight and heavy rain.
pg091_n0024_easy_read: It is recommended to grow seedlings in trays. This helps to reduce shock to the plants during transplanting.
pg091_n0025_easy_read: Transplanting seedlings from ordinary nurseries with bare roots can cause transplanting shock.

pg092_n0005_easy_read:
Move the seedlings from soil nurseries or seedling trays to a permanent seedbed when they are:
- 3 - 4 weeks old
- about 6 - 10 cm tall
- have 4 true leaves
pg092_n0006_easy_read: Before moving them, harden off the seedlings.
pg092_n0007_easy_read: Do this by reducing watering and shade in the nursery a few days before taking the seedlings to the main field.
pg092_n0008_easy_read:
Plant the seedlings:
- 25 - 35 cm apart in a row
- 30 - 40 cm apart between rows
pg092_n0009_easy_read:
To mark the spaces, use:
- a long, straight wooden pole
- a marked rope
pg092_n0010_easy_read: It is best to transplant seedlings when the weather is cool.
pg092_n0011_easy_read: This helps to reduce transplanting shock.
pg092_n0012_easy_read:
After transplanting, water the plants a little.
Do not water them too much.
pg092_n0013_easy_read: Too much water can cause diseases such as damping off and root rot.
pg092_n0017_easy_read: In normal conditions, water the crop plants about 2 to 3 days each week.
pg092_n0018_easy_read:
But think about:
- the soil type
- the weather
- the age of the plant
pg092_n0019_easy_read:
You can use these methods to water the plants:
- drip
- sprinkler
- watering can
- furrow
pg092_n0023_easy_read: To help the crop grow well, use nitrogenous fertilisers, for example, CAN, at least 3 times.
pg092_n0024_easy_read: Apply the first fertiliser 2 weeks after the plants are in the field.
pg092_n0025_easy_read: Apply the other 2 times 2 weeks apart.
pg092_n0026_easy_read: For each plant, 1 tablespoon of fertiliser is enough.
pg092_n0030_easy_read: Keep the fields free from weeds during the whole growing season.
pg092_n0031_easy_read: We use different methods to manage weeds.
pg092_n0032_easy_read:
These methods include:
- applying mulch
- pulling weeds by hand
- hoeing by hand
pg092_n0033_easy_read: It is best to manage weeds early, when they are small and easy to pull out.
pg092_n0034_easy_read: Do this before the plant canopy, or the top part of the plant, shades the space between the plants.
pg092_n0035_easy_read: As the plants grow, they cover the space between them.
pg092_n0036_easy_read: This cover stops weeds from growing.

pg098_n0009_easy_read: In this chapter, you will learn how to grow bulb onions, from the beginning to selling them.
pg098_n0010_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you earn money and have onions for your meals.
pg098_n0013_easy_read: "It offers a good chance to grow a strong crop that many people need and that kitchens around the world use."
pg098_n0016_easy_read: An onion is a bulb vegetable.
pg098_n0017_easy_read:
An onion has a short stem under the ground.
It has fleshy leaves at the base.
These leaves form a bulb.
pg098_n0018_easy_read: The bulb stores food for the onion plant.
pg098_n0019_easy_read:
Onion is usually a biennial crop.
This means it takes 2 growing seasons to complete its life cycle.
pg098_n0020_easy_read: In the 1st season, a seed grows into a plant with leaves and a bulb.
pg098_n0021_easy_read: Nutrients then build up in the bulb.
pg098_n0022_easy_read:
In the 2nd season, a plant grows from the bulb.
It produces flowers and then seeds.
pg098_n0023_easy_read: Onion bulbs can have different colours, such as red, white, and yellow.
pg099_n0003_easy_read: Bulb onions are very popular. People eat them like other spices.
pg099_n0004_easy_read: This means you can add onions to your meals to make the food taste better.
pg099_n0005_easy_read: Onions also have nutrients that are good for our bodies.
pg099_n0006_easy_read:
Onions contain minerals such as:
- calcium
- iron
- potassium
pg099_n0007_easy_read: These minerals help our bodies use food well and work properly.
pg099_n0008_easy_read:
Onions also have vitamins:
- B6
- B9
- E
pg099_n0009_easy_read: These vitamins also help our bodies use food well and work properly.
pg099_n0010_easy_read: So, onions taste good and they are also good for our health.
pg099_n0014_easy_read: Growing onions is 1 way to earn money.
pg099_n0015_easy_read: This is how you can grow onions well.
pg099_n0016_easy_read: Choose the place where you will grow your onions.
pg099_n0017_easy_read: If the area is big, make sure you have enough water and enough workers.
pg099_n0018_easy_read:
Think about how to prepare your soil for planting.
Think about how to take care of the soil and keep it healthy.
pg099_n0019_easy_read: Decide if you will hire people to help with weeding or use herbicides to kill weeds.
pg099_n0020_easy_read: Also, plan how to deal with onion pests and diseases if they happen.
pg099_n0022_easy_read: Before you start growing onions, it is important to know which types of onions people prefer.
pg099_n0023_easy_read: This is why you need to do a market survey.
pg099_n0024_easy_read: Go to the markets and see what people are buying and how much they are buying.
pg099_n0025_easy_read:
This will help you decide:
- which type of onions to grow
- how much to grow
- when to grow them
- how to get the best prices
pg099_n0026_easy_read: Finally, think about where and how you will store your onions if the market is not good at harvest time and you need to wait for better prices.
pg099_n0027_easy_read: Growing onions can help you a lot if you plan well and make your onion business successful.

pg099_n0047_easy_read: This section will guide you through the process of growing onions.
pg099_n0048_easy_read: We will start by choosing the best place for growing onions.
pg099_n0049_easy_read:
Then we will:
- prepare the seedbed
- select the right onion variety
- raise seedlings in the nursery
- transplant the seedlings
pg099_n0050_easy_read:
We will also learn how to:
- manage water
- manage nutrients
- deal with weeds
- deal with insect pests
- deal with diseases
pg099_n0051_easy_read: Remember, successful farming needs careful planning and regular work.
pg100_n0005_easy_read:
Think about these things:
- the type of soil
- the soil pH level
- the altitude of the place
- the amount of rainfall
- the temperature needed
pg100_n0006_easy_read: Good conditions can help onions grow big and healthy.
pg100_n0007_easy_read: Onions can grow in many types of soil. But onions grow best in loamy soil that drains well and has enough organic matter.
pg100_n0008_easy_read: The soil pH should be 5.5 to 6.8.
pg100_n0009_easy_read: The place should be at an altitude of 0 - 1900 m above sea level.
pg100_n0010_easy_read: Rainfall of 500 - 700 mm per year is good. But most onions are grown with irrigation.
pg100_n0011_easy_read: The best temperature for onions is 15 to 25 degrees Celsius.
pg100_n0012_easy_read: Higher temperatures can make onions form bulbs faster. But the bulbs become smaller.
pg100_n0013_easy_read: Lower temperatures can make onions start to form flowers early instead of bulbs in the 1 growing season.
pg100_n0017_easy_read: You can grow onions on a small scale in different seedbeds, including improvised seedbeds.
pg100_n0018_easy_read:
Improvised seedbeds can be made from these materials:
- used containers
- tyres
- sacks
- polythene bags
- pots filled with soil or other growing media
pg100_n0019_easy_read: For large-scale production, farmers grow onions in open fields or greenhouses.
pg100_n0021_easy_read: Follow these steps to prepare seedbeds in an open field:
pg100_n0025_easy_read: Dig the soil to a depth of at least 25 - 30 cm.
pg100_n0026_easy_read: Then make the soil smooth and level. This creates fine soil.
pg100_n0029_easy_read:
Make the seedbeds based on these things:
- the season
- the type of irrigation
- the field condition
pg100_n0032_easy_read: During land preparation, add about 25 - 40 tons of manure or compost per hectare. This is equal to 20 kg/m².
pg100_n0035_easy_read: Spread about 20 g/m² of inorganic fertiliser, such as Di-Ammonia Phosphate (DAP) or Triple Sulphate Phosphate (TSP).
pg100_n0036_easy_read: For a small seedbed, measure the area of the seedbed.
pg100_n0037_easy_read: Then work out how much to use on the seedbed.
pg100_n0039_easy_read: Remember, these steps are for open fields.
pg100_n0040_easy_read: If you use improvised seedbeds, you may need to change the steps to fit the materials you have.
pg100_n0041_easy_read:
For example:
- you may need to add more soil if you use containers or pots
- you may need to use different types of compost or manure
pg100_n0042_easy_read: Always try to use what you have and what is available in your area.
pg100_n0047_easy_read: Some varieties are hybrids. Other varieties are not hybrids.
pg100_n0048_easy_read: Table 7.1 shows some of these varieties.
pg100_n0049_easy_read: Remember, these varieties are only examples.
pg100_n0050_easy_read: People are always developing new types of onions.
pg100_n0051_easy_read: Keep learning about new onion varieties that you can grow.

pg101_n0055_easy_read: When you choose which onion to grow, think about these factors:
pg101_n0059_easy_read: Disease resistance: Some onion varieties resist diseases better than others.
pg101_n0060_easy_read: Choose a variety that resists diseases. This helps you get a healthy crop.
pg101_n0063_easy_read: Market demand: Think about what your possible customers prefer.
pg101_n0064_easy_read: In Tanzania, people often use onions in many dishes. So, onion varieties with good flavour and a longer shelf life are often more popular.
pg101_n0067_easy_read: Growth duration: The time an onion variety takes to mature can affect your choice.
pg101_n0068_easy_read: If you want a quicker harvest, choose a variety that matures early.
pg101_n0069_easy_read: Always learn more. Ask local crop extension workers or experienced onion farmers for advice.
pg101_n0070_easy_read: This will help you choose the best onion variety to grow.
pg101_n0074_easy_read: People do not usually sow onion seeds directly in the field.
pg101_n0075_easy_read:
We use nursery beds. The nursery beds can be:
- raised
- sunken
- flat
pg101_n0076_easy_read: These beds should be level so that water does not collect in 1 place.
pg101_n0077_easy_read: If water collects and stays, it can create good conditions for fungal diseases to grow.
pg101_n0078_easy_read: Use between 5 - 7 kg of seed per hectare.
pg101_n0079_easy_read: This depends on the space between the plants and the onion variety.
pg102_n0004_easy_read: Ask seed sellers or local crop extension workers about the best time to sow and the amount of seed to use.
pg102_n0005_easy_read: These are the steps for growing onion seedlings in the nursery:
pg102_n0009_easy_read:
Make lines across the nursery bed.
Leave 15 - 20 cm between the lines.
Make the lines 1 - 1.5 cm deep.
pg102_n0012_easy_read: Put the seeds thinly in the lines.
pg102_n0013_easy_read: Cover the seeds lightly with fine soil.
pg102_n0016_easy_read: Spread light, dry grass mulch on top.
pg102_n0019_easy_read: Water lightly to avoid too much moisture.
pg102_n0020_easy_read: Too much water can make the ‘damping off’ disease develop more easily.
pg102_n0023_easy_read: The seeds start to grow after 5 - 10 days.
pg102_n0025_easy_read: If you delay this step, the seedlings will become too thin and slender.
pg102_n0028_easy_read: Water when needed to keep the soil moist for the seedlings.
pg102_n0031_easy_read: Put up shade about 1 m high to protect the seedlings from strong sunlight.
pg102_n0034_easy_read:
Check the plants often.
Deal with any pest or disease problems.
pg102_n0035_easy_read: At this stage, it is very important to check and control the ‘damping-off’ disease and cutworms.
pg102_n0039_easy_read: Do transplanting during the cool part of the day.
pg102_n0040_easy_read:
Plant the seedlings after 35 - 50 days.
You can also plant them when they have 3 - 5 leaves and a stem as thick as a pencil.
pg102_n0042_easy_read:
To make field management easy, divide the field into plots.
Water the plots before transplanting.
pg102_n0043_easy_read:
2 hours before transplanting, water the nursery well.
This makes it easier to uproot the seedlings.
pg102_n0044_easy_read:
When planting, leave 15 - 20 cm between rows.
Leave 7 - 10 cm between seedlings in the rows.
pg102_n0045_easy_read: Plant the seedlings about 2 - 3 cm deep.
pg102_n0046_easy_read: After transplanting, water the seedlings more often until they are well established.
pg102_n0048_easy_read: The planting method can change based on the type of onion and what people want in the market.
pg102_n0049_easy_read: You can also use tools such as dibblers to help you plant at the right distance.
pg102_n0050_easy_read: Figure 7.2 shows examples of transplanting dibblers.
pg103_n0003_easy_read: Figure 7.2: Examples of dibblers for transplanting
pg103_n0008_easy_read: Onion plants need more water as they grow. They need less water when they are older.
pg103_n0009_easy_read: Stop watering 10 - 15 days before you plan to harvest the onions.
pg103_n0010_easy_read: There are different ways to water onions. These include furrow irrigation and modern methods such as drip irrigation.
pg103_n0014_easy_read: Besides organic manure added during land preparation, onions also need inorganic fertiliser.
pg103_n0015_easy_read:
Add 180 kg of nitrogen per hectare at different times:
- 60 kg before planting
- 60 kg at the leaf stage
- 60 kg at the 4th week
pg103_n0016_easy_read: Too much nitrogen can be harmful.
pg103_n0017_easy_read: If you add too much nitrogen late, the onion leaves will grow too fast. This will affect proper bulb formation.
pg103_n0018_easy_read: Also, apply 170 kg of potassium per hectare.
pg103_n0019_easy_read: Before transplanting, add 110 kg of potassium. Then add 60 kg of potassium 7 - 8 weeks before harvest.
pg103_n0020_easy_read: Your teacher and a local agricultural extension worker can help you choose the recommended type and amount of fertilisers.
pg103_n0022_easy_read: Managing weed pests in onion fields
pg103_n0024_easy_read:
Onion plants cannot compete with weeds for:
- space
- water
- nutrients
pg103_n0025_easy_read: Use a special herbicide to kill perennial weeds before you start land preparation or before planting.
pg103_n0026_easy_read: Use another herbicide immediately after transplanting.
pg103_n0027_easy_read: Do not use a hand hoe at this stage. It can hurt the onions.
pg103_n0028_easy_read: If possible, cover the soil with mulch.
pg103_n0029_easy_read: Mulch can stop weeds from growing.
pg103_n0030_easy_read: You can use leaves or straw as mulch.
pg103_n0031_easy_read: Use different methods together to control weeds.
pg103_n0032_easy_read: Do not depend on only 1 method.
pg103_n0033_easy_read: You can ask local crop extension workers or agricultural input suppliers for advice.
pg103_n0034_easy_read: Local crop extension workers or agricultural input suppliers can advise you on the best method to use.
pg103_n0035_easy_read: It is important to keep the field free from weeds so the onion plants grow healthy.
pg104_n0005_easy_read:
Onions are often attacked by:
- thrips
- onion maggots
- nematodes
pg104_n0006_easy_read:
Onions can also get these diseases:
- purple blotch
- onion bacterial soft rot

pg110_n0015_easy_read: Tomato is a fruit vegetable that can grow all year.
pg110_n0016_easy_read: Growing tomatoes can bring more profit when farmers grow them out of season.
pg110_n0017_easy_read: Tomato has vitamins A, B, and C.
pg110_n0018_easy_read: Tomato also has minerals such as iron and phosphorus.
pg110_n0019_easy_read: Tomato also has a special substance called lycopene.
pg110_n0020_easy_read: Lycopene helps to protect our bodies from some diseases, for example heart disease and cancer.

Tomato varieties are grouped by how they grow:

pg111_n0005_easy_read: (a) Determinate tomatoes: This type of tomato grows to a certain height. It forms a compact, bush-like shape.
pg111_n0006_easy_read: Determinate tomatoes stop growing taller when they start to produce fruit.
pg111_n0007_easy_read: Figure 8.2 (a) shows how determinate tomatoes grow.
pg111_n0011_easy_read: (b) Indeterminate tomatoes: These tomatoes keep growing. They keep making new leaves and flowers.
pg111_n0012_easy_read: Indeterminate tomatoes need support to grow upright. Farmers also remove the side branches.
pg111_n0013_easy_read: Indeterminate tomatoes are good for screen house farming.
pg111_n0014_easy_read: Figure 8.2 (b) shows how indeterminate tomatoes grow.
pg111_n0018_easy_read: (c) Semi-determinate tomatoes: These tomatoes grow in a way between determinate and indeterminate tomatoes.
pg111_n0019_easy_read: Semi-determinate tomatoes live longer than determinate types.
pg111_n0020_easy_read: The pictures in Figure 8.2 (c) show how semi-determinate tomatoes grow.

pg113_n0015_easy_read: Tomatoes grow well in well-drained soil, such as sandy loam or clay loam that is rich in organic matter.
pg113_n0016_easy_read:
The soil should be slightly acidic.
The pH should be between 5.5 and 6.5.
pg113_n0018_easy_read:
Tomatoes grow well at these temperatures:
- 20 - 25°C in the day
- 15 - 17°C at night
pg113_n0019_easy_read: Temperatures above 35°C or below 10°C can harm the tomato plant.
pg113_n0020_easy_read: Tomatoes need more than 600 mm of rainfall in 1 growing season.
pg113_n0021_easy_read: Too much rain can cause diseases on the leaves.
pg113_n0022_easy_read: Also, watering at irregular times can damage tomato fruits.
pg113_n0023_easy_read: Tomatoes need at least 6 hours of direct sunlight during flowering.
pg113_n0024_easy_read: Too much sunlight can damage the fruits.
pg113_n0025_easy_read: To choose a good place for growing tomatoes, look for a place that gets at least 6 hours of direct sunlight each day.
pg113_n0029_easy_read: You can grow tomatoes outdoors or indoors.
pg113_n0030_easy_read: You can grow tomatoes in soil or in soilless growing media.
pg113_n0031_easy_read: These are the steps for preparing land for growing tomatoes:

pg115_n0005_easy_read: You can grow tomato seedlings in 2 ways: in trays or in the soil.
pg115_n0011_easy_read:
Choose trays with cells.
Examples are:
- 105

pg115_n0014_easy_read: Fill the trays with soil, such as compost or peat moss.
pg115_n0017_easy_read: Put 1 seed in the middle of each cell, 0.5 cm deep.
pg115_n0020_easy_read: Cover the seed with soil, but do not add too much soil.
pg115_n0023_easy_read: Keep the trays safe and away from the sun and rain. Then:
pg115_n0026_easy_read: Water the trays with a sprayer to keep the soil moist.
pg115_n0028_easy_read: After 20 to 30 days, the seedlings are ready to move.
pg115_n0034_easy_read: Make a seed bed that is 50 to 100 cm wide and 15 to 20 cm long.
pg115_n0037_easy_read: Add well-decomposed manure to the soil.
pg115_n0040_easy_read: Clean the soil with dry grass and straw, or with chemicals.
pg115_n0043_easy_read: Water the soil, but do not use too much water.
pg115_n0046_easy_read: Make rows in the soil 15 to 20 cm apart.
pg115_n0049_easy_read: Put seeds in the rows and cover them with soil.
pg115_n0052_easy_read: Cover the seeds with dry grass mulch. Then water them lightly.
pg115_n0055_easy_read: Remove the grass after 5 to 7 days, when the seeds have germinated.
pg115_n0058_easy_read: Protect the seedlings by putting shade over them. Then:
pg115_n0061_easy_read:
Do these things as needed:
- Water the seedlings
- Remove weeds
- Control pests
pg115_n0063_easy_read: After 20 to 30 days, you can move the seedlings to the main field.
pg115_n0067_easy_read: Seedlings are ready to move to the main field about 20 to 30 days after sowing. They are about 12 to 20 cm tall.
pg115_n0068_easy_read: Before transplanting, harden the seedlings for 1 week by watering them less.
pg115_n0069_easy_read: This helps the seedlings stay strong when you move them.
pg115_n0071_easy_read: Important practices for transplanting the seedlings are:
pg115_n0075_easy_read: Make holes about 10 cm deep and 10 cm wide.
pg115_n0076_easy_read: Then move each seedling with its soil from the nursery into the holes. Cover the seedlings firmly with soil.
pg115_n0079_easy_read:
If you are transplanting seedlings in raised beds or flatbeds, space them:
- 60 to 90 cm apart between the rows
- 50 to 60 cm apart between the plants in the same row
pg115_n0082_easy_read:
If you are growing seedlings with drip irrigation, space them:
- 120 to 150 cm apart between the rows
- 30 to 50 cm apart between the plants in the same row
pg116_n0005_easy_read:
If you are growing indeterminate seedlings with drip irrigation, transplant them as follows:
- 150 cm between rows
- 50 cm between plants in the same row
pg116_n0008_easy_read: After you move the seedlings, water them immediately.
pg116_n0009_easy_read: The amount of water and how often you water depend on how wet the soil is.
pg116_n0012_easy_read: To keep the right number of plants in the field, replace dead plants 10 days after transplanting. This is called gap filling.
pg116_n0014_easy_read: It is better to transplant seedlings from a ground nursery early in the morning, in the evening, or on a cloudy day.
pg116_n0015_easy_read: This helps to reduce transplant shock.
pg116_n0016_easy_read: Seedlings prepared on trays can be transplanted at any time.
pg116_n0020_easy_read: Tomatoes need enough water to grow well.
pg116_n0021_easy_read: As tomatoes grow more, they need more water.
pg116_n0022_easy_read: This is especially important after tomatoes are moved from their pot to the garden, and when they are flowering and making fruits.
pg116_n0023_easy_read: The best time to irrigate tomatoes depends on the season.
pg116_n0024_easy_read: In the dry season, you can irrigate the plants 3 to 4 times a week.
pg116_n0025_easy_read: In the wet season, you can water them less often.
pg116_n0026_easy_read:
You can irrigate tomatoes in different ways, including:
- furrow irrigation
- drip irrigation
pg116_n0027_easy_read: You can also water only the base of the plant with a bucket or a hose pipe.
pg116_n0028_easy_read: It is important to water tomatoes. But too much water can also harm them.
pg116_n0029_easy_read: So, it is best to irrigate tomatoes when the soil is dry.
pg116_n0033_easy_read: There are 2 main sources of nutrients to help tomatoes grow well.
pg116_n0034_easy_read:
The 1st source is organic manure, for example:
- farmyard manure
- compost manure
pg116_n0035_easy_read: The 2nd source is chemical or industrial fertilisers.
pg116_n0036_easy_read: If you use only organic manure, apply about 12 - 25 tons per hectare in each cropping season.
pg116_n0037_easy_read:
For high-yield tomato varieties, apply:
- 100 - 150 kg/ha of nitrogen
- 65 - 110 kg/ha of phosphate
- 160 - 240 kg/ha of potash
pg116_n0039_easy_read:
Apply industrial fertilisers in this range:
- 40 - 120 kg/ha of nitrogen
- 30 - 90 kg/ha of phosphate
- 30 - 90 kg/ha of potash
pg116_n0040_easy_read: When you apply industrial fertilisers, do not let them touch young or wet plants. They can burn the plants.
pg116_n0041_easy_read: How a tomato plant takes up nutrients depends on the type of fertiliser and how you apply it.
pg116_n0042_easy_read:
You can apply the fertiliser directly to the soil:
- about 10 cm away from the stem
- about 5 cm deep
- using the ring method or the dibbling method
pg117_n0003_easy_read:
There are also foliar fertilisers.
They dissolve in water.
They come as liquid or powder.
pg117_n0004_easy_read:
Foliar fertilisers contain different macro and micronutrients.
People apply them to the leaves.
The leaves absorb them.
pg117_n0005_easy_read:
It is very important to ask a local extension worker or a competent registered agro dealer about:
- the right amount of fertiliser
- the best way to apply fertiliser
pg117_n0011_easy_read:
1 week after transplanting:
Use a complete NPK fertiliser with high phosphorus, for example 10:40:10, at the manufacturer’s recommended rate.
pg117_n0012_easy_read: Repeat this once in the 3rd week after transplanting.
pg117_n0015_easy_read:
When new leaves appear, 2-3 weeks after transplanting:
Use an NPK fertiliser with high nitrogen, for example 20:10:10, at the manufacturer’s recommended rate.
pg117_n0018_easy_read:
When flowers form, 4-6 weeks after transplanting:
Use a complete NPK fertiliser at the manufacturer’s recommended rate to promote flowering and fruit development.
pg117_n0019_easy_read: A tomato plant can continue to flower and produce fruit for 3-4 months.
pg117_n0023_easy_read:
Trellising is a way to support tomato plants.
It uses lines held by posts at set spaces.
pg117_n0024_easy_read:
Posts about 3 m long are placed 1.5-2 m apart.
Refer to Figure 8.3 (a).
pg117_n0025_easy_read: Trellising is good for indeterminate tomato varieties.
pg117_n0026_easy_read:
Staking is a way to support tomato plants.
It uses wooden poles or metal rods.
pg117_n0027_easy_read:
Place the stake firmly 15 cm beside the growing plant.
Tie the plant to the stake in stages as it grows.
Refer to Figure 8.3 (b).
pg117_n0028_easy_read: Staking is suitable for semi-determinate tomato varieties.
pg117_n0029_easy_read: Trellising and staking keep the plants and fruits firmly off the ground.
pg117_n0030_easy_read:
A combination of poles and ropes is also used to support tomato plants from the sides.
Refer to Figure 8.3 (c).
pg117_n0031_easy_read:
Trellising and staking in tomatoes reduce losses from:
- fruit rot, when fruits touch the soil
- sunburn, when foliage does not shade the fruits

pg118_n0009_easy_read: It stops the plants from touching the ground.
pg118_n0010_easy_read: This makes it harder for diseases to spread from the soil to the plants.
pg118_n0013_easy_read: It helps the plants grow upwards and use more vertical space.
pg118_n0014_easy_read: This helps farmers grow more crops in a small area.
pg118_n0017_easy_read: It helps more air and sunlight reach the plants.
pg118_n0018_easy_read: This keeps the leaves dry and makes disease less likely.
pg118_n0021_easy_read: It keeps the plants away from the paths.
pg118_n0022_easy_read: This makes farm work easier, for example harvesting.
pg118_n0026_easy_read: Pruning helps tomato plants grow better.
pg118_n0027_easy_read: Pruning is important for indeterminate tomato plants.
pg118_n0028_easy_read: When we prune, nutrients go to making tomatoes instead of extra branches.
pg118_n0029_easy_read: This makes the tomatoes grow faster and bigger.
pg118_n0030_easy_read: Pruning also helps keep the plant healthy. It lets in more air and reduces humidity.
pg118_n0031_easy_read: You can prune by pinching off the extra branches or by using a hand pruner (refer to Figures 8.4 (a) and (b)).
pg118_n0032_easy_read: Remember, not all tomato plants need pruning.
pg118_n0033_easy_read: Pruning only applies to indeterminate varieties.
pg118_n0034_easy_read: Determinate and semi-determinate varieties do not need pruning.
pg119_n0005_easy_read: Figure 8.4 (b): Pruning with a hand pruner
pg119_n0009_easy_read:
Mulching means covering the soil with a layer of:
- dry grass
- straw
- plant remains
See Figure 8.5.
pg119_n0010_easy_read:
If you use grass straw, make sure the material has no seeds.
This helps to stop weeds from spreading.
pg119_n0011_easy_read:
Mulching helps the soil keep moisture.
It does this by stopping or reducing evaporation.
pg119_n0012_easy_read:
Mulching also helps to:
- reduce soil erosion
- control weeds, especially broad-leaved weeds
pg119_n0013_easy_read: When mulch breaks down, it adds organic matter to the soil.
pg119_n0015_easy_read: Figure 8.5: Grass mulch in the tomato garden
pg119_n0019_easy_read:
Control weeds as soon as crops start to grow.
At this stage, weeds can badly affect plant growth.
This can lead to low crop yields.
pg119_n0020_easy_read:
Start weed control with correct land preparation.
Use cultural practices to control weeds, such as:
- manual hoeing
- mulching
pg120_n0004_easy_read: The following farming practices can be used together for good weed control in tomatoes:
pg120_n0008_easy_read:
Before transplanting, do deep tillage.
Expose the soil to sunlight.
This helps to destroy weed seeds.
pg120_n0011_easy_read:
Remove any remains of the previous crop.
Use clean farming practices to stop new weed seeds from getting into the field.
pg120_n0014_easy_read:
Keep the field free from weeds for 4 – 5 weeks after transplanting.
This reduces weed competition and helps to prevent low yield.
pg120_n0017_easy_read: Regularly do hand weeding between the plant rows.
pg120_n0020_easy_read: Apply mulch that has no weed seeds.
pg120_n0023_easy_read:
Plant different crops in the field each season.
Plant the same crop again only after at least 3 growing seasons.
This is crop rotation.
pg120_n0024_easy_read: Crop rotation breaks the life cycles of crop pathogens and pests.
pg120_n0028_easy_read: Several pests and diseases can harm tomatoes.
pg120_n0029_easy_read:
It is important to know what the pests and diseases are.
It is also important to know how they harm the crop.
pg120_n0030_easy_read: You also need to know how to control them.
pg120_n0031_easy_read: The following are some of the pests and diseases.
pg120_n0036_easy_read:
What they do:
They feed on sap from tomato plants.
This causes:
- leaves to curl
- leaves to turn yellow
- spread of plant viruses
pg120_n0038_easy_read:
How to identify them:
Look for tiny insects with soft bodies on the underside of leaves.
Refer to Figure 8.6.
pg120_n0040_easy_read:
How to manage them:
- Spray affected plants with a solution of soap, cow urine, or rabbit urine.
- Intercrop with other crops.
- Use recommended pesticides.
pg120_n0042_easy_read: Figure 8.6: Aphids on a tomato leaf
pg121_n0006_easy_read: What they do: They feed on the underside of tomato leaves. This causes yellowing, wilting, and the spread of viral diseases.
pg121_n0008_easy_read:
How to identify them: Look for tiny white insects on the underside of tomato leaves.
Refer to Figure 8.7.
pg121_n0010_easy_read:
How to manage them:
- Use a kerosene and soap spray.
- Plant resistant cultivars with hairy leaves.
- Encourage natural predators.
- Rotate crops.
pg121_n0012_easy_read: Figure 8.7: Whiteflies on the underside of a tomato leaf
pg121_n0017_easy_read: What they do: Larvae and caterpillars feed on tomato leaves and fruits.
pg121_n0019_easy_read:
How to identify them: Look for larvae and caterpillars.
Look for damaged leaves and fruits.
Refer to Figure 8.8.
pg121_n0021_easy_read: How to manage them: Apply the recommended insecticides.
pg121_n0023_easy_read: Figure 8.8: Bollworm fruit damage and an adult moth
pg121_n0028_easy_read: What they do: They attack tomatoes. They cause white to yellow spots on the leaves.
pg121_n0030_easy_read:
How to know them:
- Look for tiny white or yellow spots on leaves.
- Check for small, red or orange mites under the leaves.
- Notice if leaves turn yellow and fall off.
- Look for a thin white or yellow cobweb-like substance on the plant.
Refer to Figure 8.9.
pg121_n0032_easy_read:
How to manage them: Keep the field free from weeds.
Use recommended pesticides.
pg121_n0034_easy_read: Figure 8.9: Tomato affected by spider mites
pg122_n0006_easy_read: What they do: They feed on plant roots. This causes the roots to swell and change shape.
pg122_n0007_easy_read: How to identify them: Look for roots that have changed shape and roots that are swollen. See Figure 8.10.
pg122_n0008_easy_read: How to manage them: Plough the soil several times. This exposes the worms to the sun.
pg122_n0009_easy_read: Rotate the crop with crops that do not belong to the Solanaceae family.
pg122_n0012_easy_read: Figure 8.10: Tomato roots with lumps caused by nematodes
pg122_n0017_easy_read: What they do: They cut the stems of newly emerged or transplanted plants at ground level.
pg122_n0018_easy_read: How to identify them: Look for stems of newly emerged or transplanted plants cut at ground level. See Figure 8.11.
pg122_n0019_easy_read: How to manage them: Keep the field free from weeds. Use recommended insecticides.
pg122_n0021_easy_read: Figure 8.11: Cutworms and tomato seedlings they have affected
pg122_n0026_easy_read: How to identify it: Look for irregular spots on the top of the leaves. See Figure 8.12.
pg122_n0027_easy_read:
How to manage it: Keep your crops free from weeds.
Use recommended preventive fungicides.
Maintain good cultural management of your crops.
pg122_n0029_easy_read: Figure 8.12: Tomato affected by late blight
pg123_n0006_easy_read:
How to identify it:
Look for yellow leaves that start at the base of the stem and move upwards.
See Figure 8.13.
pg123_n0007_easy_read:
How to manage it:
- Keep your field free from weeds.
- Do not water too much.
- Control insects in the soil.
- Control nematodes in the soil.
pg123_n0009_easy_read:
Figure 8.13:
Tomato affected by fusarium wilt
pg123_n0014_easy_read: It is caused by a lack of calcium.
pg123_n0015_easy_read:
How to identify it:
Look for sunken, brownish-black spots on the fruits.
See Figure 8.14.
pg123_n0016_easy_read:
How to manage it:
- Keep your plants well watered.
- Use mulch to reduce the amount of nitrogen fertiliser you apply.
- Give your plants enough calcium.
pg123_n0018_easy_read:
Figure 8.14:
Tomato fruits affected by blossom end rot
pg123_n0023_easy_read:
This is a physical problem in tomato fruits.
It is caused by too much exposure to hot, bright sunlight.
pg123_n0024_easy_read:
How to know it:
Look for pale white or yellow patches on tomato fruits.
See Figure 8.15.
pg123_n0025_easy_read:
How to manage it:
- Choose tomato varieties that can handle heat.
- Give your plants balanced nutrients.

pg124_n0043_easy_read: Tomatoes take about 70 - 90 days to mature and be ready for harvesting. This depends on the variety and the climate.
pg124_n0044_easy_read:
Signs that tomatoes are mature include:
- bigger fruit size
- a change in skin colour
- more juice and sugar content
pg124_n0045_easy_read: The main sign is the change in fruit colour.
pg124_n0046_easy_read: Tomatoes can be harvested at 6 different stages, depending on market demand, as shown in Figure 8.16.
pg125_n0011_easy_read: The tomato surface is completely green.
pg125_n0015_easy_read: The tomato has a clear change in colour from green to tarnish-yellow.
pg125_n0019_easy_read:
Some tomatoes change colour from green to:
- tarnish-yellow
- pink
- red
- a mix of these colours
pg125_n0028_easy_read: About 30%-60% of the tomatoes have changed to pink or red.
pg125_n0032_easy_read: About 60%-90% of the tomatoes are pinkish-red or red.
pg125_n0036_easy_read: More than 90% of the tomatoes are red.

pg125_n0039_easy_read:
Harvest tomatoes in the morning or late evening.
This helps to keep their quality and make their shelf-life longer.
pg125_n0040_easy_read: Remove the fruits from the plants by gently twisting or turning them from the stem, without the fruit stalk.
pg125_n0041_easy_read: However, harvest cherry tomatoes in bunches.
pg125_n0042_easy_read:
When harvesting, do not drop the fruits.
Put the fruits gently in a harvesting container.
pg125_n0043_easy_read: Postharvest management of tomatoes includes the following:
pg125_n0045_easy_read:
(a) Sorting:
Do sorting and grading under shade.
This helps to avoid the bad effects of rain, heat, and sunlight, which can make tomato fruits spoil faster.
pg125_n0047_easy_read:
(b) Packaging and transporting:
People commonly pack tomatoes in:
- bamboo crates
- wooden crates
- plastic crates
pg125_n0048_easy_read: However, stackable plastic and wooden crates are the best.
pg125_n0050_easy_read:
Lining the crates can stop fruits from getting bruised.
But it may stop air from moving around.
pg125_n0051_easy_read:
Packaging helps to protect tomatoes from:
- pests
- loss of moisture
- damage
pg125_n0053_easy_read: Transport tomatoes in covered trucks with ventilation.
pg126_n0003_easy_read: (c) Storage: Store tomatoes at 12 - 15°C for the best results.
pg126_n0004_easy_read:
You can store tomatoes in a charcoal cooler or a zero-energy cooling chamber.
The temperature there is a little higher than this.
pg126_n0005_easy_read: You can store your tomatoes for 2 – 14 days.
pg126_n0007_easy_read:
(d) Marketing: You can sell tomatoes:
- at the farm
- at the local market
- at distant markets
pg126_n0008_easy_read: Common container sizes are 20-litre plastic buckets and crates.
pg126_n0009_easy_read:
At lower levels, these are popular:
- 10-litre buckets
- 5-litre buckets
- bunches
pg126_n0010_easy_read: Prices can change quickly, often within 1 week.
pg126_n0011_easy_read:
In Tanzania, tomato prices are usually low from August to October.
Tomato prices are usually high from December to May.

pg128_n0018_easy_read: Poultry is a general name for birds that people keep at home or on farms.
pg128_n0019_easy_read: Poultry includes several species, like the birds in Figures 9.1 (a) to (f).
pg128_n0020_easy_read:
These birds are:
- chicken or domestic fowl
- turkey
- duck
- goose
- guinea fowl
- pigeon
pg128_n0021_easy_read:
Poultry production, or poultry farming, means keeping birds for home use or for business.
People keep them for eggs or meat.
pg128_n0022_easy_read:
Some poultry species can be kept for decoration or for game and sports.
These include:
- peafowls
- parrots
- partridges
pg128_n0023_easy_read: The poultry species in Figures 9.1 (a) to (f) can be kept for home use or for business.
pg128_n0027_easy_read:
People rear poultry in different ways.
The ways differ in:
- how the birds are kept in a place or allowed to move freely
- how the birds get feed
- how people collect the birds' products
pg128_n0032_easy_read: Visit the school poultry unit and poultry farms near you.
pg128_n0034_easy_read:
Observe and ask about the ways used to:
- keep the birds in a place
- give the birds feed and water
- collect the birds' products
- record production and sales, both digital and manual
pg128_n0036_easy_read: Summarise what you found and the lessons you learnt in this activity in your portfolio.
pg128_n0038_easy_read:
The choice of a poultry production system depends on several factors.
These factors are:
- available land
- type of poultry
- climate conditions
- available labour
- the amount of capital the farmer can and is willing to invest
pg128_n0039_easy_read: As you learn the different poultry production systems, you will understand how these factors affect the choice of system.
pg128_n0040_easy_read: There are 3 main poultry production systems.
pg128_n0041_easy_read:
The 3 poultry production systems are:
- free-range systems
- semi-intensive systems
- intensive housing systems
pg128_n0045_easy_read: In the free-range system, birds move freely during the day to look for food.
pg128_n0046_easy_read:
At night, people lock the birds inside a house.
This protects them from bad weather and predators.
pg129_n0003_easy_read:
This system is suitable only where there is enough land.
This helps keep the right stocking density and avoids overcrowding.
pg129_n0004_easy_read:
Fields, parts of fields, or plots can be left without crops.
This lets birds move freely from 1 plot to another to look for food.
pg129_n0005_easy_read: You can rear nearly 250 adult birds per hectare with this system.
pg129_n0006_easy_read: Figure 9.2 shows an example of the free-range system of poultry production.
pg129_n0008_easy_read: Figure 9.2: Example of the free-range system of poultry production
pg129_n0011_easy_read: A free-range system of poultry production is preferred for small-scale organic production of poultry meat and eggs.
pg129_n0012_easy_read: With this system, housing costs and capital investment are low.
pg129_n0013_easy_read:
However, this system can have some problems:
- Losses from predatory animals can be high.
- Wild birds may bring diseases if proper care is not taken.
- Scientific management practices may be hard to use.
pg129_n0019_easy_read: Provide secure housing for the chicken at night.
pg129_n0020_easy_read:
It is best to build the house above the ground on slats.
This allows good ventilation and cooling.
pg129_n0023_easy_read:
Give the chicken extra feed in the evening when they return to the house.
For example, give them grains.
pg129_n0026_easy_read: Laying birds must have clean, dry, dark places called nests to lay their eggs.
pg129_n0027_easy_read: There should be 1 nest for every 5 birds in the house and the dry
pg130_n0003_easy_read: Put grass or other dry litter in the nests.
pg130_n0004_easy_read:
(d) Protect mother hens and their young chicks from:
- predators
- rain
- cold
- wind
Provide a box or a shelter made of blocks on the ground.
pg130_n0005_easy_read:
(e) Cull:
- unproductive birds
- old laying birds
- extra male birds
pg130_n0009_easy_read: In this system, birds are reared partly in houses and partly in fenced areas.
pg130_n0010_easy_read: When people use this system in a permanent area, there should be a poultry house followed by a run.
pg130_n0011_easy_read:
At night, birds stay in the houses.
During the day, birds can go into the runs.
pg130_n0012_easy_read:
The houses should stay in one place.
Fence the runs with wire mesh or other suitable fencing materials that are available locally.
pg130_n0014_easy_read:
The runs must have plants or suitable forage.
This gives the birds green forage.
pg130_n0015_easy_read:
The fencing of the runs can also be designed to allow rotational runs.
This is especially useful when forage grows inside the run.
pg130_n0016_easy_read: In this system, 1 hectare can hold about 750 birds on average.
pg130_n0017_easy_read:
With this system, you can use scientific management methods to some extent.
This system also uses land more economically than a free-range system.
pg130_n0018_easy_read:
However, fencing costs a lot.
The run also needs routine cleaning and removal of litter materials.
pg130_n0019_easy_read: Figure 9.3 shows an example of a poultry house and a run.
pg130_n0021_easy_read: Figure 9.3: Poultry house and run (semi-intensive system)
pg131_n0003_easy_read: If the runs are not permanent, they are not fenced. In that case, movable houses are better to use.
pg131_n0004_easy_read: Fold houses and coops are common movable houses for poultry.
pg131_n0005_easy_read: Fold houses are small movable houses. They have a run attached to them.
pg131_n0007_easy_read: To care for poultry in a semi-intensive system, do the following:
pg131_n0011_easy_read: Rotate the runs. This gives grass time to grow. It also allows disease-causing organisms to die.
pg131_n0014_easy_read: Put nests inside the house for the birds to lay eggs.
pg131_n0017_easy_read: Give fresh feed and water every day.
pg131_n0018_easy_read: Wash the feed and water containers every day.
pg131_n0021_easy_read: Follow the programmes for vaccinating and deworming the birds.
pg131_n0024_easy_read: You can keep chicks in a special brooding box or in a small area made for them (brooder).
pg131_n0028_easy_read: In this system, birds stay inside houses. They stay either on the ground or on wire-netting floors in cages or slats.
pg131_n0029_easy_read: This housing system is more efficient, convenient, and economical for modern commercial poultry production.
pg131_n0030_easy_read:
It has 3 categories:
- deep litter system
- slatted floor system
- cage or battery system
pg131_n0031_easy_read: These sub-divisions of the intensive poultry system are explained further here.
pg131_n0034_easy_read: In this system, the floor of the house can be made of rough concrete or rammed earth.
pg131_n0035_easy_read: Then cover the floor with dry litter materials. The depth should be about 8 cm in the broiler house and 15 cm in the layers’ house.
pg131_n0036_easy_read: However, for egg-laying birds, add a 5 cm layer of litter material every 2 weeks until it reaches the right depth.
pg131_n0037_easy_read: The birds stay inside the house all the time.
pg131_n0038_easy_read:
Keep these inside the house:
- feed
- water
- nests
- perches
pg131_n0039_easy_read:
You can use several litter materials. The choice depends on cost and availability. These materials include:
- rice husks
- sawdust
- old newspaper
- wood shavings
- chopped straw
- dried leaves
- crushed nutshells
pg131_n0041_easy_read: In the deep litter housing system, the welfare of birds is maintained to some extent.
pg131_n0042_easy_read: The system also gives manure. The manure is useful in crop production.
pg131_n0043_easy_read: Bacterial and parasitic diseases may be a problem. This is because birds have direct contact with the litter.
pg131_n0044_easy_read: Respiratory problems may also happen because of dust from the litter.
pg131_n0045_easy_read: Also, the cost of litter may add to the production cost if it is not readily available.
pg132_n0002_easy_read:
Available.
Figure 9.4 shows an example of birds kept in a deep litter system.
pg132_n0004_easy_read: Figure 9.4: Example of a deep litter system for keeping birds
pg132_n0006_easy_read: When poultry droppings build up, they make the litter thick.
pg132_n0007_easy_read: It is very important to keep the litter dry.
pg132_n0008_easy_read: Mix the litter regularly to do this.
pg132_n0009_easy_read: If the litter gets too wet, it can form lumps.
pg132_n0010_easy_read: This is bad for the poultry.
pg132_n0011_easy_read: When the litter is wet, harmful micro-organisms can grow in it.
pg132_n0012_easy_read: So, stir the litter often to break up the build-up of these harmful micro-organisms.
pg132_n0013_easy_read: If there are more chicken droppings than litter, add fresh litter.
pg132_n0014_easy_read:
This helps to keep the litter dry.
It also reduces the build-up of ammonia, which is harmful to poultry.
pg132_n0015_easy_read:
When the litter becomes more than 30 cm deep, remove it.
Then bring in fresh litter.
pg132_n0016_easy_read: Follow the procedures you have already learnt for bringing in fresh litter.
pg132_n0019_easy_read: In this system, birds are kept in a house with a slatted floor.
pg132_n0020_easy_read:
This floor can be made of:
- iron rods
- plastic
- treated wooden poles

The floor is usually 0.6 - 1 m above the ground.
This helps the droppings to fall through the slats.
pg132_n0021_easy_read:
Wooden poles or iron rods can be placed along the length of the house.
Leave 2.5 cm spaces between the rods or poles.
pg132_n0022_easy_read: The house should have a roof made of water-proof material.
pg132_n0023_easy_read: If the poultry pen has an iron roof, put insulation under the roof.
pg132_n0024_easy_read: Because this building is large, feeding, watering, and egg collection should preferably be done from outside the house.
pg132_n0025_easy_read: Figure 9.5 shows a part of a slatted floor poultry system.
pg133_n0003_easy_read: Figure 9.5: Example of a slatted floor system
pg133_n0006_easy_read: The slatted floor system for poultry is good.
pg133_n0007_easy_read: This system needs less space for each bird.
pg133_n0008_easy_read: There is no need for bedding or litter.
pg133_n0009_easy_read: It is easy to clean the droppings because the droppings fall through the slats.
pg133_n0010_easy_read: This system also helps to keep the house clean.
pg133_n0011_easy_read: This system stops parasites and diseases from spreading because the birds do not touch their droppings.
pg133_n0012_easy_read: This system also allows a lot of air to enter the house.
pg133_n0013_easy_read: However, this system costs more to start than regular solid floors.
pg133_n0014_easy_read: It is hard to get feed back if the feed falls through the slats.
pg133_n0015_easy_read: This system also limits how much you can use the building.
pg133_n0016_easy_read: Flies can enter through the slats. This makes the fly problem worse.
pg133_n0020_easy_read: This system is mainly used for commercial egg production.
pg133_n0021_easy_read: In this system, poultry stay in compartments surrounded by bars or wire.
pg133_n0023_easy_read: The cage is large enough for limited movement. It allows a bird to stand and sit comfortably.
pg133_n0024_easy_read: The cages are usually made of strong galvanized wire. They can be placed on stands on the floor of a house or hung from the roof.
pg133_n0025_easy_read: The number of birds in each cage can be 1 to 4. This depends on the cage size, the size of the bird, and the farmer’s preference.
pg133_n0027_easy_read: The cages are arranged in rows or layers called tiers.
pg133_n0028_easy_read: The number of tiers can be 3 to 6.
pg133_n0029_easy_read: The cage should have a sloping floor so eggs can roll easily for collection.
pg134_n0003_easy_read:
Drinkers are fixed to the outside of the cages.
But nipple drinkers use a pipeline that passes through the cages or above them.
pg134_n0004_easy_read: In medium-scale egg production, people feed the birds and collect the eggs by hand.
pg134_n0005_easy_read: In large-scale poultry farms, farmers can use automatic feeding trolleys and egg collection belts.
pg134_n0006_easy_read:
The cage type decides how workers collect the droppings.
They collect the droppings:
- in trays below the cages
- on belts
- on the floor
- in deep pits under the cages

It is hard for the birds to catch pathogens that cause infections.

pg134_n0025_easy_read: Bad habits such as egg eating and pecking are minimal.
pg134_n0028_easy_read: Workers can easily identify sick birds and separate them for treatment.
pg134_n0031_easy_read: Workers can easily identify birds that are not productive and cull them.
pg134_n0034_easy_read: Birds have more protection from internal parasites and illnesses from the soil.
pg134_n0037_easy_read: Eggs crack less because the birds cannot peck the eggs, and the eggs are cleaner.
pg135_n0005_easy_read: It is easy to collect eggs.
pg135_n0008_easy_read: There is a lower death rate.

pg135_n0022_easy_read: The bird lies on its side. This makes it look like it has paralysis. So, people call it cage paralysis or cage layer fatigue.

pg136_n0029_easy_read: Incubation in poultry production is the process of giving a fertile egg the right conditions so that it hatches into a chick.
pg136_n0030_easy_read: For a chick to develop, the egg must be kept at the right temperature, humidity, and ventilation.
pg136_n0031_easy_read: Brooding is the special care given to chicks immediately after hatching to keep them healthy and alive.
pg136_n0032_easy_read: In poultry, incubation and brooding can happen in 2 ways. Female birds can do it naturally. A farmer can also do it artificially by using incubators and brooders.
pg136_n0033_easy_read: When you choose the right type of incubation and brooding for your poultry farming enterprise, you need to know well how each type works.
pg136_n0034_easy_read: You also need to know the advantages and disadvantages of each type of incubation and brooding.
pg136_n0035_easy_read: These are some important features of natural and artificial incubation and brooding.
pg136_n0039_easy_read: In small-scale production, female birds incubate eggs naturally by sitting on them in the nest.
pg136_n0040_easy_read: This keeps the eggs warm enough to hatch.
pg136_n0042_easy_read: Different poultry species have different incubation periods, or hatching times. Refer to Table 9.1.
pg136_n0043_easy_read: After hatching, female birds do natural brooding.
pg136_n0044_easy_read: Female birds keep chicks warm and protect them from predators.
pg136_n0045_easy_read: Some kinds of birds are better at brooding than others.
pg136_n0046_easy_read: For successful natural incubation, it is important to find and use birds that sit well on eggs.
pg136_n0047_easy_read: The farmer should give clean water and high-quality feeds to both female birds and chicks.
pg136_n0048_easy_read: Table 9.1 shows the incubation periods for different poultry species. Figures 9.7 (a) and (b) show natural incubation and brooding.
