pg137_n0049_easy_read: This system does not need a lot of money to start.
pg137_n0052_easy_read: When conditions are suitable, more eggs hatch than in artificial incubation.
pg137_n0055_easy_read: This applies to small-scale poultry breeders or home flocks.
pg137_n0058_easy_read: You do not need special skills.
pg137_n0064_easy_read: The chance of disease infection and parasite infestation is high.
pg137_n0067_easy_read: A broody bird takes care of only a few eggs.
pg137_n0070_easy_read: A broody bird may die before hatching. Then the whole batch is lost.
pg137_n0073_easy_read: Hatching may be poor because the environment is not controlled.
pg138_n0005_easy_read: On commercial farms with many birds, farmers use egg incubators for artificial incubation.
pg138_n0006_easy_read: One machine can hold from 60 eggs to 1 million eggs.
pg138_n0016_easy_read: Many chicks can hatch at the same time.
pg138_n0019_easy_read: It is easy to carry out sanitary measures.
pg138_n0022_easy_read: You can remove infertile eggs from the incubator at any stage of incubation.
pg138_n0025_easy_read: The supply of chicks is constant.
pg138_n0031_easy_read: The starting cost and running cost are high.
pg138_n0034_easy_read: It needs skilled labour, so the labour cost is high.
pg138_n0037_easy_read: Egg contamination is very likely if the eggs come from contaminated sources.
pg138_n0040_easy_read: Chick production may stop completely if the machines break down, especially where spare parts and technicians are not reliably available.
pg138_n0044_easy_read: When many chicks need to be reared at the same time, farmers use artificial brooding.
pg138_n0045_easy_read: Farmers do this by keeping chicks in a structure called a brooder. The brooder provides feed, water, and heat.
pg138_n0046_easy_read: Artificial brooding starts when chicks are one
pg139_n0003_easy_read:
Brooding starts when chicks are 1 day old.
It lasts for 4 to 6 weeks, depending on the weather.
pg139_n0004_easy_read:
However, chicks can stay in the brooder for 6 - 9 days in hot areas.
In cold areas, chicks can stay in the brooder for 12 - 21 days.
pg139_n0005_easy_read:
Most brooders should be round.
Corners make chicks crowd together.
pg139_n0006_easy_read:
You can also use a square brooder.
Make the corners round with plywood or boxes.
pg139_n0007_easy_read: In large commercial poultry farming, the brooding house should be at least 100 metres from other buildings on the farm.
pg139_n0008_easy_read: Figure 9.9 shows chicks in brooder rings.
pg139_n0012_easy_read:
Keep these brooder temperatures:
- Day 1 - 2: 34 - 35°C
- Day 3 - 4: 32 - 33°C
- Day 5 - 6: 30 - 31°C
- Day 7: 29 - 30°C
- Day 8 onwards: 28 - 30°C
pg139_n0013_easy_read: All types of chicks need about the same brooder temperature.
pg139_n0014_easy_read: A brooder can use different heat sources.
pg139_n0015_easy_read:
These heat sources include:
- gas brooder lamps
- electric bulbs with 100 Watts
- infrared bulbs
- charcoal burners
- clay-pot burners
- lanterns
pg139_n0016_easy_read: Figures 9.10 (a) to (d) show some examples of heat sources for brooders.
pg140_n0007_easy_read:
Manage the temperature and humidity in a brooder well.
This helps chicks live comfortably.
pg140_n0008_easy_read:
Use an accurate thermometer and hygrometer to check the temperature and humidity regularly during the process.
A digital thermometer and hygrometer are better.
pg140_n0009_easy_read:
You can check the temperature and comfort in the brooder by watching how the chicks respond to the brooder temperature and other conditions.
For example, look at how the chicks spread out, as shown in Figures 9.11 (a) to (d).
pg141_n0003_easy_read:
When the temperature is right, the chicks spread out evenly.
Their noise shows they are comfortable.
The chicks stay as shown in Figure 9.11 (a).
pg141_n0004_easy_read:
When the temperature is too low, the chicks crowd near the heat source in the brooder.
They make loud and continuous unhappy sounds to seek attention.
pg141_n0005_easy_read: The chicks can spread out as shown in Figure 9.11 (b).
pg141_n0006_easy_read:
When the temperature is too high, the chicks stay away from the heat source.
They make no noise.
They pant and drop their heads and wings.
pg141_n0007_easy_read: The chicks can spread out as shown in Figure 9.11 (c).
pg141_n0008_easy_read:
Sometimes chicks show extreme discomfort.
This may happen because of:
- uneven light distribution
- outside noise
- unpleasantly cold air blowing through a brooder
pg141_n0009_easy_read:
This way of spreading out of the chicks, shown in Figure 9.11 (d), needs to be checked.
Find the real cause and provide a solution.

pg141_n0017_easy_read: The goal of a poultry farm is to make money through good management.
pg141_n0018_easy_read: But the farm must be planned carefully to do that.
pg141_n0019_easy_read: Before you start a poultry farm, think about a few things.
pg141_n0024_easy_read: When you choose a site for a poultry farm, there are important factors to consider.
pg141_n0025_easy_read: Thinking about these factors will help you choose the right site for a poultry farming enterprise.
pg141_n0029_easy_read:
(i) Local government laws:
Make sure the farm is in an area where the local government allows poultry farming.
pg141_n0031_easy_read:
(ii) Wind direction:
Choose a place that uses the wind direction well.
This helps to reduce pollution from the poultry house.
It also helps to stop diseases from spreading from one poultry house or farm to another.
pg141_n0033_easy_read:
(iii) Natural terrain and landscaping:
Look for a site where the natural landscape can reduce construction costs.
pg141_n0035_easy_read:
(iv) Good drainage, avoid flood-prone areas:
Find an area with good drainage.
Avoid places that flood easily.
This helps to prevent flooding and water-related problems.
pg141_n0037_easy_read:
(v) Easy manure disposal:
Choose a site where it is easy to dispose of poultry manure.
pg142_n0005_easy_read: Many parasites and diseases can harm poultry.
pg142_n0006_easy_read: It is important to know which parasites and diseases are common in your area.
pg142_n0007_easy_read: Knowing this will help you prevent and control the parasites and diseases.
pg142_n0008_easy_read: For example, a farmer should know which diseases need vaccination and when to give the vaccinations.
pg142_n0009_easy_read: The farmer should also know other ways to control parasites and diseases.
pg142_n0013_easy_read: It is important to find reliable sources of good-quality poultry stock.
pg142_n0014_easy_read: Look for stock that is affordable and good quality.
pg142_n0015_easy_read: You can ask other poultry farmers about their experience.
pg142_n0016_easy_read: When you order chicks, do it early.
pg142_n0017_easy_read:
When you place an order, say:
- how many chicks you want
- what kind of poultry you want
- when you want them
pg142_n0018_easy_read: Some hatcheries also sell older birds called growers. Growers can be a good option for poultry kept for egg production.
pg142_n0022_easy_read: Before you start a poultry farm, find out about the markets in your area.
pg142_n0023_easy_read: This will help you decide how big your farm should be.
pg142_n0024_easy_read:
There are 2 types of markets for poultry products:
- open or free markets
- contracted or formal markets
pg142_n0025_easy_read: It is important to work out how much you will be able to sell.
pg142_n0026_easy_read: This helps you decide the size of your farm and how much you can produce.
pg142_n0030_easy_read: In a poultry farm, capital means all the things needed to make the farm work.
pg142_n0031_easy_read: This includes buildings, equipment, and other things that help the farm produce well.
pg142_n0032_easy_read:
We also need money for things like:
- paying workers
- buying supplies such as chicks and feed
pg142_n0033_easy_read: All these things together are called capital.
pg142_n0034_easy_read:
There are different kinds of capital. For example:
- fixed capital for buildings and equipment
- operating capital for things needed every day
pg142_n0035_easy_read: We also need money to buy all these things. This money is called liquid capital.
pg142_n0036_easy_read: It is important to have a good balance of these different types of capital.
pg142_n0037_easy_read:
There are different ways to get the money we need. For example:
- save money over time
- borrow from banks or other places
- get grants or donations from people who want to help
pg142_n0041_easy_read: There are 2 ways to get feed for your birds.
pg142_n0042_easy_read: 1 way is to make the feed yourself at home.
pg142_n0043_easy_read: This means collecting different ingredients and mixing them by following a formula.
pg142_n0044_easy_read: It may be cheaper, but it takes a lot of work.
pg143_n0003_easy_read: Some ingredients are only available at certain times of the year.
pg143_n0004_easy_read: So, the ingredients may not always be easy to find.
pg143_n0005_easy_read: Another way to get feed for your chickens is to buy it from companies that make chicken feed.
pg143_n0006_easy_read: You can buy it directly from the company or from shops that sell it.
pg143_n0007_easy_read: Many companies make chicken feed. You can choose the feed that is better for your birds. You can use the company's reputation or get help from poultry experts.
pg143_n0011_easy_read: Poultry kept in intensive systems produce a lot of manure.
pg143_n0012_easy_read: If you have many chickens, the manure can cause problems in the area around the farm.
pg143_n0013_easy_read:
For example, a bird that weighs 1.8 kg can produce:
- 0.11 kg of manure each day
- 0.80 kg each week
- 3.5 kg each month
- 41.50 kg each year
pg143_n0014_easy_read: We need to manage poultry manure in a way that is good for the environment.
pg143_n0015_easy_read: There are different ways to handle poultry manure in the right way.
pg143_n0016_easy_read: We need to choose the best option for the environment, plants, and animals on the farm.
pg143_n0017_easy_read: Here are some ways to deal with poultry manure:
pg143_n0020_easy_read: (i) Spreading: You can spread poultry manure on fields where crops grow.
pg143_n0021_easy_read: You can use poultry manure instead of artificial fertilisers.
pg143_n0022_easy_read: The amount of manure you can spread depends on the quality of the soil. Usually, you can spread about 4 - 15 tons of manure per hectare.
pg143_n0024_easy_read: (ii) Composting: You can mix poultry manure with other materials to make compost.
pg143_n0025_easy_read: Compost is good for the soil. It can help plants grow well.
pg143_n0027_easy_read: (iii) Selling: Some people may want to buy your poultry manure.
pg143_n0028_easy_read: They can use the poultry manure to make natural fertilisers.
pg143_n0030_easy_read: (iv) Feeding fish: You can put fresh poultry manure in ponds where fish live.
pg143_n0031_easy_read: The manure will fertilise the pond.
pg143_n0033_easy_read:
(v) Feeding other animals: You can use processed chicken manure to feed animals such as:
- cattle
- goats
- sheep
pg143_n0034_easy_read: These animals have special stomachs that can handle processed chicken manure.
pg143_n0038_easy_read: Infrastructure is important for poultry farming.
pg143_n0039_easy_read:
Infrastructure includes:
- roads
- transport
- access to markets
pg143_n0040_easy_read: These things help the poultry farm run smoothly.
pg143_n0041_easy_read: In places like Tanzania, urban and peri-urban areas have better infrastructure than rural areas.
pg143_n0042_easy_read: That is why it is easier to have big poultry farms in
pg144_n0004_easy_read: It is also important to put the poultry houses near a road or railway that goes to the main market.
pg144_n0005_easy_read: This makes it easy to bring in supplies such as poultry feed and take out products such as eggs and birds to sell.
pg144_n0006_easy_read: Services for poultry farming include water supply and electricity.
pg144_n0007_easy_read: Water supply and electricity help the poultry farm to run smoothly.
pg144_n0008_easy_read: It is important to have another source of power in case power from public sources goes off.
pg144_n0009_easy_read: This is especially important for places such as hatchery units or brooders.
pg144_n0010_easy_read: It is also important to have enough clean and safe water for the poultry farm to work well.
pg144_n0014_easy_read:
We have to make sure that:
- everything happens at the right time
- everything stays clean
- records are kept well
pg144_n0015_easy_read: This needs someone who knows what he or she should do to make sure that everything is done the right way.
pg144_n0016_easy_read: So, as a poultry farmer, it is important to always be ready to learn the best way to take care of poultry.

pg145_n0016_easy_read:
Different types of chickens have different characteristics, such as:
- body size
- growth rate
- egg-laying ability
- resistance to diseases
pg145_n0017_easy_read:
You need to know the characteristics of different chicken breeds.
This will help you choose the most suitable breed for your farming goals and conditions.
pg145_n0018_easy_read:
Some chicken breeds are better for meat production.
Other breeds are known for high egg production.
pg145_n0019_easy_read:
When you understand the types and breeds of chickens, you can make informed decisions about:
- breed selection
- feeding requirements
- overall management practices
pg145_n0020_easy_read:
This understanding will also help you plan and use suitable housing and management systems.
You can base this on the specific needs of the chicken breed you are working with.
pg145_n0022_easy_read: Kinds of chickens can be grouped by type.
pg145_n0023_easy_read: Type of chicken is a term that describes the bird's general shape and form for its function.
pg145_n0024_easy_read:
There are 4 basic types of chickens:
- egg-type
- meat-type
- dual-purpose chickens, for both meat and eggs
- ornamental chickens
pg145_n0026_easy_read:
Egg-type chickens:
This group includes chickens developed especially for egg production.
pg145_n0027_easy_read: Egg-type chickens are usually lighter than meat-type chickens.
pg145_n0028_easy_read:
Egg-type chickens do not easily go broody.
This means they do not want to sit on their eggs to hatch them.
pg145_n0029_easy_read: Egg-type chickens are called layers or eggers.
pg145_n0031_easy_read:
Meat-type chickens:
This group includes chickens developed for meat production.
pg145_n0032_easy_read: Meat-type chickens are heavier than egg-type chickens.
pg145_n0033_easy_read: Meat-type chickens do not tolerate the high temperatures of the tropics as well as egg-type chickens do.
pg145_n0034_easy_read: Meat-type chickens lay only a few eggs.
pg146_n0003_easy_read: However, in commercial meat production, farmers sell these chickens before the chickens start laying eggs.
pg146_n0007_easy_read: This group of chickens is bred to produce both eggs and meat.
pg146_n0008_easy_read: This type of chicken is common in tropical areas.
pg146_n0009_easy_read:
These chickens are medium in weight.
They sometimes go broody.
pg146_n0012_easy_read:
This group includes chickens that people keep for their special beauty.
People do not mainly use these chickens for egg production or meat production.
pg146_n0013_easy_read:
People can rear these chickens and sell them to earn money.
People can also keep these chickens in recreational gardens for show, and charge money for the services provided.
pg146_n0014_easy_read: However, ornamental chickens are not common in Tanzania.
pg146_n0015_easy_read:
Examples of ornamental chickens are:
- Phoenix
- Brahma
- Polish
- Orloff
- Ayam
- Silkie
- Dwarf chickens
- Long Crower chickens
pg146_n0016_easy_read: Figures 10.1 (a) and 10.1 (b) show some ornamental chickens.

pg147_n0010_easy_read: Chickens come in different colours, sizes, and other traits or characteristics for each type.
pg147_n0011_easy_read:
A chicken breed is a group of chickens that share some traits, for example:
- feather colour
- egg colour
- type of comb
pg147_n0012_easy_read: A comb is the fleshy growth on a chicken's head.
pg147_n0013_easy_read:
In most cases, breeds are named by where they come from.
But people also focus on developing important economic characteristics, for example:
- meat quality
- meat quantity
- egg quality
- egg quantity
pg147_n0014_easy_read:
There are 2 types of breeds:
- exotic breeds, which come from foreign countries
- indigenous breeds, which come from local countries
pg147_n0018_easy_read: Exotic chicken breeds are either pure breeds or hybrids.
pg147_n0019_easy_read: A pure breed means offspring that come from true breeding.
pg147_n0020_easy_read: True breeding is a way of producing offspring that have the same phenotype as the parents.
pg147_n0021_easy_read: Phenotype means characteristics that can be seen or measured easily.
pg147_n0022_easy_read:
Exotic pure breeds are grouped into 2 types:
- heavy breeds
- light breeds
pg147_n0023_easy_read: Heavy chicken breeds usually have heavy body weight and are good for meat production.
pg147_n0024_easy_read:
Heavy breeds give a valuable carcass.
So, they are more suitable for meat production than egg production.
pg147_n0025_easy_read:
Examples of heavy breeds are:
- New Hampshire
- Rhode Island Red
- Cornish
- White Plymouth Rock
pg147_n0026_easy_read: Light breeds are usually small and mature early.
pg147_n0027_easy_read: People mainly rear light breeds for egg production.
pg147_n0028_easy_read:
Examples of light breeds are:
- White Leghorn
- Ancona
pg147_n0029_easy_read: Because light breeds are small, they are not very suitable for meat production.
pg147_n0030_easy_read: Exotic purebred chickens are rare in poultry farming, except in breeder farms.
pg147_n0034_easy_read: Farmers can cross different pure breeds to produce hybrids.
pg147_n0035_easy_read: These hybrids usually show better fitness than their purebred parents.
pg147_n0036_easy_read: People develop broiler hybrids for specific fitness characteristics in meat production.
pg147_n0037_easy_read:
Examples are:
- heavy weight
- fast growth
- feed efficiency, which means more body weight gain for each unit of feed eaten
- conformation, which means the characteristic shape and form
- hardness to living conditions
- meat yield
- reduced fat content
- product uniformity
pg147_n0038_easy_read: In the same way, layer hybrids are developed for certain traits.
pg148_n0003_easy_read: They have good production. They are hard to living conditions. They also have better eggshell quality and colour.
pg148_n0005_easy_read: There are many kinds of hybrids.
pg148_n0006_easy_read:
The most common hybrids are:
- light hybrids
- medium hybrids
- heavy hybrids
pg148_n0007_easy_read: People keep light and medium hybrids for egg production. People keep heavy hybrids for meat production.
pg148_n0008_easy_read: Figures 10.2 (a) to (f) show examples of hybrids. People developed these hybrids by crossing pure exotic breeds of chickens.

pg149_n0013_easy_read: There are several indigenous breeds in Tanzania and in other countries in Africa.
pg149_n0014_easy_read: However, these breeds are different in their genes and in their physical features.
pg149_n0015_easy_read:
This means they do not have similar genes that control traits passed from 1 generation to the next.
They also do not have similar characteristics that people can easily see or measure.
pg149_n0016_easy_read: Instead, they are groups of chickens that come from and fit better in a particular set of ecological conditions.
pg149_n0017_easy_read:
These chickens have some similar characteristics.
These characteristics make them different from chickens from other ecological conditions.
pg149_n0018_easy_read:
These chicken groups come from places with a given set of ecological conditions.
So, people call them ecotypes, not breeds.
pg149_n0019_easy_read:
Examples of local ecotypes found in Tanzania are:
- Kuchi
- Ching’wekwe
- Singamagazi
- Unguja
- Pemba

pg150_n0003_easy_read: Indigenous chickens survive very well in our country.
pg150_n0004_easy_read:
Indigenous chickens are strong.
They can live in different weather.
They can also cope with diseases that are common in their areas.
pg150_n0005_easy_read:
Indigenous chickens can find food easily.
They also take good care of their young ones.
pg150_n0006_easy_read: For these reasons, many small farmers prefer to keep indigenous chickens.
pg150_n0007_easy_read:
These chickens do not produce as many eggs or as much meat as exotic or commercial chicken breeds.
But people prefer the flavour of their eggs and meat.
pg150_n0009_easy_read: Hybrids of local indigenous chickens and exotic chickens

Local indigenous ecotypes fit well in our local conditions.

pg151_n0013_easy_read: Chicken housing means keeping chickens in a special building made for them.
pg151_n0014_easy_read: The purpose of housing chickens is to keep them safe from very hot or very cold weather.
pg151_n0015_easy_read: Housing chickens also keeps them safe from bad weather like rain and storms.
pg151_n0016_easy_read: Housing also protects chickens from animals that may harm them and from people who may steal them.
pg151_n0017_easy_read:
Housing also stops other animals from reaching the chickens, such as:
- rodents
- wild birds
pg151_n0018_easy_read:
To meet the purpose of housing chickens, a person needs to know the basic needs of a chicken house and follow these points:
- good design
- proper location
- correct position
- a suitable floor
- walls
- a roof
- enough living space
- basic equipment
- proper farm layout or arrangement
pg151_n0022_easy_read: A good chicken house needs enough space for the birds to live comfortably.
pg151_n0023_easy_read: Chickens need a very suitable temperature to produce well.
pg151_n0024_easy_read: The temperature chickens need in their environment changes with age.
pg151_n0025_easy_read: Chicks should start at 35°C in the 1st week after hatching.
pg151_n0026_easy_read: Then reduce the temperature slowly to 20°C - 24°C by the 5th week.
pg151_n0027_easy_read: Broilers kept at temperatures below 18°C are heavier than similar broilers kept at 18°C - 35°C. But they use feed less well.
pg151_n0028_easy_read: Laying chickens produce the highest number of eggs and the biggest eggs at 13°C - 24°C.
pg151_n0029_easy_read: In the same way, chickens use feed best when the temperature is between 21°C and 24°C.
pg151_n0030_easy_read: When the environment gets hotter, chickens eat less and their behaviour changes.
pg151_n0031_easy_read: Within the temperature range of 5°C - 30°C, feed intake reduces by about 1.6% for every 10°C rise in temperature.
pg151_n0032_easy_read: When the temperature goes above 24°C, chickens produce fewer eggs and the eggs become smaller.
pg151_n0033_easy_read: If the temperature keeps rising and reaches 38°C or higher, chickens can die.
pg151_n0034_easy_read: When the weather is very hot and humid, chickens are more likely to die because their bodies find it harder to cool down by breathing.
pg151_n0036_easy_read: Poultry houses should also have enough airflow, or ventilation.
pg151_n0037_easy_read:
Good ventilation in poultry houses is needed to remove these from the air and litter:
- dust
- ammonia
- water vapour
pg151_n0038_easy_read: The living area in a chicken house should be dry, and the light
pg152_n0003_easy_read: They should be spread out evenly.
pg152_n0004_easy_read: Protect the chicken house from vermin and wild birds.
pg152_n0005_easy_read:
The chicken house should be well arranged inside.
It should also last for a long time.
pg152_n0009_easy_read: Location is an important thing to think about for chicken housing.
pg152_n0010_easy_read: Here are important things to think about when choosing a location.
pg152_n0011_easy_read:
No matter the type of house, every chicken house should be:
- on land that drains well
- protected from floods
- easy to reach from the road
pg152_n0012_easy_read: The chicken house should also be in a place where it is easy to get inputs such as chicks and feed.
pg152_n0013_easy_read: The chicken house should also be near a good market.
pg152_n0017_easy_read:
Chicken houses should be:
- well ventilated
- fairly cool in hot areas
- protected from strong winds
pg152_n0018_easy_read: Put curtains in the chicken house to protect the chickens from wind, especially during brooding.
pg152_n0019_easy_read: In hot areas, the long side of the house should run from east to west.
pg152_n0020_easy_read: This will stop direct sunshine from falling on the birds.
pg152_n0021_easy_read: In cold areas, it is best to build houses facing south or south-east to get the most sunlight.
pg152_n0022_easy_read:
The distance between 2 houses for birds of the same age group should be at least 18 m.
This allows proper ventilation.
pg152_n0023_easy_read:
However, the young stock house should be 45 to 100 m away from houses with adult stock.
This helps to prevent diseases.
pg152_n0024_easy_read: To avoid ventilation problems, an open-sided house should not be more than 9 m wide.
pg152_n0025_easy_read: The height of the house depends on the temperature of the place.
pg152_n0026_easy_read: In general, the height of the house should be 2.4 - 3 m from the foundation to the roof line.
pg152_n0027_easy_read: A taller house helps to reduce the temperature inside.
pg152_n0031_easy_read:
The floor of the house should be:
- moisture-proof
- free from cracks
- easy to clean
- rat-proof
- durable
pg152_n0032_easy_read:
The types of floors in use are:
- all-litter floors
- all-slate floors
- slate and litter floors
- wire and litter floors
- sloping wire floors
pg152_n0033_easy_read: The walls and partitions must be strong enough to support the roof and withstand heavy winds.
pg152_n0034_easy_read:
There can be big changes.
This depends on the climate, and on whether construction materials are available and affordable.
pg152_n0035_easy_read: Every main door and rear door of the chicken house should have a footbath with disinfectant for disease control.
pg153_n0005_easy_read: Chicken house roofs must not let water through.
pg153_n0006_easy_read: Roof insulation keeps the building cool in hot weather.
pg153_n0007_easy_read:
If an area gets very hot during the day, it is good to paint the roof with special paint that reflects sunlight.
For example, use aluminium paint.
pg153_n0008_easy_read: A roof overhang of 0.9 m helps to stop rainwater from splashing into the house.
pg153_n0009_easy_read: The weather and the age of the birds decide how big the side openings should be.
pg153_n0010_easy_read: In an open-sided house with wire mesh, usually 1/2 to 2/3 of the side wall area stays open.
pg153_n0011_easy_read: In places where it stays very hot, more than 2/3 of the side wall area may stay open for proper ventilation.
pg153_n0012_easy_read:
In brooder houses, 1/2 of the area stays open.
In grower and layer houses, 2/3 stays open.
Cage houses need maximum ventilation.
pg153_n0016_easy_read: The floor space and equipment in a chicken house depend on the rearing system and the size of the birds.
pg153_n0017_easy_read: In a free-range system, 1 chicken needs about 20–30 cm² of floor space in the house.
pg153_n0018_easy_read:
In a deep litter system, the minimum floor space is:
- 30 cm² for each broiler
- 50 cm² for each layer chicken
pg153_n0019_easy_read:
In hot areas, the floor space can be increased a little.
You can do this by keeping fewer birds in the same area.
pg153_n0020_easy_read: In a slatted floor system, the stocking space in a house is 6 to 8 birds per square metre.
pg153_n0021_easy_read: In the cage system, the recommended cage size for 1 bird is 30 cm × 45 cm × 45 cm.
pg153_n0022_easy_read:
The number of birds in each cage can be 1 to 4.
This depends on:
- the cage size
- the size of the bird
- the farmer’s preference
pg153_n0023_easy_read: In semi-intensive systems, especially house and run, the living space in the house depends on the environmental conditions.
pg153_n0024_easy_read: A stocking density of 4–5 birds per square metre in a house can be used.
pg153_n0028_easy_read: It is important to arrange the farm well.
pg153_n0029_easy_read:
Build livestock houses in relation to:
- places where feed is stored
- places where manure is disposed of
- other important farm facilities
pg153_n0030_easy_read: This helps to make sure labour is used properly.
pg153_n0031_easy_read:
Each animal should have enough space to rest.
The farm should also have well-arranged facilities such as feeding and watering troughs.
pg153_n0032_easy_read:
This helps to improve animal yield.
It also makes the operator’s work easier.
pg153_n0033_easy_read: Feed storerooms should be near the animal houses.
pg153_n0034_easy_read: In general, keep feed in the middle of the building where the animals live and feed.
pg154_n0003_easy_read: It is important to plan the main path in the middle of the main chicken house carefully.
pg154_n0004_easy_read: Do this by making sure it is easy to reach the feed stores and the places for collecting eggs or broilers from the birds' area.
pg154_n0005_easy_read: There should also be isolation rooms for new chickens and sick chickens.
pg154_n0006_easy_read: Put the isolation rooms in a corner of the main house so that other chickens cannot reach the new and sick chickens.
pg154_n0007_easy_read: Also, put the quarantine sheds at the entrance of the farm.
pg154_n0008_easy_read:
This makes it easier to separate:
- new birds bought from outside
- birds coming back from a market or other places where they may have faced a risk of infection
pg154_n0012_easy_read: Chicken houses should be designed so people can care for the birds easily and so the birds can produce without stress.
pg154_n0013_easy_read: Chicken houses should also be designed to keep a comfortable temperature inside by removing too much heat and moisture from the birds.
pg154_n0014_easy_read: Poultry farmers commonly use 2 main types of chicken houses.
pg154_n0015_easy_read: The 2 types are closed houses and open-sided houses.
pg154_n0018_easy_read: A closed house is fully enclosed and has no windows.
pg154_n0020_easy_read: The conditions inside a closed house are kept as close as possible to what the birds need to stay healthy and comfortable.
pg154_n0021_easy_read: Extractor fans or ventilators remove air from the house and bring fresh air in through intake openings.
pg154_n0022_easy_read: Artificial light is used inside the house.
pg154_n0023_easy_read: A closed house is usually more than 13 metres wide.
pg154_n0024_easy_read: Closed houses are also called controlled environment houses.
pg154_n0025_easy_read: This type of house is not common in our country.
pg154_n0028_easy_read: In our country, open-sided houses are the most common type.
pg154_n0030_easy_read: In open-sided houses, usually 1/2 to 2/3 of the side wall area is left open, but it is covered with wire mesh.
pg154_n0031_easy_read: In places where the temperature stays high, more than 2/3 of the side wall may be left open for proper ventilation.
pg154_n0032_easy_read: Curtains are often used to stop the house from becoming too cold at night.
pg154_n0033_easy_read: Open-sided houses use the free flow of air through the house for ventilation.
pg154_n0034_easy_read: Open-sided houses work well in most places, except where temperatures are extremely cold.
pg154_n0035_easy_read: People also prefer open-sided houses because they are cheaper.
pg154_n0036_easy_read: In general, a chicken house should not be expensive. It should be strong, durable, comfortable, and safe.
pg154_n0037_easy_read: Figure 10.4 shows an example of an open-sided poultry house.
pg155_n0003_easy_read: Figure 10.4: Example of an open-sided chicken house
pg155_n0008_easy_read: (a) Widths: The width should be 12.6 m or less.
pg155_n0009_easy_read: Houses wider than 12.6 m will not get enough ventilation in hot weather.
pg155_n0011_easy_read: (b) Heights: Most open-sided poultry houses have a stud height of 2.4 m.
pg155_n0012_easy_read: The stud is the distance from the foundation, or base of the building, to the roofline or top.
pg155_n0013_easy_read: Most parts of Tanzania are always hot. So, the recommended stud height of the house is 3 m.
pg155_n0014_easy_read: The centre height should be 5.2 m.
pg155_n0016_easy_read: (c) Lengths: You can choose any length that is convenient for you, depending on how level the land is.
pg155_n0017_easy_read: However, 10.3 m is recommended for small units.
pg155_n0019_easy_read: (d) Foundation: A solid and suitable foundation should support the building.
pg155_n0020_easy_read: Use concrete and other materials that termites cannot damage.
pg155_n0021_easy_read: How smooth and level the foundation is will determine how smooth and level the finished building is.
pg155_n0023_easy_read: (e) Floor: You can use a concrete floor or a rammed earth floor.
pg155_n0024_easy_read: However, for disease-control programmes, a concrete floor or a similar floor is required.
pg155_n0025_easy_read: This type of floor is also needed when the soil is dense and can absorb and transfer water from the lower subsoil.
pg155_n0026_easy_read: But in some areas with sandy soil, a concrete slab is not used when birds are kept on the floor.
pg156_n0003_easy_read:
(f) Walls:
In a hot tropical climate, such as Tanzania, only the bottom 30 cm of the front and back sides can be covered.
Leave the rest open with wire mesh.
pg156_n0004_easy_read: If cages are used, a roof over the cage may be enough.
pg156_n0005_easy_read: High-quality wire mesh for the sides is a good investment.
pg156_n0006_easy_read:
A fishing net can also be used instead of wire mesh.
But a fishing net is difficult to clean and disinfect.
pg156_n0008_easy_read:
(g) The roof:
The roof can be made from any roofing material.
pg156_n0009_easy_read:
The recommended roof shape is a gable roof.
Its pitch should be from 1/4 to 1/3.
pg156_n0010_easy_read:
You can insulate the roof by using a thatch roof.
A thatch roof gives the best cooling effect in the house.
pg156_n0011_easy_read: If thatch cannot be used, it is best to use aluminium sheets.
pg156_n0012_easy_read:
Aluminium sheets reflect heat from the sun.
They are also easy to take care of.
pg156_n0013_easy_read:
The roof sheets must be thick enough.
They must also be fixed well to the frame.
This stops strong winds from blowing them away.
pg156_n0014_easy_read:
If galvanized iron sheets are used for roofing, cover them with palm branches or similar materials.
This reduces heat absorption.
pg156_n0015_easy_read:
If other materials are used, it is best to paint the roof white to reduce heat absorption.
These materials include:
- fibre-cement plates
- galvanized steel plates
- tiles
pg156_n0016_easy_read: If the white paint is taken care of well, it can make the building cooler by 3 to 8 degrees Celsius on hot days.
pg156_n0020_easy_read: A good chicken house needs the right equipment for keeping birds.
pg156_n0021_easy_read: The equipment makes it easy for birds to get food, water, and other things they need.
pg156_n0022_easy_read:
The equipment in a chicken house depends on:
- how the chickens are raised
- the kind of chicken
- the age of the chicken
pg156_n0023_easy_read:
A well-built chicken house must have the equipment needed for production, such as:
- feeders
- drinkers
- perches
- nests
- catching devices
- broody coops
- other necessary items
pg156_n0024_easy_read:
The equipment must be:
- durable
- fairly simple to make
- movable
- easy to clean
- easy to disinfect
pg156_n0028_easy_read:
Feeders and drinkers should be made so that:
- they are easy to fill
- they are easy to clean
- feed or water is not wasted much
- birds cannot stand or roost in them and dirty the feed or water
- birds can reach feed and water easily
- each bird has enough feeding or drinking space
- feeders and drinkers are high enough so birds cannot scratch litter into them
pg156_n0029_easy_read:
You can buy ready-made feeders and drinkers in different designs.
You can also make them on a farm by using locally available resources.
pg156_n0030_easy_read:

Figures 10.6 (a) to (e) show examples of drinkers.

pg159_n0003_easy_read:
Laying nests:
Laying nests should be:
- big enough
- easy to clean and disinfect
- dark inside
- cool
- well ventilated, especially in hot areas
pg159_n0004_easy_read: The nests should also be in a convenient place.
pg159_n0005_easy_read: It is important to remember that hens like privacy when they lay eggs.
pg159_n0006_easy_read: So, hens like nests that are a little dark inside.
pg159_n0007_easy_read: Nests should have a perch so birds can enter easily.
pg159_n0008_easy_read:
The perch is usually placed 10 – 15 cm above the floor.
This helps birds jump into the nests easily.
pg159_n0009_easy_read:
Nests should be comfortable and safe.
Put litter material on the nest floor.
The nests should also be built well.
pg159_n0010_easy_read: The nests must have a lip to stop the litter material from spilling out.
pg159_n0011_easy_read:
The nests must also have a sloping roof.
This stops birds from sitting or sleeping on the nest roof.
pg159_n0012_easy_read:
There are 2 types of nests:
- individual nests
- communal nests
pg159_n0016_easy_read: An individual nest should be 31 cm long × 35 cm wide × 35 cm high.
pg159_n0017_easy_read: There should be 1 nest for every 4 hens.
pg159_n0018_easy_read:
People usually build individual nests in groups:
- 5 nests across
- 2 or 3 rows high
pg159_n0019_easy_read:
Individual nests should have sloping roofs.
This stops birds from sitting or sleeping on them.
pg159_n0020_easy_read: The bottom part of individual nests should move easily for cleaning.
pg159_n0021_easy_read: Because many areas of Tanzania are hot, it is better to use wire mesh at the back of the nests instead of solid material.
pg159_n0022_easy_read: Figure 10.7 (a) shows an example of individual nests.
pg159_n0028_easy_read:
These are boxes with no partitions.
Each box is about 2.4 m long and 0.6 m wide.
There is an opening at each end.
Birds use the openings to enter and leave.
pg159_n0029_easy_read:
Each nest has a sloping cover.
The cover is hinged, so it can be opened to collect the eggs.
pg159_n0030_easy_read:
A communal nest that is 1.8 m long by 0.3 m wide by 0.6 m high is enough for 50 hens.
Refer to Figure 10.8 (b).

pg160_n0008_easy_read: Layer chickens and dual-purpose chickens kept in systems other than cages should have perches.
pg160_n0009_easy_read:
Perches are horizontal wooden bars or poles in chicken houses.
Birds use them to sleep or sit on.
pg160_n0010_easy_read:
Birds naturally roost in high places.
So perches give birds a place they like.
pg160_n0011_easy_read:
The most common perches are:
- 5 cm by 8 cm pieces
- 5 cm by 10 cm pieces

These pieces are placed on the edge.
The upper corners are rounded.
pg160_n0012_easy_read:
Each bird needs about 15 cm of perch space.
This depends on the breed.
pg160_n0013_easy_read: The perches should be 20 – 25 cm apart.
pg161_n0005_easy_read: This is a nest or cage. People use it to keep broody birds in one place and stop broodiness.
pg161_n0006_easy_read: Broody coops have wire mesh at the bottom. This stops chickens from sitting down and staying inactive.
pg161_n0010_easy_read: The main carrying device in poultry farming is a transport crate, also called a carrying crate.
pg161_n0011_easy_read: People use these crates to hold and carry chickens and other poultry birds.
pg161_n0012_easy_read:
Catching crates should be:
- strong
- easy to put chickens into
- easy to take chickens out of
- made so that birds cannot escape
pg161_n0013_easy_read: The size of the crates depends on the size of the birds kept in them.
pg161_n0014_easy_read:
People can make the crates from:
- plastic
- wood
- other suitable materials
pg161_n0015_easy_read: There are ready-made crates. There are also farm-made crates that use locally available materials.

pg162_n0022_easy_read: Feed costs make up 70 - 80% of the total cost of raising chickens.
pg162_n0023_easy_read: Chicken farmers should make sure that spending these high costs is reasonable.
pg162_n0024_easy_read: An animal keeper keeps feed costs low and keeps the quantity and quality of products as high as possible.
pg162_n0025_easy_read: Birds, like other animals, need balanced feed.
pg162_n0026_easy_read:
A balanced feed has enough:
- energy
- proteins
- vitamins
- minerals
pg162_n0027_easy_read: Birds also need enough water all the time.
pg162_n0029_easy_read:
Balanced feeds can be packed in different forms.
Chickens also get them in different feeding methods.
pg162_n0030_easy_read:
Farmers can buy balanced ready-made chicken feeds from authorised distributors.
They can also make the feeds on the farm with advice from livestock extension workers or chicken experts.
pg162_n0034_easy_read:
There are different forms of feed for chickens.
The right form depends on the type of birds being fed.
pg162_n0035_easy_read:
These forms include:
- mashes
- pellets
- crumbs
pg162_n0037_easy_read: Mash feeds: These feeds are made by grinding feed ingredients into fine particles.
pg162_n0038_easy_read: This is the most common form fed to poultry in our country, but it is most suitable for layers.
pg162_n0039_easy_read:
Mashes are easy to make.
They keep the birds active.
Birds also take more time to feed, so they are less bored.
pg162_n0040_easy_read:
However, birds may pick only the bigger particles.
This leaves some nutrients uneaten.
This can cause deficiencies.
pg162_n0042_easy_read:
Pellet feeds: These are balanced feeds.
After mixing, they are pressed into pellets of different sizes.
Pellets are like small tablets.
pg163_n0003_easy_read: because the birds pick the big particles.
pg163_n0004_easy_read: Pellet feeds are best for broilers.
pg163_n0005_easy_read: Pellet feeds do not cause nutrient deficiency because each particle is balanced.
pg163_n0006_easy_read: However, pellet feeds may cause unwanted behaviour in birds.
pg163_n0007_easy_read: This happens because birds eat fast and then stay idle.
pg163_n0010_easy_read: People make crumble feeds by passing pellets through a cracker or pellet disintegrator. This makes a feed that is between mash and pellets.
pg163_n0011_easy_read: Crumble feeds have the same advantage as pellets because people mostly feed them to young chicks.
pg163_n0012_easy_read: This feed helps chicks get all the nutrients in the ration.
pg163_n0013_easy_read: This feed also reduces wastage and improves feed efficiency.
pg163_n0014_easy_read:

pg163_n0020_easy_read: Feeding chickens well helps them grow fast.
pg163_n0021_easy_read: Most feeding methods work better for birds kept in confinement than for birds under free range.
pg163_n0022_easy_read:
The suggested methods for feeding birds are:
- ad libitum feeding
- restricted feeding
- free choice feeding
pg163_n0025_easy_read: This means giving feed to an animal at all times.
pg163_n0026_easy_read: People do ad libitum feeding gradually. They increase the amount of feed as the animal eats. They continue until the animal leaves at least 15% of the feed that was offered.
pg163_n0027_easy_read: People commonly use ad libitum feeding for fast-growing birds, for example, broilers.
pg164_n0003_easy_read:
Restricted feeding:
In this method, birds get a limited amount of feed each day.
This amount meets the best body needs of the birds.
pg164_n0004_easy_read:
Restricted feeding is commonly used for:
- pullets for all types of production
- layers
- special-purpose birds, for example, birds used for research
pg164_n0006_easy_read:
Free choice feeding:
In this method, chickens always get different types of feedstuffs.
The chickens choose what they need to eat.
pg164_n0007_easy_read: In this method, birds usually choose from 3 types of feedstuffs.
pg164_n0008_easy_read:
The 3 types of feedstuffs are:
- an energy source, for example maize, rice bran, sorghum, or wheat
- a protein source, for example fish meal or oil seedcake meals
- vitamins and minerals
pg164_n0009_easy_read: With this feeding method, birds can balance their diet well if each feedstuff is in the feeder.
pg164_n0010_easy_read: This feeding method is commonly used for game birds and indigenous chickens.
pg164_n0011_easy_read: With this method, no labour is needed to mix the feed.
pg164_n0015_easy_read:
Fresh fodders are green plant materials.
People feed them to animals such as chickens.
pg164_n0016_easy_read: For chickens, fodders are extra food.
pg164_n0017_easy_read: Fodders are important for chickens because they help chickens grow strong and healthy.
pg164_n0018_easy_read: Fodders also help chickens lay better eggs with a strong yellow yolk.
pg164_n0019_easy_read: Chickens can use many types of fodder.
pg164_n0020_easy_read: One example is vegetable crop residues.
pg164_n0021_easy_read: Another example is leaves from leguminous trees.
pg164_n0022_easy_read:
Leaves from leguminous trees are rich in nutrients.
They can be a very good source of fodder for chickens.
pg164_n0024_easy_read:
If natural sources of fodder are not available or are not enough, people can make fodder by sprouting grains or growing it from grains.
This is called hydroponic fodder.
pg164_n0025_easy_read: Sprouting grains into fodder is a good way to reduce the cost of animal feed.
pg164_n0026_easy_read: For example, 50 kg of whole grain can become up to 300 kg of fodder by sprouting it.
pg164_n0027_easy_read:
The grains used include:
- sorghum
- finger millet
- bulrush millet
- wheat
- barley
- maize
- paddy
pg164_n0028_easy_read: People grow these grains in a nutrient-rich solution, not in soil.
pg164_n0029_easy_read: People put the grains in a tray or container for about 1 week to grow.
pg164_n0030_easy_read:
This fodder has:
- vitamins
- minerals
- other nutrients that chickens need
pg164_n0031_easy_read: Chickens eat both the sprouts and the seed residue left from the fodder.
pg164_n0032_easy_read: A big benefit of this fodder is that it gives chickens a continuous supply of nutritious feed.
pg164_n0033_easy_read: Growing this fodder can also help you save money on chicken feed.

- Bulrush millet

(ii) Soak the seeds:
Put the seeds in a container, such as a bucket.

(iii) Drain the water:
After 8 hours, drain the water from the container.

You can buy a ready-made nutrient solution from a gardening store.
pg165_n0018_easy_read: Or, you can make your own nutrient solution.

You can buy it from the market.
pg165_n0020_easy_read: Make sure the fertiliser has micronutrients.
pg165_n0021_easy_read:
Add about 10 grams of this fertiliser to each litre of water.
Then mix well.
pg165_n0022_easy_read: Add about 5 grams of magnesium sulphate to each litre.
pg165_n0023_easy_read: Stir the mixture well so everything mixes properly.
pg165_n0025_easy_read:
(v) Spread the seeds:
Spread the seeds evenly on a growing tray.
pg165_n0026_easy_read: The tray should have small drain holes.
pg165_n0027_easy_read:
These holes let extra water drain away.
This stops the plant roots from staying under water.
pg165_n0028_easy_read:
If the roots stay under water, they cannot breathe.
The plants can become stressed or die.
pg165_n0029_easy_read:
You can use winnowing baskets as growing trays for hydroponic fodder.
They are easy to get.

Winnowing baskets can be found in many places.

pg166_n0003_easy_read:
(vi) Water the seeds:
Use the nutrient solution to water the seeds 2 - 3 times a day.
pg166_n0004_easy_read:
Keep the seeds moist all the time.
Do not let the seeds become wet.
pg166_n0006_easy_read:
(vii) Grow the seeds:
Put the tray in a warm place indoors.
pg166_n0008_easy_read: The seeds will sprout and grow into grass.
pg166_n0010_easy_read:
(viii) Harvest the fodder:
After 7 days, the fodder is ready.
pg166_n0011_easy_read: The fodder should be green and about 15 centimetres tall.
pg166_n0013_easy_read:
(ix) Feed the chickens:
Give the fodder to the chickens.
pg166_n0014_easy_read: You may spread the fodder on plate feeders.
pg166_n0017_easy_read: Always keep the place clean when growing hydroponic fodder.

This helps to keep your chickens safe and healthy.

pg166_n0038_easy_read: Good management of chicken health helps a poultry farmer to increase production and profits.
pg166_n0039_easy_read: To achieve this, poultry farmers should be able to tell the difference between healthy chickens and sick chickens.
pg166_n0040_easy_read: This will help a farmer notice unhealthy chickens and find the causes and solutions.
pg166_n0041_easy_read:
The following sections explain:
- the meaning of animal health
- the signs of healthy and unhealthy chickens, including poultry vices
- the causes of poor health or illness in chickens
- the general management of chicken health
pg167_n0005_easy_read: Health means the body is in good condition. All body organs and systems are normal and work properly.
pg167_n0006_easy_read: It means being free from diseases and abnormalities.
pg167_n0007_easy_read: Ill health is any change from the normal state. It is also any process that stops an animal's body from working normally.
pg167_n0011_easy_read: Poultry farmers must watch birds closely. This helps them keep each bird, flock, or herd healthy and productive.
pg167_n0012_easy_read: When an animal is ill, it shows signs or behaviour that are different from a healthy animal.
pg167_n0013_easy_read: These are some signs and behaviours of a healthy chicken that a poultry farmer should know.
pg167_n0016_easy_read: The eyes are bright, clear, and shiny. They are fully open. They have no discharge or swelling.
pg167_n0019_easy_read: Both nostrils are clear and open. There is no discharge from the nostrils.
pg167_n0022_easy_read: The chicken breathes with its mouth closed, except when the weather is very hot.
pg167_n0025_easy_read: In most chicken breeds, the wings stay close to the body.
pg167_n0026_easy_read: A few breeds have wings that point down. So, study the breed characteristics to know what is normal for your breed.
pg167_n0027_easy_read:
The wings should not:
- bend
- hang down heavily
- look twisted
pg167_n0030_easy_read: The feathers are spread evenly. There are no large bare patches.
pg167_n0031_easy_read: A healthy bird keeps its feathers smooth and flat when it is active.
pg167_n0032_easy_read: Hens kept with a cock often have bare patches on the back and at the base of the neck near the back.
pg167_n0033_easy_read: These patches happen because of scratching during mating. This is normal.
pg167_n0034_easy_read: However, some kinds of chickens are different. Their feathers are twisted or curled. Examples are Frizzle and Polish chickens.
pg167_n0037_easy_read: The skin looks smooth and unbroken. It has no open sores or swelling.
pg167_n0040_easy_read: A healthy chicken's legs look smooth.
pg167_n0041_easy_read: The scales can be seen, but they lie quite flat, like skin.
pg167_n0042_easy_read: The 3 front toes of a chicken point straight ahead. The feet should not turn outward.
pg167_n0043_easy_read: The feet should not be webbed. Webbing is skin that connects the toes. In rare cases, webbed feet appear as a genetic defect.
pg167_n0046_easy_read: This is the opening where the chicken passes out faeces and eggs.
pg167_n0047_easy_read:
A healthy cloaca is:
- clean
- pinkish-red
- moist
- free from faeces stuck on it
- free from wounds or sores around it
pg167_n0048_easy_read: The vent should not stick out. It should not be bloody or dry.
pg168_n0003_easy_read: Droppings or faeces: A healthy chicken passes firm droppings with white caps on them.
pg168_n0005_easy_read: Mental state: A healthy chicken notices things quickly and reacts quickly. In a place with light, the chicken stays away from people it does not know.
pg168_n0006_easy_read: A chicken that does not move or resist when someone holds it is likely to be sick.
pg168_n0007_easy_read: When it is dark, chickens are calm and quiet. This is normal.
pg168_n0009_easy_read: Activity level: A healthy chicken is usually active during the day.
pg168_n0010_easy_read: Some chickens get scared easily and jump a lot. Other chickens are calm but still active.
pg168_n0011_easy_read: In very hot weather, all chickens are less active.
pg168_n0014_easy_read: Normal growth or egg production: Healthy chickens should grow to the right weight for their age.
pg168_n0015_easy_read: If chickens are kept for eggs, they should lay eggs as expected.
pg168_n0017_easy_read:
Other normal behaviours: Healthy chickens should show normal behaviour in:
- eating
- drinking
- walking
- perching
pg168_n0019_easy_read: Note: Any unusual signs or behaviours in chickens show that the chickens are not healthy.
pg168_n0022_easy_read:

pg168_n0029_easy_read: Chickens can get sick for many reasons.
pg168_n0032_easy_read:
Poor feeding: If chickens do not get enough good feed, they can get nutritional problems.
For example, they may peck each other or eat their eggs.
pg168_n0034_easy_read: Poor housing, hygiene and biosecurity: If chickens live in dirty or unsafe places, they can get sick.
pg168_n0035_easy_read: Biosecurity means keeping people, animals, and plants safe from harmful germs and diseases.
pg168_n0036_easy_read: If biosecurity is poor, germs can spread and make chickens sick.
pg168_n0038_easy_read: Injuries from poor handling: If people treat chickens badly or chicken houses are not well made, the chickens can get hurt.
pg168_n0039_easy_read: This can cause problems such as broken bones or wounds.
pg169_n0003_easy_read: Parasite infestation: Parasites are living things. They live in or on another living thing, called a host, and they can harm it.
pg169_n0004_easy_read: Parasites can live outside the body or inside the body.
pg169_n0005_easy_read:
External parasites live on the chicken's body.
Examples are:
- fleas
- lice
- mites
pg169_n0006_easy_read:
Internal parasites live inside the chicken's body.
An example is roundworms.
pg169_n0007_easy_read: Parasites can cause problems in chickens.
pg169_n0008_easy_read:
Parasites can:
- compete with chickens for food
- make chickens lose their appetite
- make chickens sick
pg169_n0009_easy_read: Figures 10.13 (a) to (d) show some parasites of chickens.
pg169_n0019_easy_read: Micro-organisms or pathogens: These are very small living things that can cause diseases.
pg169_n0020_easy_read: Diseases happen when these harmful micro-organisms, or pathogens, enter a chicken's body.
pg169_n0021_easy_read: Examples of these pathogens are bacteria and viruses.
pg169_n0022_easy_read: However, some diseases happen when chickens do not get enough nutrients from food, for example, vitamins.
pg169_n0023_easy_read: Diseases often spread from 1 chicken to another chicken. This usually happens more often than spread from mother to chick.
pg169_n0028_easy_read: Direct contact with an infected chicken;
pg169_n0031_easy_read: Touching litter that has been contaminated;
pg169_n0034_easy_read: Breathing in tiny particles in the air that carry disease; and
pg169_n0037_easy_read: Eating feed or drinking water that has been in contact with infected animals or disease carriers such as insects and wild birds.
pg170_n0003_easy_read: Figures 10.14 (a) to (d) show some signs of disease in chickens.
pg170_n0005_easy_read: Figure 10.14 (a): Unhealthy chickens with a dirty vent and drooping wings.
pg170_n0007_easy_read: Figure 10.14 (b): Eggs with soft shells. This shows an unhealthy condition.
pg170_n0011_easy_read: Figure 10.14 (c): Chickens with a tilted head and paralysis in the legs and wings.
pg170_n0015_easy_read: Figure 10.14 (d): Chickens with blisters on the comb and wattles.
pg170_n0017_easy_read: It is important to note this:
pg170_n0019_easy_read:
(a) Parasites and diseases can cause problems for chickens, for example:
- discomfort
- blood loss
- death
pg170_n0020_easy_read:
To prevent this, we must keep the chicken's environment clean.
We must also use the right treatments recommended by a veterinarian.
pg171_n0003_easy_read: (b) If you used any drugs on your flock, follow the drug withdrawal period.
pg171_n0004_easy_read: This is important. It helps prevent the sale of products that have drug residues.
pg171_n0005_easy_read: The withdrawal period is the time after using a drug when the drug can no longer be found in the animals' products.
pg171_n0006_easy_read: It is important to follow this period. It helps make sure the products you sell to customers are safe and of good quality.
pg171_n0010_easy_read: Chickens can also have bad habits (vices).
pg171_n0011_easy_read: These bad habits are usually caused by poor management.
pg171_n0012_easy_read:
Some common bad habits in chickens are:
- cannibalism
- feather pecking
- egg eating
pg171_n0015_easy_read: These bad habits are usually caused by stress.
pg171_n0016_easy_read: Birds can peck each other. This can lead to death.
pg171_n0017_easy_read: This can happen when birds are not managed well or when their conditions are not part of their normal routine.
pg171_n0018_easy_read: Figures 10.15 and 10.16 show cannibalism and feather pecking, in that order.
pg171_n0023_easy_read: To manage cannibalism and feather pecking in chickens, you can:
pg171_n0027_easy_read: Give birds enough space for their age, type, and care system.
pg171_n0030_easy_read: Reduce the brightness of the light. Use dim lights or place the building so light does not hit the long side.
pg171_n0033_easy_read: Provide enough feeders and drinkers, using the recommended ratio for the floor space and number of birds.
pg171_n0036_easy_read: Give birds the right amount of balanced feed for their needs.
pg171_n0039_easy_read:
Use measures to control external parasites such as:
- flies
- lice
- mice
pg171_n0042_easy_read: Ventilate the houses to bring in fresh air and remove bad smells.
pg171_n0045_easy_read:
Keep birds busy by hanging fodder such as:
- vegetables
- edible tree leaves
pg171_n0048_easy_read: Isolate birds that have been pecked to stop more pecking or death. Then treat the pecked birds.
pg172_n0005_easy_read:
Use beak trimming only as a last option.
Trim the birds' beaks only if other methods have failed.
pg172_n0006_easy_read:
Do not trim the beaks of free-range birds.
Free-range birds need their beaks to pick food.
pg172_n0009_easy_read: Birds can start eating their eggs if they find eggs that are broken or have soft shells.
pg172_n0010_easy_read: If this habit does not stop, it can spread to other birds.
pg172_n0011_easy_read: This habit shows that people are not taking good care of the chickens.
pg172_n0017_easy_read: There are several ways to stop chickens from eating eggs.
pg172_n0022_easy_read: Give chickens enough good food and a safe place to live.
pg172_n0025_easy_read: Keep the inside of the laying nest dark.
pg172_n0028_easy_read:
Improve the quality and amount of feed.
Give enough minerals to help keep egg shells strong and of good quality.
pg172_n0031_easy_read: Make sure eggs do not stay in the nests overnight after the last collection.
pg172_n0034_easy_read: Give clean water at all times to stop thirst.
pg172_n0037_easy_read:
Trim a beak if it is too long.
This is called de-beaking.
pg172_n0041_easy_read:
There are 2 ways to manage parasites and diseases:
- preventive
- curative
pg172_n0042_easy_read: Preventive ways focus on control measures against the
pg173_n0003_easy_read: To treat diseases caused by parasites, disease-causing agents, or their vectors, use drugs and chemicals.
pg173_n0007_easy_read:
Preventive measures for poultry parasites and diseases include:
- vaccination
- control of vectors
- use of prophylactics
- quarantine or isolation
- sanitation
- proper nutrition
pg173_n0008_easy_read: The preventive measures are explained below:
pg173_n0012_easy_read: Vaccination means putting a vaccine into an animal's body to protect it from a specific disease.
pg173_n0013_easy_read: A vaccine is a biological product given to an animal's body. It helps the body produce antibodies against specific diseases caused by micro-organisms.
pg173_n0014_easy_read: Vaccines can be given to animals in different ways. The way used depends on the type of vaccine and the manufacturer's instructions.
pg173_n0015_easy_read: Give all vaccines with technical advice from extension workers or qualified veterinarians.
pg173_n0017_easy_read: It is important to follow the manufacturer's instructions for storing and giving vaccines.
pg173_n0018_easy_read: In general, store vaccines at a low temperature of 2°C to 8°C. Do not expose vaccines to direct sunlight.
pg173_n0019_easy_read: Treat the water before you give vaccines through drinking water.
pg173_n0020_easy_read: A teacher or a livestock extension worker can help with this.
pg173_n0021_easy_read: Observe the birds carefully. Make sure every bird takes the vaccine within the allowed time.
pg173_n0022_easy_read: After that, clean the drinkers well and refill them.
pg173_n0023_easy_read: Do not give a vaccine to sick animals or animals taking medication until they fully recover.
pg173_n0024_easy_read: Wait at least 2 days after the last dose.
pg173_n0025_easy_read: Also, do not mix water that contains a vaccine with vitamin supplements.
pg173_n0029_easy_read: This means giving healthy animals drugs at regular times to prevent infection.
pg173_n0030_easy_read: Chickens, especially layers, may be given coccidiostats through feed or water where there is a high risk of coccidiosis.
pg173_n0031_easy_read: Coccidiosis causes severe losses in young and growing chickens.
pg173_n0032_easy_read: A coccidiostat is a substance given to birds. It stops or slows the growth of protozoa parasites that cause coccidiosis.
pg173_n0033_easy_read: Start giving coccidiostat in the 3rd week. Continue it as a prophylactic programme.
pg173_n0034_easy_read: However, to reduce the risk of resistance to 1 coccidiostat, it is common to use different coccidiostats in each production cycle or even within the same cycle.
pg173_n0035_easy_read: Deworming with proper anthelmintics every 60–90 days is another form of prophylaxis against intestinal worms.
pg173_n0036_easy_read: Do all prophylactic measures under the supervision or advice of a qualified veterinarian.
pg174_n0005_easy_read: When highly infectious diseases such as avian influenza break out, the movement of birds and bird by-products is restricted. This helps to stop the disease from spreading to other areas.
pg174_n0006_easy_read: In the same way, keep sick birds away from healthy birds. This helps to stop the disease from spreading.
pg174_n0010_easy_read: This includes practices that stop disease-causing agents from spreading.
pg174_n0011_easy_read: These are hygienic measures that people can use to prevent parasites and diseases in poultry:
pg174_n0015_easy_read: Use an all-in all-out system. This reduces the risk of contamination.
pg174_n0016_easy_read: This system means you remove all birds from a room or building. Then clean and disinfect the room or building before bringing in a new batch.
pg174_n0019_easy_read: Do not allow people to enter the brooder house or poultry premises without permission.
pg174_n0022_easy_read:
Provide a room at the entrance with:
- a special dustbin for waste
- a place to wash hands with soap and running water
- a place to change clothes and shoes
pg174_n0023_easy_read: Use footbaths also. Manage them properly.
pg174_n0026_easy_read: Everyone must change shoes when entering or leaving a poultry house.
pg174_n0029_easy_read: Clean the drinkers and disinfect them at least once a week.
pg174_n0035_easy_read: Control vermin, flies, and other external parasites.
pg174_n0039_easy_read: Feed animals properly with enough good-quality feed. This helps to prevent nutritional deficiency diseases, for example, avitaminosis.
pg174_n0040_easy_read: It also stops animals from becoming weak and having poor growth and production.
pg174_n0044_easy_read: A well-designed chicken house gives the best conditions inside. For example, it gives good ventilation.
pg174_n0045_easy_read: This helps to reduce the chance of some parasites and diseases. It helps to keep the birds healthy.

pg174_n0053_easy_read: Kill external parasites by using pesticides:
pg174_n0054_easy_read: This helps to control external parasites that can cause ill health in chickens.
pg174_n0057_easy_read: Treat sick birds by using drugs and chemicals:

pg177_n0005_easy_read: This stage includes a brooding period.
pg177_n0006_easy_read: The brooding period is the time from hatching until the chicks no longer need artificial heat.
pg177_n0007_easy_read: The brooding period is the most important and hardest stage in chicken management.
pg177_n0008_easy_read: At this stage, people usually rear chicks in brooder houses away from the other chickens.
pg177_n0009_easy_read: Choose a brooder that is easy to use, low-cost, and works well.

pg177_n0014_easy_read: Prepare the brooder at least 2 weeks before the chicks arrive.

pg177_n0016_easy_read: If the number of chicks is small and easy to manage, cover the litter with pieces of paper.

pg177_n0034_easy_read: The general characteristics of good chicks are:
pg177_n0038_easy_read:
The feathers are dry.
They are not too moist.
pg177_n0041_easy_read:
The chicks are alert and curious.
Their eyes are clean, open, and bright.
The eyes should not be dull or closed.
pg177_n0044_easy_read:
The navel is dry and well closed.
It is not open.
It has no remains of yolk.
pg177_n0047_easy_read:
The chicks are active and move with an upright posture.
Their legs are not bent.
pg177_n0050_easy_read:
The chicks have no other abnormality.
For example:
- crooked beak
- stiff neck
- bent neck
pg178_n0005_easy_read: You must heat the brooder for the needed period.
pg178_n0006_easy_read:
The length of time depends on:
- the weather outside
- how fast the birds grow feathers
pg178_n0007_easy_read: Start heating the brooder 12 - 48 hours before the chicks arrive.
pg178_n0008_easy_read:
During this time, adjust the heater to about 35°C.
Measure this temperature 5 cm above the litter at the edge of the brooder.
pg178_n0009_easy_read: This temperature is enough for the chicks on the 1st day.
pg178_n0011_easy_read: If possible, use thermometers before you put the chicks in the brooder.
pg178_n0012_easy_read: After the first 2 days, you may remove the thermometers.
pg178_n0013_easy_read: As the chicks grow older, reduce the temperature at the rates you already learnt.
pg178_n0014_easy_read:
Use the chicks' behaviour as your guide, as you learnt in the previous Chapter.
Refer to Figures 9.11 (a) to (d).
pg178_n0015_easy_read: The figures will help you regulate the heat supply or take corrective measures.
pg178_n0016_easy_read: When the chicks have full feathers, you do not need to provide heat.
pg178_n0017_easy_read: You may increase the brooder heat above the guidelines if the chicks seem cold, especially during stress from vaccination or beak trimming.
pg178_n0018_easy_read: This will help to keep the birds comfortable at all times.
pg178_n0022_easy_read: Ventilation means fresh air moving through an enclosed space.
pg178_n0023_easy_read:
Good ventilation is important because it:
- provides oxygen
- removes ammonia gas
- removes carbon dioxide gas
- removes dust from the brooder
pg178_n0024_easy_read: Good ventilation also removes bacteria that spread through the air.
pg178_n0025_easy_read: Control the air movement in the brooding house so that it keeps an even temperature and fresh air.
pg178_n0026_easy_read: This helps to give young chicks the best conditions they need.
pg178_n0027_easy_read:
Chicks are easily affected by cold and strong wind (draughts).
So, you must protect them.
pg178_n0028_easy_read: To do this, hang curtains along the full length of the walls.
pg178_n0029_easy_read:
The size of the opening for fresh air in the brooder house depends on the weather.
The opening must let in fresh air without making the birds cold.
pg178_n0030_easy_read:
As the chicks grow older, you may open the curtains more during the warm hours of the day.
Keep the curtains closed during the hot hours of the day.
pg178_n0031_easy_read: The common curtains used are made of plastic-like materials.
pg178_n0035_easy_read: Lighting is one important part of successful egg production.
pg178_n0036_easy_read: Treat lighting as a continuous process from day-old chicks to the end of the laying cycle.
pg178_n0037_easy_read: The lighting programme should match the growing period.
pg178_n0038_easy_read:
This is because the length of the day directly affects sexual maturity.
It also affects egg size, especially in early production.
pg178_n0039_easy_read:
During the brooding period, give:
- 23 hours of light for the first 2 - 3 days
- 22 hours of light up to the 3rd week
pg179_n0003_easy_read: After that, reduce the light by 2 hours each week until the chicks get 12 hours of light in week 8.
pg179_n0004_easy_read: The light should be bright enough for the chicks to find feed and water easily.
pg179_n0005_easy_read: After a few days, you can reduce the brightness.
pg179_n0006_easy_read: Table 11.1 shows the recommended lighting schedule for this period.
pg179_n0007_easy_read:
Different breeds need different lighting.
Follow the lighting programme from the chick distributor or a poultry expert.
pg179_n0008_easy_read: In open-sided houses, which are common in our country, it can be hard to control the light brightness.
pg179_n0056_easy_read: The best relative humidity for chicks is between 70% and 80%.
pg179_n0057_easy_read: High humidity prevents dehydration and cannibalism.
pg179_n0058_easy_read:
To keep this high humidity in the first days, you may need to do 1 of these things:
- Place a pan with water near the heat source.
- Spray water on the walls or floors.
pg179_n0059_easy_read:
As the birds grow, droppings and breathing add extra humidity.
Good ventilation must remove this extra humidity.
pg179_n0060_easy_read: Wet litter may be caused by humidity that is higher than the recommended level.
pg179_n0061_easy_read: This may increase the risk of diseases such as coccidiosis.
pg179_n0065_easy_read: Feed the chicks with chick starter mash from day 1 to day 28 (4 weeks).
pg179_n0066_easy_read:
Chick mash has high amounts of:
- protein
- energy
- minerals
- vitamins
- trace elements used as additives
pg179_n0067_easy_read:
1 plate feeder can serve 65 - 70 chicks.

pg180_n0004_easy_read: Use feeds from feed companies or make feed at home with easy-to-find materials to reduce feed costs.

pg180_n0006_easy_read: Put some feed in front of the chicks on plate feeders (see Figure 10.5 (a)) or on sheets of paper. Do this until the chicks learn to eat from hopper feeders (see Figure 10.5 (b)).
pg180_n0007_easy_read: Arrange feeders and drinkers in separate rows.
pg180_n0008_easy_read: Alternate the rows of feeders and drinkers so chicks can reach feed and water easily (see Figure 9.9).
pg180_n0009_easy_read: Make sure the chicks have enough room to rest, eat, and drink.
pg180_n0010_easy_read: Place feeders well. Allow 7 - 12 cm for each chick up to 8 weeks.
pg180_n0011_easy_read: Use the right feeders for chicks at different growth stages.
pg180_n0013_easy_read: Place drinkers on raised wire platforms or boards if possible.
pg180_n0014_easy_read:
Provide enough water space:
- 1.5 cm per chick for trough-type drinkers.
- 1 round automatic drinker for 70 - 100 chicks.
- 1 nipple drinker for 20 chicks.
pg180_n0015_easy_read: Adjust the drinkers to the birds' shoulder height. This helps stop litter from getting into the water.
pg180_n0016_easy_read: Clean the drinkers well. Refill the water often.

pg181_n0005_easy_read: During the brooding period, the recommended stocking density is 50 chicks per square metre.
pg181_n0006_easy_read: If you increase the housing density, you must also increase the feeding space.
pg181_n0007_easy_read: This is because the chicks need more floor space as they grow.
pg181_n0008_easy_read:
Start with 64 cm² of floor space for each chick in the 1st week.
Then add 64 cm² for each chick every week until the birds are 5 - 6 weeks old.
pg181_n0012_easy_read: Follow all the measures you learnt in the previous chapter to protect chicks from parasites and diseases.
pg181_n0013_easy_read: If disease appears, treat the chicks immediately with advice from a veterinarian.
pg181_n0014_easy_read:
Chicks must get the correct vaccines at the right time against:
- Newcastle
- Infectious Bursal disease (Gumboro)
- Fowl pox

The first vaccine against Marek’s disease is given at the hatchery.
If necessary, the other vaccines are given on the farm.

pg182_n0021_easy_read:
This stage is called the growing period.
The chickens in this stage are called pullets or growers.
pg182_n0022_easy_read: How growers are managed greatly affects how they perform in the laying stage.
pg182_n0023_easy_read:
So, manage growers well in these areas:
- housing
- stocking rate
- feeding
- lighting
- parasite management
- disease management
pg182_n0024_easy_read:
Other parts of grower management include:
- culling
- beak trimming
pg182_n0028_easy_read: In large poultry farms, growers must be moved from the brooding house to the growing house at the age of 4 – 6 weeks.
pg182_n0029_easy_read: However, in small and medium poultry farms, people commonly use the same house for brooding and growing pullets.
pg182_n0030_easy_read: The average for birds on litter floors is 8 - 10 birds per square metre.
pg182_n0031_easy_read: The house should have good air flow.
pg182_n0032_easy_read: A suitable temperature of about 24°C must also be kept.
pg182_n0033_easy_read: If the layers will later be reared in a battery cage system, move the pullets to cages at 16 weeks of age.
pg182_n0035_easy_read: During the growing period, litter should have 20 to 30% moisture.
pg182_n0036_easy_read:
This moisture level is important for:
- better feathering
- improved feed use
- normal growth
- lower ammonia in the house
- control of some diseases, for example, coccidiosis
pg182_n0037_easy_read: You can determine the condition of the litter by holding it.
pg183_n0003_easy_read:
Pick up a handful of litter.
Squeeze it tightly.
Then open your hand.
pg183_n0004_easy_read: If the litter is in good condition, cracks will form in the squeezed litter.
pg183_n0005_easy_read:
The litter will not make a solid ball.
It will not fall apart in a heap.
pg183_n0006_easy_read: If possible, use special devices to measure the moisture percentage in the litter.
pg183_n0007_easy_read: Pullets that will later be kept in deep litter laying houses must have perches placed well.
pg183_n0011_easy_read: At the growing stage, change the feed from chick starter to grower mash until the chickens start laying at 3%.
pg183_n0012_easy_read: Grower mash has less energy and less protein than chick mash.
pg183_n0013_easy_read: This helps to control how fast the growers grow.
pg183_n0014_easy_read: Do not let pullets grow and mature before the right age.
pg183_n0015_easy_read:
If the breeder does not give a management guide, use restricted feeding for pullets.
Refer to Table 11.4.
pg183_n0016_easy_read:
Give the daily feed allowance 2 times a day.
This helps to control feed selection and encourage feed intake.
pg183_n0017_easy_read: Do this at the same time every day.
pg183_n0018_easy_read: Give them 60% of their feed in the morning and 40% in the afternoon.
pg183_n0019_easy_read: Feed sick birds, and birds that have just had vaccination or beak trimming, without restriction until they feel better.
