pg184_n0003_easy_read: You should keep checking the growth of pullets.
pg184_n0004_easy_read: Use the flock's average weight gain to make feeding decisions.
pg184_n0005_easy_read: If the birds are too heavy during the weekly weighing, reduce the daily feed amount.
pg184_n0006_easy_read: If the pullets are too light, increase the daily feed amount.
pg184_n0007_easy_read: Give pullets vitamin supplements after weekly weight measurement to help them recover from stress.
pg184_n0008_easy_read: When you change the type of feed, add the new feed slowly and reduce the old feed.
pg184_n0009_easy_read: For example, you can change from chick starter to grower mash like this:
pg184_n0012_easy_read: Day 1: 75% chick starter mash and 25% grower mash
pg184_n0014_easy_read: Day 2: 50% chick starter mash and 50% grower mash
pg184_n0016_easy_read: Day 3: 25% chick starter mash and 75% grower mash
pg184_n0018_easy_read: Day 4: 0% chick starter mash and 100% grower mash
pg184_n0020_easy_read: Give pullets enough space to reach the feed.
pg184_n0021_easy_read: If you use restricted feeding, provide enough feeders.
pg184_n0022_easy_read: This helps all birds eat at the same time when you give the feed.
pg184_n0023_easy_read: When there is not enough feeding space, aggressive birds eat more feed than calm birds.
pg184_n0024_easy_read: Adjust the feeder height so that the bottom of the trough is level with the backs of the birds.
pg184_n0025_easy_read: When the trough is lower than the birds' backs, the birds peck out more feed. This wastes feed.
pg184_n0027_easy_read: Also, give pullets water all the time.
pg184_n0028_easy_read: Provide enough drinkers and arrange them well in the pullet house.
pg184_n0029_easy_read: A 10-litre round plastic drinker can serve up to 50 pullets.
pg184_n0030_easy_read: Pullets need 2 times as much water as the amount of feed they eat. They need even more water when the temperature is above 21.5°C.
pg184_n0031_easy_read: Adjust the drinkers as you already learnt in chick management.
pg184_n0032_easy_read: Clean the drinkers well and refill the water often.
pg184_n0036_easy_read: Raise growers without extra light until they are 13 weeks old.
pg184_n0037_easy_read: This helps control sexual maturity so it happens at the planned time.
pg184_n0038_easy_read: After 13 weeks, increase the light slowly to 16 hours each day (refer to Table 11.5).
pg184_n0039_easy_read: This encourages sexual maturity and sets the laying age at 17 - 18 weeks.
pg184_n0040_easy_read: A light brightness of 3-watt/m<math><msup><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math> is enough for this purpose.
pg184_n0041_easy_read: Very bright light is not recommended.
pg184_n0042_easy_read: You have to know the daylight in your local area. If necessary, use artificial light to complete the required light schedule.
pg184_n0043_easy_read: Light, whether natural or artificial, affects the pituitary gland at the base of the brain. This stimulation causes mature pullets to start producing eggs.
pg185_n0085_easy_read: Follow the hygiene measures you learnt in the previous sections during the whole growing period of the birds.
pg185_n0086_easy_read: Continue with the vaccination programme for the growing stage.
pg185_n0087_easy_read:
The vaccines include:
- Newcastle vaccine every 75 – 90 days
- Fowl pox vaccine in the 10th week of age
pg185_n0088_easy_read:
Continue using prophylactics to control parasites and diseases during the growing period.
Do this with advice from a qualified veterinarian.
pg185_n0089_easy_read:
Also continue regular deworming every 60 - 90 days by using proper anthelmintics.
Do this with advice from a qualified veterinarian.
pg185_n0090_easy_read:
Manage the litter well.
For example:
- remove wet spots around the drinkers
- replace them with clean, dry litter
This helps reduce the build-up of coccidiosis disease-causing agents.
pg185_n0091_easy_read: Do this together with efforts to reduce water spillage from the drinkers.
pg185_n0095_easy_read: This means cutting down the beak of a bird by a properly trained person.
pg185_n0097_easy_read:
People do this to prevent:
- egg eating
- cannibalism
- other vices
pg185_n0098_easy_read: People also do this to stop feed from spilling out of the feeders.
pg185_n0099_easy_read:
This can be done by using:
- an electric debeaker
- a manual debeaker
Refer to Figures 11.1 (a) and (b).
pg185_n0100_easy_read: Usually, the person trims less than 1/3 of the upper beak.
pg186_n0007_easy_read:
During the rearing (growing) period, check the age of the birds.
Then check if the beak is overgrown.
pg186_n0008_easy_read: If the beak is overgrown, do debeaking.
pg186_n0009_easy_read:
Trim the beaks when the birds are about 10–12 weeks old.
Do this before laying.
pg186_n0010_easy_read:
Beak trimming at this age causes less stress to the birds.
The beaks will also not regrow much.
pg186_n0011_easy_read: Figures 11.2 (a) and (b) show a chicken with an untrimmed beak and a trimmed beak, in that order.
pg186_n0019_easy_read: Remove all poor or inferior birds from the flock because they are not productive.
pg186_n0020_easy_read:
These birds may:
- carry and spread diseases
- take up space that good layers can use
- eat feed and increase feed costs unnecessarily
pg186_n0021_easy_read: Therefore, cull inferior, crippled, injured and deformed layers every week.
pg186_n0025_easy_read: When you need to catch chickens for culling or for other purposes, use a poultry-catching tool.
pg186_n0026_easy_read: The poultry-catching tool catches birds quietly, comfortably and safely.
pg186_n0027_easy_read: Pullets should also be handled one by one when they are
pg187_n0003_easy_read:
to be moved from 1 house to another.
For example, from the growing house to the laying house, when the laying house is different from the growing house.

pg188_n0003_easy_read: 8. What are the main things to consider about lighting for layer growers, and why is it important to increase light for pullets slowly?
pg188_n0007_easy_read: Put birds in the laying house just before the laying period starts.
pg188_n0008_easy_read: Laying starts when the birds are 17 - 20 weeks old.
pg188_n0009_easy_read: Laying lasts for 12 to 14 months for the best production.
pg188_n0010_easy_read:
During this period, observe these important management areas:
- feeding
- providing water
- ventilation
- parasite management
- disease management
pg188_n0011_easy_read: It also includes following hygiene and biosecurity measures, as discussed in earlier chapters.
pg188_n0012_easy_read: In the cage system, put the birds into the cages a few days before the laying period starts.
pg188_n0013_easy_read: This helps the birds get used to the new confinement.
pg188_n0017_easy_read: Continue to follow the housing management practices you have already learnt, especially keeping the house clean.
pg188_n0018_easy_read:
Also provide the chickens with:
- laying nests
- enough living space
- lighting
- ventilation
pg188_n0021_easy_read: Laying boxes are also called laying nests.
pg188_n0022_easy_read: Place the laying nests in the laying house well before the hens arrive, preferably in the 16th week.
pg188_n0023_easy_read: Put plenty of good, clean litter in the nest boxes, such as wood shavings or other nesting materials. This helps to stop eggs from cracking.
pg188_n0024_easy_read: Place the nest boxes lower than the perches.
pg188_n0025_easy_read: This will stop chickens from roosting in the nest boxes. It will also help to keep the chickens and eggs clean.
pg188_n0028_easy_read: At this stage, keep 4 - 5 birds per m² in a deep litter system.
pg188_n0029_easy_read: In battery cages, do not keep more than 12 birds in 1 cage.
pg188_n0030_easy_read: Usually, you can keep 2 – 10 hens in 1 cage. This is equal to 18 hens per m².
pg188_n0033_easy_read: For the best laying, give layers 16 hours of light each day until final culling.
pg188_n0034_easy_read: So, give layers artificial light for some hours.
pg188_n0035_easy_read: Decide the hours of artificial light by the length of daylight in that area.
pg188_n0036_easy_read: In the same way, houses for laying birds should have good ventilation to allow air to move.
pg189_n0005_easy_read:
Feed the birds 2 times a day.
Use the right feed.
Place the feeders with space between them so the birds can move freely in a deep litter system.
pg189_n0006_easy_read:
A laying bird needs the right amount of layers mash each day.
The amount depends on the weight of the breed.
pg189_n0007_easy_read:
Feed each breed as follows:
- Light breeds: 110 – 115 g per bird per day
- Medium breeds: 120 g per bird per day
- Heavy breeds: 130 – 140 g per bird per day
pg189_n0008_easy_read: Give layers cool and clean water all day.
pg189_n0009_easy_read:
Check if the birds drink a normal amount of water.
If there is a problem in the flock, the birds drink less water.
pg189_n0013_easy_read: During this period, there are 2 types of culling.
pg189_n0014_easy_read:
The 2 types of culling are:
- culling non-laying birds after the laying peak
- culling the laying flock after economic laying ends
pg189_n0017_easy_read: Culling non-laying birds means finding the birds that do not lay eggs and removing them from the flock.
pg189_n0018_easy_read:
Well-reared layers reach the laying peak 1 month after laying starts.
If the birds are not well managed, this can take up to 2 months.
pg189_n0019_easy_read:
The laying peak can be at about 24 weeks of age.
At this time, laying is 90% or more.
pg189_n0020_easy_read: You can use several characteristics to identify non-laying hens and laying hens.
pg189_n0021_easy_read: An experienced poultry expert must carry out this identification exercise.
pg189_n0022_easy_read: It is also good to isolate the identified non-laying birds for some days.
pg189_n0023_easy_read: This helps the poultry farmer check if the isolated birds are truly not laying eggs.
pg189_n0024_easy_read:
The culling exercise can disturb the flock.
This can reduce egg production.
pg189_n0025_easy_read: To reduce this bad effect on the flock, do culling at night.
pg189_n0028_easy_read: From 24 weeks of age, well-managed layers can lay productively for 12 – 14 months.
pg189_n0029_easy_read: After this period, laying drops to 50%.
pg189_n0030_easy_read: At this stage, it is no longer economical to keep the birds.
pg189_n0031_easy_read: If egg prices are not very high, or if the feed is not very cheap, you should cull the birds and replace the flock.
pg189_n0033_easy_read: The culling process can start from the 10th month of the laying period.
pg189_n0034_easy_read: This will help remove non-productive chickens and reduce the work of managing non-laying hens.
pg189_n0035_easy_read: Table 11.6 shows the characteristics that help you tell the difference between good layers and poor layers.

pg190_n0025_easy_read: Very long, thin and sharply pointed
pg190_n0044_easy_read: Large, soft and free from fat
pg190_n0046_easy_read: Small, hard and with thick fat
pg190_n0073_easy_read: 3 - 4 fingers between the pubic bones and the keel bone
pg190_n0074_easy_read:
2 - 3 fingers between the 2 pubic bones
(refer to Figure 11.4 (a))
pg190_n0077_easy_read: 1 - 2 fingers between the pubic bones and the keel bone
pg190_n0091_easy_read: To avoid losing the egg market, the new flock that replaces the old flock should start laying when the final culling is done.
pg191_n0005_easy_read: Handling and adding value to table eggs has several important parts.
pg191_n0006_easy_read: First, people collect eggs from egg-laying hens.
pg191_n0007_easy_read: Egg producers should follow local rules and practices.
pg191_n0008_easy_read: Next, people inspect the eggs for quality and defects.
pg191_n0009_easy_read:
People grade the eggs by:
- quality
- size
- weight
pg191_n0010_easy_read:
Then people carefully pack the eggs in cartons or trays.
They also label them with the right information.
pg191_n0011_easy_read:
Proper storage is very important.
It keeps the eggs fresh and of good quality for the time they need to be stored.
pg191_n0012_easy_read:
It is important to handle eggs safely.

pg191_n0015_easy_read:
In the poultry farm or unit, people should collect eggs from the laying house at least 2 times a day:
- early morning
- late afternoon
pg191_n0016_easy_read: This practice helps to prevent eggs from getting dirty and breaking.
pg191_n0017_easy_read: This practice also reduces the chance of contamination and egg eating.
pg191_n0020_easy_read:
People inspect eggs to identify and remove these eggs:
- dirty eggs
- eggs with wrinkled shells
- cracked eggs
Keep them separate from normal eggs.

pg192_n0003_easy_read:
If you need to clean dirty eggs, use a cloth soaked in warm water.
Wipe the eggshell gently.
pg192_n0004_easy_read: But clean eggs as little as possible.
pg192_n0005_easy_read: This means it is easier to keep the place where hens lay eggs clean than to clean dirty eggs later.
pg192_n0006_easy_read: You can do this by cleaning the nest boxes and keeping fresh bedding as often as possible.
pg192_n0007_easy_read: You can also keep eggs clean by putting perches higher than the nest boxes.
pg192_n0008_easy_read: This is because chickens like to rest in the highest part of the house that they can reach.
pg192_n0009_easy_read: So, if the perches are higher than the nest boxes, chickens will be less likely to rest in the nest boxes and dirty them.
pg192_n0012_easy_read: Grading is used in places where eggs are sold in different classes.

pg193_n0009_easy_read: When you stack eggs in trays, always put the broad end on top.

pg193_n0011_easy_read: Also, the narrow tip is usually thicker and stronger. It helps support the weight of the egg.
pg193_n0015_easy_read: The egg storage room or area should be clean. It should have no strong smells. It should be away from rodents.
pg193_n0016_easy_read: Eggs can stay in good condition at a temperature of 10°C or lower.

pg193_n0018_easy_read: For less than 7 days, you can store table eggs in a cool room. The temperature should not go above 20°C.
pg193_n0019_easy_read: When the temperature in the egg storage room or area is above 20°C, the eggs lose a lot of quality and weight.
pg193_n0020_easy_read: For 6–8 weeks, table eggs should be kept at about 8 - 10°C. The relative humidity should be 85%.

pg199_n0019_easy_read: Chickens that people raise only for meat are called broilers.
pg199_n0020_easy_read: Commercial broilers are best raised from day 1 to 3 - 8 weeks of age. At this age, they reach market weight of 1.5 - 2 kg.
pg199_n0021_easy_read: The chicken breed you should keep depends on the demand in your area and the availability of the day-old chicks.
pg199_n0022_easy_read: The weight of the chicken you want to sell should also depend on market demand.
pg199_n0023_easy_read: A larger chicken can be sold for more money because it gives more meat.

pg199_n0028_easy_read: During the rearing period, give the birds 23 hours of light and 1 hour of darkness. This helps prevent stress if power fails.
pg199_n0029_easy_read: The preferred stocking rate is 10 - 12 birds per m2. This rate is for birds expected to grow to about 1.5 - 2.5 kg market weight.
pg199_n0030_easy_read: The birds should have feed available at all times during the rearing period.
pg200_n0005_easy_read: You can feed broilers by using 1 of these 2 programmes:
pg200_n0010_easy_read:
Three feed types feeding schedule:
This schedule means feeding the birds with 3 types of feed at different stages.
pg200_n0011_easy_read:
The 3 feeds are:
- broiler starter crumbles or mash
- broiler grower pellets or mash
- broiler finisher pellets or mash
pg200_n0016_easy_read: Give broiler starter crumble or mash from day 1 up to day 14 (2 weeks).
pg200_n0019_easy_read: Give broiler grower pellets or mash from week 3 to week 4.
pg200_n0022_easy_read: Give broiler finisher pellets or mash from week 5 up to marketing weight.
pg200_n0026_easy_read:
Two feed types feeding schedule:
This schedule means feeding the birds with 2 types of feed.
pg200_n0027_easy_read: The 2 feeds are broiler starter crumbles and broiler finisher pellets or mash.
pg200_n0032_easy_read: Give broiler starter crumble from day 1 up to day 21.
pg200_n0035_easy_read: Give finisher pellets from day 22 up to market point.
pg200_n0037_easy_read:
These feeds can be:
- commercial feeds from feed companies
- homemade feeds from local ingredients or materials, mixed locally to reduce feed costs
pg200_n0038_easy_read:
Make sure you get help from a feed expert.
The feed expert can help you get a good formula for the feed you want to make.
pg200_n0039_easy_read: Give vitamins and minerals to the chickens to avoid nutritional disorders.
pg200_n0041_easy_read: Each feeding schedule has advantages and challenges.
pg200_n0042_easy_read:
The 1st schedule uses starter, grower, and finisher feed.
It supports balanced growth and development of the chickens.
But it can cost more.
pg200_n0043_easy_read:
The 2nd schedule uses starter and finisher feed, without grower feed.
It can cost less.
But it may not give the chickens the same level of nutrients for proper growth and development.

This section is about chickens that are crossbreeds.
They come from indigenous chickens and superior cocks for meat production or egg production.
It also includes dual-purpose hybrids.
pg216_n0040_easy_read: These chickens are made to be suitable for both meat production and egg production.
pg217_n0003_easy_read: These chickens can live in normal environments, just like indigenous chickens.
pg217_n0004_easy_read:
You can rear these chickens in all poultry farming systems:
- intensive
- semi-intensive
- extensive or free-range
pg217_n0005_easy_read: Examples of dual-purpose hybrid chickens are:
pg217_n0007_easy_read:
(a) Sasso:
Sasso is a hybrid chicken. It comes from crossing indigenous hens with a superior meat cock.
pg217_n0008_easy_read: Sasso can be reared for meat and eggs.
pg217_n0009_easy_read: If you rear Sasso for meat and give it fattening feed, it can weigh more than 2.5 kg in 70 - 90 days.
pg217_n0010_easy_read: If you rear Sasso for eggs, it starts laying eggs at 20 weeks of age. It can lay up to 240 eggs during its laying period.
pg217_n0012_easy_read:
(b) Kuroiler:
Kuroiler is a hybrid chicken. It comes from crossing indigenous hens with a superior egg-laying cock.
pg217_n0013_easy_read: Kuroiler is also reared for meat and eggs.
pg217_n0014_easy_read: If you rear Kuroiler for eggs, it can lay 190 - 250 eggs in 30 months.
pg217_n0015_easy_read: Kuroiler starts laying eggs at 5 months. Local chickens start laying eggs at 6 months.
pg217_n0016_easy_read: Kuroiler lays eggs for 2 years if you take good care of it.
pg217_n0017_easy_read:
Kuroilers are also good for meat:
- Cocks can weigh up to 5 kg.
- Hens can weigh 3.5 to 4 kg.
pg217_n0019_easy_read:
(c) Tanbro:
Tanbro chickens grow fast. They also have larger bodies than local chickens. This makes them very good for meat.
pg217_n0020_easy_read: If you rear Tanbro for eggs, it can lay 180 - 220 eggs in 81 weeks.
pg217_n0021_easy_read: Tanbro starts laying eggs at 19 - 21 weeks of age.
pg217_n0022_easy_read:
Tanbro is also good for meat:
- Pullets can weigh up to 1.5 kg in 7 weeks.
- Pullets can weigh 2 kg in 9 weeks.
- Cocks can weigh 4 kg if they are well cared for.
pg217_n0023_easy_read: These chickens resist disease better than meat chickens or egg chickens.
pg217_n0025_easy_read: In Tanzania, there are several types of dual-purpose hybrid chickens.
pg217_n0026_easy_read:
The chicken you choose to rear depends on:
- what you want to achieve
- what people in your area need
pg217_n0027_easy_read:
To choose the right hybrid, think about:
- where you live
- the type of chicken people like
pg217_n0028_easy_read: It is good to ask livestock extension workers or experienced poultry farmers for their opinions.
pg217_n0030_easy_read: Looking after dual-purpose hybrid chickens is almost the same as looking after other types of chickens.
pg217_n0031_easy_read: The main difference is how you feed them.
pg217_n0032_easy_read: This depends on whether you are raising the chickens for meat or eggs.
pg217_n0033_easy_read: The feeding schedule for chickens raised for meat is:
pg217_n0035_easy_read: (a) From day 1 to day 18, or until the chickens weigh 400 grams, give them broiler starter crumble.
pg217_n0036_easy_read: If the chickens reach 400 grams before day 18, start feeding them broiler grower pellets.
pg218_n0005_easy_read: From day 19 to 35, feed the chickens broiler grower pellets.
pg218_n0008_easy_read: From day 36 until you sell the chickens, feed the chickens broiler finisher pellets.
pg218_n0010_easy_read: The feeding schedule for dual-purpose hybrid chickens raised for eggs is:
pg218_n0014_easy_read: For the first 2 weeks, feed the chickens broiler starter crumble.
pg218_n0017_easy_read: From 2 to 10 weeks, change to layer starter mash.
pg218_n0020_easy_read: From 10 weeks to 4 months, feed the chickens layer grower mash.
pg218_n0021_easy_read: This is the time when the chickens start laying eggs.
pg218_n0024_easy_read: At 5 months, feed the chickens complete layer mash until final culling.
pg218_n0028_easy_read: It is important to check the bird’s health and change the feeding schedule when needed.
pg218_n0029_easy_read: Sometimes, commercial dual-purpose chicken feed is available and costs less.
pg218_n0030_easy_read: This can lower your cost of production.

In this chapter, you will learn about duck production.
You will learn about:
- the general importance of duck production
- breeds of ducks

pg220_n0010_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you do duck production as a business.
This can help you employ yourself or get a job.
It can also help you earn profit.
pg220_n0013_easy_read: "Enhances farm diversity, provides valuable eggs, meat, and can be used as natural pest controller"
pg220_n0017_easy_read: You may have seen the birds in the pictures labelled Figure 14.1.
pg220_n0019_easy_read:
Ducks have broad bills.
Broad bills are large, flat beaks.
These beaks help ducks eat food from water.
pg220_n0020_easy_read:
Ducks also have webbed feet.
Webbed feet have skin between the toes.
This makes it easier for ducks to swim and walk on water.
pg220_n0021_easy_read: Raising ducks is called duck farming or duck production.
pg220_n0022_easy_read:
As you start to learn about duck production, think about how ducks may affect:
- your life
- your family
- your school
- your local area
pg220_n0023_easy_read:
As you learn about this topic, keep asking questions.
Enjoy learning new things about ducks.
pg220_n0027_easy_read: People often keep ducks for eggs and meat.
pg220_n0028_easy_read: If people raise ducks in a free-range system with little feed, the ducks can weigh about 1.8 kg and lay 60 to 80 eggs a
pg221_n0004_easy_read: Some duck breeds, including local breeds, can weigh more than 2.95 kg.
pg221_n0005_easy_read: In an intensive system, some ducks can lay up to 300 eggs in 1 year.
pg221_n0006_easy_read: Adult male ducks, called drakes, can weigh about 2 kg.
pg221_n0007_easy_read: Ducks from improved breeds can grow to 4.5 kg if people care for them well. Female ducks, called hens, can weigh 3.5 kg.
pg221_n0008_easy_read: In an integrated system, farmers can raise ducks with fish.
pg221_n0009_easy_read:
This system helps to:
- increase fish production
- improve fish quality
- reduce feed costs for ducks
pg221_n0010_easy_read: This system also increases farmers’ output and income.
pg221_n0011_easy_read: However, ducks can eat small fish that weigh less than 4 grams.
pg221_n0012_easy_read: Even with this challenge, the benefits of this system are greater than the problems.
pg221_n0013_easy_read: Ducks can survive in hard conditions and diseases.
pg221_n0014_easy_read: Ducks eat less because they can eat forage like ruminants.
pg221_n0015_easy_read: Ducks live longer and can bring profit.
pg221_n0016_easy_read: Ducks need affordable housing. So, farmers can raise ducks for food or products for sale at low cost.
pg221_n0020_easy_read: Several duck breeds do well in warm and tropical climates. These breeds are also suitable for Tanzania.
pg221_n0021_easy_read: Some duck breeds are suitable for tropical conditions, including Tanzania:
pg221_n0026_easy_read: Indian Runner ducks stand up straight and run in a special way.
pg221_n0027_easy_read: Indian Runner ducks are excellent foragers, which means they eat grasses. So, they can adapt well to free-range conditions.
pg221_n0035_easy_read: Muscovy ducks have a unique appearance. They have a red face and caruncles, which are fleshy growths, around the eyes.
pg222_n0005_easy_read: Khaki Campbell ducks are known for laying many eggs.
pg222_n0006_easy_read:
Khaki Campbell ducks are a light breed.
They can live well in different climates.
pg222_n0007_easy_read: Khaki Campbell ducks are also very good at finding food.
pg222_n0014_easy_read: White Pekin ducks are popular for meat production.
pg222_n0015_easy_read: White Pekin ducks like spending time outdoors.
pg222_n0016_easy_read: White Pekin ducks are fairly good at finding food.
pg222_n0021_easy_read:
These duck breeds can live in tropical conditions.
But they still need proper care and management to stay healthy and well.
pg222_n0022_easy_read:
To raise ducks well, you must provide:
- proper housing
- clean water
- proper feeding
- mating or breeding

pg223_n0016_easy_read: Looking after ducks is like looking after chickens.
pg223_n0018_easy_read: We need to think about duck housing and feeding.
pg223_n0019_easy_read: We also need to manage mating and incubation and keep ducks healthy.
pg223_n0020_easy_read: Each of the following parts will help you take care of your ducks well.
pg223_n0025_easy_read: Ducks need shelter, and they do not like wind or too much sunlight.
pg223_n0026_easy_read: When ducks rest, they need a dry and sheltered nesting place.
pg223_n0027_easy_read:
Housing for ducks is important.
It protects ducks from harsh weather and predators.
It also makes egg collection easier.
pg223_n0028_easy_read: Here are some important points to think about when giving ducks housing:
pg223_n0031_easy_read: (a) You can keep ducks in a normal house or in a simple shed made from materials available locally.
pg223_n0033_easy_read: (b) The housing should protect ducks from wind, rain, and sun.
pg223_n0034_easy_read: The housing should have enough ventilation and a dry bed.
pg223_n0036_easy_read:
(c) Ducks usually lay eggs at night or in the morning, between 6:00 a.m. and noon.
So, housing helps prevent losses from predators and makes egg collection easier.
pg223_n0038_easy_read:
(d) If possible, use a free-range system and let ducks spread out.
Or keep only 1 flock.
This can reduce feeding and penning costs.
pg223_n0040_easy_read: (e) The recommended space for free-range ducks is about 0.5 hectares for every 100 ducks.
pg223_n0042_easy_read: (f) The entrance should be big enough for the biggest duck to enter the housing easily.
pg223_n0044_easy_read:
(g) If ducks range freely, it is important to:
- rotate enclosed ranges
- provide shade
- provide shelter from bad weather
- avoid keeping ducks confined for too long during the day
pg224_n0005_easy_read: Give ducks enough space to get feed and drinking water.
pg224_n0008_easy_read: If ducks are kept for egg production, the house should have light for about 14 hours. This helps egg production.
pg224_n0012_easy_read: In an intensive system, each duck needs 3,710 - 4,650 cm² of floor space.
pg224_n0013_easy_read: In battery cages, each duck can use 1,350 cm² of floor space.
pg224_n0014_easy_read: In a semi-intensive system, ducks need 2,790 cm² of floor space in the night shelter. They also need 929 - 1,395 cm² for the outside run.
pg224_n0015_easy_read: Layer ducks should have laying nest boxes.
pg224_n0016_easy_read:
A nest box of this size is enough:
- 30 cm wide
- 45 cm deep
- 30 cm high
pg224_n0017_easy_read: Provide 1 nest box for every 3 ducks.
pg224_n0019_easy_read: In a semi-intensive system, the run can have a pool.
pg224_n0020_easy_read: Ducks need water for more than drinking. They also need water for bathing and entertainment.
pg224_n0021_easy_read: Ducks naturally enjoy swimming and splashing in water.
pg224_n0022_easy_read: Ducks can even dive under water to find food.
pg224_n0023_easy_read: Wait until ducklings are at least 5 - 6 weeks old before you introduce them to water.
pg224_n0024_easy_read:
This helps ducklings to:
- grow bigger
- develop their feathers
- handle temperature changes better
pg224_n0026_easy_read: To manage a water pool in duck farming, the pool needs enough water space. The water quality must also stay good.
pg224_n0027_easy_read: Keep the ducks’ water pool clean and free from contaminants. Clean it regularly and change the water.
pg224_n0031_easy_read:
Feed ducks a balanced diet. The diet should include:
- carbohydrates
- proteins
- vitamins
- minerals
pg224_n0032_easy_read: You can feed ducks with locally available feeds or commercial feeds from authorised distributors.
pg224_n0033_easy_read: Feed ducklings on a starter diet from hatching to 4 weeks of age. Then change to grower feed after 2 weeks.
pg224_n0034_easy_read:
These feeds can be:
- mash
- crumble
- pellet
pg224_n0035_easy_read: If special duck feeds are not available, you can use standard poultry feeds.
pg224_n0036_easy_read: Wet mash is commonly used. It should be fed as a wet mash.
pg224_n0038_easy_read: If ducklings are brooded artificially, feed them as soon as you place them in the brooder.
pg224_n0039_easy_read: Do not feed ducks on poultry feed that contains a coccidiostat. It can harm ducklings.
pg224_n0040_easy_read: Change ducks to grower feed at 5 weeks of age. Use this feed until the ducks reach sexual maturity at 24 weeks of age.
pg224_n0041_easy_read: During the development stage, from 8 - 24 weeks, feed each duck 150 grams per day.
pg224_n0042_easy_read: If wet mash is used, mix it with 40% water and
pg225_n0003_easy_read: Give 115 grams of wet feed in the morning and in the evening.
pg225_n0004_easy_read:
2 weeks before laying, increase the daily feed ration.
Give 220 grams per day for dry mash.
Give 330 grams per day for wet mash.
pg225_n0005_easy_read:
Give ducklings grit regularly.
This is especially important if ducklings do not forage for their food.
pg225_n0006_easy_read:
Giving grit helps ducklings control how much they eat.
It also helps proper digestion.
pg225_n0008_easy_read:
During the laying period, from 25 - 66 weeks, increase the ducks' feed intake.
Give 325 grams per day if you use dry mash.
Give 485 grams per day if you use wet mash.
pg225_n0009_easy_read: Ducks are expected to reach the 50% egg-laying stage at about 25 - 26 weeks of age.
pg225_n0010_easy_read: From the 50% egg-laying stage onwards, give each duck at least 0.5 kg of feed per day.
pg225_n0011_easy_read: Any feeder that can feed chickens can also feed ducks.
pg225_n0012_easy_read:
Layer ducks in an intensive system are fed 2 times a day.
Feed them in the morning and in the evening.
pg225_n0013_easy_read: Give layer ducks an amount of feed that they can finish in about 10 - 15 minutes.
pg225_n0014_easy_read:
Layer ducks can eat mash or pellets.
Wet mash is preferred.
pg225_n0015_easy_read:
For feeding:
- 1 long feeder can be used by 20 ducks.
- 1 round feeder can be used by 10 - 15 ducks.
pg225_n0016_easy_read:
As well as proper nutrition, ducks also need grit.
Grit is important for digestion and overall health.
pg225_n0018_easy_read:
Ducks need clean water.
Provide it in standing troughs with wire mesh.
This stops ducks from wetting their bodies.
pg225_n0019_easy_read:
Arrange the drinkers so ducks can put their bills under the water.
This helps ducks clear their nostrils by squirting water through them.
pg225_n0020_easy_read: Keep feeders and waterers clean to protect the health of the flock.
pg225_n0023_easy_read: Ducks do well in integrated farming systems, such as duck-cum-fish farming.
pg225_n0024_easy_read:
In these systems, ducks get most of their feed from the pond.
This feed includes:
- aquatic weeds
- insects
- larvae
- earthworms
pg225_n0025_easy_read: At the same time, fish can use waste from duck droppings and feed particles that fall into the pond.
pg225_n0026_easy_read:
When ducks can move freely on the pond surface, their droppings fertilise the pond.
This helps natural food grow for fish and ducks.
pg225_n0030_easy_read:
Male ducks are called drakes.
1 drake can serve 6 female ducks.
pg225_n0031_easy_read: However, if the farmer wants more fertile eggs, 1 drake should serve only 4 ducks.
pg225_n0032_easy_read: Ducks usually start laying eggs when they are about 5 - 6 months old.
pg225_n0033_easy_read: The highest egg production happens about 5 - 6 weeks after ducks start laying.
pg225_n0034_easy_read: To produce many eggs, ducks need 14 hours of light.
pg226_n0003_easy_read: Duck eggs can be incubated naturally or artificially.
pg226_n0004_easy_read: Commercial duck breeds cannot incubate their eggs because they are non-broody.
pg226_n0005_easy_read: For natural incubation, farmers choose broody chickens and ducks to hatch duck eggs.
pg226_n0006_easy_read: Most duck eggs take 28 days to hatch, except in a few breeds.
pg226_n0007_easy_read: On day 10 or 11, people usually candle the eggs to check development.
pg226_n0011_easy_read: Ducks are generally strong against parasites and diseases.
pg226_n0012_easy_read: However, several parasites can affect ducks.
pg226_n0013_easy_read:
Examples of parasites that can infest ducks are:
- lice
- mites
- fleas
- flukes
- roundworms
pg226_n0014_easy_read: Flukes are flatworms. They can infect the liver, gallbladder, and intestine of ducks.
pg226_n0015_easy_read:
Signs of fluke infection include:
- weight loss
- anaemia
- jaundice
pg226_n0016_easy_read:
Roundworms can infect the intestines of ducks. They can cause:
- weight loss
- diarrhoea
- anaemia
pg226_n0017_easy_read: Duck lice are small insects. They feed on the feathers and skin of ducks. They cause irritation and possible secondary infections.
pg226_n0018_easy_read: Practical ways to manage parasites in ducks include the following:
pg226_n0022_easy_read:
Practise good hygiene:
- Wash your hands well before and after handling ducks.
- Keep duck food and water clean.
pg226_n0025_easy_read:
Check ducks regularly for signs of parasites, such as:
- weight loss
- lethargy
- diarrhoea
pg226_n0028_easy_read:
Use approved pesticides, such as powders or sprays, to treat external parasites such as:
- fleas
- mites
- lice
pg226_n0031_easy_read: Clean the duck houses and runs well to prevent re-infestation.
pg226_n0034_easy_read: Deworm ducks regularly to prevent intestinal worms.
pg226_n0037_easy_read: Quarantine new birds to prevent external parasites from spreading to the whole flock.
pg226_n0039_easy_read: Also, diseases such as duck viral enteritis, avian influenza, duck plague, and fowl cholera can affect ducks.
pg226_n0040_easy_read: In general, people can manage diseases in ducks in the following ways:
pg226_n0044_easy_read: Vaccinate ducks against common viral diseases. Do this with advice from a veterinarian or poultry experts.
pg226_n0047_easy_read: Provide ducks with clean and hygienic housing conditions.
pg226_n0050_easy_read: Ensure ducks get balanced feed and proper nutrition to prevent nutritional disorders.
pg226_n0053_easy_read: Monitor duck health regularly and detect symptoms early.
pg226_n0056_easy_read: Isolate sick ducks to prevent the spread of diseases.

pg227_n0038_easy_read: Duck products, for example meat and eggs, are important to farmers and to the country's economy.
pg227_n0039_easy_read: People buy these duck products to cook tasty meals.
pg227_n0040_easy_read: Selling ducks or duck products helps farmers earn money.
pg227_n0041_easy_read: For farmers to make a good profit, duck eggs and meat should be handled well and sold at a fair price.

This sub-section gives a short overview of:

pg228_n0006_easy_read: For more detailed information and specific rules, get more information and advice from poultry extension workers or experts.
pg228_n0009_easy_read:
Collect duck eggs at least 2 times a day:
- early morning
- late afternoon
This helps keep the eggs fresh.
pg228_n0010_easy_read: Handle the duck eggs carefully. This helps prevent cracks and damage to the shells.
pg228_n0011_easy_read: Use clean containers to collect the duck eggs.
pg228_n0014_easy_read: Handle the duck eggs with clean hands. This helps prevent contamination.
pg228_n0015_easy_read: Clean the duck eggs by gently wiping off any dirt.
pg228_n0016_easy_read: Do not wash the duck eggs. Washing can remove the protective coating.
pg228_n0019_easy_read: Grade the duck eggs by size and quality.

pg228_n0021_easy_read:
Label the packages with relevant information for:

pg228_n0022_easy_read: Follow hygiene and biosecurity practices. This helps make sure the duck eggs do not get contaminated during processing.
pg228_n0025_easy_read: Use clean containers to store the duck eggs in a cool, dry place. This helps keep them fresh.
pg228_n0026_easy_read: Also, keep the duck eggs away from contaminants and predators.
pg228_n0027_easy_read: Follow storage guidelines. This helps make sure the duck eggs are safe to eat.
pg228_n0028_easy_read: Check the duck eggs regularly for damage or spoilage. Throw away any damaged or spoiled eggs.

pg228_n0039_easy_read: For more detailed information and specific rules, get more information and advice from poultry extension workers or experts.
pg229_n0003_easy_read: Duck meat handling and value addition:
pg229_n0004_easy_read:
Slaughter and process ducks in a clean and hygienic place.
This helps to keep the meat safe and of good quality.
pg229_n0009_easy_read:
Do not feed the ducks for 12 - 24 hours before slaughter.
